News.title: Gen Z clocks 36 hours a week on their phone – and it's not always to talk
News.content:
Gen Z clocks 36 hours a week on their phone – and it's not always to talk

Gen Z clock over 36 hours a week on their phones, yet voice calls rank seventh in usage as adults spend nearly four days a year doing 'life admin' for others.

Vogue Williams takes on the role of Tesco Mobile’s data warden

Brits dedicate nearly four days annually on their mobile phones handling 'life admin' tasks - for other people. Research involving 2,000 adults revealed they tackle numerous duties daily for loved ones via their phones, such as family organising (22%), social planning (17%) and serving as an unofficial therapist (14%).

‌



‌



These unofficial 'roles' consume an average of one hour and 50 minutes weekly, adding up to just over 95 hours annually - equivalent to almost four full days. However, most are happy to do so, reporting the responsibilities make them feel useful (38%), trusted (29%) and needed (26%).

‌



The research also showed Gen Z dedicates an average of more than 36 hours weekly overall to their mobiles - yet phone calls rank only seventh amongst the most frequent activities they use them for.

‌



View 2 Images Vogue Williams spoke to the public about their phone usage (Image: PinPep)

Social media apps (67%), WhatsApp (64%) and listening to music and podcasts (59%) emerged as the primary ways Gen Z utilise their devices. Watching videos or streaming content (59%), online banking (58%) and taking photos or videos (58%) also placed higher than actually using their phone to ring someone (56%).

However, for those aged 65 and above, making and receiving calls remain the most frequent uses for a mobile (78%), alongside sending text messages (72%).

‌



Spanning the generations, WhatsApp has emerged as the primary method people maintain contact through messages and calls, surpassing their phone's built-in messaging service.

To mark the importance of everyday connections, Tesco Mobile enlisted TV personality and presenter Vogue Williams as its first-ever 'Data Warden', hitting the streets of London to reward unsuspecting members of the public caught using their phones to keep in touch with others.

‌



Rather than being handed a penalty, those spotted on their phones – whether making calls to friends, scrolling, sending voice notes or messaging loved ones – were surprised by Vogue with 'Phoney Fines', a mock fine designed purely to reward them.

Each 'Phoney Fine' concealed a surprise gift card, honouring everyday connections with Tesco Mobile Pay as you go Essentials.

‌



View 2 Images Vogue surprised unsuspecting phone users across London with 'Phoney Fines’ (Image: PinPep)

Vogue Williams said: "We're always being told we spend too much time on our phones, and I'm definitely guilty of being glued to mine.

‌



"But half the time we're checking in on friends, making someone laugh or helping sort the latest drama.

"I love that Tesco Mobile is celebrating those everyday moments and giving something back to people for staying connected."

‌



The research also revealed that 76% of those surveyed believe the everyday interactions they have via their mobile devices play a crucial role in maintaining strong relationships.

Indeed, 42% have had their spirits lifted by something received on their phone, be it a funny photo (62%), a thoughtful message (58%) or good news from someone (56%). Meanwhile, 60% feel a greater sense of closeness to someone when they regularly exchange photos or videos.

‌



According to the OnePoll research, Brits take an average of one hour and 17 minutes to respond to a message. People appear split on the etiquette of messaging, with more than a quarter (27%) admitting they feel guilty about replying to a text straight away, while nearly as many (24%) confessed to taking hours or even days to respond.

While Gen Z considers a video call the ideal way to feel truly connected with someone, those aged 65 and over still prefer a good old-fashioned phone call to get the job done.

Laura Joseph, chief customer officer at Tesco Mobile, said: "Our phones play an important role in helping us stay connected, and it's often the small interactions that matter most."

News.title: 'A little rich of him': Why the Tories have no right to lecture Labour on border control
News.content:
'A little rich of him': Why the Tories have no right to lecture Labour on border control

Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp laid into Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood earlier this week when she unveiled a massive overhaul of settlement rules for migrants

View 3 Images

Tory criticism of Labour's immigration reforms is a "little rich" after their record in power, the Mirror's Political Editor Lizzy Buchan has said.

‌



‌



Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp laid into Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood earlier this week when she unveiled a massive overhaul of settlement rules for migrants. Under the plans, half a million people face longer waits for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) as the standard wait to qualify will double from its current five years. High earners and NHS staff will be among those who can apply sooner.

‌



Ms Mahmood announced a carve out for care workers as she rowed back on controversial plans to make them wait up to 15 years to qualify. Mr Philp accused her of carrying out a humiliating U-turn - and claimed she'd bowed to pressure from within her party.

‌



Speaking to the Mirror's Nicola Thorp on the Sense Check show, Lizzy said it was difficult for the Tories to attack Labour after their record in Government on immigration. Net migration surged after Brexit, peaking at 944,000 in year ending March 2023. It was dubbed the "Boris wave" by critics.

Shabana Mahmood's huge changes to UK immigration rules explained in full READ MORE :

View 3 Images Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp tried to attack Shabana Mahmood over immigration reforms (Image: Jordan Pettitt/PA Wire)

Lizzy said: "The Conservatives were in charge when so many people came over. As was Chris Philp. I think it's quite hard for the Conservatives to really land blows with those kinds of attacks considering they not only allowed lots of people to come here legally during those years when Boris Johnson was PM and after, but also they allowed the asylum system to get out of control.

‌



"They started housing people in hotels. They're responsible for so much of that. So I think it's a little rich of him to say that. And actually... these reforms are really tough. [They are] far more hard line than anything the Conservatives did."

Mr Philp authorised use of asylum hotels as an immigration minister in the pandemic, which ramped up under the Tories. Labour has pledged to end use by the end of this Parliament.

‌



View 3 Images Lizzy Buchan Mirror Political Editor said 'The Government are trying to bring immigration under control and therefore starve Farage and his gang of that argument and that ability to kind of whip people up."

Nigel Farage was nowhere to be seen in the Commons when Ms Mahmood delivered her statement on Monday - choosing instead to deliver an "emergency" press conference outside of Parliament.

‌



Asked about Reform's response, Lizzy said: "It's a bit of a tricky one for Reform in a way because they want to get rid of ILR completely and replace it with, I think, rolling sort of five-year visas. But the plans are quite tough, and so it's not that easy for him to come at Shabana Mahmood... So I think it's quite tricky for them.

"Actually, that's part of why Labour's doing it, really. It takes some of the air out of what Reform are trying to argue about Britain's immigration system being totally out of control. The Government are trying to bring it under control and therefore starve Farage and his gang of that argument and that ability to kind of whip people up."

News.title: Helicopter crashes close to Florida beach days after jet disaster - One missing and two injured
News.content:
Helicopter crashes close to Florida beach days after jet disaster - One missing and two injured

One person is missing and two others have been injured after a helicopter crashed in the waters off Key Biscayne in Florida

View Image A helicopter crashed into the water near Nixon Beach (Image: 7Skyforce)

One person is missing and two others have been injured after a helicopter crashed into the water in Florida.

‌



‌



The small aircraft went down in the waters off Key Biscayne, in Miami-Dade County, shortly before 11.30am local time (4.30pm GMT) on Wednesday.

‌



Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Department said crews were called at 11.26am to reports of a helicopter crash near Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park. It said three people were reported to be involved in the incident and that two were rescued and taken to hospital. The whereabouts of the third person were not immediately known.

‌



Footage taken by a 7Skyforce helicopter shows what appears to be the wreckage of a helicopter submerged in the water, with its yellow skid floats visible above the surface.

On Sunday, a Learjet 60, which was travelling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas, crashed on a street near Greenacres in Palm Beach County, Florida, around 75 miles north of Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park.

News.title: Brits back Andy Burnham on slavery apology as Ed Miliband says taxpayers won't be hit
News.content:
Brits back Andy Burnham on slavery apology as Ed Miliband says taxpayers won't be hit

The legacy of the transatlantic slave trade has dominated Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s first trip to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua

View 2 Images Andy Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband play steel pans during a visit to Hells Gate Orchestra Steel Pan Yard in St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

British people have endorsed Andy Burnham’s stance to consider an apology for slavery but oppose reparations as the Prime Minister held crunch talks with Commonwealth leaders.

‌



‌



The legacy of the transatlantic slave trade has dominated the PM’s first trip to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua. Ahead of the summit, Mr Burnham signalled he is open to a formal apology for Britain’s vile role in the trade of enslaved people but has been clear reparations are not on the table.

‌



A poll for YouGov found Brits support issuing an official apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade by 52% to 37%. But 65% are opposed to paying reparations to affected countries, with only 21% in favour.

‌



Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband reiterated that British taxpayers will not pay a penny more as a result of Mr Burnham’s “new approach” to the Commonwealth. Speaking to BBC Newscast, he accused previous governments of a “sweep under the carpet” approach to slavery but ruled out extra financial contributions.

John Healey rejects slavery reparations calls as Antigua PM wades into row moments after Charles meeting READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham has opened the door to a formal apology on slavery (Image: Kin Cheung/Press Association)

Asked if taxpayers would contribute more, he said: "No. And that’s – for us, that’s never been what it’s about. And that’s why it’s been important that you know, and I did have this conversation with our partners in advance. I said, ‘look, we are going to say we are willing to say that we’re open to an apology, but we’re not going to shift our position on reparations.’

‌



“It’s not for us. It’s not the right answer. It’s not practical. It’s not feasible for us, but there are things we can work on co-operatively.”

He added: “And you know there’s been a lot of acceptance of that, and I mean people have been honestly a bit bruised by the past, what happened in the past, the sense that we just really just wanted to sweep this issue under the carpet and not confront it.

‌



“My sense is there’s a bit of a sigh of relief that OK well at least you know at least there’s a sense of we’ve got a shared interest now in moving the Commonwealth on.”

He also criticised what he described as a “sorry, not sorry” from Sir Tony Blair, who in 2006 expressed “deep sorrow and regret” for Britain’s involvement in the slave trade but stopped short of an official apology.

‌



Commonwealth members have welcomed the shift in position on an apology from the British state. A communique to be signed at the end of the summit is expected to welcome the UK’s promise of structured dialogue over the issue.

Music-mad Mr Burnham tried his hand at playing the steel drum on Wednesday, performing a rendition of Mary Had a Little Lamb alongside the Hell's Gate steel orchestra.

‌



Director Khan Cordice told him “you’re a musician”, to which Mr Burnham replied: “I play a little music.” He was later joined by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband for a duet.

The PM previously showed off his skills when he was handed a guitar by a Ukrainian soldier on a visit to Kyiv, playing “Rusholme Ruffians” by The Smiths.

Article continues below

:: YouGov surveyed 2,258 adults living in Great Britain between November 2 and 3 ::

News.title: Vance sensationally turns on Trump's war as VP fights for his political future
News.content:
Vance sensationally turns on Trump's war as VP fights for his political future

JD Vance has turned on Donald Trump's Iran war, saying it is the reason for the Republican disaster in the midterm elections, as he weighs his own political future and a possible run for president

View 2 Images JD Vance said the Iran war was the reason for the disaster in the midterm elections (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

United States Vice President JD Vance has turned on Donald Trump's Iran war, blaming it for the disaster in the midterm elections.

‌



‌



In a nationwide romp, Democrats ousted Republicans from coast to coast, with many surprising places in between, as voters rejected the president’s party for the promise of something different for the country.

‌



And Vance has been quick to blame the war in Iran as he weighs his political future and a possible run for president in 2028.

‌



Vance listed all the other reasons the party lost in an X post - and appealed to Republican voters to give the party another chance.

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance said.

View 2 Images JD Vance appears to be positioning himself for a run for president (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Donald Trump faces two-year nightmare after Republican wipeout in midterms READ MORE :

US steps up Iran war fears and moves military assets into Middle East as UK becomes more of a terror target READ MORE :

His message was that backers of the Iran war should take responsibility for the defeat, with Trump having championed the conflict.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," he said.

‌



The results have set up a divided government, with Congress poised to reassert itself as a coequal branch ready to challenge Trump and reverse course after two years of unified Republican control.

And Trump has been consulting with advisers on whether Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth should be sacked, stated CBS News sources. While it has also been reported that blame is expected to land on Adm Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen Dan Caine, who both played big roles in guidance on the Iran war.

‌



The Iran war has led to an increase in inflation globally and it appears that rising prices as well as the state of the democracy were the main reasons for the poor showing by the Republicans.

Democrats are promising a 100-day agenda starting with efforts to lower the costs of gas, groceries and other goods, as well as bills to reverse cuts to the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid healthcare programmes. They’re also ready to launch a robust oversight agenda to, as House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries says, “hold the crooks accountable.”

‌



Impeachment — of the president or his Cabinet members — is also an option. The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Rep Robert Garcia of California, issued a one-sentence warning: “Lawyer up.”

Sen Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, issued his own one-word missive: “Subpoenas.” Democrats will be under pressure to quickly show that they have solutions for the high gas and grocery prices, the war in Iran and concerns about the direction of the country.

‌



For Jeffries and his leadership team, it will be their first time in the majority, managing a class of newcomers including a handful of far-left democratic socialists.

With the majority in the 435-member House well past the 218 needed and the Senate Democrats holding at least 54 of 100 seats in that chamber, Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer will have room to manoeuvre.

News.title: Half of new parents feel lonely - even with friends and family around
News.content:
Half of new parents feel lonely - even with friends and family around

New research discovered more than of half parents felt lonely during the first 1,000 days of having a baby, despite most having friends and family around them

View 3 Images Parents have three sources of support on average (Image: Getty Images)

More than half of new parents experience loneliness, despite two thirds having a 'village' around them for support. A study of 4,339 parents, including 500 from the UK, with children aged three and under found 53% have felt lonely during the first 1,000 days after welcoming a child.

‌



‌



On average, parents have three sources of support, lower than the eight recommended by paediatricians in a separate survey. Immediate or extended family (70%), themselves or their partner (72%), and friends (51%), most often make up what if often classified as a 'village. Yet, 66% feel their village isn't as strong as it was 20 years ago.

‌



View 3 Images Two thirds say their 'village' isn't the same as what it was 20 years ago (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The findings come from The Pampers Baby Report: The Village Barometer . The report is based on Europe-wide research and informed by further statistical review by UNICEF’s Office of Research Innocenti and insights from Natasha Kirkham, professor of developmental psychology.

At the heart of the report is the Village Barometer, which surveyed 4,339 parents and 425 paediatricians across nine countries to create a new measure of how supported parents feel by the people, services, and systems around them.

It looks across five areas of early parenthood to reveal where families feel well supported, where pressures are greatest, and where their wider ‘village’ could make the biggest difference.

‌



Professor Natasha Kirkham said: “The first 1,000 days are an important foundation for child health and development, but the message should not add pressure to parents.

“Babies do not need perfect conditions, they need a healthy, nurturing and responsive environment around them.”

‌



View 3 Images Parents are surviving on just over 5 hours of sleep a night (Image: Getty Images)

It revealed sleep disruption may be an additional contributor to parents feeling isolated, with those in the UK losing an average of five-and-a-half hours of sleep every week after having a child.

‌



Modern parenting is also shaped by a constant flow of information, with 42% of parents polled across Europe feeling overwhelmed by parenting advice.

This is a concern echoed by healthcare professionals, as 95% of paediatricians think access to too many sources of advice can overwhelm parents.

‌



But 41% believe modern life is not designed with babies in mind, underlining the role of workplaces, services, and everyday environments in shaping how supported families feel.

The report also highlighted the importance of play, which is widely recognised as essential for early childhood development, as an area where many parents feel under pressure.

‌



While 90% of UK parents felt play is very or extremely important for their baby’s development, 70% of all European parents have experienced some form of pressure, guilt, or judgement around playtime.

In the UK specifically, 47% feel confident supporting their baby's development through play – compared to 64% of all parents across Europe.

‌



Nearly half (45%) of all polled reported not having enough time, whereas 38% cited tiredness, stress, or a lack of mental space.

Federica Pompei, senior vice president and general manager, Pampers, said: “The first 1,000 days of a baby’s life are one of the most joyful, emotional and transformative periods for any family, but every beautiful milestone can also bring a thousand new questions.

Article continues below

“As a mother, I know how much it matters to know that you are not navigating those moments alone.”

News.title: Rapist husband 'invited two men in one night to sexually abuse his wife'
News.content:
Rapist husband 'invited two men in one night to sexually abuse his wife'

The husband, already convicted of offences in relation to the sexual abuse, would film the men in the bedroom of the marital home — and even asked one to leave an online review

View 5 Images Jonathan Kirk — not the husband — arrives at court (Image: Peter Byrne/Press Association)

A husband who drugged and raped his wife over a 20-year period invited two men in a single night into their home to abuse her — even asking one to leave an online review, a court heard.

The husband, jurors heard, would go online and arrange for others to visit his marital home, where he would film and picture them abusing his unconscious partner, before sharing the footage online. A jury heard on two occasions two men visited the property — one after the other in the early hours — where they would sexually assault the woman.

The husband, in his 60s, who cannot be named, has already admitted to drugging his wife to rape and sexually abuse her over more than two decades, between 2004 and 2025. Nine men are now on trial at Manchester Minshull Street crown court accused of a range sexual offences. Four other men have pleaded guilty to a variety of offences.

View 5 Images Sean Peers has already pleaded guilty (Image: MEN MEDIA)

The court has heard one defendant had referred to the case of Gisèle Pelicot in messages to the husband — and a jury has heard police found more than one million sexual abuse images on the husband’s phone after he was arrested.

Louise Oakley KC prosecuting said, on September 15, 2024, the husband arranged for two men to visit their marital home to sexually abuse his unconscious wife. Graham Brougham, 74, and Sean Peers, 38, attended one after the other.

The court heard Brougham left the house at 2.22am but the husband “was not satisfied”, with Peers then arriving around 3.15am. Both men have pleaded guilty and will be sentenced later.

It is alleged the husband later shared the images he had taken of the sexual abuse, with another defendant, Daniel Rayner, who allegedly sent the response “so when can I come over and play if you're pimping her out”.

View 5 Images Graham Brougham will be sentenced at a later date (Image: MEN MEDIA)

One month later another man, Keith Fotheringham, 59, visited the house and sexually abused the wife. He has also pleaded guilty. Within five minutes of Fotheringham leaving the house, the husband was sharing the images he had taken.

Ms Oakley told the court that heading into 2025 the husband “doesn’t appear to have had any New Year’s resolutions to stop his offending on his wife. If anything, his resolve to satisfy his own perversity continued.”

On February 9, Philip Wild, 58, allegedly attended the marital home, with the court hearing he was “fully aware” that the wife “was not conscious and not able to consent to any sexual activity”.

As the sexual abuse took place the wife didn’t “show any real signs of being conscious, she was snoring, she was unconscious”, the court heard.

When Wild left, after 3am, the husband “was not sexually satisfied” and went on the Fabswingers site to see if there was anyone else close enough to come round, it is said.

View 5 Images Jordan Wallace, from Wythenshawe, Manchester, is on trial (Image: Peter Byrne/Press Association)

Ms Oakley told the court his message was answered by Mohammed Sabir, 29, who used the handle ‘Kashmiri Spice’. The two men were strangers but Sabir visited the marital home after 4.30am, the jury was told.

‌



The court was told Sabir was aware the wife “was not conscious and not able to consent to any sexual activity”. Both men filmed her on their phones when in the bedroom, the court heard.

The court was told the husband later asked Sabir to leave a review on Fabswingers as he wanted to find other “liked minded individuals”.

‌



In the review, which was shown to the jury, Sabir is alleged to have said it was “really easy” to arrange a meet and how it was his first time “f***ing someone’s wife in front of them”.

View 5 Images Alan Keelan is one of the men on trial (Image: MEN MEDIA)

‌



The court heard Sabir asked about returning to the house on March 15, messaging “she leathered tonight”. But the husband told him it wasn’t possible as his wife wasn’t drinking for Lent, jurors heard.

In April, the husband resumed contact with Rayner saying needed something to help him with the abuse, the court was told. Rayner allegedly told him: “I have used some stuff from Thailand” and “I have also got sleeping pills if you can crush them and put them in her food”. The court heard he also offered to send the husband some GHB to mix in his wife’s drink.

Article continues below

The nine men on trial, who deny a range of offences, are David Graves, 60, of Ilkeston, Derbyshire; Daniel Rayner, 42, of Whitstable, Kent; Philip Wild, 59, of Stockport; Mohammed Sabir, 28, of Stockport; Jonathan Kirk, 43, of Stockport; Jordan Wallace, 31, of Wythenshawe, Manchester; Alan Keelan, 42, of Wythenshawe; Robert Stewart, 70, of Stockport, and Richard Townsend, 38, of Heywood, Greater Manchester.

The case continues.

News.title: British citizen tests positive for Ebola in DRC after deadliest-ever outbreak
News.content:
British citizen tests positive for Ebola in DRC after deadliest-ever outbreak

A British citizen has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo as the country faces its deadliest-ever outbreak of the disease

View 3 Images It is the first confirmed case of a British national contracting Ebola (Image: Xinhua/Shutterstock)

A British citizen who is in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has tested positive for Ebola, the UK Government has confirmed.

‌



A Foreign Office spokesperson said the UK has "well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this", adding that "those processes have been activated".

"The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low," the spokesperson added. The Foreign Office has said it will share further information "in due course as appropriate".

More than 5,000 people have died out of more than 10,000 confirmed infections this year in the DRC's deadliest-ever Ebola outbreak, which began in May.

View 3 Images There have been more than 10,000 confirmed cases since the outbreak began in May (Image: Xinhua/Shutterstock)

Pregnant Brit mum and unborn baby die suddenly abroad as heartbroken family pay tribute READ MORE :

There are no approved treatments or vaccines to combat the disease, which is caused by the Bundibugyo virus. A fatality rate of 48.6 per cent was reported at the end of last month.

The World Health Organisation has warned that the outbreak is on course to surpass West Africa's 2014-2016 epidemic, which killed more than 11,000 people.

Last week, an Ebola patient was medically evacuated from Nigeria to Switzerland.

Since May, two patients have been medically evacuated to Germany and one to the Netherlands. A fourth case was reported in France in July. All four people worked in healthcare or humanitarian roles in affected areas of the DRC, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.

View 3 Images More than 5,000 people have died from Ebola in the DRC this year (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Uganda also reported cases of Ebola around the time the DRC declared an outbreak, but the virus had been contained by July, with 20 confirmed cases and three deaths.

Health officials in Kenya, which recorded its first-ever Ebola case on October 6, have expressed optimism over the country's progress in containing the outbreak, with no new infections reported.

On Tuesday, Kenya's Ministry of Health released five Ebola patients after they tested negative for the virus and showed no symptoms, leaving only two patients undergoing supportive care.

The ministry also announced the release of 46 people who had been identified as contacts of the first Ebola patient and placed under quarantine for 21 days.

A further 20 contacts were released last week, while the final batch of 52 people is expected to complete quarantine and be released next week.

News.title: The last time a Kansas Democrat was in the Senate, the Wizard of Oz was in cinemas
News.content:
As the founding pastor of the United Methodist Church of the Resurrection, Hamilton told voters his faith is what inspires his belief that the government should help care for the poor and vulnerable.

But some took issue with his positions; Richard Friedeman, a lawyer and Republican Party chair of Kansas' Barton County, accused the pastor of being "very, very liberal - and he has the ability that liberal pastors have of telling you one thing and turning right around and telling somebody else the opposite".

Friedeman was cautiously optimistic on Election Day as he discussed the race from his Great Bend home, saying he believed Marshall, a personal friend and "good Republican voter," had "done a good job" during his time in office.

But he conceded that the Republican party was embattled.

"I think there's going to be a reckoning for the way Trump has alienated so many people ... I think it's going to be hard for awhile," he said.

His prediction proved true, as voters in Republican strongholds like Iowa, South Carolina and Texas turned out for Democratic candidates.

Even in Mississippi, the heart of America's bible belt, the race was neck and neck at the time of publication - a feat once thought nearly impossible for the Democratic Party.

Most pundits and pollsters are viewing these historic victories as rebukes of Trump's second-term agenda, such as aggressive immigration policies, a war in Iran and global tariffs that have contributed to the rising cost of living.

The day before the election, on a rainy afternoon filled with squalls and hail, dozens of Hamilton supporters turned out for a last-minute canvas in the university town of Lawrence, Kansas. Among them were retired teacher Sharron Witters, 77, and her husband Lynn, 78, a former forestry professor and pastor of 25 years.

As evangelical Christians, they said Hamilton's candidacy motivated them to put out signs on their lawn and knock on doors for the first time. They set out with maps and lists, as Sharron navigated their silver VW SUV from address to address in a well-heeled Lawrence neighborhood.

Hamilton, Sharron said, "doesn't sound like a politician".

"What a delight to stand and listen to somebody whose sentences make sense," she said.

"Wouldn't it be wonderful if he actually motivated people to work across the aisle?

She noted how other evangelical Christians had backed Trump "because he said, 'I'm against abortion'".

But she and her husband, "felt, from the very beginning, that [Trump] was a wolf in sheep's clothing".

News.title: Democrats won Congress in a blue wave. Now comes the hard part.
News.content:
The presumptive next speaker of the US House of Representatives had reason to be giddy Tuesday night: Next year, Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress after a blowout victory.

"Today begins the great American comeback," an ecstatic Hakeem Jeffries declared.

Election night was a fever dream for Democrats. In January, reality will likely set in.

After months of promises on the campaign trail â to investigate corruption; lower the costs of healthcare, groceries and petrol; and curtail the Iran war â they will now begin the much tougher process of putting plans into action.

A shift in the balance of power in Washington doesn't necessarily mean Democrats will immediately get to start checking items off their legislative wish list. Democrats have Congress, but Republican President Donald Trump still has the power to reject legislation.

"We need to prove we can get stuff done, actually deliver answers to their concerns and questions about low wages and rising costs in particular," US Senator Chris Coons, a Delaware Democrat, told the BBC.

"The Democratic Party is still deeply unpopular â we are less unpopular than the Republican Party, much less unpopular than Donald Trump."

News.title: Five reasons why Republicans lost so badly
News.content:
From coast to coast, voters across the US have been grappling with the soaring cost of essentials. That anger was palpable on the ground in key races.

"Gas prices, grocery prices, everything's going up," one North Carolina voter told the BBC ahead of the elections, adding that she had switched her vote from Republican to Democratic this election.

Prices increased by 3.7% in the year to September, driven higher by fuel and energy prices. Average US retail diesel prices in early October were just shy of the record of $6.52 (Â£4.83) per gallon seen in September, according to government data.

Almost eight in 10 voters (79%) said inflation had caused them and their family a severe or moderate hardship in the past year, according to data from voter polls.

And more than six in 10 respondents laid the blame for that at the feet of Trump, saying they thought higher than usual prices were because of the president's policies.

News.title: Everything you need to know from the US midterm elections
News.content:
Talarico's supporters went beserk as the projected results arrived at an election-night party, wrote the BBC's Gary O'Donoghue. Attendees hugged, kissed and drank to a reality they dared not believe would come true.

Hinojosa became the first Latina to be elected governor of the state.

Among the other states where history was made by the Democrats were Kansas, where Adam Hamilton took a closely-fought Senate seat - giving the state its first Democratic senator for nearly a century.

Senior party figures who cheered the results included Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is now poised to take over as the Speaker of the lower chamber of Congress.

"Today begins the great American comeback," he told a crowd of supporters.

If Jeffries' colleagues choose to keep him as the leader of their party's delegation in House, he will be the next Speaker, taking over from Republican Mike Johnson and becoming the first black person to fill that role.

News.title: Huntingdon train attack passengers thought stabbing was a 'joke'
News.content:
Some train passengers initially remained sitting down and thought a man was joking after he told people "I've been stabbed, run", a court has heard.

Anthony Williams stabbed 10 people on the train which made an unscheduled stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November last year.

Cambridge Crown Court heard the first person who was stabbed, Jonathan Gjoshe, later asked hospital staff "am I going to die today?".

Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 10 counts of attempted murder, and four other alleged attempted murders in earlier incidents in Peterborough and London.

A second stabbing victim said Williams ran away when his pet cockapoo fought back, and another said he threw luggage at the attacker to fend him off.

Jurors have seen CCTV footage of Williams' attack, which took place on the York to London King's Cross LNER service, after it had left Peterborough.

The court was played a video interview with Gjoshe, who said he was on his phone in carriage J at the time and initially thought Williams was someone he knew.

"I've made eye contact with himâ¦ he's pulled a knife, but I just think it was the way he's poked me, the way he's stabbed me, it was a bit weird because it was slow."

Gjoshe said that once he felt a shock "that's when the adrenalin kicked in" and he jumped over the train table.

He said his whole arm was "drenched with blood" and went through the carriage telling people "I've been stabbed, run", but said some other people on the train remained "sitting down, thinking it was a joke".

"It was like a movie, it was quite horrific."

He spent four days in hospital and asked staff "am I going to die today or not? please tell me this".

News.title: Brigitte Bardot inheritance row deepens after private letter to partner leaked
News.content:
A row over the inheritance of late screen legend Brigitte Bardot has intensified after a private letter was made public which appears to show her cutting off relations with her last partner.

Dated November 2022 â three years before she died at her home in Saint Tropez â the hand-written note accuses Bernard de Chiara, her companion of more than 30 years, of "patiently destroying me day after day".

The leaked letter is a useful weapon for the other side in the Bardot legacy battle - the animal rights foundation that bears her name - which is accused by de Chiara of rushing to dispose of her estate without regard for friends and intimates.

A week ago de Chiara, who is 85, was forced to leave the seaside house known as La Madrague which he shared with Bardot from the early 1990s.

After being looked after financially by her for so many years, he is reported to possess neither a bank account nor a social security card.

He was also furious after the Brigitte Bardot Foundation organised a sale in September of household objects mainly taken from the late actress's Paris flat. The sale raised nearly â¬1m (Â£835,000), shared between the Foundation and Bardot's only son Nicolas Charrier.

"I found it extraordinary that just a few months after Brigitte's death, they already wanted to make a souvenir out of her. I did not appreciate that one bit," de Chiara said.

In the letter, which begins "Bernard, it's a failure!", Bardot said she had given "everything" in the hope of finding a "companion would could offer back my love, share my joys and immense sorrows... who is happy at the life I am giving him."

But she concluded: "Today I have reached the end-point of my distress... I am so in need of a shoulder, a support, a tenderness, a presence â which you are incapable of giving."

Widely known under the adopted name d'Ormale (a pun on the French dort mal â sleeps badly), de Chiara was a businessman and one-time associate of far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen.

News.title: World must 'unite' to ease cost of living pressure, PM Burnham says after US midterms
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said the results of the US midterm elections meant there was an "opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living".

Speaking to broadcasters from the Commonwealth leaders summit, the prime minister promised to push for a resolution to the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine in the wake of the US elections that saw Donald Trump's Republicans suffer heavy losses.

He said he couldn't ease cost of living pressures until the US's conflict in Iran had been resolved.

Responding to the midterm results, the US president acknowledged that rising fuel prices - caused by the Iran war - had played a part in his party's defeats.

Speaking to Fox News, President Trump said: "People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that."

Giving his reaction to the results, Burnham said the voters in the US have said they want to "see the world coming together and focusing on the things that matter to people".

Asked whether he thought the results might make the US president more unpredictable, Burnham said: "President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living.

"That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we've made moves.

"But I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia.

"These are the things we have to focus on now, and I hope the world has a moment to do that.

"And certainly, in my calls with leaders, that is what I will be asking everybody to do."

News.title: UK national tests positive for Ebola virus in DR Congo
News.content:
A British national who is in the Democratic Republic of Congo has tested positive for Ebola, the UK government has confirmed.

A spokesperson said the UK "has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this" and that the risk to the public remains low.

It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DR Congo, which has so far led to more than 5,000 deaths.

The Foreign Office did not confirm whether the patient would be brought back to the UK for treatment, though a UK resident who was exposed to the virus in July was flown back for medical attention, as have previous nationals infected abroad.

Reuters news agency reported the most recent patient is a healthcare worker and would be brought to the UK, citing an internal document BBC News has not seen.

A UK government spokesperson said: "The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated.

"Further information will be shared in due course as appropriate. The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low."

Imported Ebola cases are extremely rare in the UK and have resulted in no deaths.

There have only been four confirmed cases of the virus in the UK - one, in 1976, resulting from a laboratory incident, and three involving health workers who were responding to an outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.

There have been more than 10,000 confirmed cases since the recent outbreak in DR Congo started in May, which has grown to become the second most deadly recorded spate of infections, behind the outbreak in West Africa.

It has since become the deadliest in the country's history, with a fatality rate of 48.6% reported at the end of last month.

News.title: Police launch inquiry after two inmates die in prison
News.content:
Two inmates have died in custody at a prison in Nottinghamshire.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) confirmed two men died at HMP Ranby - a Category C training and resettlement prison near Retford - on Wednesday.

Nottinghamshire Police said it was working with the Prison Service to establish the circumstances around the deaths.

A spokesperson for the Prison Service: "As with all deaths in custody, the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman will investigate, and we will respond to its findings in due course."

A spokesperson for East Midlands Ambulance Service (EMAS) said: "I can confirm that both yesterday and today, EMAS attended HMP Ranby.

"As there is an ongoing investigation, it wouldn't be appropriate for us to comment further."

Det Insp James Oakton, of Nottinghamshire Police, added: "An investigation has been launched at HMP Ranby following the deaths of two prisoners on Wednesday.

"We are working closely with the prison service to establish the circumstances surrounding these deaths, and a thorough investigation is under way.

"The families of those involved are being supported, and our thoughts are with them at this difficult time."

During the last full inspection of the prison in February 2025, HM Inspectorate of Prisons found 23% of prisoners at Ranby tested positive for drugs and a quarter said they had developed a drug or alcohol habit while serving their sentence.

Inspectors also raised concerns about the condition of the prison.

News.title: Miliband says slavery apology will not bring cost for UK taxpayers
News.content:
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has insisted the government's willingness to consider formally apologising for the UK's role in the transatlantic slave trade will not lead to higher costs for the British taxpayer.

The prime minister has said the UK will not pay reparations to affected countries, but declined to say whether his new approach could involve additional taxpayer money.

Speaking on the BBC's Newscast podcast, Miliband said previous British governments had a "sweep it under the carpet" attitude to the pain and consequences of slavery, citing what he described as former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair's "sorry not sorry" remarks on the issue nearly two decades ago.

In 2007, Sir Tony said the UK's involvement in the slave trade was a matter of "deep sorrow and regret".

"Tony Blair did sort of do a kind of sorry not sorry situation. He kind of expressed sorrow, and then said sorry, and then it was walked back by number 10," Miliband said.

Miliband said the former prime minister's approach was still referred to and came up in a recent conversation between Andy Burnham and the Prime Minister of Barbados Mia Mottley.

In addition, Miliband claimed, he and Burnham inherited a more recent mess, which is how the last Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) played out in Samoa two years ago.

Miliband said: "On the second day as my time as foreign secretary, I was told, 'look, one of your tasks is CHOGM 2024, which happened in Samoa, didn't go well.' To use sort of diplomatic speak, it ended up in a sort of punch up, a sort of verbal punch up about this whole issue."

He added: "This has really been hanging around as an issue for the Commonwealth for sort of 20 years, really. But it's grown and grown."

Given that, Miliband said, "we thought it was right to confront this issue and not to just try and sort of pretend that it didn't exist".

News.title: Fourth arrest after Halloween party stabbings
News.content:
A fourth boy has been arrested after five teenagers were stabbed at a Halloween party in Hampshire.

Police were called shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday to a home in Park Road in Chandler's Ford where an "unknown group" had gained entry to the event over a garden fence.

One boy, 17, remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition. The other four boys, who all suffered serious injuries, have since been discharged.

A 16-year-old from Southampton has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. Police have been given an extra 36 hours to question a 16 and 17-year-old, also from the city, who were held on Monday morning on suspicion of the same offence.

A 16-year-old boy from Bristol remains in custody having been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder on Monday night.

Two witnesses told the BBC a fight started after a group came in over a garden fence, although they said the motive for the stabbings was unclear.

One of the teenagers said: "I was [standing] in the hallway near the exit and I saw someone I know pull up their shirt and say 'I've been stabbed'.

"And then I later saw him lying outside the front of the house with someone compressing his wound."

The other witness said: "A big group of people started shouting and then a fight broke out and then we just heard the dad tell everyone to leave.

"And that was when we saw someone injured on the floor."

Police cordoned off parts of Park Road and the adjoining Valley Road.

The five boys who were stabbed had been invited to attend the supervised party.

News.title: Kellogg's admits snap, crackle and pop is quieter after uproar over Rice Krispies recipe change
News.content:
Kellogg's has told the BBC the "snap, crackle and pop" sound made by its Rice Krispies may be noticeably quieter after an uproar over the cereal giant's recipe change.

Rice Krispies and Coco Pops are no longer being made with whole rice grains, with the tiny toasted puffs being made using corn flour and rice flour instead.

A Kellogg's spokesperson said retaining the iconic sound had been a "huge focus" when designing the new recipe, but that customers "might notice that the sound may be quieter and not as instant as before".

The firm was responding to complaints online that the taste of the breakfast staples had changed, with some fans adding they missed the "pop" sound.

Kellogg's said it had adapted the recipes due to "changing weather conditions" that have disrupted supplies of some grains and cereals.

The cereal giant said the new versions had been "carefully assessed for taste, appearance and texture", but some shoppers said their children would no longer eat them.

Some expressed dismay that the taste and texture were "totally different" and dubbed the change "grim" and "disgusting".

"There's no snap, crackle and pop in these," a parent named Dani wrote on TikTok. "My toddler won't eat them."

Lauren, also posting on TikTok, added that she had been eating Rice Krispies every day for breakfast "for years and years".

"I had a bowl of the new recipe and you can immediately tell the difference," she said. "They don't have the snapping sound when you put in the milk."

Jessicake meanwhile said they tasted "weird and stale".

The "Snap, Crackle and Pop" - made when milk is added to the puffed rice - has been a centrepiece of the brand's marketing since the 1950s.

Kellogg's insisted the snap, crackle and pop is "still there, but consumers might notice that the sound may be quieter and not as instant as before".

Recipe changes are notoriously difficult for big brands. Chocolate makers are constantly accused of reducing cocoa content in their products and debates rage online over whether ketchup ingredients have changed.

When Scottish fizzy drink Irn Bru cut its sugar content in 2018, fans famously stockpiled crates of the old version.

No changes are being made to Rice Krispies products in the US and Canada, which are owned by a separate company.

Kellogg's said the recipe change in the UK would help "maintain consistent quality" as extreme weather takes a toll on crops and pushes up ingredient prices.

Extreme weather in Spain in 2022 and 2023 in particular had reduced availability of the types of rice the company uses for its breakfast cereals, the company said

Rice Krispies, launched nearly a century ago, are sold around the world and come in variations such as vanilla and strawberry flavours in some markets alongside the widespread chocolate-flavoured Coco Pops version.

"We appreciate that even small changes to a much-loved product can feel noticeable and that's why we have approached this with a lot of care and consideration," Kellogg's said.

The firm said it appreciated the customer feedback and would "continue to look at ways to make [its] products even better in the future".

The cereals have already undergone some change, with reductions in salt content in the 1990s and lowered sugar in 2018. The company said Rice Krispies and Coco Pops will continue to meet UK food standards on levels of fat, salt and sugar in food.

A backlash against processed foods in recent years, especially those low in fibre and high in sugar, has put cereals generally under the spotlight from healthy eating advocates.

Kellogg's stressed the cereals contain no artificial colours, flavours or sweeteners and the nutritional benefits in each bowl, such as fibre, Vitamin D and iron are staying the same.

However, the new recipes mean packaging will now include a "contains wheat gluten" warning.

Previously packaging said the products "may contain gluten" because they were made in a factory handling other cereals and there was a risk of cross-contamination.

News.title: Palestine Action ban undermined confidence in anti-terror laws, Supreme Court told
News.content:
The banning of Palestine Action has led to a "crisis in confidence" in the UK's anti-terrorism laws and triggered unprecedented civil disobedience from law-abiding protesters, the Supreme Court has been told.

Opening a major legal challenge to the group's proscription last year, lawyers for co-founder Huda Ammori said that no other protest organisation had been treated the same way.

They told the five justices that the UK's highest court had never before had to consider whether banning a group under terrorism legislation was compatible with freedom of speech and protest.

Twenty-seven protesters were arrested outside the Supreme Court on Wednesday as the hearing took place, the Metropolitan Police said.

Lawyers for Ammori told the court that thousands of elderly people, many veterans of other radical causes, had been arrested for holding up signs supportive of the group since its proscription.

Home Office figures seen by the BBC indicate that there have been more than 4,000 arrests so far at protests in which people have held up signs supportive of the group.

In practice, many demonstrators have been arrested more than once, with 1,200 charges authorised by prosecutors to date. Those trials are in limbo until the outcome of this case.

Henry Blaxland KC told the court that "far from depriving Palestine Action of the oxygen of publicity" and "far from discrediting its brand", proscription of the group has had the opposite effect.

"All it's done is to pour fuel on to a fire of one of the most publicly-contested issues of our time," he said.

"It was disproportionate to do that and in my submission completely unnecessary."

During often tense exchanges with the judges, Ammori's team accepted that Palestine Action could not be described as an ordinary and peaceful protest group.

They said that its members had carried out "direct action" protests by occupying or vandalising firms linked to Israel's military - with only three of 385 incidents assessed by the Home Secretary as constituting an offence under the Terrorism Act.

The UK's definition of terrorism includes incidents of serious damage to property for a cause - and at least two break-ins at defence firms have been described in criminal courts as having caused millions in damage.

Raza Husain KC, for Ammori, said that the judges had to put aside allegations of criminality - for which the state had many powers - and consider whether the Home Secretary's decision to label the group as terrorists had been disproportionate.

"Palestine Action was proscribed on the basis of less than one per cent of its actions over five years assessed as falling within the outer limits of a definition of terrorism," he said.

"The Home Secretary's own experts confirmed the vast majority of its direct action would not constitute an act of terrorism on the basis that any damage to property is typically more minor. Common tactics include graffiti, petty vandalism, occupation, and lock-ons."

One Palestine Action member has been convicted and jailed of fracturing a police officer's back with a sledgehammer - but the court was told that the group had never advocated such violence.

News.title: Man hid woman's body in freezer for three years, jury told
News.content:
A man killed a woman and hid her body in a freezer for almost three years while he took out credit cards and loans in her name, a jury has been told.

George Gordon, 65, is accused of murdering his friend Delia McInerney in April 2023, days before she was due to move to Portugal for a "new life".

Her dismembered body was found in Gordon's flat in St Helens along with her five dead guinea pigs in January this year.

Gordon, who did not appear in the dock at Liverpool Crown Court, has admitted killing Delia but claims it was self defence and denies her murder.

The trial heard the pair had been friends for many years and Delia, who was 62 at the time of her death, had lived with him at his flat in Gerards Court when she was not travelling abroad or staying at her house in Anfield, Liverpool.

News.title: Daniel Thomas faces trial in 2027 over migrant site accusations
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas will stand trial next year over claims he entered a restricted zone at a migrant processing centre in Dover.

Thomas, 37, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, denies the charges linked to the alleged incident at Western Jet Foil in Dover on 31 March.

Appearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court via video link on Wednesday, he was told he is due to stand trial at the same court from 1 June.

He also denies charges of racially aggravated harassment and using threatening words or behaviour in Dover on 1 April, obstructing a person engaged in a lawful activity in Dover on 6 April, and entering and remaining in Dover Docks without having lawful business or permission on both days.

Thomas had originally pleaded guilty to going into the restricted zone, but later vacated his plea and pleaded not guilty after the court heard he may have received incorrect advice from his solicitor at the time.

His trial is scheduled to last two days, with another case management hearing due to take place on 18 November.

Additional reporting by the Press Association.

News.title: Chloe Mitchell murder accused 'dismembered body', court told
News.content:
This article contains details that some may find distressing

The man accused of killing Chloe Mitchell murdered her at his house before dismembering her body and disposing of it in wheelie bins, a court has been told.

Brandon Rainey, formerly of James Street, Ballymena, denies murdering the 21-year-old in June 2023 and preventing the lawful burial of her remains.

At Belfast Crown Court on Wednesday morning the prosecution opened its case against Rainey.

Crown barrister David Russell KC told the jury it was the prosecution's case that Chloe Mitchell and Rainey had been in "an on-off relationship" and that he killed her in the early hours of 3 June, sometime between 00:36 and 05:18 BST.

"We say a wealth of evidence will show beyond reasonable doubt that the accused murdered her and disposed of her body in a way that prevented her burial," Russell said.

The jury heard that weeks before Chloe Mitchell's death Rainey ordered a range of knives.

The jury was also told that Rainey had conducted multiple online searches about Jack the Ripper.

Jurors were told Chloe Mitchell had significant addiction issues and was last seen alive by two of her friends in the company of Rainey in his flat in James Street shortly before her death.

The court also heard that one of her friends later told police that Rainey had made a comment while they were at his flat that he would "love to chop someone up and melt them in the bath" but then claimed he was joking.

When Chloe was discovered to be missing, one of those friends contacted Rainey, who told her she had only stayed about 15 minutes and left after an argument "to go to Belfast to see some fella," the court was told.

Jurors were told that after denying murdering Chloe when interviewed by the PSNI, Rainey later told a male how he killed her in his James Street flat in Ballymena.

Rainey told this male he knew how to cut her up and get rid of her body as he'd watched the TV programme Dexter, the court heard.

Extensive searches were launched by police to try to find Chloe Mitchell.

Her dismembered remains were found by a police officer on 11 June in two bins in James Street.

News.title: Rosie O’Donnell declares Trump ‘regime is over’ as celebrities react to midterm bloodbath
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Rosie O’Donnell has rejoiced at the Democrats flipping the Senate and the House, joining a slew of other celebrities in celebrating Donald Trump becoming a “lame duck” president.

The former talk show host – who now resides in Ireland after leaving the U.S. due to her outspoken disdain for Trump – took a victory lap in a nine-minute TikTok video.

She told her followers: “It’s a beautiful morning in the world. The Trump regime is over. Thank you America. We gave a very loud and clear message to Trump and his sycophants, his criminal friends: we’ve had enough.”

“I’m so proud of our country. Let the investigations begin people. This is a glorious day. You don’t get to define us, you madman. I love you America,” she said.

She continued: “Really, and this is a glorious day. Now, I feel sorry for the people who have to clean up the White House after Mr. Ketchup Thrower gets all his rage out.”

open image in gallery ‘I’m so proud of our country. Let the investigations begin people. This is a glorious day. You don’t get to define us, you madman. I love you America,’ Rosie O’Donnell said ( Rosie O'Donnell / TikTok )

“He released a statement saying that if he had been on the ballot, it would have been a landslide,” she added. “Listen, delusional, diaper Don, that's not the truth, buddy.

“It was bigger than a blue wave. It was bigger than a tsunami.”

The Democrats took control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives as voters in conservative strongholds shunned the Republican Party, which lost Texas, Maine, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and both Carolinas.

Voters also elected the country's first Black female governor, the first Native American female governor, the first Native female senator and the first openly gay male U.S. senator, in a historic night for U.S. politics.

Celebrities across the U.S. have been celebrating the blue wave. The Chicks waved fans printed with the words “F*** Trump” onstage at a Los Angeles concert Tuesday night.

“Well hello Los Angeles,” said Natalie Maines onstage at the Dolby Theater, as the band members fanned their faces, smiling.

open image in gallery The Chicks waved fans printed with the words “F*** Trump” onstage at a Los Angeles concert Tuesday night as they celebrated the Democrats flipping the Senate and the House ( Getty Images )

“Welcome to our blunami night,” Maines told the roaring crowd. “So glad we can enjoy this night together. Texas is blue. The Senate is blue. The House is blue. This was gonna be a very different night if that wasn’t the case. Welcome to the 20th anniversary of Taking the Long Way.”

The Chicks, from Dallas, Texas, have often wielded sharply worded criticism at President Donald Trump, and performed at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago in 2024. In May, Maines condemned his presidency and said: “Democracy is disappearing right before our eyes.”

Oscar-winner Viola Davis celebrated the historic victory of Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became the first Black female governor in U.S. history.

“We the people .....THE PEOPLE!!” she wrote on Instagram. “We are the orchestrators of this nation....and we have spoken...through our vote....CONGRATULATIONS, my sistah.”

open image in gallery Viola Davis celebrated the historic victory of Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became the first Black female governor in U.S. history ( PA )

Hacks star Hannah Einbinder toasted Abdul El-Sayed’s historic Senate race victory in Michigan, and posted a clip of herself doing a Haley Stevens impression after the prominent Michigan Democrat endorsed El-Sayed’s Republican opponent at the eleventh hour earlier this week.

Einbinder teased the impression on her Instagram Stories on Tuesday night: “If our guys (gender neutral) win tonight, I will debut my perfect Haley Stevens impression.”

open image in gallery ‘Hacks’ star Hannah Einbinder toasted Abdul El-Sayed's historic Senate race victory in Michigan ( Getty )

Hours later, Einbinder posted a clip of herself in a bar delivering on her pledge. “As promised,” she wrote in a caption to the video, which featured her saying: “We’re gonna give ’em a little bit of energy, a little bit of pow, a little bit of stick it to ’em, cos that’s the Michigan way.”

She then reposted a graphic with words: “Mazel tov, Abdul.”

Singer Mandy Moore posted a series of stories as the results came in overnight, saying, “Texas, this keeps getting better and better…”

She wrote: “Thank you America. Thank you, everyone who voted. Turns out starting endless wars, taking away healthcare, kidnapping people in the streets, and on and on and on isn’t what the country at large stands for.”

Happy Days actor Henry Winkler responded to a post on X from social media personality Joanne Carducci, asking him: “Checking in — how are you all feeling right now?!!!”

Winkler replied: “Dreams do come true.”

open image in gallery Henry Winkler said ‘Dreams do come true’ after the midterms election result ( @hwinkler4real / X )

Actor John Leguizamo posted a celebratory video in his bathrobe, saying: “We did it. This is redemption time! We got the first Latino governor in California… wooo!”

“It’s incredible, what wins. But it’s time to fix this mess,” he said.

Hocus Pocus star Bette Midler said: “I am overjoyed. What a great, great night! Thank you, America! You’ve saved your beloved country!”

open image in gallery Bette Midler said voters ‘saved your beloved country’ ( @bettemidler / Instagram )

Reality star Kim Kardashian shared a photo of herself on Wednesday with the caption: “GOOD MORNING AMERICA.”

Actor Pedro Pascal shared the results in Texas, writing: “SOBBING” on his Instagram stories.

He reposted several other infographics, including a picture of Texas colored in blue with the white heart in the middle, and another post celebrating Deb Haaland as the first Native American woman to be elected governor in the U.S., following her result in New Mexico.

The Breakfast Club star Molly Ringwald had encouraged fans to vote earlier in the day, and then celebrated the result in California.

“What a night! Congratulations to [Governor Xavier Becerra]! I was so happy to have met him along with his lovely wife Dr. Carolina Reyes supporting Planned Parenthood #california #plannedparenthood #choice,” she wrote on Threads. She also shared an emoji of a blue wave to signify the Democrats' sweep.

News.title: Ban on ketchup sachets is down to Burnham and not the EU, says No 10
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Downing Street has denied plans by Andy Burnham to ban tomato ketchup sachets are a result of the prime minister’s new closer ties with the European Union.

No 10 says any such ban would be ministers’ own decision following a consultation, after it was revealed that Mr Burnham was considering stopping cafes and restaurants from giving out sachets of ketchup, mayonnaise and vinegar.

The EU has outlawed single-use plastic packaging for condiments in the catering sector on environmental grounds.

Billions of ketchup sachets are used worldwide each year ( Getty Images )

Estimates suggest there are up to 199 million tonnes of plastic waste polluting the world’s oceans, and every year around a million birds and over 100,000 sea mammals die from eating and getting tangled in plastic waste.

Environmental campaigners who want a ban on the sachets say that 855bn of them are used every year globally, and many are thrown away without even being opened.

The sachets are being prohibited in Northern Ireland, under post-Brexit arrangements that require the nation to follow certain EU rules.

It had been thought the government wanted to extend that ban to Britain, as part of a push to align the UK with European Union rules.

But the prime minister’s official spokesman said: “A ban on single-serving sachets is not in the scope of any agreement with EU partners. It is not part of our EU reset for food and drink.

However, he did not rule out a ban, adding: “If any consultation on single-use sachets is taken forward, it will be solely as a result of the UK choosing to do so.”

In response to a written question in parliament, environment minister Emma Hardy said: “The EU's ban on the sale or provision of single-serving sachets or containers of ketchup, mayonnaise, sugar, salt, oil and vinegar will apply in Northern Ireland under the Windsor framework but will not apply in the rest of the UK under EU-reset.

“A consultation regarding UK alignment is being planned.”

Later this month, Mr Burnham will end one of the most damaging consequences of Brexit by agreeing to align with EU standards on food and drink to end costly and burdensome border checks.

The prime minister is due to meet EU leaders on 20 November, when he is expected to unveil a deal with Brussels worth 0.4 per cent of the UK GDP.

It will lead to a halt to border checks on food and drink, a new youth mobility scheme and a much closer working partnership with the bloc.

The deal will also allow passports for UK pets taken into the EU to resume for the first time since the UK left the bloc.

Mr Burnham plans to use the summit to launch a new discussion on options for the UK beyond the next election, including a manifesto pledge on rejoining the bloc.

News.title: Jury awards $200K to Mexican tourist in ‘fart police’ translation mixup that led to excessive force
News.content:

A Mexican tourist attacked by a police dog after Colorado police officers shouted commands in Spanish - which nonsensically translated to “fart police” - has been awarded more than $200,000 in damages.

Salvador Alonso Guerrero-Salmeron, a professional musician, was staying at a home in Aurora in March 2023 when a SWAT team made an early morning raid to arrest a tenant in another room. The musician was renting the room while promoting his band and performing shows, court records show, and he had no connection to the suspect, according to a civil lawsuit he later filed, The Denver Post reports.

Images from police body-cam footage show officers waking Guerrero-Salmeron, who does not speak English, before he holds up his ID and visa. In footage shown during his civil trial, officers point guns at him and speak Spanish. A police dog then bites the man’s elbow while he holds a document in his other hand.

It is unclear exactly what officers were trying to communicate but they used a loudspeaker with the apparent intent to warn residents that a police dog was at the scene. Officers repeatedly shouted commands in English and poorly pronounced Spanish, saying: "Pedo policía pedo la madera." A translator’s report later determined this meant: "Fart police, fart the wood," according to court records.

“You just ordered the taco plate,” one police officer noted as the commands were given, according to the report.

open image in gallery The Mexican man was unarmed and holding up his tourist visa and identification when the police dog latched onto his arm for around 15 seconds during a March 2023 raid in Colorado ( Arapahoe County District Court )

During the encounter, police ordered their dog to bite Guerrero-Salmeron and the canine latched on to his arm for around 15 seconds. Guerrero-Salmeron was arrested and charged with failing to obey a police order, a municipal offense that prosecutors later dropped.

Guerrero-Salmeron filed a civil lawsuit last month accusing Aurora Police Department officers of using excessive force and pursuing a malicious prosecution.

The musician said he neither heard nor understood the commands, according to the complaint. He said that the use of force was unnecessary because he posed no threat to officers and was attempting to identify himself.

The Post reported that during the raid, Guerrero-Salmeron had texted the building’s landlord believing intruders were breaking in and attacking someone downstairs, unaware the shouts were coming from police officers.

On Tuesday, a jury found Officer Robert Wong, the police dog handler, liable for excessive force and Officer Grant Peet liable for malicious prosecution. Jurors cleared two other officers named in the lawsuit, Oscar Pena and Jeremiah Miles.

Attorneys for Wong and Peet defended their actions, arguing that using the police dog was reasonable under the circumstances. They said Guerrero-Salmeron had failed to follow police commands for more than an hour and that officers had reason to believe he could be armed or preparing to attack them.

The jury awarded Guerrero-Salmeron $200,000 in damages. Guerrero-Salmeron's attorneys, Joshua Landy and Luke McConnell, told The Independent that the verdict "sets the record straight."

"What makes this verdict particularly significant is that the jury didn't stop at finding excessive force," the attorneys said in a statement. "The jury also found that an officer maliciously prosecuted an innocent man and imposed punitive damages for that conduct."

The Aurora Police Department declined The Independent’s request for comment.

News.title: Donald Trump humiliated in US midterms as Democrats seize control of Congress
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Donald Trump received a crushing blow in disastrous US midterms as the Democrats seized control of Congress, leaving the president’s second term in office in tatters.

Win after win for the Democrats in both the House of Representatives and the Senate demonstrated an overwhelming rejection of Trump’s policies and presidency.

Vice president JD Vance squarely placed the blame on the war with Iran, saying it would take an “honest conversation” about the conflict to reconcile where “we go from here”.

Pressure fell on Secretary of State for War Pete Hegseth, who was expected to be in the firing line for the overwhelming defeat.

The spiralling cost of living and failed tariff policies were also critical to the Republican loss.

Trump wasted no time in blaming the Republican candidates themselves for the rout, ranting on Truth Social on Tuesday night: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

open image in gallery Donald Trump was said to have spent Tuesday evening seething in the residence as results came in (pictured October 30) ( AFP/Getty )

The president was unusually quiet in the hours after the result, accused of hiding in his private residence at the White House as results flooded in.

A source close to the president told the Daily Mail that the president spent the evening sat in the dark in the White House residence, “watching Fox News barely uttering a word and paralyzed into silence”.

Trump made an appearance at the White House to praise the work being done on his ballroom and the Reflecting Pool on Wednesday.

He told reporters JD Vance’s comments blaming his party’s historic midterm election defeat on the war with Iran were “largely true”.

The president added: “But at the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again, because long-term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.

“The Iran thing we had to do, and ‌we ​continue to ‌do ⁠it.”

He again insisted that the Republicans would have won if he was on the ballot, but said “you can’t transfer the love [from my rallies] to the candidates.”

Asked if he was worried the Democrats would now try to impeach him, he said: “No, not even a little bit. I think it would destroy the Democrat Party if they did that.”

According to exit polls by SSRS, half of voters nationwide said they saw the midterms as an opportunity to rebuke the president, while three-quarters said they were “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the way the country is headed.

In the early hours, after the polls closed, Trump was ultimately forced to concede that the Democrats “did a good job”, congratulating them on their historic win.

“I don’t view it as a hit on me,” he said in a call to Fox News. “I think we’ve had the greatest two years in the history of the presidency in terms of the economy, in terms of all the things we’ve done.”

The midterms produced several firsts for both parties as in Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of any US state, while Byron Donalds, in Florida, became the first Black Republican governor in the US.

open image in gallery Abdul El-Sayed, and his wife, Sarah Jukaku, react on stage after his victory, in Detroit ( Reuters )

Democrat Gina Hinojosa will become the first Latina governor in Texas, while Democrat Xavier Becerra will be California's first Latino governor. Abdul El-Sayed will became the first Muslim elected to the Senate after his resounding win in Michigan.

The Democratic wave flooded huge swathes of the country, eroding some the firmest of Republican bastions. In Texas, James Talarico became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988.

And in Kansas, Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat since the Great Depression nearly a century ago, while in Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown claimed a seat that belonged to JD Vance only two years ago.

The Democrats focused their campaign on corruption and affordability, while capitalising on the unpopularity of the Iran war, while the Republicans under Trump attacked Democrats over culture war issues, portraying their opponents as radicals.

Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump's administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation.

Trump offered some insight into his plan to obfuscate Congress, sharing a picture on his social media platform of one of his iconic red baseball caps featuring one word: “Veto.”

On Sunday, ahead of the elections, he had said he expected to issue presidential vetoes for “a month or two” until he can reach compromises with the Democrats.

Dr Rebecca Stone, associate professor of US History at the University of Warwick, told The Independent that Trump’s knee-jerk ‘veto’ reaction reveals how he intends to play out the rest of his presidency.

“There is no limit to the number of vetoes a president can wield,” she explained. “While they can be overridden by a two-thirds majority vote in both the House and the Senate, such a feat would require the support of at least a few elected Republicans.”

Liverpool resume their Champions League campaign at Fenerbahce bidding to bounce back from a bitter Premier League defeat to Arsenal at the weekend.

The Reds, bruised from their first loss to Arsenal at home for 14 years, travel to struggling Fenerbahce aiming to resume what has been a successful start to their European adventure, with nine points from their opening three games.

They’ll be reunited with an old friend at the Sukru Saracoglu Stadium in the form of interim manager Dirk Kuyt, who spent six years at Anfield and stepped into the hot seat at the Turkish club after Ismail Kartal’s resignation last month.

Liverpool midfielder Trey Nyoni starts once again as Reds deal with Ryan Gravenberch’s injury absence. The teeanger impressed despite defeat to Arsenal on Sunday and is rumoured to be close to signing a new deal.
