Sports.title: Ocon's F1 story is one of success, even if this is the end
Sports.content:
There's really not much reason to think otherwise: it looks increasingly likely that this could be the end of Esteban Ocon's active Formula 1 career. A career blessed with plenty of highlights, a handful of podiums and a victory scored behind the wheel of a car that wasn't capable of winning on merit.

He made a lot of the opportunities that came his way - not just on the track, but throughout his career. And even if it ends now, that career has already become far more than anyone could reasonably have expected, given where he started.

There aren't many stories like his in modern F1, with kids from modest backgrounds - without wealthy families or rich sponsors behind them from an early age - reaching the pinnacle of motorsport, let alone achieving what Ocon has managed.

But his abrupt departure from Haas could well mark the end of that chapter of his racing career. Things could change. He could still return, because he's still one of the best drivers in the world. It's just very difficult to see how right now.

It's almost impossible to imagine Ocon on the grid when the 2027 season begins in Bahrain - if it begins in Bahrain - with most seats already taken and those potentially still available having plenty of candidates queuing up for them. And there's little reason to believe he'd suddenly jump ahead of the others.

There's still a question mark over Cadillac's second seat. But there's Colton Herta, with his American passport, and Yuki Tsunoda as another possible option. Liam Lawson's future hasn't been confirmed either, but Red Bull isn't suddenly going to add a 30-year-old Frenchman to the pool of candidates for its junior team. That's essentially a fight between Lawson and 19-year-old Bulgarian Nikola Tsolov.

What's more likely is that Ocon would once again have to find a place on the substitutes' bench, waiting for an opportunity until somebody slips in the shower.

Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

And there are plenty of examples of drivers who have eventually made it back after choosing that route. Even on the current grid, Alex Albon, Valtteri Bottas and Nico Hulkenberg are examples. Ocon himself belongs in that group: he returned to racing with Renault in 2020 after spending a year on the sidelines as Mercedes' reserve driver.

But, as uncomfortable as the truth may be, the way Ocon's 2026 season ended so suddenly makes the prospect of a comeback even less likely than it would have been had he simply finished the year with Haas.

There's no point speculating about what actually happened between him and the team. And it would be wrong to give more visibility to the rumours flying around.

What we do know is that something happened during the Mexico Grand Prix weekend. And whatever it was, it was enough for Haas to take Ocon out of the car and hand it to Ryo Hirakawa, a driver with no previous F1 starts, who made his grand prix debut at the age of 32 - something we hadn't seen since Andre Lotterer jumped into a Caterham at Spa in 2014.

Whatever happened, it was serious enough not only for Haas to sideline him for the weekend, but also to decide that he wouldn't race for the team again this season.

Yes, perhaps the situation was also convenient for Haas. It now has an opportunity to give Rafael Camara, its future driver, some actual race experience. That will certainly be useful for the Brazilian, but also for the team, which can identify areas to work on, get to know him better and benefit from all the other things that come with running a young driver in a grand prix.

But Haas wouldn't have shown Ocon the door just for that.

When a driver disagrees with his team, it's certainly not ideal. When it gets to the point where the team takes him out of the car, it's worse. And when the driver in question is Esteban Ocon, it's difficult not to talk about his reputation and see Mexico 2026 as another stain on it.

Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Reputation is a tricky thing.

It's often formed according to its own rules, through freak circumstances and, nowadays, through the mystery of social media algorithms. When there's something to hate, the modern world provides more than enough tools to multiply the effect, exaggerate it beyond recognition and turn the whole thing into a farce.

But reputation exists. And Ocon has a reputation for being a somewhat difficult character to work with.

After all, his previous spell with a team ended in a remarkably similar way, with Alpine asking him to vacate his cockpit before the end of the 2024 season.

And then there's the whole outcry over his collisions with team-mates.

It's not actually as bad as the social media hate suggests, and many of those incidents weren't even his fault. If you go back and look at the incidents themselves, the picture isn't nearly as clear as the usual social media reaction would have you believe.

But it is what it is. And it's also true that anyone considering Ocon as a future driver will inevitably have that preconception about him - however fair or unfair it may be.

Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team, Laura Mueller, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

There's a puzzling disconnect between that image and the person we see in interviews.

Believe it or not, Esteban Ocon is one of the nicest people in the F1 paddock to talk to. Friendly, chatty, very polite. Yet there are enough people who would tell you that he can be difficult to deal with at times.

We talked about it when I interviewed him for GP Racing magazine a couple of years ago. We'd visited him at his training centre in the south of France and then had a long conversation in the car on his way home to Geneva.

I told him that a sporting director from an F1 team had once described Ocon to me as one of the most brutal guys when it came to discussions in the stewards' room.

I asked whether he thought that was part of his character. And he agreed that he understood what people might be talking about.

"But yeah, when there's something that has to be said, especially in Formula 1, it has to be said," he told me back then. "We have no time to waste here. So, it's important to be straightforward. Maybe I'm too straightforward at times, but well… I'm not going to let anything go after I've worked so hard to get where I am. You see how many hours I put in every day here - and I don't want to get, you know, eaten alive by doesn't matter who it is, be it some team manager, team principal, or a world champion.”

And we talked about how that part of his character was perhaps formed in the early days of his career, when his future depended not only on results but also on his ability to stand his ground and be as pushy as necessary to secure support.

Esteban Ocon, Alpine F1, celebrates on the podium Photo by: Jerry Andre / Motorsport Images

His family had sold their house to fund his karting career, but they simply couldn't provide enough money for him to progress through the junior formulas.

He needed to be a fighter, because nothing was handed to him.

And you've got to admire that - just as you've got to admire his whole journey.

“That's probably the right way to put it: I had the weight of my family on my shoulders, from a very young age,” he said. “And I’m not saying it to seek pity: it was worth trying and we succeeded to end up where we wanted to be - and now everything is good. But it's clear that I had to deal with these sorts of pressures, I had to be tough when it mattered, and I had to be heard when people were not necessarily listening, or weren’t convinced. And, you know, to make these businessmen, investors listen to you, when you're 13 or 14, and really pay attention, is not easy.”

It's probably not right to look at this as though it has now become a problem for him in Formula 1. Because he made it this far thanks to being who he is. And a decade-long career at the pinnacle of motorsport, with a grand prix victory to his name, is something nobody will ever take away from him.

As sad as it may be, perhaps that's simply all there was for Ocon in Formula 1.

There's a certain irony in the fact that what could turn out to have been Ocon's final F1 weekend as a race driver was also the weekend Kimi Antonelli won the world championship with Mercedes.

Because Ocon was once Toto Wolff's favourite kid, too. Wolff even said it was only a matter of time before Esteban would drive for the Silver Arrows.

It was never meant to be. And perhaps there was a reason for that, too.

Esteban Ocon, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Chris Graythen / Getty Images

Ocon is undeniably fast. You don't have a 10-year career in F1 without being fast, let alone win a grand prix. But Formula 1 is also Formula 1. And only the absolute best, with the complete package required to reach championship level, actually get there.

There's no denying that, in terms of pure speed, there are far more drivers capable of winning a world championship than there are actual world champions. There's luck. There are circumstances, which play a huge role in how careers develop. And some of those things simply didn't fall into place for Ocon. Or perhaps his complete package wasn't convincing enough at the right moments - for Wolff, for example, to put him in a Mercedes when the opportunity arose.

After all, Ocon was available when Lewis Hamilton decided to leave for Ferrari. But by then, Toto already had a new favourite kid.

And he was ultimately proven right.

Whatever happens next, even if Ocon never finds his way back onto the grid, there's no reason to look back at his career with pity or regret. Because the career he's had is one that thousands of drivers would give almost anything to have. It's a bit sad - and even silly - that it could end like this. But it's certainly not what he deserves to be judged on.

And also...

As difficult as it looks now, even if it seems impossible, we're talking about someone who's already made an impossible dream come true: a kid from a small French town, whose dad was a mechanic, making it all the way to F1.

Don't count him out just yet.

And whatever happens next, he deserves to be praised for what he's already achieved.

Sports.title: Mercedes takes blame for Russell's poor Mexico GP: "We let him down"
Sports.content:
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has admitted to ‘letting George Russell down’ at Formula 1’s Mexico Grand Prix, with the Briton’s bid for victory derailed within seconds by a technical issue.

Russell was starting from the front row alongside Lewis Hamilton at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, and his initial getaway was good enough to retain that position and take the polesitter’s slipstream, but his Silver Arrow encountered an energy deployment issue.

By the time he got to Turn 1, Russell was down to sixth. A few corners later, he was attacking Isack Hadjar but failed to back out going into Turn 6 and tapped the Red Bull into a spin, landing a 10-second penalty.

As a consequence, Russell was sixth again by the time the red flag was waved for Valtteri Bottas’ hefty crash, as the penalty dropped him behind Lando Norris, and he failed to make any inroads during the second part of the race.

After the chequered flag, the 28-year-old congratulated team-mate Kimi Antonelli for his world title but did not stick around; Mercedes excused him from his media duties, landing a €5,000 fine from the FIA.

“I saw George after the race on the FIA scales, and obviously he's distraught about the situation,” Wolff said. “It was a great show of sportsmanship to go and see Kimi. I have known George for such a long time and I know for a racing driver this is a catastrophic moment.

George Russell, Mercedes, Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

“Maybe today the race was a little bit a picture of his season. This was a race for him to win. We had the pace in the car and we let him down on the first straight. The energy delivery is not what we have thought it should be.

“I'm very much with him, at the moment. I've been in situations where he's very difficult to cope. Him not doing the media work or leaving the track is absolutely understandable. Him staying would have actually surprised me. That's absolutely honoured.”

This wasn’t the first time a lack of energy deployment caused trouble for Russell; it also happened at Spa-Francorchamps down the Kemmel Straight, leading to a collision with Hamilton. The Briton retired on the post.

Russell was also struck by other mechanical problems, notably power unit failures that caused retirements from the lead in Canada and third in Malaysia.

“Definitely he has had bad luck at some point in the season,” Antonelli admitted when asked if Russell would ‘give him a big push’ in 2027. “He has had a little bit more than me, being honest. I've also had my moments in Silverstone and Barcelona. Also, after Silverstone, we had to trash our new PU because it had a problem in it, and we had to take an earlier penalty, which was in Monza.

“Definitely, we've had our bad moments, but still, he will definitely come back. You know, he's super quick. He has shown this season that when he's on it, it's very hard to beat.

George Russell, Mercedes, Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

“So it's just about, you know, on my side, keeping focused on myself, keep trying to raise the bar, keep improving, keep developing, because I think it's not going to be only a matter of George at the end of this season, but also for next season, Red Bull, especially with Max [Verstappen], Ferrari and McLaren, eventually, we're all going to be up there, and it's going to be a tight fight. So, it's going to be important to be on top of the game, not only against my team-mate but against all the others.”

Russell eventually posted a long message to Instagram on Monday evening, delving into his emotions following the weekend’s events.

“Now feels like a pretty suitable moment to speak from the heart. This season started off exactly how I had hoped but it very quickly unravelled with tough luck and poor performances,” wrote the Australian GP winner, who took only two more victories in the next 18 grands prix.

“It’s been the first proper season of my career where I’ve had more bad days than good. Has it been tough to deal with? Yes, very. Has it been tough to pick myself up week in, week out? Yes, very. Confusion at times? Often. All I know is that I’ve given it my all and 2026 was not meant to be my year.

“I want to sincerely congratulate Kimi on what has been an absolutely incredible season. You truly deserve the Championship.

“Thank you to the team for producing the best car and power unit this season; it’s been inspiring to see everyone coming together over four tough years to bring Mercedes back to the top.

“Now, all I can promise is that for the rest of this season, and into the next one, I will be giving my absolute all to rediscover the performance I have been capable of producing for the majority of my career and fingers crossed a little bit of luck returns.

“Thanks for all the support.”

Russell still has a chance to clinch his highest-ever finish in the drivers’ championship, having taken fourth place in 2022 and 2025. He currently lies fourth, again, with 250 points – 11 and nine points adrift of Verstappen and Hamilton respectively.

Additional reporting by Roberto Chinchero and Ronald Vording

Sports.title: Herta to contest FP1 for Cadillac in Brazil to obtain final superlicence point
Sports.content:
Cadillac test driver Colton Herta will conduct his sixth Friday practice session of the Formula 1 season at this weekend's Brazil Grand Prix to collect his missing FIA superlicence point required to race in the series.

Herta, who has been building up for an F1 campaign with private testing, FP1 sessions and a troubled F2 campaign, needs 40 points to obtain the required FIA superlicence. Cadillac believed the former IndyCar ace had reached that threshold last week in Mexico, but it soon emerged the Californian was still one point shy amid confusion over his previous IndyCar results.

Cadillac will now rectify that error by handing Herta another Friday FP1 session in Sergio Perez's car, which yields a single point. Teams are only required to run a rookie in four FP1 sessions per year, but Sao Paulo will be Herta's sixth of the season as the squad is keen for Herta to finally obtain the licence.

That allows the team to keep its options open as it considers retaining incumbent Valtteri Bottas for a second year alongside Perez, or handing Herta his F1 debut in 2027.

"I’m really looking forward to getting back behind the wheel of the MAC-26 for another FP1 session," Herta said. "Interlagos is such an iconic, historic track, and driving an F1 car around there is going to be an awesome experience.

"Every time I’ve stepped into the car this year, from Barcelona to Budapest, COTA and Mexico City, I’ve felt more comfortable and better integrated with the engineering team.

"My goal for Friday morning in Brazil is the same: execute the run plan cleanly, give Checo and the engineers the best possible setup data to start their weekend, and keep building on my progress in the car. I’m grateful to the team for giving me this opportunity."

Valtteri Bottas, Cadillac Photo by: Chris Graythen / Getty Images

Cadillac heads to Brazil after a bruising Mexico weekend, which ended with Bottas suffering a high-speed crash in the race due to a sudden front-left suspension failure. Team principal Marcin Budkowski said the team had "implemented mitigations" to avoid a repeat.

"Following our post-race investigations, Valtteri suffered a suspension failure, and we have implemented mitigations going forward," Budkowski said.

"I’m also pleased to see Colton return to the MAC-26 for another FP1 outing, stepping in for Checo. His growth in the car across his sessions has been impressive, and his feedback remains invaluable to our 2027 development programme."

Herta's bid to obtain his superlicence hit a snag when his car broke down in Monza, leaving the 26-year-old short of the 100km threshold required for the session to award a point. In Brazil, 24 laps of the Interlagos circuit will satisfy that requirement.

Sports.title: Ocon to skip the rest of F1 2026 with Camara to debut for Haas in Brazil
Sports.content:
The Haas Formula 1 team has decided that Esteban Ocon will not race again for the squad, with 2027 rookie Rafael Camara getting an early debut this weekend on home soil.

Following increasingly strained relations between Ocon and the squad, a heated argument in Mexico proved the final straw that made team principal Ayao Komatsu decide to bench the Frenchman.

Reserve driver and Toyota protege Ryo Hirakawa replaced him from Saturday onwards in Mexico, going on to score a point on debut in 10th place. The team has now confirmed Ocon, who is a free agent next year, will not return.

"We have now notified Esteban Ocon that he will not return to a race seat with TGR Haas F1 Team this season," Komatsu explained.

"Such decisions are never made lightly, as was the case in Mexico City - but then, as now, we feel this is firmly in the best interest of the team moving forward.

"The conversations that ultimately unfolded between the team and Esteban remain an internal matter, and we will continue to respect the private nature of closed-door situations."

Ferrari junior Camara, who had already been signed by Haas to replace Ocon for 2027, will take the wheel of the VF-26 at the Brazilian Grand Prix.

The 21-year-old, who currently leads the Formula 2 standings and made a stellar impression on Haas in private testing, will have the opportunity to begin his F1 career several months ahead of schedule.

The final green light came on Tuesday afternoon, although Camara had already been placed on standby during the Mexico Grand Prix weekend following Ocon's sudden removal from the Haas line-up.

It is not yet confirmed whether Camara or Hirakawa will race for the team in the remaining rounds at Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi, with it likely being a combination of both drivers.

Rafa Camara has conducted private testing in older machinery with both Ferrari and Haas. Photo by: Davide Cavazza

Camara has never driven a 2026 F1 car, but will not arrive at his high-pressure home debut unprepared. During the season, he has completed five Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) outings, four at the wheel of Ferrari's SF-25 and one driving the Haas VF-25.

The latter took place in August at Portimao in Portugal and played a crucial role in convincing the US-owned team of his natural ability.

"Looking ahead, we've chosen Rafael Camara to drive alongside Ollie Bearman at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix," Komatsu confirmed.

"Having excelled in his TPC outing in August, we know Rafael's capabilities and we're looking forward to welcoming him into the team this weekend and working with him through his Formula 1 debut driving the VF-26 in Brazil."

The change of plans will also have consequences for Ferrari. Friday morning's FP1 session, originally allocated to Camara, will instead be handed to Dino Beganovic, giving the Swedish driver another opportunity to get behind the wheel of the Maranello team's car.

Sports.title: Why Bearman is yet to be announced as a Haas driver for F1 2027
Sports.content:
With Oliver Bearman firing on all cylinders in his sophomore Formula 1 campaign, it feels odd that Haas has been able to confirm the identity of Esteban Ocon's replacement in the second seat for 2027 before announcing Bearman is staying put for a third year.

There is no real doubt that Bearman will stay where he is, with both parties keen to continue for another season into 2027.

“I think it's very clear. I want to continue with Haas and that's definitely my goal," Bearman said in Mexico on Thursday. "It's not really in my hands. If it was up to me, it would have already been announced a long time ago, but there are a few bigger picture things that we're working on."

Team principal Komatsu added: "I don't like to go into the details of our contract, but Ollie is showing amazing potential. He's contributing a lot to the team's success and we want to grow together. We want to move up the grid as a team.”

And while Komatsu had to dismiss unsubstantiated rumours over Bearman's pay demands, holding up a deal as "absolute nonsense", the real reason behind the delay is not about 2027, but about what happens next.

Autosport understands that should Ferrari be unable to guarantee him a seat in 2028 - after three years of being loaned out to customer team Haas - then Bearman will have the freedom to part ways with Maranello. It is this "bigger picture" that Bearman was referring to in his answer, and a picture that has become increasingly clouded in recent months.

Oliver Bearman, Scuderia Ferrari, Jeddah 2024 Photo by: Mark Sutton

Bearman is still on course to complete the full Ferrari Driver Academy pathway, all the way from F4 to a race seat with the Scuderia - Charles Leclerc being the only driver thus far to have completed the entire trajectory.

But a new road block has emerged in the shape of Lewis Hamilton, who has regained form this year and exercised the contractual option that secured his place at Ferrari for 2027. While Bearman initially looked like a perfect successor to Hamilton, the seven-time world champion's recent comments in the media about his longevity do not portray a man who is walking away from Ferrari and F1 anytime soon. Leclerc, meanwhile, has already agreed a long-term contract extension until at least 2030.

So, if Ferrari isn't able to guarantee Bearman a seat for 2028 and the 21-year-old Briton would be free to explore other options, it makes sense that there is a need right now to clarify certain aspects of his long-term future before formally announcing an extension with Haas.

Komatsu stressed that there is no disagreement regarding the desire to continue the partnership. “I don't think I can go into the details of the what's the hold up, but it's very clear from both parties that they want to continue working together,” he said.

"We work really well together, push each other. He brings a lot to the team and then we are growing together so our intentions from both parties are fully aligned. We're trying to find a solution to work together next year and I'm sure we will”.

The Bearman camp's priority, then, seems to be about ensuring that another year at Haas does not tie him down longer than necessary and potentially limit future opportunities. The paradox is that all parties involved appear to be pursuing compatible objectives. Haas wants to retain Bearman, the driver wants to keep racing, and Ferrari has every interest in protecting a young talent in whom it has invested for years.

Oliver Bearman, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

What complicates the picture is the impossibility of guaranteeing today what might happen two seasons from now. For Bearman, therefore, the issue is not finding a seat for 2027. The real challenge is ensuring that the seemingly inevitable decision to remain at Haas does not become an obstacle to his prospects for 2028.

That delicate balance is what is currently being worked out behind closed doors. And it is probably the most likely explanation for an announcement that, only a few weeks ago, appeared to be nothing more than a formality.

Sports.title: McLaren to bring upgrades to Brazil GP with F1 2027 in mind
Sports.content:
McLaren will introduce upgrades to its MCL40 Formula 1 car at this weekend’s Brazil Grand Prix, featuring a front wing concept which is expected to feature on its 2027 challenger.

The team had surged to the front when it substantially updated the MCL40 in Hungary, with Lando Norris winning that race and the following one at Zandvoort, but it has since slipped back in the pecking order despite introducing another comprehensive upgrade package in Baku and further new parts in Austin.

McLaren had the fourth-quickest car in the last four qualifying sessions, with a 0.511s deficit to pole position and a 0.236s gap to the third-fastest challenger on average, but is still working away at improving the MCL40 – with an eye on 2027.

“We’ve got some updates coming to the car across the front wing, rear wing and some floor components as part of our normal development cycle,” said Peter Prodromou, chief technical officer, aerodynamics. “The aim is to make up ground, improve our performance over the remaining races and build momentum into next year.

“Sao Paulo has been a good circuit for us in the past and is a fairly representative track, so we’re hopeful these upgrades can help us take another step towards the front.

“The season isn't over yet: these upgrades are designed to improve the car now and help us in our fight for third in the championship. While the learning we take from these upgrades will feed into next year’s development, we also expect to carry over the concept of the new front wing into the launch specification of next year’s car.”

Peter Prodromou, McLaren Technical Director Aerodynamics Photo by: McLaren

McLaren has a 17-point deficit to third-placed Red Bull but has scored just 59 points to its rival’s 152 across the last five rounds.

The Mexican race was still encouraging, with Norris taking fifth just 12 seconds adrift of race winner Max Verstappen, yet the reigning world champion wasn’t optimistic for the next few rounds.

“If we look at Baku and stuff, I think we're still going to be struggling for pace,” he said on Sunday evening. “So we need to improve the car in certain tracks and certain areas still a lot more.

“Today it was good, but I'm not convinced that if we go back to the tracks we struggled at we'd be good all of a sudden. It's just today suited us, but I don't want to rely on a bit of hope and luck on performance.

“We know what we need to improve on, it just takes time, and hopefully we can have a better day in Brazil.”

Sports.title: The reason behind Honda’s power unit lasting five laps in Mexico GP
Sports.content:
In its Mexico Grand Prix preview, Honda’s Shintaro Orihara had described Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez as “a very challenging track for the power unit”, but he perhaps didn’t expect Aston Martin’s weekend to go so awry.

Despite decent pace and mileage in free practice – Fernando Alonso was just 0.769s down on pacesetter Charles Leclerc in FP2, with the AMR26s covering a whopping 144 laps across all three sessions – it all went wrong in the competitive sessions.

Honda did fix some driveability and turbo lag issues between FP3 and qualifying, but Alonso encountered “abnormal signals on the water systems” on Saturday afternoon, which didn’t prevent him from outqualifying Lance Stroll; still, both cars were out in Q1, four tenths down on the Q2 cut-off time.

In the race, the pair retired after five laps due to cooling issues.

“We knew that with the special high-altitude circumstance of Mexico City, we would face some additional challenges compared to other racetracks for the cooling,” said Orihara, Honda’s trackside general manager and chief engineer, following the race.

“However, we found that our ERS cooling circuit was under heavier stress than anticipated and this is why we had to stop the car in different sessions.

Lance Stroll, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

“Despite completing a series of laps during the practice sessions, the issue occurred today and during qualifying yesterday.

“At each race this year, we need to learn for 2027, even the hard lessons. We have a lot of data that we can bring back to this circuit next year, including on the turbo lag, and we will work on the solutions.”

Orihara pointed out on Thursday that in previous years the MGU-H supported the turbo, therefore reducing lag, but the new, simpler power units no longer feature that device – and that too was a problem with the thinner air at Mexico City’s high altitude.

While a frustrated Stroll only gave laconic answers to the media at the end of the weekend, Alonso was slightly more loquacious and underlined the scale of the challenge for Aston Martin and Honda.

“The car is very good,” the Spaniard said. “The problem is just, we cannot do more laps than a certain number, apparently, with the engine. Hopefully we learned a lesson and we come next year more prepared.”

But the Adrian Newey-designed machine had potential – even in Mexico. It’s fair to say Alonso and Stroll didn’t get much of a chance to show what they could do in the race; yet, putting the Spaniard’s quickest three sectors together on Sunday (he pitted on lap three, which prevented him from completing a decent lap), he was nearly as quick as Williams’ Carlos Sainz, despite presumably having a much heavier car with a full tank of fuel.

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

“On Thursday, when we sat together, we said this is a track that has a lot of low-speed corners,” Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack said. “And if we get the driveability under control, that we can be competitive. For example, corners like the stadium section, [Turns] 4-5-6, low-speed stuff.”

Reliability therefore is the crux of the issue – as well as keeping morale up. “It's difficult for everyone to keep the motivation high in such situations, and we are struggling all year already,” Krack admitted.

“We had a very difficult start of the year, then the period when we introduced the upgrades and the ADUO, we [had] a bit better results. Now, we have more trouble in terms of reliability. In Texas, we had different issues with incidents. You know, it's part of racing.

“The thing is, everybody tries his best, everybody is motivated to do better, and I have no doubt about the motivation. We don't have to motivate them, it's motivating them the highest possible.”

And if anyone is staying motivated, that will be Alonso. “I’m doing my best every time, every lap I do, every morning I wake up, every preparation I do, every food I take – everything is focused on performing at my best behind the wheel,” he insisted again, despite his seventh retirement of the season.

Additional reporting by Luis Ramirez

Sports.title: Cracked sump almost put Antonelli out of Mexican Grand Prix | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Mercedes has revealed Andrea Kimi Antonelli came close to retiring from the Mexican Grand Prix.

The team discovered the new world champion’s car had developed a fault in its power unit in the final laps.

Mercedes’ deputy team principal Bradley Lord described it as “a sign of the fact that this is Kimi’s year and things are rolling with him.”

“We got the car back after the race, took the floor off the bottom, [and found it was] covered in oil,” he told High Performance Racing. “Sump cracked.”

Antonelli was already detecting signs of trouble from his Mercedes power unit. “Kimi said he thinks about four laps from the end he could start to feel the engine just starting to struggle. So [he was] right on the edge of retirement [from] that race and yet it held together.”

The Mercedes driver lost almost two seconds on the final lap of the race, though he said that was because he was crying. He would still have clinched the title had his engine failed, but a retirement would have robbed him of the iconic photograph with Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton he wants to put on his wall.

Lord also shed more light on the loss of power George Russell suffered on the run to turn one at the start of the race, which allowed several of his rivals to overtake. “He’s taken the lion’s share of these technical problems and quirks and we had another one on Sunday,” said Lord.

“He was in prime position for going for the lead into turn one and then [has] a de-rate out of nowhere because of one of the complex bits of the energy rules mean he’s back in P5, P6 and caught up in the [mess] with Hadjar.

“It was a little bit like Spa, the start of the race there where he was so well positioned and then it just became that collision at turn four.”

Sports.title: Stats: Hirakawa is sixth one-off starter to score a world championship point | 2026 Mexican Grand Prix stats and facts
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen won the race and the new world champion finished third: this year’s championship-deciding race resembled last year’s, though the similarity was superficial.

There may have been three drivers still in contention but this wasn’t a down-to-the-wire nail-biter: Andrea Kimi Antonelli’s coronation was virtually assured before he even set foot in Mexico.

Third place ensured Antonelli succeeds Lando Norris as F1’s second new world champion in as many years. That hasn’t happened since 2010 when Sebastian Vettel became the fourth new world champion in a row, following Kimi Raikkonen, Lewis Hamilton and Jenson Button.

Norris’s reign as world champion therefore lasted less than a calendar year. At 329 days, this is the sixth-shortest individual duration as champion. However others who had short spells as champion won the title more than once, giving them longer reigns:

Shortest reigns as world champion (days)

*Died before winning the championship

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Antonelli’s championship success produced several notable statistics which were previously covered here:

Lewis Hamilton became the oldest driver to claim pole position for a grand prix in his lifetime. At 41 years and 297 days old he is the most senior pole-winner since another Ferrari driver, Mario Andretti, took pole position for the 1982 Italian Grand Prix. Hamilton is the fifth-oldest driver ever to claim a pole position in F1.

Oldest F1 pole-winners

Driver Race Track Age Giuseppe Farina 1954 Argentinian Grand Prix Buenos Aires 47y, 78d Juan Manuel Fangio 1958 Argentinian Grand Prix Buenos Aires 46y, 208d Jack Brabham 1970 Spanish Grand Prix Jarama 44y, 16d Mario Andretti 1982 Italian Grand Prix Monza 42y, 195d Lewis Hamilton 2026 Mexican Grand Prix Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez 41y, 297d

Hamilton’s pole position was his first for over three years. That’s well short of the longest spell between consecutive pole positions: Raikkonen went 3,262 days (over eight years) between his pole positions in the 2008 French Grand Prix and 2017 Monaco Grand Prix.

That record-extending 105th pole position for Hamilton was a close thing: he beat George Russell by just nine-thousandths of a second. But that was three times the scale of his last pole-winning margin. Hamilton beat Verstappen to pole by just three thousandths of a second in Hungary three years ago.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Unexpectedly, 17 places behind Hamilton on the grid was Ryo Hirakawa, who arrived in Mexico only expecting to take part in the first practice session. However Haas’s shock decision to replace Esteban Ocon after Friday’s running handed Hirakawa his grand prix debut at the age of 32 years and 239 days. That made him the oldest debutant since Andre Lotterer made his one-off appearance for Caterham in the 2014 Belgian Grand Prix – he was older by 39 days.

It’s not uncommon for a driver to take part in practice and then be replaced due to illness or injury. Occasionally, teams swap drivers between garages if damage leaves them with only one car available, as happened with Logan Sargeant and Alexander at the 2024 Australian Grand Prix.

But it is very unusual to see a healthy driver begin a race weekend with a team and then be replaced someone else. The last time something akin to Ocon’s substitution happened was when Ensign attempted to run Ricardo Londono-Bridge in the 1981 Brazilian Grand Prix.

The race moved to Jacarepagua that year and the Colombian driver took part in the then-customary pre-event acclimatisation session for the new circuit on Wednesday. However the FIA refused to grant him a superlicence, so Ensign replaced him with Marc Surer.

Hirakawa’s surprising weekend continued as he scored a point despite originally taking the chequered flag in 13th place. Penalties for Oscar Piastri and both Alpine drivers meant Hirakawa, like Arvid Lindblad earlier this year, finished his first grand prix inside the points.

As it stands, Hirakawa will not take part in any more races – Rafael Camara will take over in Brazil. F1’s rules only allow Haas to use a total of four drivers all season, unless they get a dispensation, and the team has an obvious reason to keep Camara in the season as he will drive for them next year.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Hirakawa therefore stands to join the tiny group of drivers who scored a point in their only start. Just six drivers can claim this unusual feat, and only one – Neville Lederle – did it driving solo in a race run to Formula 1 regulations:

Single-start points-scorers

Driver Race Position Points Notes Joie (George) Chitwood 1950 Indianapolis 500 5th 1 Shared car with Tony Bettenhausen Dorino Serafini 1950 Italian Grand Prix 2nd 3 Shared car with Alberto Ascari Eric Thompson 1952 British Grand Prix 5th 2 Formula 2 regulations Oscar Galvez 1953 Argentinian Grand Prix 5th 2 Formula 2 regulations George Amick 1958 Indianapolis 500 2nd 6 Neville Lederle 1962 South African Grand Prix 6th 1

It remains to be seen whether Ocon will return to start another race. At the beginning of the season the Mexican Grand Prix was due to be his 200th career start. Without him, the number of race-winning drivers on the grid has fallen to 12.

Finally, Verstappen’s sixth win at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez makes it the venue he’s scored the most wins at. He could equal that with a sixth win at Yas Marina next month – if the race takes place.

Sports.title: On This Day: Penske makes final CART appearance as longest season ends | Brief
Sports.content:
The end of CART’s longest-ever season, 25 years ago today, marked a watershed moment in the series’ battle with the rival Indy Racing League, formed by a split five years earlier.

Cristiano da Matta won the 21st and final event of the 2001 campaign at the Fontana superspeedway. However the season was marked by rows over technology, the controversial cancellation of a race in Texas on safety grounds and the appalling Lausitzring crash which almost claimed the life of Alex Zanardi.

Significantly, the 2001 finale saw the last appearance of the powerhouse Penske team before it defected to the IRL. Over the coming years rival engine manufacturers followed them and CART fell into bankruptcy. The two series reunited in 2008 and Roger Penske’s organisation purchased the merged IndyCar series in 2019.

Sports.title: Official: Ocon will not return to drive for Haas, Camara to take over in Brazil | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Haas has confirmed Esteban Ocon will not return to drive for them following his shock ousting for the team last weekend.

Rafael Camara , who was due to make his Formula 1 debut for the team next year, will take over Ocon’s car from this weekend’s round in Brazil.

Ocon participated in Friday’s second practice session in Mexico and was due to remain in the car for the rest of the weekend. However Haas unexpectedly announced on Friday morning that Ocon’s place had been taken by Ryo Hirakawa, the team’s test driver who participated in the first practice session driving Ocon’s car.

Ocon subsequently issued a statement confirming there had been a difference of opinion between him and the team but strongly denying any claims “physical violence was used to resolve any differences”. He challenged race engineer Laure Mueller’s instruction regarding tyre strategy during second practice.

Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu has not explained the team’s reasons for dropping Ocon.

“We have now notified Esteban Ocon that he will not return to a race seat with TGR Haas F1 Team this season,” he said in a statement issued by the team. “Such decisions are never made lightly, as was the case in Mexico City – but then, as now, we feel this is firmly in the best interest of the team moving forward.

“The conversations that ultimately unfolded between the team and Esteban remain an internal matter, and we will continue to respect the private nature of closed-door situations.”

Haas announced last month that Ocon won’t return to drive for the team next year. Camara will therefore make his debut at his home race this weekend.

The team has not given any indication who will drive for them at in the final three rounds of the championship. Komatsu said Camara “excelled in his TPC [Testing of Previous Cars] outing in August.”

“We know Rafa’s capabilities and we’re looking forward to welcoming him into the team this weekend and working with him through his Formula 1 debut driving the VF-26 in Brazil,” he added.

Sports.title: Spotlight: Verstappen puzzled by engine braking: ‘It just decides by itself what to do’ | Formula 1

Max Verstappen said he couldn’t explain the engine braking problems he reported on his radio during the latter stages of the Mexican Grand Prix.

“It happens randomly,” said Verstappen, who won the race despite. “The engine just decides by itself what to do, to be honest. So, I don’t know.

He suspected the problem was linked to the demanding conditions at the track. “We don’t know, sometimes it just happens. It’s not very consistent.

Sports.title: “Silly” power unit rules prevent passing, says Hamilton: “The engine can go faster” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1’s power unit rules made it harder for drivers to race at the Mexican Grand Prix, according to Lewis Hamilton.

The Ferrari driver spent the final laps of the race trying to attack race leader Max Verstappen . He said he was unable to do so because of the limits on energy deployment. This causes the effect known as “clipping”, where the amount of power being delivered drops.

“You can’t overtake here,” said Hamilton in the post-race press conference with Verstappen and Andrea Kimi Antonelli. “I think it’s something the FIA need to [address]. It’s just quite bad, I’m sure these guys would agree.

“We have this clip at the end of the straight where you can’t go past a certain speed, so everyone just follows. It’s the silliest thing when you are behind and you have a little bit more power in the slipstream. You should be able to go past that to have a chance to overtake.

“The engine can go faster, it’s just they have these silly clips. It’s the worst engine profile setting that I think they’ve probably ever had in this sport and it doesn’t provide great racing. So today you probably didn’t see much overtaking, unfortunately, because of that.”

Other drivers warned before the race that the “speed limiter” would inhibit overtaking. F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali has rejected criticism of the series power units and said fans “don’t understand” what clipping is.

Hamilton acknowledged other factors make overtaking especially difficult in Mexico. The high altitude means the air pressure is lower which makes it harder to keep cars cool when running in traffic. He also thinks the track’s configuration could be improved.

Sports.title: Antonelli says doubters “added fuel to the fire” in his world championship pursuit | Formula 1
Sports.content:
New world champion Andrea Kimi Antonelli says he was driven to disprove those who said he wasn’t ready for Formula 1.

Mercedes brought him up through the junior ranks quickly, skipping Formula 3 entirely and only spending a single season in Formula 2. Antonelli made his F1 debut last year, aged just 18, with Mercedes’ works F1 team rather than one of their customers.

Antonelli’s first season did not go entirely smoothly. He endured a nine-round spell during which he failed to score on seven occasions.

However he was competitive right from the start of his second season and quickly overtook team mate George Russell in the championship. Antonelli clinched the title yesterday with four rounds to spare.

He said that had been a satisfying response to those who suggested he wasn’t ready for F1.

“It’s always good to shut off some of the noise,” said Antonelli. “I think in many ways it does help to add fuel to the fire, the fact that some people said that I didn’t belong in Formula 1 or I wasn’t ready for it.

“At some points last year, it probably looked like that I wasn’t ready for it. But I think last year, being able to experience those moments made me much more ready ahead of this year. Experiencing really low and difficult situations, high-pressure moments, really helped me to face certain situations this year, and definitely they made me mature a lot as a driver and as a person.”

Antonelli clinched the title with nine grand prix wins, the most of any driver. But he admits there was room for improvement in his performance. “I’ve had moments where I could have done better, a lot better. It’s just a constant learning process.

“But I think last year, being able to race [with] Mercedes, obviously [going] straight under the spotlight, made me grow much, much faster than if I would have gone to a smaller team, for example.”

Sports.title: Deontay Wilder vs Jai Opetaia Announced For Fury-Joshua
Sports.content:
Deontay Wilder faces Jai Opetaia on December 11 at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium, serving as the co-feature to Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua on Netflix, Ring Magazine announced today. On paper, it sounds massive.

In reality, the matchup leans heavily on Wilder’s legacy rather than any guarantee of a thrilling contest. The real question is whether the former champion has anything left to offer, or if he is simply being set up as a marquee name on Opetaia’s resume.

Opetaia makes the jump from cruiserweight to take on a veteran whose present-day form is a massive question mark. Wilder once captivated audiences because someone was practically guaranteed to hit the canvas. Yet recent setbacks have drained that aura. Bouncing back against Tyrrell Herndon and Derek Chisora did little to prove he can still run with top-tier heavyweights. Herndon brought virtually zero profile, while outpointing Chisora hardly signals a career renaissance.

Because of that decline, Wilder becomes an ideal target for Opetaia. He delivers elite name value, championship pedigree, and the lingering threat of a highlight-reel finish. At the same time, his age and physical mileage make him a vastly safer proposition than young, dangerous contenders like Daniel Dubois, Agit Kabayel, Filip Hrgovic, or Moses Itauma.

Opetaia’s camp likely would not jump at those fights with anywhere near the same eagerness. Even someone like Bakhodir Jalolov would represent a much rougher initiation into the heavyweight division. Those challenges would force Opetaia to prove his mobility, punching power, and chin hold up against heavyweights who are in their prime.

Targeting Wilder lets Opetaia chase the spotlight without taking on that degree of risk. Even an explosive stoppage victory would leave plenty of doubts about how he matches up with the division’s elite.

Wilder still holds one classic trump card. If that trademark right hand lands cleanly with full power, Opetaia could be out cold before his slick boxing fundamentals take control. Opetaia showed vulnerability against Huseyin Cinkara, raising genuine concerns about how he handles elite heavyweight firepower.

That equalizer only matters if Wilder actually pulls the trigger. With his history of shoulder trouble, the real capability of that weapon remains unclear until fight night. If he looks tentative, sluggish, and unable to establish respect, Opetaia could roll over him early.

That is the major gamble with putting this bout in the chief-support slot. A faded Wilder getting dominated may generate flashy clips for social media, but it makes for a lopsided, disappointing viewing experience. His name dresses up the marquee, yet it remains to be seen how many fans still view him as must-watch TV.

Opetaia would gain far more credibility by testing himself against a top heavyweight contender or booking a cruiserweight collision with David Benavidez. Wilder offers a different prize entirely, letting Opetaia look devastating against an opponent fans remember as terrifying.

Whether Wilder still has any of that venom left will determine if this co-main event actually delivers on its billing. Wilder has looked completely faded, uncoordinated, and gun-shy for a long time. His legs are gone, his punch resistance has evaporated, and the explosive athleticism that once compensated for his lack of basic boxing fundamentals is nowhere to be found.

Putting him in with someone as sharp, fast, and aggressive as Opetaia feels cynical. For the organizers and Opetaia’s handlers, it checks cynical commercial boxes: It is built to lure casual and older viewers. Those fans remember the destructive knockout artist who ruled the WBC division and had the trilogy with Fury. They see the name, assume it is an explosive heavyweight collision, and either tune into Netflix or buy into the buzz.

The result offers almost no real sporting substance. Hardcore fans see right through it. If Opetaia blasts out a 41-year-old, fragile shell of Wilder, what does it prove? It tells us nothing about how Opetaia handles a legitimate, prime heavyweight contender who can absorb shots and fire back.

Yet, the highlight reel will be circulated everywhere, marketed as Opetaia making a devastating statement in the heavyweight division. The casual viewers will dismiss it regardless. If Wilder looks dreadful, clumsy, and gets wiped out in a round or two, casuals will simply view the whole thing as a sad mismatch featuring a washed fighter rather than crediting Opetaia as an elite heavyweight force.

It ends up in that weird circus middle ground: too lopsided and artificial to earn respect from hardcore purists, and too sad of a spectacle to leave casual viewers satisfied once the opening bell actually rings.

Sports.title: Paulie Malignaggi Says Osleys Iglesias Is Too Good For Canelo
Sports.content:
Paulie Malignaggi knows the Canelo Alvarez matchmaking blueprint inside out. His belief that Osleys Iglesias is “too good and not popular enough” points to a familiar formula: target a credible foe with just enough flaws for Canelo to exploit.

Because of that, Malignaggi considers Lester Martinez a far more realistic candidate to be selected for Canelo’s next opponent in 2027. Martinez brings real grit to the table, yet his technical limits give Canelo’s corner a clear path to victory. Iglesias presents a far uglier package involving size, elite craft, plus power.

“I think at the moment [Iglesias] is probably too good and not popular enough,” Malignaggi explained to Boxing King Media.

Malignaggi drew a direct line between Iglesias and the way David Morrell missed out on Canelo during his undisputed championship run. As he sees it, Morrell and David Benavidez brought too much threat with too little commercial upside. Malignaggi views Iglesias through that exact lens, even if Canelo’s camp hasn’t formally turned down the Cuban.

The argument is simple. An elite boxer can easily earn a title shot on merit while packing enough danger to price himself out of the running. Martinez strikes a far more appealing balance for the Mexican superstar.

“He’s continued to win, but has looked a little bit flawed, just flawed enough to where you’re saying, you know what, that might be a guy we could pick off here,” Malignaggi noted.

Lester battled Christian Mbilli to a grueling draw last year, proving his durability over 10 hard rounds. Yet that contest revealed his limitations. He would make Canelo sweat, though an elite counterpuncher would find plenty of clean openings. Malignaggi pointed out that Martinez lacks a consistent jab, handing Canelo room to dictate terms.

Iglesias, meanwhile, possesses a powerful jab that spells trouble. His right hand could easily cause more headaches than Terence Crawford’s, purely through reach advantages. Iglesias leans on his pedigree in the Cuban amateur system to control range, making Canelo eat leather long before he enters punching distance.

Slipping into the pocket is just as risky. Iglesias hides a vicious right hook that travels on an unorthodox arc courtesy of his long frame, catching opponents blind as they surge in. Factor in his southpaw stance alongside genuine power in both fists, and Canelo faces a nightmare puzzle.

Martinez delivers some name recognition with hardcore fans, along with clear technical flaws. Iglesias brings pure stylistic poison with minimal mainstream buzz. Martinez would come to fight, but his flaws make him beatable for the aging Canelo. Iglesias has the exact skillset that keeps his phone silent.

Sports.title: Agit Kabayel Faces Another Aging Heavyweight In Nelson Hysa
Sports.content:
Agit Kabayel defending his WBC belt against 42-year-old Nelson Hysa on November 28 continues a habit of feasting on past-prime heavyweights. Kabayel holds wins over far superior opposition, making this soft showcase completely useless for proving how he stacks up against the division’s dangerous young lions.

The Merkur Spiel-Arena in Düsseldorf stages this mismatch between the German titleholder and the obscure Albanian. Hysa (25-0, 23 KOs) provides flashy numbers for promotional posters, yet he walked into this championship opportunity without defeating a single credible top-15 contender.

“This is the fight we wanted to make,” promoter Frank Warren said when announcing the event.

For Kabayel (27-0, 19 KOs), this matchup continues a blatant habit of feasting on guys past their expiration date. Zhilei Zhang had already blown out 41 candles before Kabayel took him out in February 2025. Arslanbek Makhmudov was 34 when they clashed in December 2023, while earlier targets Kevin Johnson and Pavel Sour had long crossed into their 40s before stepping through the ropes.

Those previous opponents brought vastly different threats to the table. Zhang owned legitimate one-punch power, having already demolished Joe Joyce and Deontay Wilder. That made Kabayel’s stoppage a genuine statement win. Getting off the canvas to fold the Chinese southpaw with a body shot proved he could take heat and execute under fire.

Yet Zhang’s gas tank betrayed him, just like his age. Kabayel capitalized on those glaring flaws, but surviving an aging slugger who runs out of petrol after three rounds does not prove he can handle the division’s elite young guns.

Makhmudov brought a completely different danger profile. He arrived younger than Zhang or Hysa, carrying an undefeated record built on chilling knockout power. Kabayel ruthlessly exposed his stiff movement and crude defense, sending the Russian power puncher down three times before the referee intervened in the fourth round. It looked devastating on screen, even if Makhmudov arrived with an empty resume propped up on weak opposition.

Even Kabayel’s masterclass against Frank Sanchez deserves a massive asterisk. Sanchez fought essentially on one leg after suffering a severe knee injury. Stripped of his wheels, the Cuban was transformed into a sitting duck along the ropes. Kabayel did not out-box or out-maneuver a prime contender; he cornered an injured man who could neither retreat nor generate leverage to fire back.

Subtract Sanchez, and what is left of Kabayel’s record? An exhausted 41-year-old Zhang who ran out of oxygen after three rounds, a crude, stiff Makhmudov who had never beaten anyone, and a string of washed 40-somethings. Taking on Nelson Hysa is not an aberration; it is just standard operating procedure.

Hysa has shown nothing to suggest he belongs in the same ring with world-class operators. Blowing out Thomas Narmo in two rounds last August was another empty showcase against a bottom-tier opponent. It offered zero proof that he can survive deep water, handle relentless body shots, or deal with someone who hits back.

Kabayel is custom-built to expose fighters at this level. His relentless assault to the midsection has dismantled far superior heavyweights. Hysa will quickly find himself drowning under steady pressure, with zero answers once the body attack starts sapping his legs.

The bigger problem is what Kabayel actually gets out of this mismatch. Beating up a 42-year-old keeps his undefeated record clean and ensures he hangs onto his WBC belt, yet tells us nothing about how he copes with prime, dangerous heavyweights who possess the youth and stamina to drag him into deep waters.

Kabayel built a solid following through his relentless engine. Asking fight fans to stomach another aging victim merely stalls the division, delaying the crucial tests against prime heavyweights everyone actually wants to see.

Sports.title: Tim Tszyu Targets Aging Erislandy Lara For Belt
Sports.content:
Tim Tszyu grabbing a second belt sounds great until you look at who is holding it. Erislandy Lara is 43, fights once a year, and represents a safe shortcut to a championship rather than any kind of statement at middleweight.

Picking up the WBA strap off a semi-retired veteran will look good on paper, but beating Lara proves nothing about where Tszyu stands against actual middleweight threats.

The December 13 date at Cbus Super Stadium in Queensland is pure home-cooked business. Lara has defended this belt just four times since picking it up in May 2021. Holding a title hostage across five years through inactivity is not dominance; it is just boxing politics at work. His points win over late sub Johan Gonzalez last December told everyone what they already knew: Lara is running out the clock.

The Cuban still knows how to survive, jab, and make opponents look bad. But expecting the slick operator from eight years ago to magically appear in Australia is wishful thinking.

Tszyu’s team knows exactly what they bought here. They get a recognized name, a major title, and an opponent old enough to be Tszyu’s father who barely fights. From a purely competitive standpoint, he doesn’t come out ahead. If Tszyu beats Lara, hardcore fans will just say he ran over a 43-year-old museum piece. If he struggles or loses, his stock completely craters. The entire maneuver is purely about leverage, optics, and business.

Casual fans and mainstream Australian sports outlets do not track Lara’s inactivity or birth certificate; they just see that Tszyu went up to 160 and captured another major title. It gives his team a shiny promotional bullet point that lasts forever, regardless of how watered down the accomplishment actually is.

Holding the WBA middleweight strap transforms Tszyu from a challenger hunting for fights into a belt-holder who dictates terms. In modern boxing, belts are chips at the negotiating table.

If Terence Crawford, Canelo Alvarez, or anyone else wants to talk big-money unification or cross-weight clashes down the line, Tszyu having a 160-pound trinket gives him contractual leverage, a higher purse split, and immediate PPV headliner status in Australia.

Since Sebastian Fundora battered Tszyu inside seven rounds in their summer 2025 rematch, Tszyu has coasted on decision wins. Beating an inactive Errol Spence Jr. at 154 was convenient, but now Tszyu gets to leap straight to a middleweight belt without trading punches with a single real contender at 160 pounds.

It is soft matchmaking dressed up as elite action. Tszyu might leave the ring wearing middleweight gold, but taking a belt off Lara’s ghost will fool nobody paying close attention.

The undercard tells the same story. Jermell Charlo steps in against Brock Jarvis, a guy already knocked cold by Liam Paro and Keith Thurman. Charlo has been sitting on the couch since Canelo took his lunch money in 2023.

Sports.title: Canelo Wants Crawford Rematch, But The Purse Demand Could Kill It
Sports.content:
Terence Crawford appears ready to talk business, yet Canelo Alvarez wanting a rematch is only part of the equation. The real hurdle sits with whether Turki Alalshikh will supply the massive purse required to draw Crawford out of retirement.

“Hurry up I don’t got forever or all day to be waiting,” Crawford posted on X.

A rematch between Canelo Alvarez and Terence Crawford makes almost zero financial sense unless someone is comfortable eating an astronomical deficit just for the ego trip of staging it.

Crawford walked away from their first meeting with the undisputed crown, his undefeated record intact, and an estimated $50 million. If he comes out of retirement, he expects a raise, not a pay cut, and talk has suggested he wants numbers pushing toward nine figures. But where does the return on investment come from?

If Turki saw real value in a second meeting, the contract would already be signed and announced. The hesitation tells you everything about how that first fight went over behind closed doors. Turki is a fan who wants value for his money. He pays for violence, drama, and events that generate genuine international buzz. Crawford delivered none of that.

Crawford took the check, executed a safe, low-risk game plan, and left Las Vegas with the belts while the broadcast limped across the finish line. Why would any backer voluntarily line up to pay Crawford another record sum to repeat that exact same performance? The market has moved past Crawford anyway. At 168 pounds, there are younger, hungry fighters who fight with bad intentions, bring high punch volume, and come at a fraction of Crawford’s price tag.

From a pure boxing standpoint, taking no damage and collecting an enormous check makes sense for Crawford’s retirement fund. From a promoter’s standpoint, spending tens of millions to watch a guy jab, reset, circle, and coast to a decision feels like burning money.

When an event bleeds cash, promoters usually swallow the loss if it generates fanatical public demand for a sequel. That demand does not exist. Nobody outside of Canelo’s immediate camp is clamoring to see Crawford repeat the same cautious tactical performance. Canelo wants redemption because that loss damages his commercial standing, but Canelo wanting to fix his record is not Turki’s problem to solve with another fortune.

Throw in Crawford wanting a raise on top of what he made previously, and the proposition becomes absurd. Paying more money for a fight that previously delivered tepid action, zero viral highlights, and heavy financial losses defies basic logic. Unless Turki decides he simply wants to throw away millions to grant Canelo a personal favor, the checkbook stays shut.

Crawford is notoriously low-key and uninterested in selling fights outside the ring, and Canelo never plays the villain to get fans interested. Neither fighter is going to manufacture an entertaining promotional run to convince casual fans to shell out top dollar.

Canelo can campaign for the matchup publicly, but he cannot bankroll it alone. Just because Turki funded their first bout does not ensure the same checkbook opens for an encore, particularly at the price Crawford likely demands.

Even Saudi backers have to look at the balance sheet when the opening event already carried massive overhead and likely finished well in the red. Sinking another $120 million to $150 million into combined purses for two quiet personalities who produced a tactical chess match the first time around is an easy way to burn cash.

Canelo might want the opportunity to erase the blemish on his record, especially after getting past Christian Mbilli to pick up the WBC belt again. But wanting revenge and convincing someone to lose tens of millions of dollars to stage it are entirely different realities.

Sports.title: Tim Tszyu Could Land Vergil Ortiz With Lara Win
Sports.content:
The winner of the Tim Tszyu vs. Erislandy Lara fight could face the winner of Vergil Ortiz Jr. vs. Keith Thurman in the first quarter of 2027, according to Chris Mannix. Tszyu will challenge Lara for the WBA middleweight title on December 12 in Australia.

The target is the first quarter of 2027. Both December fights have to play out, and the winners would still have to make a deal.

Boxing executives love mapping out tournament brackets on paper, but they constantly ignore whether the American public actually cares enough to buy the final product.

Neither Ortiz Jr. nor Tszyu has established real pay-per-view drawing power in the United States. Tszyu sells tickets in Australia, but putting him behind a stateside paywall has always yielded modest numbers. Ortiz produces exciting scraps, yet his profile remains largely confined to hardcore followers rather than mainstream sports fans. Expecting casual buyers to drop $60 to $80 on DAZN PPV for Ortiz against Tszyu was already a massive stretch.

If the upsets hit, the whole concept falls off a cliff.

Keith Thurman has fought only once in nearly five years, and Erislandy Lara turns 44 next spring. A Lara-Thurman clash in 2027 belongs in a time capsule from 2017, not on a premium pay-per-view platform. Lara’s safety-first, counter-punching style has always been poison for commercial metrics, while Thurman’s long stretches of inactivity killed off whatever casual fanbase he once commanded.

Building an expensive pay-per-view model around two fights that could easily produce Lara vs. Thurman is promotional Russian roulette. If the favorites slip, the networks are left holding the bag on an unsellable relic.

Lara can make Tszyu look bad by taking half a step back and catching him with the straight left when he reaches. Tszyu will have to cut off the ring and make Lara work after he lands, because following him around gives the champion time to pick his shots and get out. At 43, how often can Lara do that if Tszyu keeps making him move? That’s the part of this fight Tszyu can exploit.

Against Ortiz, Tszyu could find himself doing the moving. Ortiz can get close behind his jab and go to the body when an opponent covers up. Tszyu likes to plant his feet to get power on his right hand, and Ortiz would give him chances to throw it. The cost is what comes back if Tszyu stays in front of him after he lets it go. He could land the cleaner shot and still spend the rest of the round trying to get off the ropes.

Thurman can spoil that pairing, and Lara can make the whole discussion academic for Tszyu. But if Tszyu wins in December and Ortiz is next, he could have only a few months to prepare for a man who will make him fight for the same ground Lara is willing to give up.

Sports.title: Jermell Charlo Takes the Safe Route With Brock Jarvis
Sports.content:
Jermell Charlo’s choice of Brock Jarvis reveals the modest ambitions of his ring return. After more than three years away, the former undisputed 154-pound champion booked a matchup designed for him to win. Jarvis brings genuine power, yet the two premier opponents on his resume stopped him inside four combined rounds. Keith Thurman did it at age 36 while shaking off a three-year hiatus himself.

Charlo (35-2-1, 19 KOs) meets Jarvis (23-2, 21 KOs) across ten rounds at middleweight. The bout serves as the co-feature to Tim Tszyu’s clash with Erislandy Lara at Cbus Super Stadium on Australia’s Gold Coast, streaming on DAZN on December 12. For Charlo, it marks his first live action since dropping a lopsided decision to Canelo Alvarez up at super middleweight in September 2023.

Thurman had sat out since 2022 prior to taking on Jarvis in March 2025. Even as an older veteran operating well past his peak, Thurman needed just three rounds to dismantle the Australian. Any thought that ring rust might leave Thurman vulnerable vanished instantly.

Before that, Liam Paro served as the only world-level name on Jarvis’s ledger, wiping him out inside a single round back in October 2022. While Jarvis rebounded from the Thurman defeat by halting the undefeated Sam Beck in four rounds last August, his record against elite opposition remains telling. His 21 knockouts look great on paper, but that power evaporates against seasoned champions.

“I’m willing to fight on a co-main event all the way in Australia because that’s how hungry I am,” Charlo said.

Charlo publicly aims for a belt in a second division, yet this booking proves he wants an easy touch before testing ranked 160-pound contenders. During his peak run, Charlo broke down Tony Harrison in the 11th round to reclaim his WBC strap, then stopped Brian Castaño in the 10th round of their rematch to unify all four belts. He excelled at solving dangerous, technical operators who gave him early fits. Jarvis has never proven he can force an elite boxer into those kinds of adaptations.

The card placement carries plenty of irony. Charlo sits beneath Tszyu, who was originally scheduled to challenge him for the undisputed crown before a hand injury forced Charlo out in early 2023. Tszyu now gets to headline for a middleweight belt against Lara, leaving Charlo to rebuild on the undercard.

An early night would deliver Charlo the tune-up he wants while setting him up for serious contenders. However, if Jarvis manages to hang around or steal rounds late, everyone will see that Charlo has lost a step. Thurman barely needed to dip into his old toolbox to erase Jarvis, setting a clear bar for what Charlo must do.

Jarvis is custom-made for the showcase. He is an aggressive puncher with zero defense against elite competition, which makes him the perfect target to get starched inside three or four rounds. Once Jermell produces a highlight-reel knockout, his team can blast the clip across social media, erase the memory of the toothless Canelo performance, and sell the illusion that the old, ferocious Charlo is fully back.

From there, the real target board is tiny. If Tszyu beats Lara, an Australia stadium showdown between Tszyu and Charlo carries built-in promotional heat from their canceled 2023 meeting, and Main Event/No Limit Boxing will back up an armored truck full of cash to stage it.

If Tszyu falls through, Ennis is the next logical target. Boots has been hunting for an established, marquee American name to build a pay-per-view around, and Charlo offers name value without the lethal threat of an active prime champion. Beyond those two, nobody in or around 154 to 160 moves the needle financially to justify the risk.

Jermell wants the reward without running the gauntlet against young, hungry killers. Knocking out Jarvis is simply the paid audition to secure the bag.

Sports.title: IBF Reorders Lindolfo Delgado vs. Arthur Biyarslanov Talks
Sports.content:
The IBF made the correct call by keeping Lindolfo Delgado in contention for its vacant 140-pound championship after his withdrawal from the Riyadh event. Following a report from Darshan Desai, the sanctioning body ordered Delgado and Arthur Biyarslanov to reopen negotiations. While Biyarslanov certainly earned quicker clarity on the status of his bout, stripping Delgado of his title shot would have been an excessive penalty for prioritizing safety and preparation.

Delgado (24-0, 16 KOs) and Biyarslanov (21-0, 17 KOs) had been scheduled to meet on the Canelo Alvarez vs. Christian Mbilli undercard. Biyarslanov traveled to Saudi Arabia as planned. Delgado remained behind after his trainer, Robert Garcia, cited regional missile threats alongside a grueling travel schedule. Under that proposed itinerary, Delgado would have had barely two days on the ground to overcome jet lag and shed final pounds.

Biyarslanov voiced valid frustration after enduring twelve weeks of camp away from home, followed by seven days of silence in Riyadh. He put in the work, made the flight, and reasonably expected direct word on whether the contest remained intact. Delgado’s camp owed him that basic communication while sorting out logistical hurdles.

Still, traveling to Riyadh is not the same as arriving with proper runway to contest a world championship. Biyarslanov got into town early and settled into fight week. Garcia faced a delayed flight plan, extended ground travel, and a dangerously compressed weight cut. Just because one camp navigated the journey without incident does not invalidate the other side’s athletic and safety concerns.

Now, the ruling brings the two undefeated contenders back to the negotiating table for the title Richardson Hitchins vacated upon moving to 147 pounds. What remains is securing a firm location and date. Biyarslanov has already invested a full training camp and traveled across the globe. Before he launches another grueling camp, he deserves concrete details on where and when this matchup will actually happen.

Ghana News.title: School is your biggest networking opportunity; make the most of it – MC Kabutey
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaian event host MC Kabutey has urged students to look beyond academic work and take advantage of the relationships and experiences available to them while in school, saying these could open doors to opportunities later in life.

Speaking on The Career Trail Season 4 on Joy Learning TV and Joy News, he encouraged young people to meet new people, explore unfamiliar interests and make themselves known within their school communities.

Sharing his experience at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), he recalled deciding to spend his first year exploring the different activities and communities on campus.

One of his discoveries was the Campus Christian Family (CCF), where students from different academic backgrounds came together to stage drama performances based on Bible stories before Sunday sermons.

He said he was fascinated by the acting, costumes and creativity that went into the productions, which inspired him to join the Communication Arts Department (CAD) when he returned for his second semester.

“That was the beginning of my theatre, acting and emceeing life. I discovered theatre, I discovered acting. And I just did it for fun because I just loved it, I was just excited about it,” he recounted.

His involvement in the department also introduced him to people who would later occupy significant positions in their respective fields.

Among them was the current Minister of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Samuel Nartey George, who was his colleague in the university's mass drama group.

“Somebody like Honourable Samuel George was my colleague in mass drama. He was technical director, I was drama director. Today he's a Minister of Communications, he's a Member of Parliament,” he said.

MC Kabutey also recounted how his interest in exploring new experiences led him to salsa dancing while at KNUST.

Although some members of the Christian community had reservations about the dance style, he said he was curious to learn it and eventually joined a salsa group at Independence Hall.

He continued dancing at the Aviation Social Centre after leaving university, where he met people including Chatterhouse Public Relations Officer, Robert Klah.

He said these experiences showed him how participating in activities outside the classroom could introduce young people to new communities and relationships they might never have encountered otherwise.

He also argued that simply knowing a prominent person does not necessarily translate into opportunities, but a relationship in which that person knows you and recognises your value could make a difference.

“Who you know is a good thing. If you know a big person, if you know an influential person, it's a good thing. But do you know what is even better than whom you know? It's who knows you,” he said.

“As you and I sit here, we know President Mahama, right? What has your knowing President Mahama done for your life? No. But the day President Mahama gets to know you like the way he knows me; that is the big deal. You know I was honored to host his 30th wedding anniversary and to host a few state events. He knows me and I know him,” he added.

Mc Kabutey urged students to see their time in secondary school and university as an important opportunity to build lasting relationships.

“The university, the secondary school, is the biggest, is your final mass congregation space you will ever be in. For the rest of your life, you will likely never, ever be confined in a space that has that many people at the same time,” he echoed.
