World.title: World Bank Says Liberia’s Economy Is Growing, But Extreme Poverty Is Rising
World.content:
Monrovia – The World Bank has released a report that detailed how mining-led growth is not creating enough jobs, and that the country is wallowing into extreme poverty

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The Bank says Liberia’s economy is growing faster, but most citizens are not feeling the benefits, stating that extreme poverty has edged up even as national output expands.



At the launch of the seventh Liberia Economic Update, World Bank Country Manager Georgia Wallen described this as the “paradox at the heart of this report”: the economy is growing, yet more people are struggling to meet basic needs.

Delivering the report, she began with the good news: Real GDP growth rose to an estimated 5.1 percent in 2025, up from 4 percent the year before. Inflation was contained, and the fiscal deficit narrowed to 2.1 percent of GDP.

Madam Wallen credited the government’s and the Central Bank’s “disciplined macroeconomic management,” which she said “deserves recognition.”

The economy has also held up against external shocks. Conflict and disruptions at maritime choke points have unsettled global energy markets and pushed up fuel prices, affecting import-dependent countries like Liberia in early 2026.

Policymakers, she noted, are moving swiftly to contain the risks while maintaining prudent policies.

Even so, extreme poverty is estimated to have climbed from 34.6 percent to 36.1 percent over the past two years. Wallen said this reflects the nature of recent growth, which has come largely from mining, a capital-intensive sector that generates few jobs and offers limited opportunities for local businesses.

According to the report, agriculture, manufacturing and small-scale services, where most Liberians earn their living, have lagged. It states that about 78 percent of workers are in vulnerable informal employment, while nine in ten firms are small or micro enterprises.

“What will it take?” Wallen asked, pointing to farmers facing high transport costs, traders running generators because electricity is unreliable, and entrepreneurs struggling with taxes.

This edition focuses on state-owned enterprises (SOEs), which provide electricity, water, port and fuel services. These services shape business costs and determine whether households have light at night. They also carry significant fiscal risks for the national budget.

The report finds that policymakers cannot see the full portfolio. Many entities do not submit financial reports, while most existing audits are delayed. Wallen called the creation of the State-Owned Enterprises Authority of Liberia (SEAL) “a significant and positive step.”

SOEs alone do not explain the jobs challenge, she indicated, but better information and accountability are practical starting points. Most recommended steps can be taken under existing law.

The report also highlights two trade-offs. The government achieved fiscal consolidation partly by cutting capital spending, which fell from 8.5 percent of GDP. The World Bank Country Chief warned that this approach has limits, since roads, electricity and other infrastructure are essential to Liberia’s growth.

And with iron ore and rubber accounting for more than 90 percent of exports, public finances remain exposed whenever global prices weaken.

Macroeconomic stability is the central foundation, she furthered, and “now is the time to use that foundation to take off.”

The choices ahead, she asserted, concern the quality of public investment, services and information as much as the quantity of growth. Government cannot do it alone; the private sector, civil society and development partners all have a role.

Presenting Chapter Two, “Beyond Growth: Addressing Structural Constraints to Job-Rich Growth in Liberia,” World Bank Senior Public Sector Specialist Bonnie Ann Siroris reveals that the government lacks the reliable information needed to assess SOE performance, fiscal exposure and value for money.

“Oversight covers less than half of the operational portfolio. Over six years, financial information was submitted for only 83 of 276 potential entity-years, while 25 of the 46 entities operating through 2025 never submitted a single return. Reporting standards also vary.”

Although the PFM Act requires International Financial Reporting Standards, entities use a mix of IFRS, public sector standards and U.S. GAAP, while some have no defined accounting basis. That, Siroris told the gathering, can make aggregated figures “very misleading.”

Audits tell a similar story. Seventeen operational entities have completed at least one audit since FY19, and 29 more are underway. Only four audits across all SOEs received unqualified opinions, while all 10 available compliance audits were adverse. Where figures could be compared, 40 percent differed by more than 5 percent between audit reports and Bureau of State Enterprises or SEAL data. The General Auditing Commission has pledged to clear its backlog by June 2028.

The SEAL Act was signed in February 2026, and the former Bureau of State Enterprises is transitioning into the new body.

But oversight is only part of the solution, Siroris noted, because boards must also fulfill their responsibilities.

A 2023 sample showed uneven attendance, and there is no portfolio-wide data on directors’ qualifications, interests or compensation. She recommended a director register, conflict-of-interest declarations, board induction and basic governance records.

The 19 reporting entities show an adjusted surplus of about $28 million for FY24, but three account for roughly $47.4 million of that total. The other 16 posted a combined deficit of about $19.4 million. The largest surplus, at NASSCORP’s core, reflects pension and investment accumulation, not distributable profit.

Those results include $15.1 million in government subsidies and $16.7 million in grants from development partners. Without them, the portfolio would record a loss of about $2.7 million.

At the end of 2025, the 19 entities reported about $815.4 million in liabilities. SOE loans on-lent or guaranteed by the government stood at about $423.3 million, with the Liberia Electricity Corporation (LEC) accounting for roughly 77 percent. Even these figures are incomplete, as there is no reconciled account of arrears, unpaid government bills, supplier claims or court judgments.

LEC’s own revenue rose substantially between FY22 and FY24, but its earnings were positive only when grant income was included, much of it non-cash. It received adverse audit opinions through FY23 and is owed about $34 million, roughly $30.8 million of which is owed by government bodies.

Siroris cautioned against interpreting a subsidy as evidence of poor performance, since it may finance a legitimate public service obligation.

By the end of FY27, the report calls for classifying the portfolio, creating verified entity and director registers, introducing a common reporting template and directing audit resources to the five highest-risk entities. By June 2028, it wants the government’s full fiscal relationship with LEC, the National Port Authority and the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company reconciled.

“Stronger SOE governance will not automatically reduce electricity costs, improve services, or create jobs,” Siroris said. Instead, it creates the conditions to identify underperformance, diagnose its causes, assign corrective action and track results.

The real task, she said, is not whether every SOE turns a profit, but whether the government, the legislature and the public can determine what each entity costs, delivers and risks, and whether the portfolio offers value for money.

World.title: Liberia: From Extraction to Eco-Prosperity, What Liberia Can Learn from Anji, China’s Bamboo Revolution
World.content:
Monrovia–Liberia’s environmental future will depend on choices that go beyond one focused. The country must determine how to manage its forests, wetlands, rivers, and agricultural landscapes while expanding employment, improving public health, and creating opportunities for rural communities.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Anji County China is one area that offers evidence that ecological protection and economic development can reinforce one another when conservation is supported by investment, effective institutions, market access, and locally relevant industries.



This President Xi Xiapin’s concept in his speech at 2020 at the 75th UN General Assembly at the United Nations on Carbon Nutrality, where following that, he launch3d an initiatie of using bamboo as a substitute for plastic.

A policy was also issued on Octover 15, 2026, by the Chinese Government, which prevented the production of plastic takeaway containers for food or shopping bags in China. This is intended to address some global problems such as Climate Change, plastic polution and other environmental problems.

With approximately 10 billion tons of plastics being produced by the world and only 10 percent being used properly and efficiently and recycling plastic remains costly. China believed that using bamboo as a substitute for plastic is an answer for the world since bamboo is totally biodegradable.

What if Liberia’s forests, rivers, wetlands ,and other natural resources could become a stronger source of jobs, healthier communities, and sustainable income for the people who depend on them? That concern is gaining relevance following a visit by Liberian media representatives to Anji County in eastern China, during a two-week media seminar, where bamboo processing, ecological conservation, sustainable agriculture, and rural tourism have helped reshape the local economy.

For Liberia, a country endowed with extensive tropical forests, freshwater systems, mangroves, and other valuable ecosystems, Anji offers a development lesson, protecting nature need not come at the expense of economic growth. Under the right conditions, conservation can become a foundation for prosperity. But translating that experience into reality will require more than admiration for China’s achievements.

Financing, infrastructure, technical capacity, environmental, enforcement, and community ownership will determine whether Liberia can turn its natural resources into sustainable livelihoods.

Liberian Health and environmental science researcher and former Chairman of the Public Health Department at the University of Liberia, Forkpah Pewee and Dr. Anthony Saah Tengbh, Environmental Scientist and Academic Chairman, Department of Environmental Studies and Climate Change at the University of Liberia say elements of the Anji model could work in Liberia if they are adapted to local conditions and supported by practical investments.

However, the Environmental Protection Agency’s position remains unclear. FrontPage Africa sought comments from EPA Executive Director Dr. Emmanuel King Urey Yarkpawolo on the lessons Liberia could draw from Anji and the role environmental regulation could play in developing sustainable enterprises.

He had not responded by the time of publication. His nonresponse does not establish opposition to the approach but leaves unanswered questions about how the country’s environmental regulator would support, oversee, and measure such initiatives.

Anji’s transformation, when conservation becomes an economic strategy. Located in Zhejiang Province, Anji County covers approximately 1,886 square kilometers and has a population of roughly 470,000. It is known for its bamboo forests, white tea, and rural landscapes.

The county was not always the green destination it is today. During the 1980s and 1990s, industrial activities, including quarrying, paper production, and other pollution-intensive operations, contributed to environmental degradation. In Yucun Village, authorities subsequently moved away from environmentally damaging activities and pursued alternative livelihoods, including tourism and other businesses linked to the natural environment.

The transition required difficult economic adjustments, as closing polluting industries initially affected some incomes. Over time, Anji increasingly linked ecological conservation with bamboo processing, agriculture, and tourism.

A 2022 peer-reviewed study of the county’s ecological conservation policies found that protected areas experienced less expansion of construction and agricultural land than the study’s modeled alternative scenario.

The areas accounted for approximately 39 percent of the county’s land but more than 80 percent of its estimated ecosystem-service value in 2015. The findings support the importance of protecting ecologically valuable landscapes, although they do not establish that conservation alone caused all of Anji’s subsequent economic growth. For Liberia, the lesson is that a forest can provide more than raw materials. Properly managed, it can also protect water sources, sustain biodiversity, support livelihoods, and attract visitors. Beyond bamboo poles, Building an industry

One of Anji’s most important achievements is its ability to turn bamboo from raw material into a broad range of finished products. The resource supports manufacturing activities involving furniture, flooring, household utensils, kitchenware, packaging, building materials, and other goods.

Bamboo shoots are also used as food, while processing innovations create additional uses for plant residues. According to figures reported by China’s State Council Information Office in June 2025, Anji’s bamboo industry recorded an output value of 19.2 billion yuan in 2024, an increase of 7 percent over the previous year.

The report also said bamboo-related income benefited more than 51,000 farming households, with average additional household earnings of 6,500 yuan that year. These figures illustrate the scale of an established Chinese industry, not an earnings forecast for Liberia.

Anji’s advantage lies in the connections between growers, processors, manufacturers, traders and customers. Each stage creates opportunities for employment and income. Liberia could adapt that principle by processing suitable natural resources locally instead of relying predominantly on raw-material sales.

Liberia’s untapped bamboo wealth, an industry waiting to grow

Liberia is not starting from zero. The country possesses bamboo and rattan resources that could support furniture-making, household products, handicrafts, selected construction materials, and other manufactured goods.

Previous technical-assistance programs have also sought to develop local skills in bamboo processing. A World Bank report on Liberia’s forest sector identified bamboo and rattan as resources with considerable commercialization potential. It highlighted limited access to processing equipment and technical skills, including the ability to split, slive, and weave bamboo as an obstacle to developing the industry.

These constraints help explain why the existence of a resource does not automatically translate into jobs and business growth. With appropriate training, equipment, and market access,

Liberian entrepreneurs could explore making chairs, tables, beds, shelves, mats, window blinds, household utensils, decorative products, and selected packaging materials. Some bamboo species also produce edible shoots, while processing residues may have other uses where technical and environmental assessments establish their viability.

These are potential opportunities, not guaranteed profitable ventures. Each product would require an assessment of raw-material supply, production costs, quality standards, customer demand, and competition from imports.

Liberia has already received bamboo-related technical assistance from China. According to a Chinese government account, a bamboo and rattan weaving program began in 2007, alongside training in vegetable production and biogas technology.

AidData’s project record reports that 55 trainees had learned to make basic household products by 2008 and that approximately 900 people had received training through the program by 2022.

Those figures document training activities but do not establish how many participants subsequently operated successful businesses. In August 2025, Liberia’s Ministry of Youth and Sports also announced the groundbreaking for a China-supported technical-assistance training facility at the Samuel Kanyon Doe Sports Complex.

World.title: Liberia: EPA Puts Gender at the Center of Climate Action, Orders Every Department to Deliver
World.content:
Opening his address, Dr. Yarkpawolo argued that environmental work cannot be separated from the people it is meant to serve. The theme of the launch, he said, reflects the kind of institution and country Liberia is trying to build

MONROVIA — The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has turned the lens on itself, unveiling its first Gender Policy and a refreshed national Climate Change Gender Action Plan, and warning its own managers that the commitments must show up in everyday decisions rather than gather dust on shelves.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Executive Director Dr. Emmanuel K. Urey Yarkpawolo made the declaration on Tuesday at the Corina Hotel in Sinkor, where the two documents were launched under the theme “Advancing Gender Equality for Inclusive Climate Resilience in Liberia.”



Gender, Children and Social Protection Minister Gbeme Horace-Kollie joined government officials, development partners, and representatives of civil society, women’s and youth groups, and persons with disabilities at the event.

“A matter of people’s lives”

Opening his address, Dr. Yarkpawolo argued that environmental work cannot be separated from the people it is meant to serve. The theme of the launch, he said, reflects the kind of institution and country Liberia is trying to build.

He painted a picture of those at the heart of the agenda: a woman farming to feed her family, a young person looking for work, and a person with a disability who deserves an equal chance to contribute. Policies, he said, must recognize their circumstances and open doors for them to take part.

Findings that shaped the policy

The EPA’s first Gender Policy did not emerge in a vacuum. According to the Executive Director, it was shaped by an institutional gender assessment, consultations with staff and stakeholders, and a review of existing policies.

The assessment credited the Agency with progress but also exposed a gap: gender considerations had not yet been woven fully into the Agency’s work.

To address that, the policy sets out practical guidance on hiring and promotion, training, leadership, workplace culture and accountability. It also tackles discrimination and sexual harassment head-on. Dr. Yarkpawolo said every employee should be able to grow professionally in a workplace that protects dignity and safety.

Linking gender to national climate goals

The second document, the updated Climate Change Gender Action Plan, takes forward an earlier plan. It was developed through research, stakeholder consultations and training, with support from UN Women, and it ties gender equality to Liberia’s national climate pledges under NDC 3.0.

The EPA’s first Gender Policy did not emerge in a vacuum. According to the Executive Director, it was shaped by an institutional gender assessment, consultations with staff and stakeholders, and a review of existing policies

The plan focuses on eight sectors: agriculture and food security, coasts and fisheries, forestry, health, water and sanitation, waste, energy, and transportation.

Its core argument, the EPA chief explained, is that climate change does not hit everyone equally. Differences in access to land, finance, information and decision-making mean some people are far more exposed than others. He pointed to a woman farmer who may read shifting rainfall patterns better than most, yet lacks the means to adapt. Climate programmes, he said, should tap such knowledge while removing the obstacles she faces.

Early steps already taken

Dr. Yarkpawolo told the audience the Agency is not starting from zero. Among the steps already taken, he said, is the elevation of the gender function to senior management, ensuring it has a stronger voice where institutional decisions are made.

The Agency has also invested in women’s skills, including international training for its women environmental inspectors. Stronger skills, he said, improve the Agency’s ability to monitor environmental conditions and protect communities.

He singled out Madam Madrid Chuka Piah, head of the EPA’s radiation laboratory, as proof of what women are contributing in specialized scientific roles.

The Agency has likewise hired persons with disabilities, whom he said strengthen the institution. Even so, he acknowledged the work is unfinished, saying the EPA must keep adapting its workplace so they can participate fully.

Tough questions ahead

With the documents now launched, the Executive Director shifted from planning to performance. The Gender and Climate Change Baseline Assessment process, he said, helped pinpoint gaps; implementation must now close them, measure progress and flag where more action is needed.

He listed the questions that will guide that scrutiny. Are women benefiting from training and promotion? Can persons with disabilities participate in a meaningful way? Are climate projects reaching those facing the steepest barriers? Do budgets actually back the promises made?

No department left out

Dr. Yarkpawolo was unambiguous about who carries the load. He expects every department to take responsibility for implementation. The Gender Unit will guide and coordinate, but managers across the Agency must bring these commitments into their daily decision-making.

Beyond the EPA’s walls, he called for cooperation across government and sustained partnership with civil society, communities and development partners. Clear responsibilities, sufficient resources and regular monitoring, he said, will determine whether the policies succeed.

The Executive Director thanked Gender Coordinator Madam Grace Biah and her team, the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, technical experts, and all others who contributed. He reserved special appreciation for UN Women for backing the update of the Climate Change Gender Action Plan.

World.title: Lwandamina names 30 for Burundi  AFCON qualifier
World.content:
Chipolopolo interim coach George ‘Chicken’ Lwandamina has named a 30-member provisional squad for Zambia’s back-to-back Group I qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations against Burundi.

The squad, announced by the Football Association of Zambia (FAZ), is a blend of foreign-based players and top-performing local stars.

In-form Zesco United striker Kennedy Musonda, fit-again Red Arrows defender Zephaniah Phiri and red-hot Red Arrows airman Ackim Mumba headline the local call-ups.

Portugal-based midfielder Chanka Zimba returns to the national fold after finding a new base, while Gift Mphande has also earned a look-in from the technical bench.

The team will set up camp in Ndola on Thursday, with foreign-based players expected to join when the FIFA international window opens on 9 November.

Lwandamina is expected to trim the provisional squad to 26 for the final stages of preparation.

Zambia will host Burundi on Friday, 13 November at the Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola, before travelling to Bujumbura for the return fixture four days later on 17 November.

The double-header is crucial for Zambia’s qualification hopes. Algeria lead Group I with four points, with Zambia second on three points. Togo are third, also on three points, while Burundi are bottom with one point after two rounds of matches.

Victory in both legs would put Chipolopolo in a commanding position to qualify for the AFCON PAMOJA 2027, which will be jointly hosted by Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania from 19 June to 17 July 2027.

Lwandamina, who took over on an interim basis, will be looking to build momentum and stability in the squad as Zambia push for a return to Africa’s biggest stage.

Some players have been excluded from this assignment as they are part of U23 squad playing Burkina Faso on 11 November in Ouagadougou and Heroes four days later.

World.title: Mambwe Maternity Annex renovated
World.content:
The Maternity Annex at Nsefu Clinic in Mambwe District in Eastern Province that was recently renovated by Painted Dogs Lagoons, at a cost of about K350, 000

has officially been handed over to the community.

The maternity annex, which was in a deplorable state, has now been given a new face-lift to provide a safe and dignified environment for mothers in the chiefdom to access maternal health services.

Speaking during the handover ceremony, Director of Health Services, Luwi Kawanda thanked His Royal Highness Senior Chief Nsefu for engaging Painted Dogs Lagoons to undertake the renovations.

Dr Kawanda also expressed gratitude to the Director of Painted Dogs Lagoons for renovating the facility.

“The improvements made to the infrastructure will ensure that mothers in the chiefdom access maternal health services in a safe environment,” she noted.

She revealed that Nsefu Clinic serves a catchment population of more than 10,000 people, hence the need for quality infrastructure.

Meanwhile, Nsefu Ward Councillor, Kalima Chibwana said he was pleased with the works done by cooperating partners and commended the community for participating in ensuring that the works were completed on time.

Mr Chibwana said the facility will serve the people in the ward and urged mothers to preserve the facility so that it continues to benefit them.

Meanwhile, Painted Dogs Lagoons Director, Peter Woeste thanked Senior Chief Nsefu for creating an enabling environment for them to do business in the chiefdom.

Mr Woeste said he was very happy to help in renovating the annex for the benefit of the community where they are doing business.

He revealed that the renovations cost about 350 thousand Kwacha.

“Our Organization also supports schools in the area by providing textbooks and other learning materials,” he said.

And Senior Chief Nsefu who was represented by his Personal Secretary, John Mbewe commended Painted Dogs Lagoons for the intervention, while calling for more support.

He requested that the main clinic building also be worked on and that staff houses are needed to enhance service delivery to the community.

He called on the Clinic Administration to ensure the facility is well taken care of so that community members receive the intended services in a timely manner.

Senior Chief Nsefu also urged people in his chiefdom to normalise taking expectant mothers to the clinic for safe deliveries.

“For the Community Resource Board (CRB), I urge you to identify areas that need support so that in future, cooperating partners doing business in the Chiefdom can help,” he said.

World.title: Mkushi man gets 3 years imprisonment for theft
World.content:
A 26-year-old man has been sentenced to three years’ imprisonment with hard labour for breaking into a shop and stealing property worth K13,600.

Vincent Mwape was convicted of break-in and theft contrary to Section 303 of the Penal Code, Chapter 87 of the Laws of Zambia.

Particulars of the offence are that Mwape, on dates unknown but between October 26, 2026 and October 27, 2026 broke into a shop belonging to businessman, Innocent Kapuka with intent to steal and stole 35 T-shirts, 16 pairs of trousers and two black speakers valued at K13,600.

The court heard that only property worth K2, 850 was recovered, leaving the complainant with a substantial loss.

In mitigation, Mwape asked the court for mercy and leniency, stating that he had a three-year-old child and a wife who depended on him.

And in passing the sentence, Magistrate Felix Lukonde, said Mwape should have considered his family before engaging in criminal activities.

“You should have considered your child before committing this crime. Out of the property stolen, only a small amount was recovered, leaving the complainant with a huge loss while you benefited,” he said.

Magistrate Lukonde described the offence as a felony, punishable by up to seven years’ imprisonment, adding that break-ins and theft were prevalent in the district.

“People have lost their hard-earned property at the hands of people like you. Therefore, you should go to jail so that you learn to stay clear of crime,” he added.

The magistrate, however, took into account that Mwape was a first offender and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment with hard labour.

World.title: Zambia’s Moody upgrade to strengthen businesses
World.content:
Zambia has strengthened its standing in the international business and investment community, following Moody’s decision to upgrade the country’s sovereign credit rating from Caa2 to Caa1, with a positive outlook.

Ministry of Information and Media Director Spokesperson, Henry Kapata, says Moody’s is one of the world’s leading credit rating agencies.

Mr Kapata says the agency assesses how likely countries and companies are to achieve their debt obligations.

He has told the media business news that investors, lenders and financial institutions use these assessments when deciding where to invest, lend money and do business.

Mr Kapata noted that the upgrade means Moody’s now considers Zambia a relatively stronger credit proposition than it did under the previous rating.

“Caa1 remains within the high-risk category, but the improvement signals progress in the country’s credit standing,” said Mr Kapata.

He notes that for Zambia, the development strengthens the country’s efforts to attract investment, build confidence among international partners and improve access to financing.

Mr Kapata observes that as investment grows, businesses can expand, industries can increase production, farmers can find larger markets and more people can access employment opportunities.

He adds that this is the practical value of strengthening the country’s economic standing, saying investment in energy, agriculture, mining, manufacturing and infrastructure can support production, create business opportunities and expand economic activity across the country.

The development comes as Zambia prepares to present the 2027 National Budget on 6 November, 2026, while the International Monetary Fund’s proposed US$1.472 billion programme awaits consideration by its Executive Board.

President Hakainde Hichilema has consistently positioned Zambia as open for business, calling for accelerated economic growth through investment and trade.

A stronger credit assessment supports that ambition by improving how international lenders and investors view the country.

World.title: Nzovu lauds adoption of Quantity Surveyors’ Standard Method of Measurement
World.content:
Government says Zambia has successfully adopted the African Association of Quantity Surveyors’ Standard Method of Measurement (SMM), making it the first country to implement the framework.

Minister of Infrastructure and Urban Development, Collins Nzovu, says the development marks a significant milestone for the quantity surveying profession, noting that Zambia had been using measurement standards dating back to 1973.

Mr Nzovu made the remarks in a speech read for him by the Ministry’s Permanent Secretary, Albert Malama, during the Zambia Institute of Quantity Surveyors 2026 Annual Conference in Lusaka today.

Mr Nzovu said the adoption of the new standards will help strengthen professional practice and improve the delivery of infrastructure projects.

He urged the government institutions, mining companies and private investors to engage quantity surveyors from the early stages of project planning to ensure cost efficiency, accountability and value for money.

The Minister noted that quantity surveyors play a critical role in preparing reliable project cost estimates, managing contracts and ensuring that infrastructure projects are delivered within budget and on schedule.

He has also called for stronger collaboration between government, industry players and professional institutions to build capacity in commercial management, digital technology, contract administration and sustainability.

Zambia Institute of Quantity Surveyors President, Timothy Musole, has called for early involvement of quantity surveyors in infrastructure, mining and energy projects to enhance value for money and ensure effective financial management.

Mr Musole says quantity surveyors should be engaged from the investment decision-making stage through construction, operation and maintenance to ensure projects are delivered within budget and provide lasting benefits.

And African Association of Quantity Surveyors (AAQS) President, Victor Odongo, called on African governments to ensure quantity surveyors are actively involved in the planning, budgeting and implementation of major infrastructure projects.

Mr Odongo indicated that involving quantity surveyors in the early stages of project development will help ensure realistic budgeting, prevent cost overruns and promote timely completion of infrastructure projects.

World.title: Govt. steps up investment in tourism infrastructure
World.content:
Government is stepping up investment in tourism infrastructure, including accommodation facilities, roads and access to tourist attractions, as the country targets five million international tourist arrivals annually by 2031.

The investment is aimed at ensuring that the country’s tourism infrastructure can accommodate the anticipated increase in international tourists, while improving the experience of both local and foreign tourists.

Ministry of Tourism Public Relations Officer, Nelly Banda, says Government is prioritising infrastructure development in emerging tourism destinations as well as improving facilities in established tourism circuits.

In an interview with the media in Lusaka, Ms Banda said one of the major interventions is the US$100 million World Bank-supported Green, Resilient and Transformational Tourism Development Project (GREAT-TDP), which is supporting infrastructure development in Nsumbu, Liuwa Plains and the source of the Zambezi River.

She also hinted that Government has launched the rehabilitation and upgrading of approximately 8.31 kilometres of selected roads in Livingstone to improve accessibility and the visitor experience.

Ms Banda added that Government is further encouraging private sector investment in hotels, lodges and conference facilities to expand accommodation capacity.

She noted that the ministry is also prioritising stronger air connectivity and improved access to tourist attractions to ensure that transport and accommodation capacity grow alongside visitor demand.

Meanwhile, Ms Banda stressed that the expansion of visa-free entry to nationals from 167 countries is another measure aimed at making Zambia more accessible and affordable to international tourists.

She said Government is also working with the private sector through the Zambia Tourism Agency to connect local tourism businesses with international buyers and travel partners.

World.title: Nkana eye top spot as they host Kansanshi
World.content:
Nkana have a golden chance to go top of Stream A – even if only for 24 hours – when they host Kansanshi Dynamos at Nkana Stadium in Wusakile on Wednesday afternoon.

Kalampa sit fourth with 10 points, just two points behind leaders Konkola Blades, who only play on Thursday. A win over Kansanshi will take Nkana to the summit.

Kansanshi are sixth with five points from five matches and are desperate to start picking up points away from home.

Nkana assistant coach Donashano Malama says the team is ready, with focus on recovery and freshness after the goalless Kitwe Derby against Power Dynamos.

“The preparations have gone well so far. We prioritised the recovery and freshness of the players. We also took some time to analyse, reflect and identify areas that needed to improve. I can confidently say that we are ready for tomorrow’s game,” Malama told Nkana FC Media.

Nkana remain unbeaten at home this season, having beaten Makeni All Stars and Nchanga Rangers in Wusakile.

“The team is very motivated, knowing that we haven’t dropped points at home. Going into tomorrow’s game, the players are equally motivated, coming from the performance in the derby,” Malama added.

Kansanshi coach Dennis Makinka is demanding more gusto from his players on the road.

“We are preparing the boys to begin picking results from away games. We are telling the boys to replicate the same energy shown in home matches when we play away,” Makinka said.

“Nkana will be playing at home, so we need to be cautious and manage their quickie frontline. We will be ready for the match.”

Meanwhile, Zanaco are hosting FC Muza in the other midweek Stream A match.

In Stream B, Red Arrows are at home to Nkwazi in Lusaka derby as Kabwe Warriors host Roan United in Kabwe.

World.title: Mundubile, Makebi Zulu to learn tomorrow where sedition case will be tried
World.content:
The Lusaka High Court sitting in Solwezi will tomorrow decide whether opposition leaders Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu should stand trial for sedition in Solwezi or have their case moved to Lusaka. Judge Edward Musona has set the ruling for Thursday, 5 November, at 14:00 hours. The date was fixed on Tuesday when the matter came up in chambers for a possible ruling. Instead, the judge directed both sides to file written arguments first. The State was given until 12:00 hours on Tuesday, while the defence has until 14:00 hours today.

Mr Mundubile, who was the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) presidential candidate in the 13 August elections, and his running mate Mr Zulu each face charges of seditious practices under Section 57 of the Penal Code. The State alleges that the two published material through livestreams on their respective Facebook pages. In those broadcasts, it is alleged, they claimed that their parallel voter tabulation showed they had won the presidential election. Earlier court proceedings heard that Mr Zulu is accused of posting that Mr Mundubile would address the nation and urging the public to remain on standby. Neither has taken plea since the matter opened in Solwezi in September.

The jurisdiction fight began on 5 October, when the defence objected to the case being heard in Solwezi. The lawyers argued that the indictment itself places the alleged offences in Lusaka, where the two were also apprehended. They relied on Section 75 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which requires criminal cases to be tried in the district where the offence was committed. They also told the court that no evidence links the alleged offences to Solwezi and that holding the trial there would make it harder to reach their witnesses. Director of Public Prosecutions Gilbert Phiri, who prosecuted the matter personally, countered that where it is uncertain where an offence was committed, proceedings may be brought in any jurisdiction where the matter properly falls.

On 13 October, Solwezi Principal Resident Magistrate Mambwe Mukonde declined to rule on the question. She found that her court lacked the authority to either try the case or transfer it to another court of equal status. She referred the matter to the High Court for determination. That referral is what brought Judge Musona to Solwezi this week.

Speaking to journalists after Tuesday’s proceedings, National Prosecution Authority Chief State Advocate Chali Hambayi said both parties had been given the chance to argue for and against the application. She said the State would file within the time allowed.

“As the State we have indicated that we shall file the motions by 12:00 hours today and the defence has also been accorded chance to file their submissions on Wednesday 14:00 hours, the learned High Court will make its ruling on Thursday, 14:00 hours,” Ms Hambayi said.

Defence lawyer Chifumu Banda, State Counsel, welcomed the timetable. He said the defence had agreed with the court’s directive and that a fixed date would bring an end to weeks of uncertainty over where the substantive case will proceed.

“This is good because we now know when the pending issue of jurisdiction will finally be determined by the court,” Mr Banda said.

The Solwezi case has already disrupted other proceedings in Lusaka. On Tuesday, the trial of Lusaka Archbishop Alick Banda, who is charged with possessing a Toyota Hilux suspected to have been unlawfully obtained, failed to start before Resident Magistrate Mwandu Nakazwe. Deputy Chief State Advocate Mercy Lungu told the court that the prosecution team was in Solwezi on the Mundubile matter. The defence, led by State Counsel John Sangwa, did not oppose an adjournment, and the case was pushed to Friday.

“The notice of hearing in the Solwezi matter was served on the State after dates for this case had already been set,” Ms Lungu said.

The sedition charges are separate from the treason proceedings that followed the post-election security operations against the opposition. The European Union Election Observation Mission, in its final report published on Tuesday, noted that the two were arrested and charged with treason and later sedition. It said the prolonged lack of official information about the arrests and the charges had heightened public anxiety. Tomorrow’s ruling will not decide guilt or innocence. It will settle only where the trial takes place, and therefore how soon plea can finally be taken.

World.title: Govt calls for mine ventilation audit
World.content:
MINES and Mining Development Deputy minister Fred Moyo has called for a baseline study across Zimbabwe’s mining sector to establish whether mines have adequate ventilation personnel and whether the profession is given sufficient priority in organisational structures.

Moyo said the proposed study should cover different classes of mines and establish where ventilation departments are positioned within their management structures.

“I have demanded that they go in and do the baseline study.
