World.title: Zimbabwe’s pig industry emerges as key driver of livestock growth
World.content:
Zimbabwe’s pig industry is recording significant growth, supported by improved genetics, modern production technologies and rising local production.

The sector’s expansion is unfolding within the framework of the Livestock Growth Plan (2021–2025), a national blueprint that prioritises improved breeding, affordable feed, biosecurity and market access across livestock value chains.

In a statement yesterday, Lands, Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Rural Development ministry permanent secretary, Obert Jiri, said the pig value chain was among the country’s fastest-growing livestock sectors, with smallholder farmers increasingly benefiting from improved breeding stock and technologies.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: PP4P champions national development through strategic knowledge exchange with China
World.content:
AS Zimbabwe advances towards its Vision 2030 goal of becoming an empowered upper-middle-income economy, human capital development and industrial modernisation remain critical national priorities.

The Presidential Programme for Professionals (PP4P) is mobilising professional expertise to support these objectives by strengthening leadership, building capacity and bridging the gap between policy and implementation.

Through strategic cooperation with China, PP4P is advancing knowledge exchange in governance, vocational education, technical skills development and industrial transformation.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: D-Day for Hwange, Chinhoyi illegal traders
World.content:
THE Hwange Local Board and the Municipality of Chinhoyi have given illegal traders operating in the two local authorities to cease operations and demolish their structures by Friday or face heavy penalties.

The impending blitz is aimed at restoring order and cleanliness across in urban areas, targets widespread illegal developments, roadside businesses, and vending stalls that have mushroomed at undesignated sites.

The operation is also targeting motor vehicle mechanics operating on public spaces, illegally- parked vehicles, abandoned vehicle shells, and buildings erected without approved municipal plans.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Government orders councils to prioritise workers’ welfare, service delivery
World.content:
Government has ordered all local authorities with outstanding salary arrears to prioritise settling their obligations to employees, or risk restrictions on foreign travel, workshops outside their jurisdictions, and purchase of vehicles for personal use.

The directive, contained in Local Authorities Circular Number 9 of 2026, dated October 20, underscores growing concern over the accumulation of salary arrears running into several months at some local authorities.

Issued by the Ministry of Local Government and Public Works, the circular describes the situation as unacceptable, citing its negative impact on employees’ welfare and livelihoods, staff morale, productivity and the capacity of councils to deliver essential services.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Africa: Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games - Kenya on Top, Madagascar on Podium, Senegal Looks to Future
World.content:
Dakar — African women's rugby made its mark at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games. At the Iba Mar Diop complex, Kenya secured gold after a spectacular final against Australia, while Madagascar took bronze. For Senegal, the host country, this first international experience opens new avenues for the development of the sport among young girls.

African women's rugby has reason to be ambitious. In Dakar, the young Kenyan women delivered one of the standout performances of the Youth Olympic Games' rugby sevens tournament, defeating Australia 17-12 in a final that went to extra time. This victory highlights the growing strength of women's rugby on the continent.

Trailing on the scoreboard, the Kenyan women found the strength to level the score (12-12) at the end of regulation time, before securing the victory with a decisive try in extra time. A hard-fought win, achieved through courage and determination, that rewards the journey of an ambitious team.

"We came here with one goal: to win gold. We came to represent Kenya," said captain Zain Hido, emotional after her team's victory.



Beyond the medal, this victory confirms the ability of young African players to compete with top-level opponents. It also sends an encouraging signal for a sport that seeks to expand its reach and increase its visibility across the continent.

Madagascar confirms its potential

Kenya was not the only African team to distinguish itself. Madagascar also achieved a remarkable performance by winning the bronze medal, confirming the potential of its new generation of players.

The Ladies Makis demonstrated consistency throughout the tournament, conceding only one defeat, against Kenya in the semi-final. This performance rewards their commitment and the efforts they made to reach this level of competition.

"This medal is for us, for our country! It's the first time for us, it's incredible," said Princia Ranaivoson, bursting with joy after this third place.

Behind this result lie weeks of preparation and the sacrifices of young female athletes forced to juggle training, studies and international ambitions.

Their coach, Dina Razafindratsara, praised the commitment of her players, whose journey testifies to the training work undertaken in Madagascar.

This bronze medal represents encouragement for Malagasy women's rugby and underlines the importance of continuing efforts in coaching, training and access to international competitions.

Senegal, a first to prepare the next generation

For Senegal, the tournament ended without a victory, but with important lessons learned. Finishing last in the standings, the Lionesses suffered a defeat against Spain (0-27), highlighting the experience gap that still separates them from some international teams.

But for this young team, the stakes went beyond sporting results. It was primarily about discovering the demands of international competition and gauging the road ahead.

"I'm proud of the girls. Today, the team represented our country well. They fought hard, even though they lacked experience," declared the national coach, Oumar Diop.

This participation is part of a dynamic of development of women's rugby in Senegal, in particular through the Rugby Rising Play program, supported by World Rugby to encourage the practice of this sport among young girls.

According to the coach, several players joined this initiative less than two years ago. Their participation in the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games therefore represented their first experience at the highest international level.

"After the Youth Olympic Games, we will continue the work, keep this team, train it and always try to compete against the best. We still have a lot of work to do," he added.

For Senegalese rugby, the challenge now is to transform this first participation into a real dynamic of development, by multiplying opportunities for competition and consolidating training systems.

An African podium that brings hope for women's rugby

With two African nations on the podium, the Dakar 2026 women's rugby sevens tournament offers an encouraging illustration of the continent's sporting potential.

Close 

Kenya's victory and Madagascar's bronze medal demonstrate the progress made by some federations, while Senegal's participation highlights the challenges still faced by countries where the sport is still developing.

Beyond individual and collective performances, these results highlight the importance of investing in training, technical coaching, and access for young girls to sports infrastructure.

For African federations, the challenge now will be to capitalize on the visibility offered by these Games to strengthen talent identification, support, and competition programs.

In Dakar, young African rugby players will not only have played matches and won medals. They will also have helped to raise the profile of their sport and pave the way for a generation of athletes determined to advance women's rugby on the continent.

The article was translated from French

World.title: Africa: How Many More COPs Before Climate Promises Become Action?
World.content:
A woman wades through floodwaters in Bor, Jonglei State, South Sudan, where communities continue to live with the effects of flooding from previous years as the country prepares for further climate-related shocks.

Every year before COP, the same question surfaces: what is the one thing Africa needs from this summit?

Ahead of COP31, the answer emerging from a World Resources Institute Africa webinar was clear: Africa must move beyond asking what it can receive from global climate negotiations and focus on what it can bring. With geopolitical tensions, energy disruptions and climate shocks exposing vulnerabilities across African economies, speakers argued that the continent must use the summit to advance practical solutions that strengthen energy security, protect food systems and mobilise climate finance.

A reinvented agency

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Olufunso Somorin, Regional Principal Officer for Climate Change and Green Growth at the African Development Bank, said these challenges were interconnected, warning that simultaneous disruptions to energy, food and economic systems could undermine the continent's development gains. He described them as a triangle of reality - when one is hit, the others strain, and when all three are hit, the development gains of recent years are at risk.

"COP of today, it is now a trade forum. It is now a marketplace."

He said that Africa needed to rethink its approach to global climate negotiations and strengthen its position as a partner in shaping climate solutions rather than simply seeking assistance. His answer was what he called a "reinvented agency". Africa, he said, must move "away from this idea of Africa that needs to be helped, to an Africa that needs to be partnered with."

He also questioned the pace of the process itself, asking that after 30 COPs, how many more does it take to get things done?

That means understanding what COP has become. "COP of today, it is now a trade forum. It is now a marketplace. And what you get out of a marketplace is largely based on who you are and what you bring to the marketplace," he said.

Strengthening energy security

Energy security was one of the key issues at COP31, with the prevailing situation of geopolitical tensions and disruptions to the global energy supply underpinning the risks of being dependent on external energy sources. Africa has significant renewable energy potential. However, the challenge remains translating these resources into reliable and affordable electricity that can support economic growth, businesses, and industrial development.

Yasmin Abdulwassie, Senior Manager for Climate in Africa at the Children's Investment Fund Foundation, said high financing costs and limited public budgets remained major obstacles to scaling up renewable energy investments. "The challenge is really translating that potential into affordable, reliable energy that can be replicated and scaled," she said.

She said philanthropy can help by funding project preparation, policy reform and investment pipelines, so that transition pathways are country-led. She pointed to South Africa's Just Energy Transition Partnership. The initiative, she said, initially announced with $8.5 billion, had grown to more than $14 billion, proof that investors back credible country platforms.

She also highlighted Senegal's Renewable Energy Investment Facility as another emerging example of efforts to attract investment and support the country's energy transition. "So that type of catalytic role that philanthropy plays is not just about unlocking finance, but helping countries turn lasting financing possibilities for economic reform," said Abdulwassie.

Somorin said that achieving universal energy access would require stronger partnerships that connect national ambitions with clear financing strategies. He cited Mission 300, which aims to connect 300 million people in sub-Saharan Africa to electricity by 2030, as an example of how shared targets and country-specific strategies can accelerate progress.

He said 37 African countries had developed national energy compacts outlining their strategies for expanding electricity access, helping attract investment from development finance institutions, the World Bank, the African Development Bank and philanthropic organisations. He said the initiative demonstrated the importance of having a collective goal while agreeing on practical steps to achieve it.

"It is a new way of defining partnership where you have a collective goal, but you also have a shared discussion on the how. How do we get there? What do we need to do differently?" he said.

Beyond energy security, COP31 is urged to give greater attention to adaptation, particularly ensuring that climate finance reaches countries and communities most vulnerable to climate change.

Abdulwassie said that the climate summit should move adaptation commitments toward "real, measurable outcomes," particularly in food systems, water and livelihood infrastructure. She set out three priorities. The first is a credible financing pathway. Countries have committed to tripling adaptation finance by 2035, but Abdulwassie said the detail is missing. "How are we going to do it? How will progress be measured?" she asked, adding that these questions need answers at COP31 and at every milestone after it.

The second is better indicators, and here she pointed to the Belém-Addis vision, a two-year process that runs toward COP32 in Ethiopia. Current metrics, she said, tend to count activities, such as how many farmers completed climate-smart agriculture training. She argued the measure should be whether a farmer's livelihood "stays intact or improves despite climate shocks," and that credible results of that kind are what attract further financing.

The third is matching national adaptation plans with investment plans. She cited a Malawi initiative, backed by philanthropy and led by the African Climate Foundation, in which more than 20 of the country's priority adaptation proposals have been matched with potential investors. The aim, she said, is to give adaptation the same investable pipelines that mitigation projects increasingly have.

Closing the adaptation finance gap

The challenge of mobilising climate finance for adaptation was also highlighted by Somorin, who said African countries needed to rethink how adaptation projects are financed and how their economic value is presented to investors.

"Adaptation is very complex," Somorin said, and the sector has made it harder by lumping everything together as "climate action." He said that adaptation remains more difficult to finance than mitigation because projects often lack the clear financial returns that attract private investors.

Put all climate projects in one finance basket, he said, and about nine in ten that emerge would be mitigation projects. They are simply easier to finance and attract capital more readily. Africa also faces a structural handicap. In every other region, he said, private capital drives climate action. Africa is the only place where public money leads.

His first proposed fix is to stop treating the two as separate. "You use mitigation finance to drive adaptation goals," he said. He gave an example of a solar-powered irrigation scheme in a semi-arid region that cuts emissions through clean energy, but it also lets farmers grow and earn all year round, which is an adaptation result. The more deliberately adaptation is built into mitigation projects, he said, the more capital will reach it.

"I argue that you use mitigation finance to drive adaptation goals," he said.

Somorin also called for a change in how investors assess adaptation projects, arguing that their wider economic benefits should be recognised alongside their immediate financial returns.

He said financiers needed to understand the distinction between financial viability and economic viability, particularly where investments generate long-term benefits that may not immediately translate into revenue. Somorin said the task is to help financiers see that the economic value is real and can be monetized, either now or later, as new markets emerge to turn it into financial returns.

Africa has documented 11 financial instruments for mitigation projects but, at best, three for adaptation. Expanding these financing options, he said, would let more resources flow and would bring non-traditional investors into the adaptation space.

Philanthropy can help unlock larger investments

While development finance institutions have a role in mobilising investment for climate action, Abdulwassie said philanthropic capital could help address some of the structural barriers preventing African countries from accessing climate finance. "Philanthropy alone, we know, cannot close that gap," she said. However, she identified three areas where it could have a catalytic impact: strengthening national institutions, developing country-led investment platforms, and building stronger partnerships across the climate finance ecosystem.

The first is institutional capacity. Where African institutions don't exist, or need strengthening, she said, philanthropic money is best spent building them. That leads to country ownership and brings "the local voice, the local agenda" to the table, alongside partners such as the African Development Bank. She pointed again to South Africa's Just Energy Transition Partnership, where philanthropic partners and multilaterals helped the government negotiate what international financing would look like. She also made a pointed aside: more grants should go directly to countries to help scale such efforts.

The second is building investment platforms with countries rather than for them. Philanthropy can provide technical expertise, convene partners and help design financing mechanisms and instruments. The models must be contextual, she said, because every country's energy pathway, food system and growth path is different.

The third is strengthening the wider ecosystem of African climate leadership. She cited philanthropic support for the first two Africa Climate Summits, the resulting Nairobi and Addis Ababa declarations, and efforts to give African countries a collective voice through the African Union during South Africa's G20 presidency.

The stakes, she said, are high: climate finance flowing into Africa is less than 2% of what is needed, nowhere near the continent's needs. Without African leadership in these rooms, she argued, the finance ambitions cannot be met.

"Bringing in that collective voice because I believe that ensures that African leadership is there to shape African priorities," she said.

Turning country platforms into action

Somorin said his experience working with country platforms at the African Development Bank had shown that strong national leadership was essential to their success.

He outlined three factors that can help these platforms move beyond coordination. First, governments need clearly defined climate goals and realistic objectives that reflect their national capabilities, political circumstances, and development priorities.

"Nothing substitutes for strong leadership," he said. He named the difference it makes by comparing Rwanda with Niger. Clear, well-structured country goals matter, he said, but so does honesty about capability. Countries that are still asking partners to help train their people, when they should be implementing, are not ready to move. Goals also have to fit a country's political and socioeconomic realities. He said, "You cannot ignore" even when they seem unrelated to climate.

Second, countries must understand the strengths of their development partners, including multilateral institutions, philanthropic organisations and NGOs, and bring them together around clearly allocated responsibilities.

Third, governments must demonstrate their own commitment by contributing resources to the initiatives they want partners to support. Somorin said that countries which tell partners they need support for 80% of a project because they will supply 20% make faster progress than those that put in nothing and ask for everything. A government that commits a set share of its budget over five years, and assigns people to learn and deliver, finds it much easier to leverage what others bring.

Building towards an African COP32

Ethiopia is set to host COP32 in 2027. Abdulwassie said African countries should begin preparing now to ensure the summit delivers beyond political commitments. She said that COP32 should not be viewed as an Ethiopian event alone, but as an opportunity for African countries to unite around shared development priorities and strengthen the continent's influence in global climate discussions.

"COP32 is not just an Ethiopian COP, but an African COP," she said.

Abdulwassie outlined three priorities for the road to COP32. First, African leaders must work together to agree on key priorities. She pointed to the African Union summit in February and the pre-COP period as chances to agree on priorities that can outlast political cycles, including the action agenda and the initiatives each presidency will announce.

Second, Africa should use the run-up to COP32 to showcase successful climate initiatives already underway, demonstrate their results and identify which approaches can be adapted or scaled up in other countries.

Third, she called for greater recognition of local voices, particularly those of young people and communities already driving climate action. She said communities' ambitions and practices need to reach leaders and be translated into action. "How do we make sure the voice of youth in particular ... is translated into action?" she asked. She warned that decisions made today would shape the world inherited by future generations.

Close 

Development partners, she said, should engage Africa not in terms of handouts but as true partners, in a relationship where Africans have resources to trade and engage with, at COP32 and beyond.

To make COP31 a success for Africa, Abdulwassie pointed to stronger continental unity, partnerships and visibility in global climate discussions.

She said African countries needed to speak with a stronger collective voice while building momentum around energy, food security and water resilience. She also stressed the importance of having more Africans present at the summit to share their ambitions, experiences and progress.

Somorin said Africa's voice and leadership must be central to global climate discussions, particularly given the continent's limited contribution to climate change and its disproportionate exposure to its impacts. The voice, agency and significance of that continent, he argued, can never be ignored, but the starting point is Africa asserting its own agency, because the global climate equation is incomplete without Africa's development and resilience.

He urged African countries to move away from the perception of a continent waiting to be helped.

"Africa should be recognised not only for its vulnerability but also for its potential to contribute to global solutions," said Somorin. "If there's any region that could play a significant role in the global solution, it is Africa."

Protecting Africa's industrialisation ambitions

Soha Benchekroun, a climate resilience and industrial development policy researcher and adviser, argued that climate negotiations must give greater consideration to Africa's right to industrialise and move up global value chains.

The aim for COP31, and for the "African COP" in Ethiopia a year later, said Benchekroun, is to make sure climate action "does not undermine our industrialization trajectories." Most African countries are only starting to climb global value chains and build manufacturing and processing capacity at home. Many have moved to restrict raw material exports and promote local processing, a trend she called positive.

The threat, she said, comes from unilateral trade measures adopted in the name of climate policy by industrialized countries: carbon border adjustments, carbon pricing and related regulations. She said the negotiated rules should seek to limit the harm of these measures to African and other developing economies. The timing is pressing, she noted, with more carbon border mechanisms on the way, including the UK's, due to start in January 2027.

"Justice and a good outcome is first about doing no harm to our African development and industrial development pathways," she said.

Benchekroun also said that the just transition debate has focused on wider energy access while giving the right to development, and industrial development in particular, only marginal attention. "We do not expect COPs to sort out our energy infrastructure challenges, nor to promote our own industrialization," she said, "but at least a good start would be to not hinder them." What lifts a continent out of poverty, she said, is infrastructure, industrial development, and local value addition, paired with ways to turn them into benefits for society.

World.title: South Africa: Voters Demand Water, Electricity and Dignity As Ramaphosa Heads to Polls
World.content:
South Africans in queuing to vote in the 2026 Local Government Elections.

Voters at Hyde Park High School in Johannesburg want the local government elections to bring better services, safer communities and leaders who listen.

Gloria Chabalala brought her daughter to the voting station to teach her about a democratic right her grandparents only enjoyed later in life.

Johannesburg voters want more than election promises. They want water, electricity, housing and safer communities.

As South Africans cast their ballots in the 2026 local government elections, voters at Hyde Park High School say they are hoping for leaders who will put their needs first.

The voting station is also where President Cyril Ramaphosa and First Lady Dr Tshepo Motsepe are expected to cast their ballots.



For residents, however, the election is about choosing leaders who can improve their daily lives.

Among those who arrived to vote was Johannesburg resident Melisa Mandy, who praised the smooth voting process and the help she received from election officials.

"The IEC is very helpful, telling us exactly where to go. It's quite an efficient and fast process," she said.

Mandy, who was born and raised in Johannesburg, said she had watched the city change over the years.

She hopes the election results will bring positive changes to the city she calls home.

"It's a special occasion today. I think it's a turning point in the country. Everyone needs to participate," she said.

For another voter, Gloria Chabalala, election day was also a chance to teach her young daughter about South Africa's democracy.

She brought her daughter to the voting station so she could see what it means to take part in an election.

Her daughter still has about 10 years to go before she is old enough to vote, but Gloria wants her to understand the importance of having a say in who leads the country.

She remembered her late father, who died in 2005.

Although he lived into his 70s, he only had the opportunity to vote a few times during his lifetime.

His experience is a reminder to Gloria that the right to vote was not always available to all South Africans.

"I was telling my daughter how important it is for her to vote because her grandparents only got to vote much later in life. It's important that they understand the importance of us being here and this right that we have," she said.

Gloria said her daughter already knows about some of South Africa's political parties and is beginning to understand the choices voters make.

But beyond teaching her daughter about democracy, Gloria wants the elections to bring real change.

Close 

She believes South Africans deserve leaders who will tackle the problems affecting their communities.

"We all deserve dignity. We all deserve water, we all deserve electricity. We all deserve housing. We don't need crime," she said.

For Gloria, these are basic needs that every community should have.

She hopes those elected will serve all residents and make decisions that put people's needs ahead of their own interests.

While Mandy hopes to see Johannesburg change for the better, Gloria wants her daughter to grow up understanding the value of voting and the responsibility that comes with choosing leaders.

Both voters see the elections as an opportunity for change, but their hopes go beyond what happens at the ballot box.

As Ramaphosa and Motsepe prepare to vote at Hyde Park High School, residents are making their own choices about who should lead their communities.

For Gloria, the real test will come after the votes have been counted.

She wants leaders who will turn election promises into working services and make sure communities have the water, electricity, housing and safety they deserve.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 4, 2026
World.content:
UN to Withdraw Peacekeeping Mission from Western Sahara

The United Nations has started preparations to withdraw its peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara. This follows Russia and the United States vetoing each other's proposals to extend the 35-year deployment. The UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) was established in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire and support a settlement between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front. The latest disagreement in the Security Council followed a US proposal to renew the mission's mandate while placing Morocco's autonomy plan at the centre of efforts to resolve the dispute. Russia rejected the proposal, arguing that it favoured Morocco's position and could prejudge questions of sovereignty. The US subsequently vetoed Russia's alternative proposal. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has expressed concern about the possibility of renewed fighting and urged both parties to exercise restraint. He also reiterated the need to respect the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination. Morocco controls most of the territory, while the Polisario Front continues to push for an independent state.

HRW Urges Ethiopia to Lift Suspension of Independent Newspaper



Human Rights Watch has called on the Ethiopian government to immediately reverse its decision to suspend the licences of The Reporter, one of the country's oldest independent media outlets and its last privately owned Amharic newspaper. The Ethiopian Media Authority announced that the publication's print and online operations would be suspended indefinitely, accusing it of repeatedly violating media laws and publishing content that undermines national interests, including foreign investment, tourism and diplomacy. Human Rights Watch said that the decision reflects an escalating crackdown on independent journalism and civic freedoms in the country. Since 2025, authorities have reportedly shut down several media outlets, deported foreign correspondents and targeted local journalists through arrests, office raids and other forms of intimidation. The organisation said the government has also increased pressure on The Reporter, including the arrest of some of its journalists. Its director for the Horn of Africa, Laetitia Bader, said that the government should lift the suspension, while Ethiopia's international partners should pressure authorities to end attacks on independent media.

Service Failures, Water Crisis, and Coalitions Set to Shape South African Municipal Elections

Service delivery failures, water shortages, electricity disruptions and rising living costs are among the key issues influencing South African voters as the country heads to municipal elections. Residents in communities like Tembisa have vented their anger at sewage in the streets, inconsistent electricity and poor local infrastructure, with some wondering if voting will make any real change. Water supply and quality have become particularly important issues with a number of areas facing prolonged shortages and aging infrastructure unable to meet demand. Water rights organisation WaterCAN said that almost 70% of the country's wastewater treatment works are in a critical state, contributing to pollution in rivers and streams. The elections are also expected to test the African National Congress's declining support, with polling suggesting the party could lose further ground and more municipalities could be governed through coalitions. Immigration has been a major theme in the campaign messages as parties look to capitalize on public concerns about illegal immigration and border management. Meanwhile, the Independent Electoral Commission is investigating more than 700 complaints relating to election misinformation, including false claims about asylum seekers being mobilised to vote. Analysts said that turnout will be crucial in determining the outcome, particularly as municipal elections have historically recorded lower participation than national polls.

Libyan Religious Body Issues Ruling Prohibiting Sale and Use of Nike Products

Libya's highest religious authority, Dar al-Ifta, has issued a religious ruling prohibiting Muslims from buying, selling, or wearing clothing bearing the Nike logo. The Tripoli-based institution argues that the American sportswear company's name is derived from the Greek goddess of victory and that its famous swoosh logo is inspired by her wings. It says wearing clothing displaying the logo amounts to promoting symbols associated with the worship of multiple gods, which it considers contrary to Islamic teachings. The religious committee has also accused Nike of supporting Israel and reiterated calls for a boycott of companies it considers supportive of the country during the war in Gaza. The ruling was approved by Libya's Grand Mufti, Sadiq al-Gharyani, but does not amount to an official government ban and carries no specified legal penalties. The institution has previously issued similar rulings against jewellery and watches bearing the logo of French luxury brand Van Cleef & Arpels. The latest decision has sparked mixed reactions on social media, with some welcoming it while others have questioned its relevance amid Libya's wider political and economic challenges.

At Least 27 Civilians Killed in Burkina Faso Attacks

Human Rights Watch said that at least 27 civilians were killed in two attacks by Al-Qaeda-linked armed group Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) in Burkina Faso's northern Yatenga province in September. The first attack took place on September 1, when more than 60 fighters stormed an artisanal gold mining site near Soubo village, killing 24 civilians, injuring at least 20 others and destroying hundreds of shelters, motorcycles and mining equipment. Witnesses said the attackers opened fire on people who were sleeping or working at the site, while some victims were shot as they attempted to escape. Four days later, an explosive device detonated on a road near Mera village, killing three people travelling on a motorcycle, including a five-year-old child and a 65-year-old woman. Human Rights Watch said that the attacks appear to constitute war crimes and has called on Burkina Faso's authorities to strengthen protection for vulnerable communities, investigate the killings and prosecute those responsible. The organisation also raised concerns about the use of improvised explosive devices, which pose a serious threat to civilians. It says the attacks come amid a wider pattern of violence by Islamist armed groups and serious abuses against civilians by government forces and allied militias.

Close 

Kenya Registers Thousands of Ethiopian Refugees Fleeing Clashes

Kenyan authorities, working with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and the Kenya Red Cross Society, have begun registering Ethiopian refugees fleeing renewed clashes in the border town of Moyale. More than 50,000 people have reportedly crossed into Kenya since fighting intensified in late October, prompting growing concern over the humanitarian situation along the border. The registration exercise began around October 31 at temporary reception centres in Marsabit County, including Harhosa and OMC camps. Officials are issuing identification wristbands to newly arrived refugees before conducting household profiling to establish their needs and coordinate humanitarian assistance. Many displaced people are currently sheltering in temporary camps, schools and churches, while others are staying with relatives and host communities. Humanitarian agencies say urgent assistance is needed, particularly food, clean water, emergency shelter, sanitation, healthcare and protection for women and children. The UNHCR, International Organization for Migration, UNICEF and other partners are working with Kenyan authorities to coordinate the response. They have appealed for approximately 8.9 million dollars to provide assistance over three months. The latest influx follows renewed clashes in Moyale, where longstanding territorial and administrative disputes between Ethiopia's Oromia and Somali regional states have escalated into violence, resulting in civilian casualties, injuries and the destruction of homes and businesses. Kenyan authorities have also increased security along the border following reports of stray bullets landing in areas on the Kenyan side.

World.title: Former NFL star recalls his scariest on-field moments following Jack Campbell injury
World.content:
Members of the Detroit Lions, notably Aidan Hutchinson, were visibly shaken when Jack Campbell was stretchered off the field earlier this week.

Unfortunately, those occurrences are not out of the norm, and former wide receiver Brandon Marshall has been on the field for a couple of those scary moments, including one that ended a career.

Marshall was a member of the Denver Broncos when his then-teammate, Dominic Hixon, was tackled by Kevin Everett on Sept. 9, 2007. Everett suffered a cervical spine injury that left doctors unsure whether he would ever walk again, but he defied the odds.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

During an interview with OutKick, Marshall also recalled a time while playing at UCF when a teammate of his was airlifted to the hospital. Defensive lineman Paul Carrington, who played 15 NFL games, was injured during a practice before the 2005 season started - he wound up playing the entire season and leading the Conference USA with nine sacks.

"Honestly, it comes with it. In those moments, you’re shocked and you’re really feeling for your teammate or the guy on the field. But once the whistle blows, you don’t get wrapped up in your emotions. You have to have a short-term memory. You’re trained to move forward," Marshall said.

CHRISTIAN MCCAFFREY GIVES ONE 49ERS QUALITY THAT SEPARATES TEAM FROM PACK AMID SUPER BOWL HOPES

The Lions on Monday announced "preliminary indications are positive" for Campbell's condition. But "out of respect for Jack and his family, we will not share further information at this time."

"It's positive, you know?" coach Dan Campbell told reporters. "So your prayers are working. Please continue to do that."

Minnesota Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson caught a pass in the middle of the field and was soon sandwiched by two Lions defenders, including Campbell. Campbell arrived at the contact while falling to his knees and appeared to have his head slanted upward, so he made contact with his facemask rather than his shoulders and arms.

Campbell immediately collapsed and lay motionless, his arms dropping to his sides. On a positive note, Campbell did not require help breathing.

"That's difficult, you know, it's difficult," Dan Campbell said. "You don't ever want to see somebody like that on the field, but when you see Jack, Jack never lays on the field ever, no matter what it is.

"And that's when you're like, it puts it in perspective … when you're in the world we're in, you know, you got to snap back, and it's not an easy thing to do."

OutKick's Armando Salguero contributed to this report.

World.title: Redistricting efforts blow up in Republicans' faces amid historic House losses
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Republicans' gambit to stave off election losses by changing congressional maps backfired in most of the country on Tuesday night.

Democrats swept both battleground House seats and areas considered safe GOP territory in an unprecedented midterm election performance, despite the best efforts by Republican-led states to redistrict in multiple states to give their party an edge.

"It was definitely the wrong move," one House Republican told Fox News Digital. "One of the truisms in politics is never to overreach. We did and that was part of the reason for the backlash."

DEMOCRAT SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN

Republicans in states that were particularly affected by redistricting had been warning their governors for months that it could be a bad idea, another person told Fox News Digital.

"It's a bridge too far, and clearly the bridge blew up behind them," that person said.

In Texas, where the GOP-led state government altered the congressional map to give Republicans an advantage in five districts, Democrats are projected to win at least three.

Reps. Vicente Gonzalez, D-Texas, and Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, managed to hold onto their seats despite Republicans' efforts, and Democrats also won the newly redrawn 35th Congressional District. The remaining two have not been called.

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

Florida Republicans are on pace to lose all four House seats they drew to favor their party. Incumbent Reps. Kathy Castor, D-Fla., and Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., are projected to win their respective altered districts, along with political newcomer Pia Dandiya in her red-leaning seat.

Rep. Darren Soto, D-Fla., who was expected to be hardest-hit by Sunshine State Republicans' efforts, is narrowly leading in a race that's still too close to call.

Overall, however, it's worth noting that Florida was a bright spot for the GOP overall on Tuesday night. Rep. Byron Donalds, R-Fla., won the race for governor and all Republican incumbents kept their seats.

Meanwhile, a push in Ohio to make districts held by Reps. Greg Landsman, D-Ohio, and Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, more favorable to Republicans also failed.

And in Alabama, Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Ala., won another term despite his seat also being altered to favor Republicans.

The process of redistricting is traditionally done after a national census, to account for population shifts in each state.

Changing congressional maps mid-decade is a controversial move that saw bipartisan pushback — though both sides ultimately took part.

World.title: Iran takes a victory lap over stunning US election results, claims 'collapse has accelerated'

Democrats weren't the only ones celebrating amid shattering defeats for Republicans in the midterm elections — Iranian leaders also took a victory lap Wednesday.

Iran cast the results — where Democrats made gains even in traditional Republican strongholds — as a rejection of President Donald Trump's war and a decisive referendum on the economic toll it took on American voters in the months before the election.

"The process of the US’s collapse has accelerated," Iran’s current Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, posted on an official English language account on X.

"Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has also served as Tehran's chief negotiator in talks with Washington, posted on X.

STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

"If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," Ghalibaf added.

Khamenei, meanwhile, appeared to signal Iran would dig in its heels rather than negotiate with the U.S.

"The Great Satan [the US] wants the surrender of the Iranian nation. The slightest inclination toward submission would cause the immense capital acquired through the blessings brought by the blood of our martyrs and the sacrifices of the entire Iranian nation to be lost," he wrote in another post on X.

"It would embolden the enemy to launch more wars, and carry out its next acts of aggression."

The declarations came after Democrats seized control of Congress Tuesday night in a political bloodbath for Republicans, delivering a major rebuke to Trump after a campaign dominated by concerns over affordability and the months-long war with Iran that the president repeatedly promised was nearing its end.

When the attacks began earlier this year, Trump said it would last a weeks — maybe a bit over a month. It has now been raging for more than eight months.

TRUMP CALLS IRAN CONFLICT A 'SOFT WAR,' INSISTS US HOLDS THE CARDS AHEAD OF MIDTERM ELECTIONS

Iran was hardly the only issue driving voters to the polls — but the conflict became increasingly intertwined with Americans' economic concerns as the war sent energy prices higher and impacted the costs of gas and most goods.

Polling ahead of Election Day showed deep public dissatisfaction with the Iran conflict.

Trump himself acknowledged after the results came in that Iran "partly" played a role in Republicans' losses, even as he continued to defend his decision to go to war.

Vice President JD Vance was much more blunt, writing in a lengthy X post: "The reason we lost is the war."

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," he continued. "Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest."

Other voices in Tehran also claimed vindication in the wake of the results.

TRUMP ADMIN THREATENS IRAN WITH 'CONSEQUENCES' AS ALLIES CONVENE AMID THREATS OF POST-ELECTION ESCALATION

Iranian Deputy Parliament Speaker Ali Nikzad called the Republican losses the "aftershocks" of what he described as Trump's defeat at the hands of Iran, while a senior official in Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's office claimed the war and U.S. support for Israel had brought Republicans an historic electoral defeat.

Trump entered the conflict predicting a short war.

In the opening days of Operation Epic Fury, the president repeatedly said the campaign would take roughly four to six weeks and soon declared U.S. forces were running "substantially ahead" of schedule. American and Israeli strikes quickly eliminated senior Iranian military leaders and battered Tehran's military infrastructure.

But the war proved far easier to start than to end.

Iran retaliated by choking commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway that before the war carried roughly a fifth of the world's oil supply, while launching attacks on energy infrastructure across the Persian Gulf. Shipping through the strait nearly ground to a halt in the early weeks of the conflict, removing millions of barrels of oil from global markets and sending energy prices sharply higher.

Iranian attacks damaged oil and energy facilities in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and elsewhere in the Gulf, further squeezing supplies. By the end of May, more than 1.1 billion barrels of crude that would ordinarily have reached global markets had been disrupted, according to the International Monetary Fund.

THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE

What Trump initially described as a matter of weeks instead stretched across much of 2026, as the administration struggled to secure lasting freedom of navigation through Hormuz and Iran retained the ability to threaten commercial shipping and its Gulf neighbors.

The economic consequences followed Americans home.

Oil prices surged after the war began, feeding through to gasoline and other consumer costs just as Republicans headed into a midterm election already dominated by concerns over affordability.

Even after U.S.-led operations restored much of the traffic through Hormuz by the fall, oil flows remained below prewar levels and Iran continued attacking commercial vessels.

A radical left-wing student group at one of New York City's most selective public high schools is facing scrutiny after signing an Instagram statement declaring "Intifada Until Victory," prompting demands for accountability and questions about what city and school officials are doing to prevent similar incidents.

The Young Democratic Socialists of America chapter at Manhattan’s Stuyvesant High School, according to an advocacy group, shared the post a day after the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 terrorist attacks that saw the murder of over 1,200 people, including American citizens.

The post was also shared by several New York City DSA college chapters, including Hunter College, the New School, City College and Lehman College, according to Politico.

Michelle Ahdoot, speaking in a video shared by the Jewish advocacy movement #EndJewHatred, urged the public to demand accountability from school officials over the student group's involvement in the post.

BACK TO SCHOOL SHOULD NOT MEAN BACK TO FEAR FOR JEWISH STUDENTS

"This is not okay," Ahdoot said.

The group has called on Stuyvesant administrators and New York City Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels to address the post.

The New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America (NYC-DSA) responded to Fox News Digital's inquiry about the Stuyvesant group's involvement in the post.

"NYC-DSA was not involved in the planning or development of this post," NYC-DSA co-chair Grace Mausser told Fox News Digital.

"We also condemn attempts to attack high school students for political reasons," Mausser added.

The statement accused the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter of silencing students seeking to protest Mayor Zohran Mamdani over Israel. The signatories also criticized Mamdani’s decision to retain NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch, describing her as a "Zionist billionaire."

PRO-ISRAEL ORGANIZATIONS CONDEMN DSA CO-CHAIR FOR SAYING OCTOBER 7 ATTACKS WERE 'INEVITABLE'

But it was the statement’s declaration of "Intifada Until Victory" that drew particular concern. "Intifada," an Arabic word meaning ‘to rise up,’ is associated with Palestinian uprisings against Israel, including the Second Intifada, when suicide bombings and other terrorist attacks killed a over a thousand Israeli civilians and seriously injured many more, according to the ADL. Some activists use the term to describe resistance to Israeli policies, while many Jews hear it as a call for violence.

Ahdoot, director of #EndJewHatred, told Fox News Digital that the phrase cannot be separated from its violent history.

"Intifada invokes Palestinian uprisings that included suicide bombings and deliberate attacks on civilians," she said. "In this context, ‘INTIFADA UNTIL VICTORY!’ is a call for violence against Jews and has NO place in a public school community."

The involvement of a high school chapter in a statement signed predominantly by college organizations has raised questions about the group's oversight, its relationship with Stuyvesant and what responsibility school administrators have when student political activity generates concerns about antisemitism.

The controversy follows previous reports of antisemitism at Stuyvesant. In May 2025, antisemitic graffiti was discovered in a boys' bathroom, prompting school administrators to condemn the vandalism and introduce additional security measures, according to the school’s student newspaper, The Stuyvesant Spectator. The newspaper reported that further antisemitic vandalism was discovered later that month.



The latest dispute comes amid broader concerns about antisemitism in New York City public schools. An August 2026 report by United Jewish Teachers documented 250 antisemitic and anti-Israel incidents across the city's public schools between Oct. 2023 and July 2026, with nearly 65% involving direct acts such as harassment, vandalism, assaults or threats.

Questions now center on whether the YDSA chapter is officially recognized by Stuyvesant, whether it operates under faculty supervision, what oversight applies to its activities and whether administrators have taken any action since the post appeared.

NYC PUBLIC SCHOOLS UNDER FIRE FOR FAILING TO ADDRESS ANTISEMITISM: 'NOT SEEING ANY ACTION'

Fox News Digital reached out to Mayor Mamdani's office, Stuyvesant Principal Seung Yu and the NY Board of Education asking what action, if any, has been taken, who is responsible for overseeing the student group and what steps are being considered to prevent similar incidents. Neither had responded at the time of publication.

Asked about the lack of response her organization received from education officials, Ahdoot said, "The silence from the NYCDOE chancellor, school and central admin and BOE officials is, frankly, deafening," She added, "The lack of immediate action and acknowledgment of the Jewish community’s concerns points to the sheer lack of care and urgency when it comes to Jewish civil rights."

"Students deserve a learning environment free from Jew-hatred, and families deserve to know that school leadership takes their concerns seriously!" she said.

World.title: 5 key insights from the NBC News Exit Poll about the blue tsunami
World.content:
It was a historic blue tsunami: The Democratic Party captured both chambers of Congress, flipping as many as seven seats in the Senate and at least 29 in the House of Representatives.

Just two years ago, the nation had been hit by a red wave. How did things turn around so dramatically?

A cocktail of crucial factors: Voters feeling fed up with the economy, Democratic candidates emerging as more well-liked, important voting blocs — including Latinos and Black men — shifting blue, opinions about the Republican Party dropping and a resounding rejection of President Donald Trump himself, according to the NBC News Exit Poll.

Here are five key insights we have gleaned about Tuesday’s stunning midterms analyzing data from the poll, which surveyed more than 79,000 voters nationwide.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

1) Americans were deeply negative on the state of the economy and gloomy about the future of the country.

An overwhelming majority of voters (75%) rated the nation’s economy as “not so good” or “poor,” the poll showed. And they soured on their trust in Republicans to handle it.

Sixty-nine percent said the U.S. economic system favors the wealthy, and only 31% said it favors most Americans. This perception came at a time when the vast majority of voters expressed concerns about the cost of living. More than 80% of voters said they were worried about the price of necessities: gas and diesel fuel, food and groceries, utilities and healthcare.

Thirty-seven percent of voters said they favored Republican control of the economy, while 43% favored Democrats — a flip in perspective from the 2024 election. Voters also blamed Trump: 65% said the president’s policies had made the economy worse. Just 27% said they had made the economy better.

A David Crowley supporter at an election night event in Milwaukee on Tuesday. Nam Y. Huh / AP

Sixty-two percent said higher-than-usual prices are more because of Trump’s policies than factors outside his control, and 65% said his tariff policies hurt the national economy.

Their frustration extended beyond the economy — and into a pessimistic view of the U.S. overall. Three in four voters said they were unhappy with how things are going in the U.S., and more than a third (38%) said they were angry about the state of the country.

More than half of voters (57%) said that life for the next generation of Americans will be worse than today; just 22% said they believed it would be better.

2) Democratic candidates enjoyed advantages on favorability, character and experience.

In an overwhelmingly negative political environment, Democratic Senate candidates emerged as well-liked in races that looked tough for them at the beginning of the election cycle, according to the poll.

Democrats above water on favorability included Jon Ossoff in Georgia, where a remarkable 59% of state voters said they viewed him favorably; James Talarico in Texas, where 52% of voters said they viewed him positively; and Josh Turek in Iowa, where 49% of voters said they viewed him favorably. All three candidates won their races.

Republicans, meanwhile, struggled to win over voters.

In two key Senate races, voters expressed negative opinions about Republican candidates’ personal character.

A watch party for the Democratic candidate for Senate, Adam Hamilton, in Overland Park, Kansas, on Tuesday. Evert Nelson / USA TODAY Network via Reuters

In Kansas, 43% of voters said Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, an OB-GYN who faced scrutiny after The New York Times reported that he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid bills, had the right character for the job. Marshall has described the story as a “hit job.”

Voter opinions were worse about Ken Paxton’s personal character. Only 34% of Texas voters thought positively of the attorney general, who has battled scandals for years and was impeached in 2023 by the Republican controlled state House before the state Senate acquitted him.

Both Paxton and Marshall lost their Senate bids.

Candidates aligned with Trump also struggled. In North Carolina, Michael Whatley was seen as too supportive of Trump (60%), and in South Carolina, where the president endorsed Darline Graham, only 35% of voters said she had the right experience.

3) After flirting with the GOP in 2024, big Democratic voting blocs swung back with a vengeance.

By ignoring or denigrating many of the new voters who were key to Trump’s victory two years ago, Republicans squandered the opportunity to cement a new coalition of voters.

Latinos, who notably gave Trump almost half (46%) of their votes in 2024, bounced back to the Democrats, who garnered 62% of Latino support in races for the House, the poll showed.

Among Black male voters, 1 in 5 went for Trump in 2024. That share shrunk to 13% for Republican House candidates this year.

Trump narrowly won men under age 25 in 2024, getting 49% of their votes compared to 48% for Democrat Kamala Harris. But young men swung dramatically away from the GOP in House races this year: Democrats swept them by a 68% to 28% margin.

On the whole, more Trump voters had buyer’s remorse (6% supported Democratic House candidates) than Harris voters (3% defected to the GOP).

4) And Trump himself was soundly rejected by voters.

Trump tried to energize his base by encouraging his supporters to vote like, “I’m on the ballot.” But the nation had largely soured on his presidency, according to the poll.

Trump’s approval rating among voters, just 38%, was the lowest Election Day rating for any president since 2008.

Forty-three percent of voters said they cast their House ballot to express opposition to Trump. Just 16% said they voted to express support for him.

Voters gave Trump overwhelmingly negative marks on key aspects of his presidency, saying that he prioritizes “his own personal interests” over the country’s (62%), that his war against Iran was the “wrong decision” (63%) and that his immigration actions had “gone too far” (57%).

5) A key distinction: It’s a blue tsunami, not a progressive earthquake.

Politicians and pundits alike mistook Trump’s 2024 victory as an endorsement of his deeply conservative plans. But the 2024 NBC Exit Poll found little evidence of an ideological shift to the right.

The story is the same this year: On key issues, voters are no more progressive than they were two years ago.

Among voters this year, 64% said abortion should be legal in most or all cases. That’s just a notch below the share of 65% in 2024.

Twenty-three percent of the electorate considered themselves liberal in 2024, while 35% called themselves conservative. Those numbers hardly budged among voters in 2026, standing at 25% liberal, 34% conservative.

Voters’ opinions of socialism remained largely negative, at 54% unfavorable and 33% favorable. Just 1 in 5 voters this year considered themselves democratic socialists. By contrast, capitalism remains relatively well-regarded in the minds of voters (57% favorable, 32% unfavorable).
