World.content:
Stocks surged on Wednesday after Democrats won commanding victories in key races across the country, making it immediately clear to investors which party would control the House and Senate.

As the earliest results began to roll in on Tuesday night, Nasdaq 100 futures plunged as much as 2.5%.

But by the following morning, the picture had changed dramatically.

The Nasdaq Composite opened higher by 1.5%. The broader S&P 500 surged more than 1.2%. The Russell 2000, which tracks small and medium sized companies, soared 2%. The Dow rocketed higher by 1,150 points at the opening bell.

Wall Street welcomed the clarity of the results, which marked a departure from previous years in which it took several days for decisive projections.

“The combination of a large Democratic majority in Congress and President Trump’s statement that he is willing to work with the opposition should act as a break on extreme policy outcomes and bring down risk premia,” said Deutsche Bank’s George Saravelos in a note Wednesday morning.

“The market is increasingly likely to interpret surprising policy shifts from the Executive as time-bound by the next Presidential election or the new domestic political configuration,” he added.

Economists at Goldman Sachs wrote that Democrats might now move to limit some of Trump’s most economically-disruptive actions.

“We expect Democrats to use fiscal deadlines to seek to limit the war with Iran, roll back selected tariffs, and reverse spending cuts enacted last year,” they said in a note.

The price of oil, which has been pushed sharply higher this year due to the Iran war, declined by more than 3%.

But, experts said that results poised a major risk to the AI boom from politicians who will now take office.

“Key market implications include incrementally negative AI sentiment on greater expectations for data center restrictions,” said strategists at Morgan Stanley.

“At the federal level, the outcome is less likely to change the outlook for data center and AI regulation, which would still need bipartisan support,” said Goldman’s economists.

“However, Democratic wins at the state and local level are likely to lead to short-term data center moratoria, potentially affecting about 45% of planned US data center capacity expansion.”

Several Democrats who won key governor’s races Tuesday have called for a pause in data center construction in their states, including Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Amy Acton in Ohio. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.

Possibly more than any other state, Texas has been a major focus for AI investors and a critical market for data centers.

Texas “is the one state with enough scale” where a slowdown could make a difference, Wolfe Research’s head of U.S. policy and politics, Tobin Marcus, wrote in a recent note.

SpaceX and Tesla, both engaged in the AI and data center businesses, plunged around 5% in early Wednesday trading. Musk, who runs both firms, was poised to become one of the biggest beneficiaries of Republican victories and spent hundreds of millions of dollars in support of GOP candidates.

Analysts at JPMorgan Chase also pointed to a potential “investigation risk” facing CEOs who have close ties to President Donald Trump.

Major companies ranging from Nvidia to Apple to NBC News’ parent company, Comcast, have donated millions of dollars to Trump’s pet projects, most notably his ballroom, and some of their leaders have regularly appeared alongside him at events.

Top Democrats have already signaled their interest in launching investigations of some of Trump’s projects in January, when their new congressional majority will give them subpoena power.

Democrats vs. data centers

Tech stocks have played more of a role than any other sector to the surge in the value of U.S. equity markets over the last two years.

Trillion-dollar companies such as Amazon, Nvidia, Microsoft and Google parent Alphabet, as well as a handful of smaller data center startups, have poured hundreds of billions of dollars into developing AI models, building data centers and buying the equipment needed to operate them.

The AI boom has been a primary driver behind the Nasdaq 100’s gain of 40% since Election Day 2024, more than the S&P 500’s roughly 30% jump.

Any widespread slowing or halting of data center construction could put those unprecedented and sweeping investments, which many of the country’s top companies have stakes in, at risk.

“Democrats winning gubernatorial races in Texas, Ohio, and Georgia—which have a significant share of the U.S. project pipeline—means new pauses and restrictions on data center development,” Evercore’s Sarah Bianchi wrote late Tuesday.

Bianchi described the outcome of the midterms as a “blue tsunami.”

She added that “2027 is shaping up to be a turbulent year as developers will be forced to adapt to a shifting policy landscape,” but cautioned traders not to get ahead of themselves.

Bianchi wrote that “the impact of any pause or moratorium will hinge on the details, such as any grandfathering, and whether projects facing prolonged disruption can relocate to other states.”

Democrats were also projected to win Senate races in a number of battleground states where data centers were a major issue during the campaign, including Georgia, North Carolina, Michigan, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas.

“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” wrote Elon Musk on X. He has also proposed putting servers for AI systems in orbit above Earth. Most experts say the idea faces significant hurdles.

Even before Tuesday’s projected results, markets had been on edge for months about whether, and how, the AI boom and the massive investments tied to it would deliver returns.

On Friday, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq both posted their worst days since mid-June after Intel and Amazon, two key suppliers to AI companies, reported mixed earnings results.

World.title: Photos: Celebration and gloom at watch parties across the U.S.
World.content:
Joy and despair punctuated election watch parties overnight after a blue tsunami swept the country’s midterm elections.

In Detroit, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed celebrated his victory over Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim senator in U.S. history. He was cheered on by a crowd of supporters — some wearing hijabs, others cowboy hats.

World.title: Democrats score key secretary of state wins ahead of the 2028 election
World.content:
Democrats won secretary of state contests in four presidential battlegrounds while making inroads in red territory, giving them election oversight authority in key states for the 2028 elections.

Democratic candidates maintained control of secretary of state offices in Arizona, Michigan and Nevada, while flipping the office in Georgia, all states that have been at the center of recent campaigns for the White House. And Democrats gained secretary of state control in the GOP-leaning states of Indiana and Ohio.

In Georgia, Democrat Penny Brown Reynolds will succeed Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, who drew President Donald Trump’s ire for rebuffing his push to overturn the state’s 2020 election results. She defeated state Rep. Tim Fleming, a former aide to outgoing Republican Gov. Brian Kemp who was endorsed by Trump.

Reynolds, who is known for a family court television show and serving in the Biden administration, campaigned as a judge who would stand up to Trump while following the law in running state elections. Fleming did not go as far as other Republicans in claiming the 2020 election was stolen, but said there were “irregularities” and called for new mail voting restrictions.

In Michigan, Democratic Lt. Gov Garlin Gilchrist bested Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini, a Republican, to succeed Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who won the state’s race for governor. Gilchrist had criticized Forlini for sharing voter data with the Trump administration and hiring a Jan. 6 protester to his office.

In Arizona and Nevada, incumbent Democrats Adrian Fontes and Cisco Aguilar fended off challenges from far-right Republicans whose careers were rooted in advancing election conspiracy theories, enjoying far better margins than they had in similar 2022 matchups.

And in Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s win in the governor’s race is also expected to give the party authority over the administration of state elections. Texas’ secretary of state is appointed by the governor, with concurrent terms.

Once an under-the-radar, downballot job, secretary of state has become a much more high-profile position amid a constant drumbeat of unfounded election fraud claims from Trump and his allies. All four battleground states saw challenges to the 2020 election results and secretaries of state in these and other states have faced a steady stream of lawsuits and threats.

In the final stretch of the midterm campaign, Democrats started targeting Indiana, Kansas, Ohio and Iowa for red-state gains. So far, they’ve won two of their targets and lost one.

Democratic state Rep. Allison Russo will be the next secretary of state of Ohio as her party also flipped Senate and gubernatorial seats in a state that has shifted to the right in recent years. Russo defeated Republican state Treasurer Robert Sprague.

In Indiana, Beau Bayh, a 30-year-old scion of a longtime Democratic family in the state, beat Republican state Rep. Max Engling. Engling had replaced Indiana’s Republican incumbent, Diego Morales, who was embroiled in allegations of corruption and ethics violations, at the party’s nominating convention.

Bayh spent more than $ 8.6 million on ads, according to AdImpact, campaigning heavily on fighting corruption. He ran at the top of the ticket in Indiana, which didn’t have any races for Senate or governor this year.

In Kansas, where voters haven’t elected a Democrat as secretary of state since 1948, the race between Democratic state Rep. Jennifer Day and Republican state Rep. Pat Proctor was too close to call, according to NBC News’ Decision Desk.

Democrats saw success elsewhere in the state, with pastor Adam Hamilton pulling off an upset over GOP Sen. Roger Marshall.

Top-of-the-ticket wins didn’t translate to secretary of state success everywhere.

In Iowa, Republican Secretary of State Paul Pate fended off a challenge from Democrat Ryan Peterman, even as Democrats won Senate and governor’s races in the state.

And In South Carolina, Republican Secretary of State Mark Hammond beat Democratic challenger Jason Belton, even as Democrat Annie Andrews prevailed in the Senate race.

World.title: Tuesday’s elections bring historic first for Black governors
World.content:
For the first time in U.S. history, multiple elected Black governors will serve at the same time after five wins in elections across the country.

They are Democrat Wes Moore, who won re-election in Maryland, Republican Rep. Byron Donalds in Florida, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Democrat David Crowley in Wisconsin and Democrat Aaron Ford in Nevada.

Before those wins, the only elected Black governors in U.S. history had been Moore; Deval Patrick, a Democrat who was elected Massachusetts’ governor in 2006; and Doug Wilder, a Democrat who was elected Virginia’s governor in 1989. None served simultaneously.

Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, overcame an enormous spending disadvantage to defeat Republican Rick Jackson, a wealthy healthcare executive who pumped more than $100 million of his own money into his campaign. She is the first woman and the first Black person to be elected governor of Georgia, and will be the first Black female governor in U.S. history.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

In an interview with NBC News last month, Donalds said the history-making aspect of his candidacy was “very special.”

“From a larger perspective, there’s so much that has been talked about in politics over the last couple decades around race. Obviously, the country has had some real negative parts of our history surrounding race,” he said. “I’m humbled to be in this position, but I think it says a lot more about the state [of Florida] than it does about me.”

Others fell short in their races.

In South Carolina, another Black Democrat, state Rep. Jermaine Johnson, lost his state’s race for governor to Republican Alan Wilson.

On the Republican side, Rep. John James lost his governor’s race to Democrat Jocelyn Benson, and Minnesota state House Speaker Lisa Demuth lost the state’s gubernatorial contest to Democrat Amy Klobuchar.

World.title: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan’s Senate race
World.content:
Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former public health official aligned with the Democratic Party’s left flank, has won Michigan’s highly hostile Senate race, defeating his Republican rival, former Rep. Mike Rogers, NBC News projects.

El-Sayed, 42, overcame a raft of Islamophobia fomented by President Donald Trump and others to become the first Muslim elected to the chamber.

He also overcame a last-minute defection from Rep. Haley Stevens, a vanquished primary rival who reneged on her pledge to support him and endorsed Rogers after she attended church with him Sunday.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

“They tried to confuse you, so let me just set the record straight,” El-Sayed told supporters early Wednesday. “I love America”

El-Sayed also had sharp words for those who had made an issue of his religion, from Rogers on up to Trump. He said he relished that it would be Vice President JD Vance, with whom he has tangled publicly, who swears him into the Senate.

“So Mike, enjoy your retirement,” said El-Sayed, referring to Rogers. “See, you chose hate, and Michigan chose hope. May we never have to see the likes of you in this state again.”

El-Sayed’s victory extends a long-running GOP drought in the state. A Republican has not won a Senate seat in Michigan since 1994. El-Sayed will succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

The clash between El-Sayed and Rogers, 63, was rated among the country’s most closely watched and aggressively fought, given El-Sayed’s alliance with progressive firebrands such as Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. El-Sayed’s criticism of the Israeli government, which he has accused of genocide, was also a consistent flash point.

Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, right, and Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., attend a church service Sunday in Detroit. Jose Juarez / AP

A group affiliated with the pro-Israel group AIPAC spent more than $30 million in an unsuccessful effort to lift Stevens over El-Sayed in the Democratic primary and re-engaged in Michigan in the closing weeks of the general election. Stevens, meanwhile, linked her defection from El-Sayed to his position on Israel and his campaign’s suggestion that she was not welcome at his campaign events after she began voicing her criticism more in the race’s closing days.

Rogers and his Republican allies tried to spin El-Sayed’s anti-Israel stance into attacks that evoked his religion and raised questions about his loyalties. Vance, in particular, routinely attacked El-Sayed — a rift that grew out of El-Sayed’s sarcastic questioning of whether Vance’s late, white Appalachian-born grandfather would have approved of his Indian American wife.

Trump’s attacks on El-Sayed’s faith went furthest.

Within days of El-Sayed’s August primary victory, Trump began falsely asserting that “jihadists” were gaining purchase in U.S. politics and government. The attacks escalated over the next three months, with Trump at one point whipping a crowd in Youngstown, Ohio, into a frenzied chant of “Deport! Deport!” He often referred to El-Sayed by his middle name, Mohamed.

El-Sayed had a handy retort for that one.

“That’ll be Sen. Mohamed to you, bro,” he said at an Oct. 25 event with Sanders.

World.title: Record number of female governors elected
World.content:
Voters in 17 states have elected female governors, setting a record in Tuesday’s election as Democrats made sweeping gains in races up and down the ballot.

With some governor’s races still unresolved, at least 10 Democratic women were projected to win their contests, and three Republican women — Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn — were projected to do the same.

Democratic women made historic gains in battleground states for their party, with former public health official Amy Acton in Ohio and state Rep. Gina Hinojosa in Texas emerging victorious in races that were not initially expected to be competitive.

In her victory speech, Hinojosa told her supporters: “I am a daughter of the Rio Grande Valley, where the people embody the work ethic and values of our great state, where no one would have imagined that one day, a little girl from the RGV would stand before you here as the next governor of the greatest state, Texas. But God had a plan, and the people of Texas had a plan, too.”

Acton in Ohio, Hinojosa in Texas, Blackburn in Tennessee, Amy Klobuchar in Minnesota, Helena Foulkes in Rhode Island and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia picked up governorships currently held by men.

Georgia voters led the historic night with an early victory for Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and adviser to former President Joe Biden, who will become the first Black female governor in U.S. history.

In her victory speech Tuesday night, Bottoms quoted the 1971 song “If I Were Your Woman.”

“Georgia, I have said over the past few days: If I were your woman,” she told supporters. “Well, now I am your woman, and here is what I will do: I will never, ever, ever stop loving you. Thank you, Georgia, for electing me as your governor.”

In Maine, Hannah Pingree was projected to win the governor’s race, keeping a woman in the highest statewide office after Janet Mills’ two terms.

Similarly, in Michigan, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson was projected to keep the Governor’s Mansion in Democratic hands, succeeding Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. In Massachusetts, New York and Arizona, Maura Healey, Kathy Hochul and Katie Hobbs were re-elected.

Several races — including one in Oregon — remained uncalled close to 2 a.m. ET. But that race also had two female major-party nominees competing.

The previous record for female governors serving at once was 14, a mark that was reached briefly last year and achieved again and sustained in the next year, after Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger and New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, both Democrats, were sworn in following 2025 election wins.

World.title: Mississippi Senate race is toss-up, with margin of under 100 votes
World.content:
Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved Wednesday morning, with Democrat Scott Colom mounting a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

With 96% of the vote in, just a few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State.

Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge, and could deliver Democrats yet another victory.

Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races Tuesday night, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. With more than four flips of GOP-held seats, Democrats secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority.

Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost of living and health care issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.

Mr. Trump won Mississippi by 20 points in 2024, and the state hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.

Speaking to supporters in the wee hours of the morning on Wednesday, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction."

"We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."

The unresolved race in Mississippi comes as Alaska's Senate race is also outstanding, leaving the size of Democrats' majority up in the air.

World.title: Trump asking advisers if Hegseth should go, sources say
World.content:
Washington — President Trump has been asking advisers around him and on the phone whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should stay in his job, following Republicans' catastrophic losses Tuesday night, multiple sources familiar with the matter tell CBS News.

Some White House aides have predicted some of the blame for GOP midterm losses will be trained on Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, who both played big roles in guidance on the Iran war.

Still, other sources said the president hasn't decided to replace Hegseth. Before the election, Democrats were already trying to impeach Hegseth, and the likelihood of an impeachment effort could increase with Democrats holding strong majorities in both chambers.

Vice President JD Vance is blaming the war for the GOP defeat. "The reason we lost is the war," he said in a lengthy post on X Wednesday morning.

One source told CBS News that GOP Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is being floated as a possible replacement for Hegseth, arguing DeSantis could go through Senate confirmation in the lame-duck period and then take the post when his term as governor expires Jan. 5.

Asked for comment about reports that Hegseth's future as defense secretary, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement that Mr. Trump "has full confidence in Secretary Hegseth." In the statement, Kelly also praised the military operations in Iran and Venezuela and Hegseth's efforts to reverse the Biden Pentagon's prioritizing of "DEI and woke ideology."

World.title: Ukraine says "insane attack" on aid center may have killed 70
World.content:
Kyiv — The death toll from a Russian missile strike on a Ukrainian aid distribution center climbed to 40, President Zelenskyy said in a Wednesday post on social media. Zelenskyy said Russia dropped nine bombs on an old school being used to distribute humanitarian aid in Ukraine's southeast Zaporizhzhia region on Monday.

"They first struck people who had come to receive humanitarian aid, and then first responders and police officers who arrived at the scene," Zelenskyy wrote, noting that rescue efforts were still ongoing Wednesday afternoon, and "more than 30 people may still be under the rubble."

Russia's Defense Ministry said a strike in the area targeted Ukraine's military, and it claimed that as many as 25 Ukrainian service members were killed. Russia denies deliberately targeting civilians, despite strikes regularly hitting apartment buildings and other civilian infrastructure.

A view of the destruction from Russian airstrikes on Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region Nov. 2, 2026, as the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry said Russian forces repeatedly struck a school where local residents regularly gathered to receive humanitarian aid. UKRAINIAN STATE EMERGENCY SERVICE/Anadolu/Getty

On Tuesday, Russia launched one of its largest attacks of the year on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, hitting facilities in 10 different regions, according to Ukraine's energy ministry.

The attacks affected the Ukrainian capital's water supply, with Kyiv residents losing running water in their homes for more than 16 hours. Kyivvodokanal, the city's water utility, said water supply and sewage pumping stations in Kyiv resumed operations on Wednesday afternoon.

Russian and Ukrainian representatives will visit the White House Friday to meet with Melania Trump, after the first lady brokered a temporary ceasefire last week to allow for civilian evacuations and humanitarian aid to move into Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine, officials in both Kyiv and Moscow said.

Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and Davyd Arakhamiia, the leader of Zelenskyy's parliamentary faction, will attend the meeting, according to Ukrainian newspaper Ukrinform.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova planned to represent Russia at the meeting, but that visa complications could affect their travel.

Zelenskyy announced Wednesday that the U.S. first lady was to receive Ukraine's highest award for women, the Order of Princess Olga, 1st Class, for her role in brokering the limited ceasefire.

He also promised a Ukrainian response to the Russian attack on the Zaporizhzhia aid center, and a day after Democrats took control of both houses of the U.S. Congress, he renewed his plea for more missile interceptors and other key military support.

"Unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack. But it, like thousands upon thousands of other war crimes Russia has committed against Ukraine and Ukrainians, demands a strong response," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "Evil always goes further if it is left unanswered. We count on a response – Ukraine needs air defense support right now. I am grateful to the partners who are taking such steps."

World.title: Vance blames Iran conflict for GOP defeats: "The reason we lost is the war"
World.content:
Washington — Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that he believes Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress because of voters' opposition to the war in Iran and suggested that the conflict may not have been worth the cost of losing the GOP's hold on the Senate.

In his first public comments since Democrats' rout of Republicans in the midterm elections, Vance said Republicans must be honest about the impact the war had on their campaigns in order to determine the best path forward for the party.

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote in a post on X. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

The vice president said many voters who backed President Trump and him in the 2024 presidential contest cast their ballots for Democrats in 2026 for four reasons: to end the war with Iran, focus on the cost of living and inflation, put America first and change the U.S. relationship to Israel.

"Our voters showed up," Vance wrote. "And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats."

The vice president highlighted Fox News host Rachel Campos-Duffy's call to reach a "diplomatic resolution" to the conflict with Iran, saying that her recommendation was "sound." Vance spent much of the spring leading U.S. negotiators in talks aimed at ending the conflict and reached an ill-fated agreement with Iran to halt the fighting that soon fell apart.

In his post, the vice president said an unnamed data analyst told him that voters who backed him and Mr. Trump in 2024 were angry and would vote for Democrats in the midterms. He said that analysis "looks prophetic now."

"Our voters did show up," he wrote. "In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026. "

Vance also said it's likely the GOP's economic messaging "wasn't sharp enough" in the closing weeks of the campaign.

"I remain hopeful about our country," he said. "To the people who are pissed off and want to say, 'II told you so': you're right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let's take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country."

Democrats are expected to hold at least 54 seats in the Senate following wins in 10 of 11 battleground states. The Senate elections in Alaska and Mississippi are unresolved and rated as toss-ups. CBS News estimates Democrats will control between 251 and 268 seats in the House when all votes are counted.

Mr. Trump launched the war in Iran in late February and had pledged at the time that it would last only four to five weeks. But it has since stretched into its eighth month, leading to a spike in gas prices.

In an interview with Fox News on Tuesday, the president suggested that the war with Iran was partially to blame for Republicans' losses, but he said "people understand the importance of what I've done."

Still, Mr. Trump has repeatedly defended his decision to go to war with Iran and told CBS News on Tuesday that Tehran must not be able to develop a nuclear weapon.

The president said the war will end "when I say it ends."

The U.S. launched limited defensive strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday. Twenty-three U.S. service members have been killed during the conflict, and 865 have been wounded, according to the Defense Department.

World.title: Frantic 911 call from hero dad who killed school shooter released
World.content:
The armed father who was hailed for his heroic actions during a deadly shooting at his daughters' elementary school in Oregon frantically called authorities before he went after the shooter, according to a recording of the 911 call released Tuesday.

"Someone's at the school, at my daughters' school with a gun. I have a gun, and I will shoot them right now if I have to," 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco told the 911 dispatcher as the Oct. 15 shooting was beginning to unfold.

Giamanco's two daughters were inside Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, when he happened to drive by the school and see the shooter begin his rampage. Giamanco's girls survived the attack.

The shooter killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher. Giamanco killed the 16-year-old shooter after rushing into the school with his handgun.

Kaylub Giamanco, who fatally shot an attacker at Silver Rail Elementary School, poses for a portrait Oct. 22, 2026, in Bend, Oregon. Saskia Hatvany/Oregon Public Broadcasting via AP

The roughly 80-second-long recording released Tuesday captures the initial chaos surrounding the shooting, which started when the gunman shot at a vehicle. Giamanco previously told Oregon Public Broadcasting he went for his gun in a panic after he saw the shooter throw his weapon over the school's fence and then climb after it.

Giamanco's first words on the 911 call were, "Oh my God."

After Giamanco described the situation to the dispatcher, the dispatcher asked exactly what happened.

"Silver Rail Elementary! Silver Rail Elementary!" Giamanco told her.

Oregon school shooting 911 call Kaylub Giamanco called 911 before he rushed inside Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, and killed the shooter. Your browser does not support the audio element.

The dispatcher asked Giamanco for his phone number and then if he knew who the shooter was.

"This is my daughters' school. I'm about to go kill this kid," Giamanco said.

The dispatcher asked again if he knew the shooter's identity.

"No, I don't f---ing know, I was just driving," Giamanco said.

Giamanco then told the dispatcher the shooter was inside the school. The dispatcher asked where. Giamanco again gave the name of the school. When the dispatcher asked where the shooter was located in the school, he provided additional details.

"God d--- it, they're f---ing shooting people. Come on!" Giamanco said.

The call ends shortly after the dispatcher asked for a description of the shooter.

"Sir, I need you to tell me what's going on," the dispatcher said. "We have help en route."

World.title: Back in the majority, Democrats have plans for a long list of Trump investigations
World.content:
Back in the majority, Democrats have plans for a long list of Trump investigations

toggle caption i Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images

Midterms coverage: Live results | Takeaways | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democrats won big in the midterm elections, but with President Trump still in the White House, the next Congress is unlikely to see much major legislation signed into law.

Instead, expect to see a lot more oversight. With public corruption and failing leadership as two of the top issues concerning voters, congressional Democrats have an ambitious agenda of investigations planned for their return to power in the House and Senate.

Their new majorities mean that they will have at their disposal the full investigatory powers of the Congress, which include the ability to subpoena records for review and compel individuals to testify before lawmakers.

Sponsor Message

Rep. Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is expected to become chair of the House Oversight committee, put it bluntly in a statement: "LAWYER UP."

The Democratic Party has a long list of investigative targets. According to conversations with Democratic House and Senate committee staffers, here are some areas the party is likely to prioritize in its oversight work.

Jeffrey Epstein

Among Democrats' primary targets: the administration's handling of — and connections to — the scandals of late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Bipartisan congressional action forced the Trump administration to release extensive documents tied to federal investigations of Epstein's crimes and other alleged offenses, though Democrats maintain that many of the records were improperly redacted or withheld from the public. They also say that the Justice Department has worked to shield Trump from damaging allegations — claims that the department's leadership has denied.

In the new Congress, lawmakers are expected to probe ties between Epstein and other powerful figures, including the president himself, which they say is part of an effort to secure accountability for victims of Epstein's crimes.

In connection with an October report, Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said, "Donald Trump says he knew Jeffrey Epstein 'just like everybody in Palm Beach knew him.' Not exactly."

Sponsor Message

"Evidence involving 11 women tells a completely different and far more damning story about their relationship and the abuse of young women and girls that took place in their network," Raskin said.

The president, for his part, has long denied any wrongdoing related to Epstein and has maintained that their relationship ended before the disgraced financier was indicted for soliciting prostitution in 2016.

Public corruption

Democrats also plan to continue their own investigations into what they describe as efforts by administration officials to advance the financial interests of the president, his family, themselves and close allies.

In particular, Democrats highlight the president's continued business interests, including Truth Social, a number of cryptocurrency projects and overseas projects involving his sons and powerful foreign investors.

toggle caption i Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

Garcia on the House Oversight Committee, has gone further, linking the high cost of living to politicians on both sides of the aisle acting in their own self-interest rather than the interest of the American public.

"Millions of dollars in dark money are flowing throughout our political system. Some members of Congress may be trading stocks based on information the public doesn't have. The revolving door between the government and lobbying for large corporations keeps spinning," he wrote last month in an MS Now opinion piece. "Americans are dealing with a cost-of-living crisis, and these abuses of power are making it worse. All the while, the wealthiest people in our country are richer than ever."

Immigration

Trump returned to office promising a stricter approach to immigration in the United States. But public support for his deportation agenda has cratered in the wake of a number of high-profile incidents involving federal immigration enforcement personnel, including the killing of two U.S. citizens in Minnesota this year.

While in the minority, Democrats have publicly documented hundreds of incidents of alleged abuse and misconduct by immigration agents and will continue that work in the new term. They are expected to hold hearings on incidents of violence, which have largely gone without congressional oversight in the first two years of the president's second term.

Sponsor Message

Democrats held a field hearing in Austin, Texas, in October on shootings by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said following the hearing that "ICE is a lawless, rogue agency that is causing generational trauma in communities across the country. House Democrats today are doing the oversight work that Republicans refuse to do — and we will continue to do everything possible to protect our communities from Trump's mass deportation agenda."

Public health

In June, Democrats released a report documenting how they believe that the Trump administration has undermined public health infrastructure and U.S. scientific research into chronic and deadly diseases. That work will continue in the new year, with a particular focus on Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Executive power

Trump's muscular use of executive power has been unrestrained by the Republican congressional majority. That is expected to change.

Committee staffers indicate that the president's pet projects — remodeling the White House's East Wing, building a monumental arch, renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, shuttering the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, paving the White House's Rose Garden, among others — will face robust congressional oversight.

toggle caption i Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

The projects are entwined in a larger constitutional fight over the appropriations process: Congress has the sole authority to decide how taxpayer dollars are spent, and the White House has repeatedly disregarded its declarations and rescinded billions of dollars in congressionally approved spending.

Iran war

Constitutional authorities delegated to Congress will also take center stage in Democrats' U.S.-Iran war oversight. The legislature has the sole authority to declare war, and presidents are required to seek authorization for the use of military force, something that has not happened for any of the Trump administration's military campaigns this term. Democrats also plan to press Pentagon officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, on the war's cost to the American public.

Sponsor Message

Even before the Democrats take control, a House impeachment vote on Hegseth could come during the lame-duck session.

More war powers votes — efforts to force the president to end the conflict, some of which have attracted limited bipartisan support — are also expected. While previous war powers votes have passed, the votes are largely symbolic and do not carry the weight of law.

Elon Musk

toggle caption i Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Technology titan Elon Musk has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican politics but has lately drawn the ire of Democrats after interruptions to his satellite internet service provider stymied Ukraine's military operations against Russia.

"We will ensure that the 120th Congress will closely scrutinize federal funding awarded to Mr. Musk's businesses, including whether these companies meet their contractual obligations, and whether adequate safeguards exist against political interference, arbitrary service restrictions, and misuse of federal resources," a group of Silicon Valley House Democrats wrote in a letter to the White House in October.

There could also be investigations into the Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency effort that decimated the government workforce in the first year of Trump's second term but failed to deliver on the promised trillion dollars in cost savings. It has remained a focus of House Oversight Committee Democrats during their time in the minority.

World.title: Abdul El-Sayed welcomes Trump's plan to cut Israel aid, calls for end to arms sales
World.content:
Abdul El-Sayed welcomes Trump's plan to cut Israel aid, calls for end to arms sales

toggle caption i Salwan Georges/Getty Images

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history in Michigan, defeating Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate as his party reclaimed control of Congress.

The 42-year-old former public health official campaigned on lowering costs, Medicare for All and getting corporate money out of politics. Rogers, backed by President Trump, repeatedly attacked El-Sayed over his Muslim faith and opposition to U.S. military aid to Israel.

But Israel and the war in Gaza became a defining fault line in the race. Haley Stevens, whom El-Sayed defeated in the Democratic primary, endorsed Rogers just days before the election amid a bitter dispute over Israel.

After a campaign marked by heated disagreements over Israel, El-Sayed now finds himself on the same side of an issue as Trump.

The president announced plans to end roughly $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel by the end of the year, though he offered no details on how the cuts would work.

Sponsor Message

Speaking to Morning Edition after his victory, El-Sayed welcomed the proposal.

"I think the president is actually right on this policy," he said. "I'd also like to see us stop selling weaponry that gets used to do the worst things, including genocide and apartheid, to Israel."

The U.S. provides Israel with $3.8 billion in annual military aid under an agreement that runs through 2028.

His argument goes beyond Israel. El-Sayed also questioned U.S. military support for Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Pakistan, saying American tax dollars should be spent at home.

Winning Michigan's Senate seat, however, doesn't mean every division within his party has disappeared.

During a visit to Michigan before the election, NPR's Michel Martin heard concerns about El-Sayed from some Jewish and Black voters. Asked whether he still had work to do to win their support, El-Sayed said the election results challenged that narrative.

"There's always more work to do. There's always more to build. There's always more conversations to have," he said.

Listen to the full interview live by clicking on the blue button above.

The digital version was edited by Treye Green.

World.title: The world is reacting to the Democrats' sweeping midterm elections victory
World.content:
The world is reacting to the Democrats' sweeping midterm elections victory

toggle caption i Allison Robbert/AP

One color dominates international headlines about the U.S. midterm election results. French newspaper Libération called the Democrats' win "une vague bleue," or blue wave, Britain's Daily Mail dubbed it a "historic blue tsunami," and The Times of India's headline ran "midterm blues for Trump."

Countries at war were also watching closely, with Ukrainian newspaper The Kyiv Independent's online headline hopeful: "Democrats seize control of Congress in blow to Trump, potential boost for Ukraine."

Russia had a different take. Rossiyskaya Gazeta, the state-run daily newspaper, suggested the results would in fact be a blow to Ukraine, which has firm support from the European Union. "Brussels, brace yourself. After the Republicans' defeat, Trump's wrath will fall on Europe," read the headline.

Sponsor Message

Iran's Tehran Times said "Call it Operation Midterms Hammer" — a play on the U.S. military's Operation Midnight Hammer strikes against Iran in June 2025. Since the United States and Israel renewed their war against Iran this February, the fallout has pushed up the price of oil and other goods, becoming a major election campaign issue. The article ran a cartoon of a man slamming a mini-Trump with a hammer in a game of whack-a-mole.

In Israel, which just held its own parliamentary elections last week, headlines focused on what the Democrats' victory means for the U.S. support of the Jewish state and its war in Gaza.

The Times of Israel ran a headline focusing on Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's triumph in the U.S. Senate race in Michigan, saying "Anti-Israel El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race, pledges no money for 'apartheid, genocide.'" A headline in Israel's Haaretz read: "Abdul El-Sayed Shows Opposition to Israel Is No Barrier to Winning Battleground States."

toggle caption i Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

Newspapers in U.S. neighbors Canada and Mexico, meanwhile, noted the results were a rebuke and setback for Trump.

Some foreign politicians celebrate, others keep silent

International leaders tend to shy away from commenting directly on the results of U.S. midterm elections, as opposed to presidential races when they routinely congratulate the winner. However, this time several have made public statements.

Sponsor Message

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that with Trump accepting the midterms results, the focus can turn to ending wars and bringing down prices.

"The world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living," Burnham told reporters Wednesday. "I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia, these are the things we have to focus on now."

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has an acrimonious relationship with Trump, was forthright in his response.

"Yesterday, American society voted against policies that only impoverish. Against hate. Against machismo. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites," Sánchez wrote on social media.

In South Africa, where diplomatic relations with the U.S. are at an all-time low after Trump falsely accused the government of persecuting its white minority, President Cyril Ramaphosa said "The people of America have spoken."

Ramaphosa made the comments as he cast his own ballot in South Africa's municipal elections Wednesday, adding: "I do think that this is going to introduce a new era in world relations. … We're hoping that on a bilateral basis there will be a coming together of minds."

A senior Russia diplomat suggested the Democratic Party's return to power in both houses of Congress bode ill for U.S.-Russian relations. "The approach of the activist wing of the Democratic Party towards Russia is extremely negative. There's nothing new in that," said Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov in an interview with the state RIA-Novosti news service. Ryabkov also signaled there would be no grand shifts in Russian foreign policy as a result.

In Germany, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius congratulated Democrats on an "historic victory," adding that Berlin's commitment to cooperating with the administration in Washington remains unchanged. He stressed that Berlin will be reaching out to both Democrats and Republicans.

toggle caption i Vahid Salemi/AP

Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere said the results are a "powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters." Speaking to Reuters, Stoere said "voices are now emerging in American politics that are closer to us than the president and the administration have stood for, for example on climate and environment, and in foreign policy and development aid policy."

Sponsor Message

A spokeswoman for China's Foreign Ministry told a daily press conference that the midterm elections "are an internal affair of the United States." She added that "China is willing to continue working with the U.S. to … strengthen communication, properly manage differences, expand cooperation, and build a constructive, strategically stable China-U.S. relationship based on the principles of respect, fairness, and reciprocity."

Japan's top government spokesman, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara, told a news conference that Japan's alliance with the U.S. remains essential for global peace and stability, regardless of the outcome of midterm elections.

The alliance "remains the cornerstone of Japan's foreign and security policy" and is crucial to "maximizing its national interests" amid an increasingly volatile and uncertain global situation," he added.

Middle East reacts

Iran's Parliament Speaker and top negotiator Mohammad ‌Baqer Ghalibaf commented on X: "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message. If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."

For Israel, the U.S. midterm results fall during a time of political uncertainty, amid coalition-building talks after Trump's ally, incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, lost his parliamentary majority in Oct. 27 Israeli elections. "In some ways Netanyahu lost two elections in the last week," said Israel-American analyst Mairav Zonstein.

Netanyahu's rivals seized on the midterm results. One Israeli opposition leader, Yair Golan, said the U.S. results reveal "just how toxic Netanyahu is among both Democrats and Republicans." Another, Yair Lapid, said the U.S. results "eliminate any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu."

Laura Cain in London, Charles Maynes in Moscow, Esme Nicholson in Berlin, Lauren Frayer in Tel Aviv, Hadeel Al-Shalchi in Istanbul, Aya Batrawy in Dubai and Anthony Kuhn in Seoul contributed reporting.

World.title: Democrats seize full control of Congress. And, which candidates made history last night
World.content:
Democrats seize full control of Congress. And, which candidates made history last night

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Democrats have gained full control of Congress for the first time since 2023, flipping both the House and Senate with significant wins in deep red states. Abdul El-Sayed defeated Mike Rogers in Michigan, and Troy Jackson defeated Susan Collins in Maine, winning their states' closely watched Senate seats. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, ending more than 30 years of Republican control, while Democratic state Rep. James Talarico won the U.S. Senate race. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton became the first Democratic senator elected in nearly a century. A record number of candidates endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America were elected to the House, growing the organization's presence on Capitol Hill. Nine states also made history with their gubernatorial picks. Take a look at how key demographics voted.

Here are 6 midterm takeaways from NPR's senior political correspondent Domenico Montanaro:

toggle caption i Cliff Owen/AP

All the signs were pointing in Democrats' direction heading into election night. But nothing indicated quite this level of a romp.

Sponsor Message

President Trump wanted this election to be about him. It was and that hurt Republicans: Trump was historically unpopular. People were frustrated with the economy and the war, and it hurt the GOP. It turns out when you wage the kind of war that you said you wouldn't get into — that drags on, raises gas prices and piles on people who were already feeling the pinch, don't be surprised when you pay the price. Republicans tried to insulate themselves with redistricting, but it didn't work: Trump strongly encouraged conservative-led states to redistrict — but it backfired. There was always the possibility that weakening safe districts could make them more competitive and that happened. It's a true cautionary tale of the "dummymander." Latinos are a true swing group in America now: Trump only lost Latinos by 5 points in 2024. In this election, they sided with Democrats by 27 points. The economy and deportation tactics were big reasons why. In a real indictment of the Trump deportation policies, the voter poll found 59% overall said they disapproved of ICE. Is Texas — and other red states — in play for Democrats or was this election a giant asterisk? Democrats won in a lot of red states. The party has needed to show it can win in red and rural areas. They did that this time. But will that last, or is it a Trump-sized asterisk? The results of this year's elections don't mean the country is enamored with the Democratic Party: The party is still unpopular and fissures within their coalition will be laid bare over the next several months in the 2028 presidential primaries. They'll have to be careful politically with how they approach leadership with the opportunity they've been handed. The polls got the direction right. If anything, they underestimated Democratic support: For a decade, polls have underestimated Republican support. In these elections, that was not the case. It's important to understand that it's hard to poll when the country has been going through as significant a political realignment as it has been in the Trump era.

Sponsor Message

President Trump lashed out early on as results showed Democrats ahead in many key races, but later congratulated the Democrats and said more than once that he would respect the outcome of the elections.



🎧 The president positioned himself as the central figure in the midterm elections, relying on his personality and appeal to supporters to counter low approval ratings and economic concerns. NPR's Franco Ordoñez tells Up First that this strategy made it more difficult for vulnerable candidates to distance themselves from him. Ordoñez says he expects there to be a confrontational relationship between Trump and the Democrats, especially as they prepare to investigate him and his family.

After the Democratic victory in the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the first Black lawmaker to be elected Speaker. Last night, Jeffries said, "We understand as House Democrats that we need to deliver dramatic change." With a Democratic majority, they'll have the chance to exert more influence in the legislative branch.



🎧 The large Democratic margins in the House and Senate will serve as a check on the White House, NPR's Barbara Sprunt says. A Democratic Senate majority will provide massive roadblocks for the president's confirmation of the future cabinet and judicial nominees. In the House, Sprunt says to expect numerous investigations. Jeffries plans to hold those involved in corruption accountable, and the House will have subpoena power to compel witnesses to testify. Democrats have a list of targets in mind already, but Sprunt says the party is cautious about pursuing a third impeachment of Trump, because it doesn't support their argument that they have more to offer than just being anti-Trump party.

Life advice

Annelise Capossela for NPR

About 1 in 20 Americans experience seasonal affective disorder (SAD), and it typically lasts for nearly 40% of the year. If you're dealing with SAD, you might feel sluggish, depressed and lose interest in activities you once enjoyed. You might also find yourself oversleeping, overeating and gaining weight. As winter approaches, NPR's Life Kit offers advice on recognizing these feelings and finding ways to boost your mood and energy.

Sponsor Message

💙 Women are more vulnerable to SAD, and the condition is more common in the Northern Hemisphere.

💙 Some people need more light. Experts often recommend SAD lamps, which are significantly brighter than typical indoor lighting.

💙 Stop eating three hours before bedtime to help your body rest. Eating within a consistent 10- to 12-hour window signals your body about the time of day, no matter what else is happening.

💙 Exercising during the day helps your body recognize its daily rhythm, keeping you alert when needed and allowing for rest in the evening.

💙 Try to reduce stress by decorating a room with bright colors, seeing a therapist to discuss your feelings, or trying meditation for relaxation.

For more guidance on how to get through SAD, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Picture show

toggle caption i Gabby Hiestand Salgado/KYUK

Typhoon Halong severely impacted small Native villages in Western Alaska last fall, destroying infrastructure and displacing more than a thousand people. A year later, many remain displaced. In Kipnuk — a village of under 200 homes — dozens of houses were swept off their foundations. The community is now mostly scattered across Alaska, and some have relocated far from their ancestral lands. Climate change increases the vulnerability of towns like Kipnuk to future storms. While most residents wish to rebuild the village in a safer location, current FEMA funding only allows for restoring what was damaged. See these photos of the town now, as its people continue to pick up the pieces.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Yuri Cortez/AFP via Getty Images

A new study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences shows that jumping spiders meet all sleep criteria and show signs of entering a rapid eye movement (REM) sleep cycle. Ancient Egyptian mummies were once marketed as medicine. Archaeologists are using chemistry to better understand how they were made. New World screwworm cases have increased to 99 since June, as the outbreak accelerates across Texas, New Mexico and Arizona.

Sponsor Message

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: 6 takeaways from Democrats' big wave on election night
World.content:
6 takeaways from Democrats' big wave on election night

toggle caption i Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

All the signs were pointing in Democrats' direction heading into election night.

But nothing indicated quite this level of a romp.

Democrats won the House and the Senate, and while that outcome was always a possibility, the depth and breadth of the Democratic victories were jaw-dropping.

Tuesday night was a reminder that the pendulum of American politics continues to swing, and politics is never permanent.

Here are six takeaways about what happened, why it happened and what it all means going forward:

1. President Trump wanted this election to be about him. It was, and that hurt Republicans

toggle caption i Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

President Trump's unpopularity has been a glaring warning sign for the Republican Party heading into election night. Since the Iran war, Trump's approval ratings slid from 48% to as low as 36% in an average of the polls.

Sponsor Message

A whopping 62% of voters in this election disapproved of his job as president, according to the voter poll commissioned by the broadcast networks and the Associated Press, which mixes pre-Election Day polling of early voters and Election Day exit polls.

Three-quarters of voters said they are either angry or dissatisfied with the direction of the country. A plurality said the economy was the most important issue, and two-thirds said Trump's policies have made economic conditions worse.

In addition to the economy, corruption rose as an issue in the last several months. The voter poll showed that 62% said Trump prioritizes his own interests more than the country's.

For all of the things that will be written about this election, the bottom line is that Trump waged the kind of war he said he wouldn't get into — one that is dragging on, raising gas prices and piling on people who were already feeling the pinch — and now he is paying the price.

If Trump was supposed to be the kingmaker in the 2028 Republican presidential primary, think again. These midterms will have heavy reverberations for the presidential election. It will likely mean more GOP candidates will enter the race, and they will be more likely to present a wider view of what the direction of the party could be — rather than simply trying to carry the Trump torch.

Sponsor Message

2. Republicans tried to insulate themselves with redistricting, but it didn't work

The fundamentals of this election seemed to mirror the 2006 midterms amid the Iraq war — the last time the Democrats won back both the House and Senate. Democratic gains in this election, though, were seen as possibly being limited by structural disadvantages — primarily through Republican efforts to tilt the playing by redistricting.

Trump strongly encouraged conservative-led states to redistrict over the last year, hoping to gain more Republican seats in the House — but that backfired, particularly in South Texas. There was always the possibility that incidentally weakening safe districts could make them competitive. Now that that's happened, it's a true cautionary tale of the "dummymander."

3. Latinos are a true swing group in America now

The reason Texas Republicans' efforts to gerrymander didn't pay off is because Latinos did not vote in this election the way they did in the 2024 presidential election.

In 2024, Trump only lost the group by 5 points. It moved toward Trump at the time, in large measure because they were upset with inflation and believed Trump would bring down prices.

Not only did that not happen over the last two years, Trump also angered many in the community because of aggressive deportation tactics that targeted more than just hardened criminals, as Trump promised.

In a real indictment of the Trump deportation policies, roughly 60% of respondents in the voter poll said they disapproved of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE. Sixty-eight percent of Hispanics disapproved of how ICE is handling its job.

To be clear, Latinos are not a monolith. Latinos in South Florida have different backgrounds and priorities than those in South Texas or those in California or New York. But the fact that the largest-growing group in the country swung strongly away from the president and Republicans makes them very important electorally — a true swing group in the country that is underrepresented at the polls and has a lot of power.

Sponsor Message

4. Are Texas and other red states in play for Democrats, or was this election a giant asterisk?

toggle caption i Brandon Bell/Getty Images

Democrats won in a lot of red states. That is important for the party heading into the 2028 presidential election. To have a real chance at expanding the presidential map, they need to figure out how to appeal to red-state and rural voters. They showed in this election they can do that, but they won't have Trump as their rocket fuel in this next presidential election.

The Lone Star State, for example, has been a majority-minority state for a while, and that demography had previously given Democrats false hope. So is Texas the new Georgia, or will it revert to its conservative roots?

The breadth of Democratic victories in Texas in this midterm is undeniable. They won up and down the ballot — Democrat James Talarico won by roughly 12 points, or 1.1 million votes, the first time Texas is sending a Democrat to the Senate since 1988; incoming Gov. Gina Hinojosa won by 7 percentage points, or almost 700,000 votes; they flipped two congressional districts, both of which were won by Trump in 2024 by at least 14 points; they won lieutenant governor; attorney general; railroad commissioner and more.

As they say in Texas, they beat 'em like a rented mule. But are Democrats renting power in the state or is it something bigger? There is going to be a lot of money spent in 2028 to see if the blue gains in Texas are more permanent. And a lot is on the line, because Texas has 40 electoral votes, and putting it in play legitimately for Democrats would reshape the electoral map in a way that would only be rivaled by the earthquake of a shift that was California going for Democrats starting in 1992. (Yes, California used to be a reliably Republican state, going for the GOP in all but one election between 1952 and 1988.)

Sponsor Message

By the way, a bonus lesson from this election is that money isn't everything. Republicans spent more than $413 million on the Texas Senate race — and lost.

5. The results of this year's elections don't mean the country is enamored with the Democratic Party

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

Democrats have the opportunity to show they can authentically represent their states and try to hold onto these inroads they made in lots of red states and districts.

They were handed the keys to Congress, and people are going to expect results. New York Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer, the once majority leader who may want to be in the job again, victoriously promised overnight that "relief is on the way."

But how? Even if Democrats have serious policy ideas to help fix economic problems in the country, they can't wave a magic wand. They won't have a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate, and they are unlikely to have an eager negotiating partner in congressional Republicans or Trump. Just before midnight on election night, Trump put out an image on his social media platform of a big red hat with the word "VETO" on it.

So Democrats are in danger of overpromising and underdelivering, which has become all too common in politics, and leads to voters becoming jaded. Democrats have to be careful with their messaging and how they govern. There will undoubtedly be more investigations and oversight of the Trump administration. But how far will they go? Another Trump impeachment attempt, for example, could be politically fraught.

No doubt, the GOP was soundly rejected Tuesday night, but Democrats aren't much better liked. The voter poll showed Republicans underwater with a 41% favorable and 59% unfavorable rating. Democrats were 47%-53%. Democrats had lower approval ratings earlier in Trump's second term, mostly because of disaffected Democrats. They rallied together to win in these midterms, but fissures on the left are simmering below the surface and are about to become far more apparent in the 2028 presidential Democratic primaries.

6. The polls got the direction right. If anything, they underestimated Democratic support

For a decade, polls have underestimated Republican support. In these elections, that was not the case. In fact, in some places they underestimated Democratic support.

Sponsor Message

For example, the national generic congressional ballot — the question of who people would vote for if the election was held the day of the poll — favored Democrats by about 8 percentage points. The voter poll looks like it turned out to be at least +18.

It's important to understand that it's hard to poll when the country has been going through as significant a political realignment as it has been in the Trump era.

World.title: Review: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is superb, streamlined and safe
World.content:
Review: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is superb, streamlined and safe

toggle caption i Nintendo

With its tale of an idyllic world despoiled by the lust for power, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time feels as relevant today as it did in 1998. Nintendo's new remake, out Thursday on the Switch 2, enshrines its place in the gaming canon for generations to come. But despite its stupendous production values and painstaking details, the game left me feeling oddly bereft.

Perhaps I should have expected as much. Ocarina of Time weaponizes nostalgia even within its narrative, as the protagonist Link ventures to save his post-apocalyptic world as an adult after first working through it as a kid. You'll uncover old characters enduring new catastrophes. You'll try to rescue everyone you meet. You'll strive to bring things back to how they were before — no, better than they were before.

Sponsor Message

Seven years stretch between Link's childhood and adult adventures. 28 years yawn between the remake and the original's release. Both in and out of the game, Ocarina of Time makes us yearn for an idealized past.

How it plays

Decent remakes evoke how you remember a game rather than re-create dated controls and chunky graphics. In myriad small ways, Nintendo has brought Ocarina of Time up to contemporary standards while (mostly) preserving its soul.

toggle caption i Nintendo

I miss the thoughtfully-composed camera angles from the original, but quickly got used to the over-the-shoulder camera the remake employs (though I was irked that it abandoned the top-down view when you sneak into Hyrule Castle). The new jump and sprint buttons made navigating the world feel more natural. Combat's smoother too, though it's still not easy to switch between targeted enemies (unlike modern third-person games like Elden Ring , where you can toggle between foes by simply flicking the right stick).

You can, thankfully, swap between items in a quick menu — the same system introduced to the series in 2023's Tears of the Kingdom and continued in 2024's Echoes of Wisdom . It's still not as fast as I'd wish (I'd have preferred a customizable wheel), but I vastly prefer it to constantly pausing to access my equipment. It made it easy to change my strategy on the fly. I'd often cast Naryu's Love and deploy Bombchus, for example, where before I'd mostly stick to the Longshot and Bow.

toggle caption i Nintendo

If you get stuck, a new "Threads of Time" quest log can point you in the right direction (though you'll likely still need to look up a guide for the convoluted Biggoron Sword quest !). And yes, the notoriously frustrating Water Temple is much more tolerable this time around. But mind your rupees! Inflation's hit Hyrule. While wallets can now carry double the cash that they used to, Great Fairy upgrades are no longer free. They can cost up to 500 rupees!

Sponsor Message

How it feels

It's the remake's aesthetic changes that stand out most. The game's astonishingly ornate textures can jar with its cartoony proportions. Ninety-eight percent of the time the translation is a clear upgrade, but other times it leads straight into the uncanny valley (Nabooru looks bizarrely yassified with huge red lips and golden eye-shadow, for example).

toggle caption i Nintendo

The animations are much more extensive — so much so that the new cutscenes, particularly in the game's opening hours, can drag down the pacing. The game also fleshes out unspoken implications and flattens rough edges. Mido, the jerk who blocks your progress in Kokiri Forest, has been subtly rewritten from bully to overbearing but well-intentioned boss. Kaepora Gaebora, the talking owl who guides your path, won't repeat himself at the slightest provocation. Navi, your fairy companion, no longer chimes in with an incessant "Hey! Listen!"

Such changes risk eroding the game's character. Still, it ultimately stands as one of the most faithful adaptations I've seen — less than the Demon's Souls remake but far more than the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy or even the Resident Evil 4 remake . It gives me hope that Ocarina of Time's surreal sequel, Majora's Mask, could receive such treatment in the future.

toggle caption i Nintendo

Yet this remake will never eclipse my memories of the first Ocarina of Time. Of course it couldn't — that game helped launch a new 3D era and defined the childhoods of a whole generation. Where once it innovated, now it represents the safest of safe bets .

But by lavishing such attention on an all-time classic — ahead of a Zelda movie next year — Nintendo has ensured it won't go out of style for at least another few decades. I look forward to sharing it with my nephews and, eventually, my own toddling son. As much as I detest how media giants can't seem to move past the hits of yesteryear, some harmonies are worth turning back time for.

World.title: Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House
World.content:
Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House

toggle caption i Alex Wong/Getty Images

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

After helping to deliver a decisive victory for House Democrats in the midterm elections, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., appears all but certain to become the first Black lawmaker to be elected speaker of the House.

Jeffries was elected House minority leader in 2022 and is the first Black politician to lead either party in the House or Senate. As speaker, Jeffries would be second in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president.

His elevation to speaker would represent the pinnacle of a nearly 14-year House tenure, a span that has seen Jeffries rise from a rank-and-file member focused on criminal justice policy to a top party lieutenant under former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then minority leader.

Sponsor Message

It's a rise that has meant securing buy-in from a diverse and often fractious House Democratic caucus — a task that may prove only more challenging as the Democratic Party now looks to make good on its promises to voters.

"This is a change election, and we understand as House Democrats that we need to deliver dramatic change," Jeffries said on Tuesday night. "Things are broken. We need a Congress that puts the American people first."

Criminal justice reform work

Born and raised in Brooklyn, N.Y., Jeffries has represented parts of the borough in Congress since 2013 and served as a leader in both the influential Congressional Black Caucus and the House Democratic caucus.

Before entering politics, Jeffries served as a lawyer in private practice and credits his time helping members of his community through a law school legal clinic as sparking his interest in criminal justice reform.

"I think over time it did inform that if I had the opportunity to go into the practice of law, or eventually public service, that I wanted to do something about the broken criminal justice system," Jeffries said in a 2023 interview with NY1.

He served for six years in the New York State Assembly, where he worked on regulating warrantless stop-and-frisk searches by the New York City Police Department. As a policymaker in Washington during the first Trump administration, Jeffries led the effort to pass the bipartisan First Step Act, which reduced sentences for some drug crimes.

Sponsor Message

That effort required working closely with President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner. He told Time that "to get things done in this town you need a coalition of unusual suspects."

"There was a real partnership [with Kushner] that produced real results," Jeffries said.

The lawmaker faced blowback from some inside his party this year for meeting privately with Kushner, first reported by The New York Times and later confirmed by Jeffries. He later said he took the meeting at Kushner's request to discuss affordability, adding that Democrats intend to hold the administration accountable.

Political identity

Jeffries was once a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and a sponsor of Medicare for All proposals, though he has long drawn skepticism from outside activists from his party's left wing. As speaker, he will have to contend with how to best incorporate, or sideline, a growing flank of Democratic Socialists of America-aligned and far-left members in the legislative process in the new term.

"There will never be a moment where I bend the knee to hard-left democratic socialism," Jeffries told The Atlantic in 2021. "Black progressives do tend to tackle issues first and foremost with an understanding that systemic racism has been in the soil of America for over 400 years."

Though the party's progressive members are as racially diverse as the rest of the caucus, Jeffries points specifically to his race as shaping his views on the drivers of America's systemic inequities.

"Hard-left progressives tend to view the defining problem in America as one that is anchored in class. That is not my experience as a Black man in this country," Jeffries said.

Jeffries also served as an impeachment manager during the Senate trial over Trump's pressure campaign on Ukraine, in which Trump withheld military aid while pushing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to announce investigations into Joe Biden ahead of the 2020 presidential election.

Sponsor Message

Like many elected Democrats, Jeffries has so far refused to commit to pursuing impeachment again in Trump's second term. He told Fox News in April that it was not a top priority for Democrats and in September told ABC that Democrats "haven't ruled anything in and we haven't ruled anything out."

Jeffries has maintained that the primary focus for the new Congress is lowering costs for Americans.

The House will hold a floor vote for speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3.

World.title: Funeral service for soldier killed in CFB Wainwright fire starts in Prince Albert, Sask.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Pte. Shaun Farrell lost his life at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Oct. 17 after a grass fire turned deadly, killing four soldiers and injuring dozens more. On Wednesday, a military service with full honours is being held for Farrell in Prince Albert, Sask.

People have gradually arrived for the military service with full honours in Prince Albert, Sask., for Pte. Shaun Farrell, taking place on Wednesday morning.

Members of the military, Premier Scott Moe and members of the public arrived before the service, as the city and ceremony retain a somber tone.

Farrell, 23, was one of four service members who died at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta on Oct. 17 when a grass fire grew out of control. Another 39 people were injured.

The service is scheduled to begin at 11 a.m. CST at the Prince Albert Armoury on Exhibition Drive. The military will also be livestreaming the service for those unable to attend in person.

Speakers at the service are expected to include military officials, Farrell's friends and the premier.

WATCH | Pte. Shaun Farrell honoured with hometown vigil: Pte. Shaun Farrell honoured with hometown vigil, military procession | Duration closed caption 2:21 The young soldier from Prince Albert, Sask., who was killed in a fire during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright on Oct. 17, made his final journey home with a military escort on Saturday. About 200 people gathered to honour Private Shaun Farrell at a vigil.

Farrell served with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, based in Edmonton. The unit was taking part in live-fire training at CFB Wainwright, preparing for a deployment to Latvia.

His family has said that Farrell's dream of a career in the military dates back to his childhood. He was born and raised in South Africa before immigrating to Canada with his family and settling in Prince Albert in 2017.

They described him as mischievous, hard-headed, loving and successful.
