WATCH | Soldier killed in Wainwright fire 'was living his dream': Saskatchewan soldier killed in Wainwright fire 'was living his dream' | Duration 1:53 The family of a Saskatchewan soldier who died in Saturday's CFB Wainwright fire says Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, was living his childhood dream with the military. His mother, Patricia Farrell, says he spoke of becoming an "army man" when he was about five.

He overcame diagnoses of dyslexia and Asperger's syndrome and graduated from Carlton Comprehensive High School.

"He had a lot of challenges that he had to overcome," his mother Patricia Farrell said at a news conference five days after his death. "And it didn't stop him, so he was definitely an achiever and he overcame … any obstacle that was put in his way."

World.title: Until the midterms, only 3 Black governors were ever elected in U.S. Tuesday saw 5 wins
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hear excerpts from Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's victory speech after he secured a win in the Michigan Senate race, becoming the first Muslim Senator in history. 'You chose hate,' he said of his Republican rival, 'and Michigan chose hope.'

With hundreds of elections taking place Tuesday night for U.S. Congress and state-level offices, there were bound to be trailblazers and candidates making history individually and collectively.

Perhaps the most remarkable outcome in that regard is the fact that in 2027, based on the results, there will be five Black governors.

When David Paterson was elevated to New York governor in 2008 as the disgraced Eliot Spitzer stepped down, history was made as Paterson and Massachusetts' Deval Patrick became the first Black governors to serve simultaneously.

Until Tuesday night, there had only been three elected Black governors in modern times. They included Wes Moore, of Maryland, who on Tuesday joined Patrick as the only Black governors to be re-elected.

Meanwhile, Abdul El-Sayed became the country's first Muslim senator, winning a Michigan contest in which he fended off accusations of antisemitism, as some Republican officials were accused of Islamophobia in their attacks on El-Sayed.

Here's more on Tuesday night's history-making U.S. midterm results:

2SLGBTQ+ wins

One of the early races called saw New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, 46, defeat Republican John E. Sununu to help get Democrats started en route to taking control of the Senate in 2027.

In winning, Pappas becomes the first openly gay male U.S. senator, moving over from the House of Representatives, where he has served the state since 2019. Wisconsin Sen. Tammy Baldwin is the only other current 2SLGBTQ+ member of the chamber.

WATCH | Chris Pappas helped Democrats regain Senate control: New Hampshire Democrat Pappas calls Senate election win a 'wake-up call for billionaires' | Duration closed caption 1:18 Democrat Chris Pappas won New Hampshire's U.S. Senate race on Tuesday, defeating Republican John Sununu and becoming the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. Pappas called the result a rejection of 'corporate special interests and billionaires' and vowed to fight for a change in direction in Washington.

At his victory party, Pappas thanked his husband, Uber executive Vann Bentley, leading to wild applause from the crowd.

"All right, the wrong person was on the ballot apparently," Pappas quipped, declaring himself the "luckiest guy because I'm married to a man that I love."

Given its far greater numbers, the House has historically seen the majority of the few dozen out members of Congress. Some won re-election on Tuesday night, including Robert Garcia and Mark Takano, both of California; Eric Sorensen, of Illinois; Ritchie Torres, of New York; Mark Pocan, of Wisconsin; Becca Balint, of Vermont; Emily Randall, of Washington; and Sharice Davids, of Kansas, who is also a member of the Ho-Chunk Nation.

The 2SLGBTQ+ politicians projected to join them as first-time members of Congress so far are Jeremy Moss, of Michigan; J.D. Ford, of Indiana; JoAnna Mendoza, of Arizona; and Marni von Wilpert, of California, who identifies as bisexual. Like the returning 2SLGBTQ+ members of Congress, all are Democrats.

Delaware Democrat Sarah McBride, who made history two years ago as the first out transgender legislator, was re-elected in the U.S. House. Transgender Democratic candidates Allison Montgomery and Bentley Hudgins were elected to state legislatures in Alabama and Georgia, respectively.

At the state level, lesbian governors Maura Healey and Tina Kotek were re-elected in Massachusetts and Oregon. Both are Democrats.

Wave of women governors

Next year, there will be 17 women governors — the most in U.S. history — with Kansas and Alaska still uncalled races.

Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms will become the first Black woman to govern in U.S. history, defeating billionaire Republican Rick Jackson in Georgia.

Keisha Lance Bottoms hugs her daughter, Lincoln, during an election-night watch party at the Atlanta Marriott Marquis on Tuesday after defeating Rick Jackson to become the nation's first Black woman governor. (Megan Varner/Getty Images)

Democrat Deb Haaland, of New Mexico, also built upon an already-established political career that saw her serve in the U.S. House and as Joe Biden's secretary of the interior. Haaland, a member of the Laguna Pueblo, will become the first woman Indigenous governor of any U.S. state.

No win was more shocking than Texas, where Republican Greg Abbott was denied a fourth term in office. Gina Hinojosa will become the first Democratic governor in Texas since the legendary Ann Richards served in the mid-1990s, and the first Latina governor of any U.S. state other than New Mexico, where Michelle Lujan Grisham and Susana Martinez have served.

LISTEN | 2 strategists on what was just seen in U.S. votes: The Current 15:06 Where do the Democrats and Republicans go from here? The midterms shifted the balance of power in Washington. What will it mean for Donald Trump and his MAGA movement? Will Democrats be able to get anything done? As both parties look ahead to 2028, we speak with Democratic strategist Michael Hardaway and Republican strategist John Feehery.

In addition to Healey and Kotek, Kathy Hochul kept New York in the Democratic column, while Republicans Kelly Ayotte, of New Hampshire, and Sarah Huckabee Sanders, of Arkansas, were also re-elected.

Democrat Amy Klobuchar, of Minnesota, and Republican Marsha Blackburn, of Tennessee, successfully moved from the U.S. Senate to the governor's offices in their states.

Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico are shown Monday at a late campaign rally in Austin. Both scored upsets in Texas, with Hinojosa elected governor and Talarico headed to the U.S. Senate. (Eric Gay/The Associated Press)

Also winning in races where the previous governors were term limited were Democrats Hannah Pingree, Jocelyn Benson and Helena Foulkes, in Maine, Michigan and Rhode Island, respectively.

And in a matchup that was bound to make representation history — Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy is Indo-American — Amy Acton became Ohio's first Jewish governor and one of a handful of Jewish women elected to gubernatorial office in the U.S.

Gubernatorial history

Jewish American incumbent governors Josh Shapiro, of Pennsylvania, and J.B. Pritzker, of Illinois, were easily re-elected, while Phil Weiser is projected to become Colorado's governor, succeeding fellow Jewish American Democrat Jared Polis.

In addition to Hinojosa, Xavier Becerra, the former California attorney general, also made history. By defeating Republican Steve Hilton, Becerra became the state's first Latino governor since Romualdo Pacheco in 1875.

Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, left, greets supporters after speaking at an election-night event in Las Vegas early Wednesday. Ford is set to become the state's next governor. (John Locher/The Associated Press)

Maryland's Moore said before winning re-election that "it was never lost on me that I'm the only Black governor in this country, and that's a title that I never wanted."

There will be four other Black governors joining him at National Governors Association meetups, including the aforementioned Lance Bottoms.

Incoming governor Aaron Ford has served as Nevada's top prosecutor since 2019. Throughout his campaign, he described growing up in poverty and going to school hungry. He explained how he became a math teacher before earning his law degree, and highlighted efforts to fight the Trump administration.

Ford and fellow Democrats worked to connect Republican Joe Lombardo with President Donald Trump's tariffs, saying they harmed Las Vegas tourism, which saw a 17 per cent drop in Canadian visitors in 2025.

Republican Rep. Byron Donalds celebrates at an election-night event with his wife, Erika, on Tuesday in Hollywood, Fla., after winning the race to become Florida's next governor. (Rebecca Blackwell/The Associated Press)

Like Ford, David Crowley is the first Black governor-elect of his state after topping Tom Tiffany in Wisconsin. Born in Milwaukee, he has spoken eloquently of overcoming a difficult childhood in which both his parents battled substance abuse issues.

Not all the history was on the Democratic side. U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds won the race to succeed Ron DeSantis to become Florida's first Black governor-elect. As a result, the Republicans keep that office, which they've held since the late 1990s.

World.title: Province's last boundary panel chair urged new panellists not to alter southern Alberta ridings. They did.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When the judge who led Alberta’s boundaries commission gave politicians a narrow path to revise his panel’s work and rescue two rural ridings from the chopping block, Justice Dallas Miller added a few provisos to protect his electoral map work.

The first condition, which the Smith government adopted, stated that “restoration of the two electoral divisions should: have no impact on any electoral division in Airdrie or containing territory south of Airdrie’s southernmost border…”

And lo and behold, where has the new boundary panel done its most controversial redrawing?

In Lethbridge, Calgary and Canmore. All south of Airdrie.

NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi has called it a “Trump-style, MAGA gerrymandered map” that safeguards UCP-held territory in southern Alberta. Adopt it, Nenshi has warned, and “we’ll see them in court.”

Premier Danielle Smith has expressed early favour for the new plan, regardless of its apparent overstepping of the conditions her side set on her new boundary advisory group.

Back in April, when United Conservatives shelved the official commission’s work, she had insisted she was accepting that majority report, just with Justice Dallas Miller’s extra recommendations which proposed modest tweaks.

"You'll see that in his Recommendation Five, he is quite prescriptive about the areas that he thinks are problematic," she told reporters.

The new panel chaired by retired judge Brian O’Ferrall, however, did not feel so fettered about sticking to the confines of what Miller and Alberta’s legislature had set out, stating in its “majority” report that the words in Miller’s fifth recommendation don’t warrant “deification.”

“It was not the ‘Fifth Commandment,’” the report states. “It was simply a bit of political ‘give and take.’”

So what did O’Ferrall’s panel give and take?

It took Lethbridge’s two urban seats and split one of them across three rural ridings that variously stretch up to 150 kilometres in each direction to the U.S. border, the TransCanada Highway, Waterton Lakes National Park and the hamlet of Manyberries, due south of Medicine Hat.

A map showing a sole Lethbridge urban seat, as well as three hybrid electoral divisions combining parts of the city with vast surrounding rural regions. (Advisory panel on electoral boundaries)

It took rural acreage communities from the formerly proposed Cochrane-Springbank riding and dispersed them among three west Calgary districts — which, Nenshi argued, gives thousands of Conservative voters to seats currently held by a trio of UCP cabinet ministers.

It took the Diamond Valley and Longview areas away from adjoining rural ridings south of Calgary and gave them to the Canmore-Banff riding on the other side of Kananaskis Country and a highway partially closed for six months every year.

Not only had Miller, the original commission’s chair, recommended against such tinkering in service of restoring a pair of rural ridings in northern and central Alberta; it’s also not clear that these southern Alberta modifications were even necessary to accommodate the un-eliminating of those two districts.

They weren’t knock-on effects caused by bringing back the riding in Rocky Mountain House and Sundre.

In the case of Springbank and Bearspaw, it was a straightforward bit of subtraction, division and addition, separate from any map work to the north.

According to population figures in the new report, Cochrane’s riding shed 9,703 people, and that same amount was split among the three Calgary ridings, without any corresponding adjustments to any other Calgary constituencies.

It leaves the redesigned Cochrane with 46,785 residents, and 13 per cent below the provincial average riding population. The redrawn Calgary-West-Springbank and Calgary-Bow-Springbank each have more than 58,000 people, nine per cent higher than average.

“Adding Springbank to Calgary Bow is said to potentially favour the party in power,” O’Ferrall’s report acknowledged. “But whether that potential will manifest itself in the next election, not even the pollsters with their voter transpositioning software know for sure.”

Springbank was moved because O’Ferrall and the panel’s UCP appointees felt that rural area had more connection to Calgary than to the small town of Cochrane to its north.

Similarly, it felt that “Lethbridge is not an isolated urban municipality,” but is the hub of southern Alberta’s agri-business, health and service district. Therefore, it partially becomes three hub-and-spoke ridings that nearly stretch from Saskatchewan to British Columbia — and, the NDP argues, erases one of Lethbridge’s politically competitive ridings and dilutes those votes in UCP-friendly zones.

LISTEN | Alberta @ Noon on the boundary revisions: Alberta at Noon 52:39 Redrawing Alberta's electoral boundaries A newly proposed electoral map could add four more ridings and heavily shift boundaries across the province. We look at the controversial changes and ask how they might impact your community in the next election.

O’Ferrall and his UCP-appointed majority dismiss complaints their work is unconstitutional as “polarizing nonsense.”

They take similar umbrage in their report with the NDP-appointed minority’s protests about the new map work in southern Alberta, saying “it can be summarized quite simply. Our proposals are constitutional; yours are not. Our proposals are non-partisan; yours are not.”

For the record, Smith’s cabinet chose O’Ferrall, a former Court of Appeal judge who has donated thousands of dollars to the UCP and federal conservatives since he retired in 2022, and served in court as lawyer for an Alberta Progressive Conservative riding association two decades ago before he was a judge.

The United Conservatives’ two appointees to the panel are Monte Solberg, a former Conservative MP and head of a Calgary-based lobby firm who has donated $2,883 to Smith’s party this year, including some while serving on the panel; and Darwin Durnie, a longtime conservative political donor and municipal public works official who has a lengthy history as a boundary-making hobbyist of sorts, having submitted maps to Alberta’s boundary commissions that propose several rural-urban hybrid ridings.

The NDP’s appointees, constitutional law professor Gerard Kennedy and former Okotoks councillor Brent Robinson, have no record of provincial donations in Elections Alberta’s database. Kennedy has donated federally, predominantly to Conservatives and some to Liberals.

Regardless of how partisan the boundary panellists are or aren’t, the partisan MLAs are set to debate the contentious report in coming days.

Smith likes the idea of Lethbridge’s hybrid ridings, similar to how Medicine Hat is divided between her Brooks-Medicine Hat seat and a UCP colleague’s Cypress-Medicine Hat.

“I represent a hybrid riding, and I think Medicine Hat is well-served by having two representatives. I think Lethbridge will be very well-served by having four representatives,” she told reporters Tuesday.

Premier Danielle Smith, who represents a rural-urban hybrid riding in Medicine Hat, said Lethbridge would be well-served by having several rural-urban hybrid MLAs instead of two city-only MLAs. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

The NDP cannot launch a lawsuit against this new riding map until the legislature approves it and puts it into effect. A successful challenge would have to argue that the ridings violate the “effective representation” guarantees in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms — such a claim could theoretically come from a political party, or the affected residents in Lethbridge or elsewhere, including the few thousand people in Springbank and Bearspaw who find themselves mixed into 50,000-person-plus seats in Alberta’s biggest city.

Original commission chair Miller, for his part, wrote in his report that he didn’t find Lethbridge or Springbank hybrids “necessarily unreasonable or procedurally unfair,” noting that some public members proposed them to the commission. But that report blurb wasn’t part of the government motion that created the do-over boundary review, unlike the one urging against any redrawing work south of Airdrie.

Smith discussed on Tuesday being ready to “assemble a legal team” ahead of a potential court challenge. When asked about Miller’s warning on southern ridings she said: “I'll take a closer look at it and talk to the lawyers about that.”

World.title: A runner died in the New York City Marathon. Have the risks changed as more people race?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

She was just a few kilometres from the finish line.

A record-breaking 61,146 runners completed the New York City Marathon on Sunday. But Rachel Apa, despite being in what her father describes as perfect health, wasn't one of them.

The 24-year-old athlete collapsed near mile 24, or about 38.6 kilometres into the 42.2-kilometre race. Despite the life-saving efforts of bystanders, paramedics and then hospital doctors, she was pronounced dead later that night, her grieving parents told the New York Times.

" It's unfathomable," her father Steve Apa, who could not be reached by CBC News, told the news outlet.

Every year, more and more people vie for the chance to lace up their sneakers and push themselves 42.2 kilometres to cross that finish line. But every year, young and seemingly healthy people also die trying — typically of heart failure or cardiac arrest.

All told, including Rachel Apa, at least six runners have died racing in marathons and half-marathons around the world in the past six months alone. Still, experts say the incidence rate is very low, given that millions of people run them every year.

Marathons aren't any riskier than they were 20 years ago, but they are far more popular, explained J ack Goodman, a professor emeritus in kinesiology at the University of Toronto, and adjunct scientist of cardiovascular research at Toronto's University Health Network.

"When the population is so large, there are bound to be more cases, rare as they are," Goodman told CBC News.

Any time you have thousands of people in the same space, based on probabilities, one of them will have a cardiac event, Dr. Christopher Labos, a cardiologist and epidemiologist in Montreal, told CBC News.

"You just hear about it more in the news because it's so shocking when something unexpected like this happens."

Rachel Apa is pictured in the 2023 field hockey roster on the athletics website for Bucknell University in Lewisburg, Pa. (Bucknellbison.com)

Risk of dying has decreased: study

Anyone who has tried to register for a marathon in the last few years can tell you how popular they've become. A record 1.3 million people have already applied to run the 2027 London Marathon. So many people have tried to register for the Boston Marathon in recent years that they've tightened their qualifying times.

In the U.S. alone, more than 29 million people completed marathons and half-marathons in between 2010 and 2023, notes a 2025 study published t he Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA). That's triple the number compared to a decade earlier, the authors add.

Overall, the risk of risk of death is about one in 150,000 runners, notes a 2019 global review in the BMJ medical journal. Typically, the risk is much higher for men, the cause is often coronary artery disease and the deaths most often occur in the last quarter of the race, the study says.

"There are infrequent deaths, which are often reported widely, and may create unnecessary alarm about the potential risks," the authors wrote.

The 2025 JAMA study points out that the risk of dying from a cardiac event during long-distance running races in the U.S. has actually gone down by about 50 per cent in recent years — likely due to more effective emergency planning, including access to defibrillators.

But the study also noted a small uptick in non-fatal cardiac events since 2020, which the authors hypothesized could be due to less access to health care during the COVID-19 pandemic, leading to reduced detection of cardiovascular disease.

Runners make their way through Queens during the New York City Marathon Sunday. (Heather Khalifa/The Associated Press)

Usually a pre-existing cause, expert says

Most often, in the case of death, there's underlying coronary disease the runner didn't know about and never caused them a problem until the race, said Goodman.

"Sudden cardiac death is, unfortunately, not a terribly uncommon first symptom of heart disease," he said.

Just last month, 24-year-old Treyton Lara collapsed at mile 20 of the Portland Marathon and died. He'd experienced a sudden cardiac arrest, his family said. In January, Julien Autissier, 33, collapsed around the 19-mile mark of the Miami marathon and died in the hospital. Doctors also suspected sudden cardiac arrest, according to the Miami New Times.

Roland Liinar, 25, died last May after collapsing in the Rimi Riga Marathon in Latvia. The same month, two other runners died after collapsing while competing in half-marathons in New York and the U.K.

Still, from a public health perspective, the problem most people have is moving too little, not moving too much, said Lagos, the cardiologist and epidemiologist. And if you're a young healthy person who trained properly for a marathon, a cardiac event is "almost certainly not going to happen in your case."

Runners cross the finish line in Central Park on Sunday. (Angelina Katsanis/The Associated Press)

'She did everything she's supposed to'

Apa, an industrial-technology product manager, had run to raise money for Parkinson's disease in honour of her grandfather. On her fundraiser page, which had raised more than $26,000 US by Tuesday evening, Apa called him her "role model."

New York Road Runners, the non-profit club that stages the New York City Marathon, said in a news release that CPR was administered to Apa by a bystander and later by event medical staff. A defibrillator was also used before paramedics took Apa to the Mount Sinai Hospital, reports The Associated Press.

The former Division I field hockey player at Bucknell University was in critical condition when she was brought to the hospital, where doctors unsuccessfully tried to save her for several hours.

Steve Apa says Rachel's cause of death Sunday was rhabdomyolysis, a rare but serious condition where the muscle cells break down and leak into the bloodstream. Rhabdo, as it is often called, can be brought on by severe physical exertion.

Exercise-induced rhabdo cases aren't tracked across Canada, CBC News has previously reported. But there was recently a spike of cases in young women in St. John's, with health officials pointing to i ntense workouts and social media competitiveness.

It was her first marathon, but Rachel was a lifelong athlete, her father told USA Today, and she had trained carefully for months.

"She did everything she's supposed to."

World.title: Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's gorgeous remake retains the original's soul
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

If you loved the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, chances are you don't remember the moments that were clunky, hard to control and kind of ugly, because the good stuff outstripped the bad by a longshot.

Now, Nintendo has remade and rebuilt the 1998 classic from the ground up, for the Switch 2 console. In doing so, they've managed to recreate the good memories from this iconic game, but with modern improvements to the visuals, responsive controls and much more.

In other words, they've avoided making this stroll down memory lane a cringe-inducing slog. The end result will feel like a comforting hug to many gamers, but its world will welcome anyone who hasn't visited before.

WATCH | What you can and can't do in the new Zelda remake: Ocarina of Time is better than you remember | Duration 2:06 Back — and not bigger than ever. That's a good thing. Nintendo's remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a better-looking version of an adventure that still holds up in 2026.

It looks way better

What hasn't changed is the classic story of the balance between good and evil. Ocarina of Time tells the interweaving tale of Zelda, a princess burdened with dark, prophetic dreams; Ganondorf, the manipulative power-hungry thief; and Link, a boy with a mark of destiny who must grow up quick — figuratively and literally, thanks to time travel — to meet the challenge.

As Link, you still navigate the Kingdom of Hyrule: a beautiful, wide world full of puzzles, weapons and enemies.

The blocky, polygonal graphics of the original version meant some of this epic storytelling had to be done in our imagination.

But on the Switch 2, the rays of the sun shine, the dust flows, the water glistens and the characters — even the weird ones — have gestures, emotions and faces with more discernable features.

Link stands in front of the Great Deku Tree. Fireflies, light and mist swirl about, showing off the graphical sea change from the original to the remake. (Nintendo)

From the stained-glass texture of your fairy companion Navi to the latex skin of the fish-like Zora people, Ocarina feels like it's giving you reasons to pay attention to details in this era of second-screen distractions. There are no graphical hiccups or bathroom-break loading screen times here.

The tools and weapons essential to your journey are colourful and responsive, from deflecting monster projectiles with your shield to the hissing of a lit bomb that you'd better throw soon.

Unlike the original, which would automatically throw Link over pits and edges, jumping now has a button, giving the player more control over combat and traversal.

It sounds the same (that's a good thing)

Speaking of those tools, they are a driving force in one of the best parts to any Zelda adventure: the sound design.

The shlink of a sword, the hyaah of our otherwise silent protagonist, the clunk-thunk of iron boots and the creak of opening a treasure chest are all still here. Nintendo has done little to improve the sound effects other than making them sound less tinny.

Yes, that includes the symphony of squelching as you navigate the insides of Jabu-Jabu, a giant fish-like creature.

Link holding the titular Ocarina of Time, with his fairy companion Navi beside him. (Nintendo)

The titular ocarina is still a satisfying woodwind to play, but now you can hum the tunes in case you forget (or don't want to bother remembering) the exact note combinations. Songs are key to game progression, and if you don't want to sing aloud, simple button presses will also work.

The musical score is just as lovely and supportive of the grand adventure as before. The castanets and guitar got me vibing through the deserts of Gerudo Valley, and I loved how the tempo slowed down as night fell over the canyon.

New voice acting and a slightly reworked script helps boost moments so you're not just mashing buttons to hurry along boxes of text on the screen. Thankfully, the melodrama of that acting and writing never overstay their welcome. Ganondorf is wonderful in brief menacing monologues, but the forest dwelling would-be-tough-guy Mido steals the show.

It feels bigger, but is actually faster

Ocarina benefits from quick pacing elsewhere, too. While it takes up more than 20 gigabytes of storage — more than 2023's Tears of the Kingdom — this adventure isn't heavily beset with tasks and side quests.

Early on, you might think the tall, vast, gorgeous world before you feels endless. But you'll quickly realize that few treasures are hidden in the walls, and slashing at shrubs won't uncover much more than a couple of rupees.

Link gets ready to ride his horse Epona. Though your horse helps the speed of traversing the map, it's a tiny world compared to modern Zelda games. (Nintendo)

But that's a good thing.

The last two Zelda games on the Switch — Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom — took the franchise into an exhaustive open world, a feature of modern games that try to keep you in these environments for dozens of hours.

Ocarina of Time, however, is focused on good level design and clever mechanics to get through them. In the later temples, for example, it's all about switching between your tools to figure out a path through a unique set of rooms.

That means this game doesn't take as long to beat — and this may be the one downside to staying true to its roots.

What used to be semi-challenging puzzles in the original now feel a little dated and are over before you know it. The same goes for the epic set-piece boss battles that you can finish in a few hits, making you wonder what all that dungeon-crawling was for. (Thankfully, another modern improvement is the ability to replay boss fights for bragging rights.)

But like some good, old memories, it's not worth interrogating. The Ocarina of Time remake is short, sweet and worth reliving — or worth making the memories for the first time.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time releases Nov. 5 on the Switch 2 and the digital version retails for $84.99, while the physical game card version retails for $99.99.

World.title: Israeli president accepts certified election results after commission denies voter fraud
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he would begin consultations with party representatives on the formation of a new government after accepting the certified results from last week's parliamentary elections, effectively pushing aside claims of voter fraud.

Herzog's acceptance on Wednesday of the results as valid dealt a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's effort to discredit the vote, in which his religious-nationalist bloc lost its majority in the Israeli parliament, or Knesset, while Arab-led parties made historic gains.

Netanyahu and his supporters have repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that the Arab-led parties had "stolen" the election, possibly with foreign assistance.

The Israeli president is required now to sit down with various party leaders to determine who to name as prime minister-designate — a process that could potentially bring Netanyahu's opponents to power.

No fraud in Israel's election, commission says

Israel's election commission said earlier on Wednesday that after a thorough investigation of all parties' claims of fraud it had found "no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results."

Netanyahu's Likud party did not respond to a request for comment.

A separate investigation by the Shin Bet intelligence service, which is headed by David Zini, a Netanyahu appointee and loyalist, into allegations of foreign interference in the election is still ongoing.

In a private meeting on Wednesday of the election committee's members, its head, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, read out an intelligence assessment from the Shin Bet saying the agency believed there had been a "widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states," including from countries hostile toward Israel.

The Shin Bet provided no evidence to explain its assertion. The Associated Press obtained a transcript of the assessment from a person who attended the meeting. The person requested anonymity to discuss a closed-door meeting.

WATCH | No clear party or leader emerged as winner in last week's election: Netanyahu, Eisenkot left jostling for power after Israel's election | Duration 1:58 Israel's Central Elections Committee says voter turnout was 77.7 per cent, the highest in two decades. But as votes are counted, no party or leader has emerged as a clear winner.

The committee has previously said that while claims about foreign actors seeking to influence the election are serious and under investigation, it does not believe that any such interference affected the results, even if it had happened.

Sohlberg reiterated that stance on Wednesday. "At this stage, these are merely suspicions, and even if they are substantiated, the scope of their potential impact is limited," he said during a ceremony to present the certified election results to Herzog.

He added that it was dangerous to cast doubt on the results and said they are legally binding.

Public trust in the electoral process is "easy to destroy, yet very difficult to repair," he warned.

What comes next for Herzog

In the Oct. 27 vote, neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the bloc of allies of his chief rival, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, secured a parliamentary majority needed to form a new government, raising the possibility of an alliance between the two rivals or an alliance between Eisenkot and some of the Arab-led parties.

Israel's president is now expected to begin a series of sit-downs with political parties. The meetings are expected to unfold over the next several days.

Herzog is then to choose the candidate — most likely Netanyahu or Eisenkot — who he believes is most likely to be able to form a coalition government, setting the stage for weeks of negotiations.

If neither man can put together a government, the country would hold a new election early next year.

LISTEN | Arab voters turned out in record numbers to vote in Israel's elections: Day 6 8:30 Why so many Palestinian citizens of Israel switched from boycotting to voting in this election Historically, many Arab and Palestinian citizens of Israel have boycotted Israel’s national elections. But this week, they turned out in record numbers. Lubna Masarwa, the Palestine and Israel bureau chief for Middle East Eye and a Palestinian citizen of Israel explains what motivated the change.

The Shin Bet had requested approval from Israel's attorney general on Tuesday to interrogate several elected officials as part of the agency's separate probe, including Ra'am party leader Mansour Abbas and other senior Arab lawmakers, Israeli media reported.

The request was sharply rejected.

"It is not permissible to interrogate citizens or elected officials without evidence to justify such action," Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said.

The Joint List of Arab parties condemned the request, calling it a "campaign of incitement" by Netanyahu and his allies designed to delegitimize the Arab vote.

A far-right ally of Netanyahu, Itamar Ben-Gvir, rejected the committee's findings that the elections were valid.

He called on the Shin Bet, over which he has no jurisdiction, to "arrest all the leaders of the Arab political parties" and to interrogate them in "basement interrogation cells until these suspicions are fully clarified."

Herzog said Wednesday that the Shin Bet investigation into possible foreign interference should play out. But he cautioned that Arab Israeli voters "must not be smeared."

"I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently," Herzog said.

World.title: Canada dismisses fears of international blowback over Russian world junior hockey ban
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's secretary of state for sport dismissed concerns Wednesday that barring Russian players from next month's world junior hockey championship in Alberta could hurt the country's chances of hosting future international events, including the Olympics.

"No, we've been unequivocal with respect to our support for Ukraine and in our insistence that Russia as well as Belarus do not compete in international events while using their national symbols," Adam van Koeverden said when asked about potential repercussions.

The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled last week that Russia must be reinstated to international competition, starting with the world juniors. Russian and Belarusian teams have been banned since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

But veteran sport lawyer Dick Pound said the international sport court has no authority to dictate which athletes Canada allows into the country.

"Short of stamping their feet and pouting, there's not much they can actually do," Pound said.

Pound, a longtime International Olympic Committee member and former CAS arbitrator, said the Canadian government has the final say on who enters the country.

"Hockey Canada, if that's where the buck stops, I'd say, 'listen, I'm sorry, we're a sport organization. We don't decide who can get entry visas into Canada, nor can CAS order the Canadian government to grant visas."'

The International Ice Hockey Federation reiterated its opposition Wednesday to the ruling ordering Russia's reinstatement, but stopped short of addressing Canada's refusal to allow Russian players into the country.

WATCH | Prime Minister shuts down Russian involvement in 2026 world juniors: Carney says Russia won't be allowed to play in upcoming world juniors | Duration closed caption 0:55 Prime Minister Mark Carney said while Russia and Belarus are supporting 'this illegal and unjustified war in Ukraine,' no athlete representing either country will be allowed to compete in Canada, including at this winter's World Junior Hockey Championship in Alberta.

PM: 'The Russians will not be there'

Prime Minister Mark Carney made Canada's position clear Tuesday while attending the Commonwealth Summit in Antigua.

"So if you're asking specifically about the world juniors, the Russians will not be there," he said.

Van Koeverden said he met Tuesday with Finland's sports minister to discuss the issue, noting that countries neighbouring Russia face different consequences from its invasion of Ukraine.

"We have a lot in common and certainly not the least of which is our support for Ukraine," he said.

Asked why Russia was being treated differently from other countries, including the United States, van Koeverden pointed to Moscow's use of international sport to advance its political interests.

"They continually use sport for nefarious reasons and purposes, so the false equivalencies aren't necessary in this regard," he said.

In a statement Wednesday, the IIHF cited logistical, security and competitive challenges with Russia's immediate return, including visa requirements and potential changes to tournament formats.

"The global impact of the decision made by the CAS Panel and the challenges it creates for all involved were significantly underestimated," the federation said.

WATCH | Russia's international hockey ban lifted by Court of Arbitration for Sport: Russia is back in the hockey world champions | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 6:59 Russia had been banned from international ice hockey competitions since 2022 following the invasion of Ukraine. The Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned International Ice Hockey Federation decisions, which excluded Russia from events in the 2026-27 season, including the men's and women's world championships. It is unclear how Russia will be included since adding another team will make for uneven groups and longer tournaments.

IIHF consulting national hockey associations

While the IIHF did not directly address Carney's announcement, it said it is consulting national hockey associations, tournament organizers and host authorities before determining its next steps. The federation said player safety and tournament integrity remain priorities. It promised more information in the coming days.

The federal government said it would use its immigration powers to prevent Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials from entering Canada to compete under their national symbols.

Ottawa said the measure was intended to prevent Russia and Belarus from using international sporting events in Canada as platforms for political legitimacy and propaganda. Athletes competing as neutrals could still be permitted to participate.

Russia's ambassador to Canada criticized the decision Tuesday, accusing Ottawa of bringing politics into sports.

"It is genuinely regrettable to see Prime Minister Carney's cabinet bringing politics onto the ice. Sport, particularly junior hockey, should be about athletic excellence, fair competition and bringing young people together," Oleg Stepanov said.

Stepanov also suggested the decision would eliminate some of Canada's strongest competition at the tournament.

Hockey Canada welcomed the government's position Tuesday and said its board would meet this week to discuss next steps. Several European hockey federations, including Sweden, Finland, Czechia and Latvia, have said their teams would refuse to face Russia.

Canada's decision came after several European hockey federations, including Sweden, Finland, Czechia and Latvia, said their teams would refuse to face Russia.

The opposition has also spread to major sponsors of next May's men's world hockey championship in Germany.

Czech automaker Skoda, the tournament's main sponsor for more than 30 years, said Wednesday it would reassess its involvement if Russia competes. German workwear manufacturer Strauss also threatened to withdraw its sponsorship, while Nokian Tyres said it would end its backing if Russia participates.

The world junior championship opens Dec. 26 in Edmonton and Red Deer, Alta., with defending champion Sweden among the 10 teams scheduled to compete.

Canada, Czechia, Switzerland, the United States, Germany, Latvia, Slovakia, Norway and Finland round out the field.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Democrats retake control of the US Congress in a heavy blow to Trump
World.content:
Democrats retake control of the US Congress in a heavy blow to Trump

4th Wednesday, November 2026 - 09:09 UTC Full article

CBS News projected a Democratic majority in the House shortly after 10 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday; with dozens of seats still to be decided, Democrats had passed the 218 needed

The Democratic Party on Tuesday regained control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate in the midterm elections, winning in Republican strongholds such as Texas, Ohio and Kansas in a heavy blow to President Donald Trump, who will govern for the remaining two years of his term with Congress in opposition hands.

CBS News projected a Democratic majority in the House shortly after 10 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday; with dozens of seats still to be decided, Democrats had passed the 218 needed. In the Senate, they secured a majority with victory in Iowa and hold at least 53 of the 100 seats, with results in Alaska and Mississippi still pending. According to El País, it is only the seventh time the party in power has lost both chambers in a midterm election.

Democrats won Senate seats in states where they had not done so for decades. In Texas, James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton; in Ohio, Sherrod Brown regained the seat from Jon Husted; in Kansas, Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton became the state’s first Democratic senator in almost a century. They also won in Iowa, with Josh Turek; in Maine, where Troy Jackson defeated Republican Susan Collins, a senator since 1997; in North Carolina, with Roy Cooper; and in South Carolina, with Annie Andrews. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, will be the first Muslim senator in US history. Republicans held seats in Florida, Idaho and Montana.

In governor’s races, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott in Texas and will be the first Hispanic woman to lead the state; Xavier Becerra will be California’s first Hispanic governor since 1875; and Deb Haaland, in New Mexico, the first Native American woman to govern a state. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds will be the state’s first Black governor.

Trump told Fox News he was “a little surprised” and that the Democrats “did a good job”, attributing part of the defeat to the Iran war and higher fuel prices. He told The New York Times he would accept the results and hoped to reach agreements with the opposition. On his social network, however, he wrote: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”, and posted an image of his cap bearing the word “VETO”, a reference to his threat to veto the new Congress’s laws.

With majorities in both chambers, Democrats will be able to block the White House’s legislative agenda and open investigations into the first half of the term. Former president Barack Obama said voters had sent “a clear message” in favour of “a politics that brings people together rather than divides them”. China said it was ready to “keep working” with Washington, and the Kremlin said it expected Trump to maintain his foreign policy. Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said “Americans have said no to war”.

Polls had identified the cost of living, corruption and the Iran war as voters’ main concerns, and turnout was at record levels for a midterm election.

World.title: Paraguay takes over Ueno Bank, with 3 million customers, and freezes its deposits
World.content:
Paraguay takes over Ueno Bank, with 3 million customers, and freezes its deposits

4th Wednesday, November 2026 - 08:27 UTC Full article

“We proceeded to close the entity; therefore, neither the app, nor the cards, nor any service of the entity is active,” said a member of the Central Bank’s board. Photo: EFE/ Juan Pablo Pino

Paraguay’s Central Bank on Tuesday took over Ueno Bank, one of the country’s largest banks, after its solvency ratio fell below 50% of the legal minimum, and froze all its assets and liabilities, including the savings of some 3 million customers and more than US$800 million in public funds. The bank immediately suspended all its services.

“We proceeded to close the entity; therefore, neither the app, nor the cards, nor any service of the entity is active from today,” said Liana Caballero, a member of the Central Bank’s board, which took the decision unanimously. According to its own figures, Ueno’s customers are equivalent to 60% of the country’s adult population, and it manages public funds including about US$380 million from the Social Security Institute, which runs pensions and public healthcare.

The Deposit Guarantee Fund covers savings of up to 75 minimum wages, about 228 million guaraníes or roughly US$38,200 per person. Those with larger balances will have to wait for the Superintendency of Banks’ final accounting. “The priority will always be small savers,” said Central Bank President Carlos Carvallo, who described the situation as “an isolated, one-off event” and said the financial system “remains sound and healthy”.

According to Carvallo, the takeover followed months of investigation that revealed loans to companies linked to the bank’s owners. On October 18, the Association of Banks of Paraguay had asked the Central Bank to report on the solvency of institutions that benefited from facilities in merger processes and warned about a bank’s credit exposure, which it did not identify, to companies in its own group. Days earlier, senators from the ruling party and the opposition had called on President Santiago Peña to dismiss the Central Bank’s leadership, which Peña backed.

Carvallo, who ran Ueno Bank before Peña appointed him to head the Central Bank in 2023, said he had signed his resignation, although he will remain in office until the bank’s resolution is complete. According to the Paraguayan press, several of the bank’s executives were detained, including its president, Miguel Vázquez.

The crisis had immediate political fallout. Vice President Pedro Alliana “paused” his bid for the ruling Colorado Party’s presidential nomination in order to “put the house in order”. The opposition Authentic Radical Liberal Party said it would push for impeachment proceedings against Peña and Alliana. “They plundered the pensioners’ money and this cannot be left like this,” said its presidential hopeful Ricardo Estigarribia, according to the newspaper ABC Color. In 2024, the Social Security Institute’s purchase of about US$32 million in Ueno bonds caused controversy; Peña, who called the reports a “media campaign”, was a shareholder in Ueno Holding, not the bank, and sold those shares in April 2025.

World.title: Trump accepts midterm defeat but says Republicans would have won “in a landslide” had he been on the ballot
World.content:
Trump accepts midterm defeat but says Republicans would have won “in a landslide” had he been on the ballot

4th Wednesday, November 2026 - 08:16 UTC Full article

“We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out,” he said

US President Donald Trump said he accepts the results of the midterm elections, in which Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress, and signalled willingness to negotiate with the opposition, but blamed the Republican defeat on his absence from the ballot and threatened to veto the new Congress’s legislation.

“I am absolutely willing to accept those results,” Trump told The New York Times. “We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out.” In a call to Fox News he admitted being “a little surprised” — “I thought we’d do better; we had tremendous rallies” — and acknowledged that Democrats “did a good job”. He told Politico he spoke with Democratic leaders at around 11 p.m. on Tuesday and would rather strike deals than spend his final two years vetoing legislation; according to NBC News, he said several newly elected Democrats had called him, though he did not name them. He cited immigration as a possible area of cooperation, according to CNBC.

His tone on social media was very different. Before polls closed on the West Coast, he wrote on his Truth Social platform: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”, despite having spent weeks urging supporters to vote “as if I were on the ballot”. An hour after his conversation with Democrats, he posted an image of a red cap bearing the word “VETO”, a reference to his threat to block the new Congress’s legislation. “It’s one of the strongest powers a president has,” he told Fox News. “They send me crazy proposals and I veto them. After a couple of months of vetoes, they ask: ‘How can we get this done?’ And we work together.”

Trump also said he would “become a Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost”, and claimed without evidence that Fox News “bears responsibility for these losses” by giving airtime to the opposition. He criticised Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott, defeated by Democrat Gina Hinojosa, for turning “moderate”, and said he had no regrets about endorsing candidates such as Darline Graham in South Carolina and Ken Paxton in Texas, both of whom lost their Senate races.

The defeat confirms the fear Trump himself voiced in January before his party’s lawmakers, when he warned that if they lost the midterms, Democrats would find “a reason” to impeach him for a third time. According to the Associated Press, impeachment of the president or members of his Cabinet “is not off the table”. With control of both chambers, Democrats will also be able to block his legislative agenda and open investigations.

Democratic leaders celebrated the result. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called it a “generational remake of the Senate map”, and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said “the American people are crying out for transformational change”.

His acceptance of the result contrasts with his refusal to concede defeat to Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election, which he still does not acknowledge. Trump will leave the White House in January 2029 and cannot run again, so the defeat also opens the race to succeed him in the Republican Party.

World.title: Markets react to the US midterms: the dollar falls and gold rises
World.content:
Markets react to the US midterms: the dollar falls and gold rises

4th Wednesday, November 2026 - 08:00 UTC Full article

The dollar index, which measures its value against a basket of currencies, remained in negative territory near 101.50

The US dollar weakened against major currencies on Wednesday morning and gold rose more than 2% to above US$4,000 an ounce as markets assessed the Democratic victory in the midterm elections, which will give the opposition control of both chambers of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency.

The dollar index, which measures its value against a basket of currencies, remained in negative territory near 101.50, and the yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note fell below 4.95%, according to financial analysis platform FXStreet. Wall Street index futures were mixed. The dollar’s biggest fall was against the Swiss franc, at 0.4%. The euro briefly rose above US$1.1250, its highest in two weeks, before easing to 1.1230, and sterling extended its winning streak to a sixth day above US$1.3450, ahead of an expected Bank of England rate rise on Thursday.

Analysts at Germany’s Commerzbank warned that “US equities, and in particular the tech-heavy Nasdaq, are likely to come under pressure today”, and that because the dollar’s recent strength had benefited from equity-related capital inflows, “dollar weakness could consolidate somewhat further in the coming hours”. In the longer term, they said a more constructive political debate in the United States, “admittedly a very remote possibility”, could reduce the political risk premium priced into the dollar.

Trump told The Wall Street Journal that the Iran war was “partially to blame” for the Republican defeat and that he has no plans for personnel changes in his administration.

World.title: Spain’s transport minister resigns after the train crash that killed at least 69 people
World.content:
Spain’s transport minister resigns after the train crash that killed at least 69 people

4th Wednesday, November 2026 - 07:44 UTC Full article

Spain’s Transport Minister Óscar Puente resigned on Tuesday, six days after a collision between two high-speed trains near the town of Urda, in Toledo province, that killed at least 69 people. Puente also said he was withdrawing his name from the Socialist Party’s lists for the snap general election on November 29.

“A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year,” he told Congress at the end of a lengthy session in which he presented new rail safety measures and faced opposition criticism. He was also referring to the crash at Adamuz, in Córdoba, on the same line, which killed 46 people in January. Puente said his decision was driven by “political dignity”. Days earlier he had said he did not intend to step down.

The People’s Party and Vox, as well as some of the government’s allies, had called for his resignation, accusing him of blaming human error for the crash to avoid responsibility for a high-speed rail system whose credibility Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez admitted was “broken”. Sánchez praised Puente, who “faced up to the situation, provided answers and solutions, and then stepped aside. Out of dignity. Of his own accord. Out of respect for the victims.”

The crash happened on the morning of October 28 on the Madrid-Seville line, when a Renfe AVE train carrying 397 passengers ran into the back of an Iryo train with 147 passengers on board, which had stopped after a failure in the computerised signalling system. Recordings of conversations between the control centre and the drivers, published by the Spanish press, show the controller authorised the AVE to continue “at normal speed” even though the Iryo train was still stationary about 25 kilometres ahead. In another recording, the Iryo driver warns the control centre that he cannot restart the train. It was Spain’s worst rail disaster since the Santiago de Compostela crash in 2013.

The resignation comes at a key moment in the political calendar, less than four weeks before the general election. According to the BBC, many analysts see the crash as a heavy blow to the prospects of the Socialist government, which polls already placed behind the People’s Party.

World.title: Cristina Kirchner meets Lula’s digital strategist in a bid to replicate his comeback in Argentina
World.content:
Cristina Kirchner meets Lula’s digital strategist in a bid to replicate his comeback in Argentina

3rd Tuesday, November 2026 - 20:16 UTC Full article

Kirchner, who is serving a final six-year sentence for corruption under house arrest and is barred for life from public office

Former Argentine president Cristina Kirchner on Monday received Brazilian lawmaker André Janones, creator of the WhatsApp channel that helped Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva win re-election, in Buenos Aires, as the Peronist opposition looks to Brazil for keys to defeating Javier Milei in the 2027 presidential election.

Janones, a federal deputy for the state of Minas Gerais, runs “Lula’s Army”, a WhatsApp channel with more than 10.4 million followers to whom he sends daily instructions to share and amplify content on social media, a strategy credited with part of Lula’s comeback against Flávio Bolsonaro on October 25. On the day of the Brazilian election, the Peronists launched their own “Peronism’s Army”, which had passed 80,000 followers after Janones’ visit.

Kirchner, who is serving a final six-year sentence for corruption under house arrest and is barred for life from public office, posed with Janones in a photo he shared on social media with the message: “Beside Cristina Kirchner to tell the world that yes, we can defeat the far right.” Lula’s channel was told to share the post, which drew more than 60,000 interactions within an hour. Janones also met Sergio Massa, the Peronists’ last presidential candidate, but not Buenos Aires province governor Axel Kicillof.

The visit came amid an internal Peronist struggle over the 2027 presidential candidacy, in which Kicillof, backed by several governors and mayors, faces the Kirchner and Massa camp. The former president, who hopes to overturn her conviction before international courts, said in an interview with The Washington Post published on Monday that she could run again: “When I recover my political rights, why not?”

Janones, re-elected as a deputy in October, has ruled out a ministerial post in Lula’s new government and returns to Brazil on Tuesday. His team denied he plans to work on the campaign of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez ahead of the November 29 general election.

World.title: The Pope arrives in an Argentina where bishops are among Milei’s firmest critics
World.content:
The Pope arrives in an Argentina where bishops are among Milei’s firmest critics

3rd Tuesday, November 2026 - 09:29 UTC Full article

Leo XIV has placed social justice at the heart of his pontificate, while Milei has called it “an aberration”
