Pope Leo XIV will arrive in Buenos Aires on Sunday on a visit that Javier Milei’s government presents as strictly pastoral, but which takes place amid tension with Argentina’s Catholic hierarchy, one of the most critical voices against the president’s austerity policies. The pontiff will begin a tour in Uruguay on Friday that will continue in Argentina from November 8 to 11 and end in Peru.

“The Pope belongs to all Argentines, not to a political party or a political colour,” presidential chief of staff Karina Milei, who led negotiations with the Church and the Vatican, has repeatedly said. The secretary of worship, Agustín Caulo, insisted it is “an apostolic tour” and that “this should not be politicised”. Authorities expect some 7 million people to follow the Pope in Buenos Aires, Claypole, Luján and Córdoba, in what Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva described as “the largest operation in our history”.

The underlying differences are well known. Leo XIV has placed social justice at the heart of his pontificate, while Milei has called it “an aberration”. A study by sociologist Sol Prieto of the National Scientific and Technical Research Council (Conicet) of documents published by the Argentine Bishops’ Conference between January 2024 and September 2026 found that 42 of the 44 referring to public policy, or 95%, take “a critical position”, on issues such as the social situation, the environment, institutional quality, the lowering of the age of criminal responsibility and a decree curbing migrants’ rights.

Ten days ago, when Milei questioned the idea that many people cannot make ends meet, the president of the Bishops’ Conference, Marcelo Colombo, replied: “That people cannot make ends meet is a fact of reality, not something that needs to be proven.” The Archbishop of Buenos Aires, Jorge García Cuerva, said the Pope “will find a wounded Argentina”. “There is no affinity, but a very strong aversion between most Argentine bishops and Milei’s government,” said researcher Fortunato Mallimaci, who identifies opposition to abortion as one of the few points of agreement.

According to El País, the government sought to limit mass gatherings but the Vatican’s position prevailed, and the Pope will celebrate open-air Masses. Two events are particularly uncomfortable for the government, according to the newspaper: the meeting with trade unionists, business leaders and social movements at the Catholic University of Argentina and the visit to the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione, a home for people with disabilities, one of the sectors hardest hit by spending cuts. The place of Vice President Victoria Villarruel, estranged from Milei, at official events also remains undecided.

World.title: Ayuso honours Kast in Madrid on the eve of the Ibero-American Summit: “We defend the same things”
World.content:
Ayuso honours Kast in Madrid on the eve of the Ibero-American Summit: “We defend the same things”

3rd Tuesday, November 2026 - 09:18 UTC Full article

Kast, on his first European tour since taking office in March, replied that Madrid “is one of the most open, free and prosperous regions in Europe” and stressed security, the focus of his government

The president of the Madrid regional government, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, on Monday awarded the region’s International Medal to Chilean President José Antonio Kast, who is in the Spanish capital for the 30th Ibero-American Summit of Heads of State and Government. “On both sides of the Atlantic we defend the same things,” Ayuso said at the ceremony.

“We are free nations and we defend our governments and liberal democracies and the rule of law, which will not yield to authoritarianism,” said the People’s Party leader, who contrasted Chile with Cuba, Nicaragua and Venezuela. Ayuso praised Chile as “an example of what a nation can achieve when it trusts its citizens” and highlighted Kast’s “commitment to freedom, security, prosperity and the defence of institutions”. “We do not want citizens dependent on power; we want them to be masters of their own lives,” she added.

Kast, on his first European tour since taking office in March, replied that Madrid “is one of the most open, free and prosperous regions in Europe” and stressed security, the focus of his government. “It is the first duty of the state. And when the state fails in that duty, the most vulnerable pay. Without security there is no order, without order there is no peace and without peace there is no freedom.”

The Community of Madrid’s International Medal, created in 2017 and purely honorary, is awarded on the regional president’s personal initiative. Previous recipients include Argentine President Javier Milei and Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa; Venezuelan opposition leaders Juan Guaidó and Edmundo González; Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky; Pope Leo XIV; and the United States, for the 250th anniversary of its independence. Manuela Bergerot, spokeswoman for Más Madrid in the regional assembly, accused Ayuso of turning the award into “the membership card of her far-right international”. A group of demonstrators protested outside the regional government headquarters.

Kast began the day with a private meeting with Vox leader Santiago Abascal, with whom he has close ties, and plans to meet Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez during the summit, which brings together the countries of Latin America with Spain, Portugal and Andorra.

World.title: Mexico’s economy nearing ‘strong’ according to the latest MND Economy Index™
World.content:
Listen to this article

THE MND ECONOMY INDEX™

Providing broad insight into the Mexican economy

MND Intelligence · Sixth edition

Welcome to the sixth edition of the MND Economy Index™, part of the MND Intelligence™ suite of data products from Mexico News Daily.

The MND Economy Index™ is a 10-pillar, 19-indicator composite index that compiles a broad range of economic data into a single score between 0 and 100, giving Mexico News Daily readers a clear, accessible picture of how the Mexican economy is performing across multiple dimensions.

In the inaugural MND Economy Index™ article, published in late May, we not only analyzed the index score — 63.4 out of 100 — but also explained what the index is, why we developed it and how it works. Click here to read (or re-read) those explanations.

In this edition of the MND Economy Index™ — which uses economic data primarily from the month of August — the index score is 74.5, an increase of 1.4 points compared to the previous score.

The score for August is the highest since we began publishing the MND Economy Index™, reflecting improvements in various parts of Mexico’s economy.

Before we look more closely at the latest index result, here is a short guide to what the overall index score means.

85–100: Exceptional — the economy performing at a high level across nearly all indicators.

— the economy performing at a high level across nearly all indicators. 75–84: Strong — strong broad-based performance with only minor areas of concern.

— strong broad-based performance with only minor areas of concern. 60–74: Above neutral — meaningful strengths, but with notable room for improvement.

— meaningful strengths, but with notable room for improvement. 50–59: Mixed — passing marks overall, more indicators above benchmark than below.

— passing marks overall, more indicators above benchmark than below. Below 50: Broad underperformance — more indicators below benchmark than above.

Mexico’s economy on the verge of a ‘strong’ assessment

As noted above, the latest MND Economy Index™ score is 74.5, an increase of 1.4 percentage points compared to the previous score. The latest score is just 0.5 percentage points below the score required for a “strong” assessment for Mexico’s economy.

Below you will see the score for each of the ten pillars that make up the index, expressed out of 10 to reflect each pillar’s exact contribution to the final composite score.

Pillars are color-coded using a traffic light system: green (a score above 7.5) indicates strong performance; yellow (5.0–7.5) signals decent performance but with room for improvement; and red (below 5.0) flags a pillar that is falling short of its benchmark. Where a pillar score has improved compared to the previous month, an upward arrow appears alongside its corresponding traffic light; a downward arrow indicates a deterioration; and a pause symbol denotes no change.

As you’ll see below, scores for four of the ten MND Economy Index™ pillars increased in August compared to the previous month. Scores for five pillars declined, while the score for one was unchanged.

Collectively, the increases were more significant than the decreases, allowing the index score to rise.

🟢 ⬇️ INFLATION (9.54)

The score for this pillar fell to 9.54 in August from 9.68 in July. Despite the decline, the inflation pillar retained its position as the top contributor to the overall MND Economy Index™ score.

Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate increased to 3.26% in August, ending a four-month streak of declines. The increase caused a slight decrease in the score for the current inflation component of the pillar as the headline rate moved away from the Bank of Mexico’s 3% target.

The score for the pillar component that considers the 12-month forward inflation forecast was unchanged as the Bank of Mexico’s outlook for the third quarter of 2027 is applicable to both July and August. The central bank is predicting a headline inflation rate of 3.2% in the third quarter of next year.

🟢 ⬆️ MONETARY POLICY (9.46)

The score for this pillar increased to 9.46 from 9.32 in July.

The Bank of Mexico’s benchmark interest rate remained at 6.50% in August after the central bank’s board voted to keep it at that level at a monetary policy meeting on Aug. 6. Therefore, there was no change in the interest rate component of the pillar score.

The increase in the pillar score was due to a decline in Mexico’s real interest rate in August — i.e., the Bank of Mexico’s benchmark interest rate minus the annual headline inflation rate.

The real interest rate in August was 3.24%, a reading 0.54 points above the 2.7% neutral midpoint.

The real interest rate in July, at 3.38%, was further away from the neutral midpoint than the reading in August.

🟢 ⬆️ MANUFACTURING SECTOR HEALTH (8.53)

The score for this pillar increased in August, rising to 8.53 from 7.9 in July.

The exports component of the pillar remained at the maximum score due to a 40.4% annual increase in export revenue in August, well above the 16.7% threshold needed for a perfect ten. Official data shows that over 94% of Mexico’s export revenue in August came from the shipment abroad of manufactured goods.

The increase in the overall pillar score was due to 4.1% year-over-year growth in manufacturing output in August. The year-over-year gain represented a significant improvement from the 1.6% increase in July.

🟢 ⬆️ ECONOMIC GROWTH (8)

The score for this pillar increased to 8 in August from 7.6 in July.

The increase was due to a higher annual economic growth rate in August. The annual growth rate in August was 3.5%, according to final data published by INEGI on Oct. 23. Year-over-year growth in July was slightly lower at 3.3%.

At her morning press conference on Oct. 26, President Sheinbaum said that growth of 3.5% in August was “very good news.”

She noted that construction, including housing and public infrastructure projects, was helping to drive growth. Sheinbaum also noted that the production of electronics in Mexico was providing momentum to the economy.

🟢 ⬆️ SOVEREIGN RISK (7.72)

The score for this pillar increased to 7.72 in August from 7.41 in July.

The score for the sovereign credit ratings component of the pillar remained unchanged in August, as there were no month-over-month changes to the Mexico ratings of Moody’s (Baa3/stable); S&P (BBB/negative); and Fitch (BBB-/stable).

The increase in the overall pillar score was due to a narrowing in Mexico’s 5-year credit default swap spread. The credit default swap spread was 77.89 basis points at the end of August, down from 87.19 basis points at the end of July. The narrower spread reflected a decrease in the market-implied cost of insuring against a Mexican sovereign default.

🟡 ⬇️ CURRENCY STABILITY (6.73)

The score for this pillar declined slightly to 6.73 in August from 6.79 in July.

The standard deviation of daily exchange rate movements decreased to 0.25% in August from 0.40% in July, leading to an increase in the score for that component of the pillar.

The decrease in the pillar score in July was due to a lower spot rate score. The score for that component declined because the peso strengthened against the US dollar in August to trade at 16.99 to the greenback at the end of the month, an appreciation of 1.9% compared to the end of July.

The exchange rate was thus more distant from the index’s 19.00 USD:MXN baseline, which is based on the 2025 average rate. This pillar penalizes significant deviation from the 19.00 USD:MXN baseline in either direction, recognizing that a peso that has strengthened too far from this benchmark can erode export competitiveness and reduce the purchasing power of remittances, just as a weakening peso raises import costs.

The spot rate component of the currency stability score will increase in the next MND Economy Index™ as the peso depreciated 6% in September to trade at 18.08 to the dollar at the end of that month.

🟡 ⬇️ INVESTMENT CLIMATE (6.46)

The score for this pillar decreased to 6.46 in August from 6.58 in July.

The decrease was due to lower annual growth on the S&P/BMV FIBRAS Total Return Index, which tracks the performance of Mexico’s listed real estate investment trusts. The index grew 24.9% annually to the end of August, down from a 27.4% year-over-year increase at the end of July.

The score for the foreign direct investment component of the pillar remained steady as the latest available data is still that published by the Economy Ministry in late August. That data shows that foreign direct investment in Mexico increased 2.1% annually in the first six months of 2026 to reach a record-high $34.96 billion. Annual FDI growth of 25% is required for a perfect score in that component of the investment climate pillar.

🟡 ⏸️ PRODUCTIVITY (6.4)

The score for this pillar remained steady at 6.4 in August after increasing to that level in July from 3.8 in June.

Data published by the national statistics agency INEGI on Sept. 10 showed that the IGPLE — INEGI’s quarterly productivity measure — increased 1.7% annually in the second quarter of 2026. That level of productivity growth was significantly stronger than the +0.1% reading in the first quarter of 2026.

INEGI will publish productivity data for the third quarter of 2026 in early December.

🟡 ⬇️ LABOR AND EMPLOYMENT (6.11)

The score for this pillar decreased to 6.11 in August from 6.18 in July. Scores for two of the pillar’s three components stayed the same while one declined.

The number of people in formal sector jobs rose 1.5% in the 12 months to the end of August, on par with the annual growth rate at the end of July.

Nominal wages were up 6.7% year-on-year at the end of August, the same increase recorded at the end of July.

Year-over-year growth in Mexico’s informality rate was 0.2 points at the end of August, up from an annual increase of 0.1 points at the end of July. In August, 55% of all Mexican workers worked in the informal economy. Lowering the informality rate is a major challenge for the Mexican government.

🟡 ⬇️ EXTERNAL INCOME (5.51)

The score for this pillar increased in August, rising to 5.51 from 5.26 in July. A year-over-year reduction in remittances in August — just the second decline this year — was a drag on the pillar score, but a strong increase in international tourism revenue more than offset it.

Incoming remittances declined 3.6% year-on-year to US $5.45 billion in August, the first decline of any month since January.

Thus, the score for the remittances component of the pillar fell sharply, although not so far as to warrant a score of zero, as that would require a year-over-year decline of 16.67%.

The pillar score increased in August as international tourism revenue grew compared to the same month of last year, whereas it declined in July. International tourist spending increased 7% year over year in August to reach $2.4 billion.

The MND Economy Index™ trend

In the graph below you can see how the MND Economy Index™ score has changed over time.

We have now calculated a total of ten index scores in the period between March 2025 and August 2026. The difference between the lowest score (56.9 in March 2025 — predating the publication of the first MND Economy Index™ article) and the highest (74.5 in August 2026) is 17.6 points.

The much higher score in this edition of the MND Economy Index™ indicates that Mexico’s economy is performing much better now than it was early in President Sheinbaum’s six-year term.

The improvement in the index score this year has been significant, increasing more than 10 points between March and August.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice is ‘67% complete,’ Sheinbaum reports: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🕊️ Government presents progress under Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice: The mañanera focused on advances made over the past year under the plan, which the government devised after the assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo on Nov. 1, 2025. President Sheinbaum said the presentation would cover areas other than security.

The mañanera focused on advances made over the past year under the plan, which the government devised after the assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo on Nov. 1, 2025. President Sheinbaum said the presentation would cover areas other than security. 📊 Sheinbaum says Plan Michoacán is 67% complete: The president said 1,680 of more than 2,500 “actions” under the plan have been completed.

Why today’s mañanera matters

A presentation on the progress made under “Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice” over the past year was the central focus of President Sheinbaum’s Wednesday morning press conference.

The government devised the plan in response to the assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo on Nov. 1, 2025, and general insecurity in Michoacán.

At the start of her Wednesday mañanera, the president noted that today’s presentation would focus on progress in areas other than security. She said that an update on the security situation in Michoacán would be presented at her press conference next Tuesday.

Data presented at Sheinbaum’s Oct. 13 mañanera showed that homicides in Michoacán declined 40.3% in the first nine months of 2026 compared to the same period of last year.

The president was accompanied on Wednesday by various high-ranking officials, each of whom spoke briefly about Plan Michoacán initiatives.

Today’s mañanera allowed the government to both highlight progress on the plan and explain how funds have been spent. Sheinbaum characterizes her weekday press conferences as exercises in transparency, a principle she says is central to her administration.

115 ‘Well-being Fairs’ held in Michoacán

Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez reported that 115 “Ferías del Bienestar,” or “Well-being Fairs,” were held across all 113 municipalities of Michoacán over the past year.

She said that officials helped Michoacán residents complete more than 1.1 million trámites (administrative procedures) at the fairs, including ones that facilitated their access to government welfare programs.

Rodríguez also noted that Michoacán residents exchanged 673 firearms for cash over the past year under the Sí al Desarme, Sí a la Paz (Yes to Disarmament, Yes to Peace) program. Those exchanges, she said, will save lives.

Key advances under Plan Michoacán

Officials presented key advances under Plan Michoacán across a range of areas. Not all of the investment they outlined is directly linked to Plan Michoacán funding. Summarized below are the presentations made by 10 officials.

Deputy Economy Minister Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez reported that work will start this month on the Bajío Industrial Park in the municipality of Zinapécuaro. He said 9.3 billion pesos (US $498.5 million) will be invested in the project. The industrial park will primarily cater to the agroindustrial and automotive sectors.

Agriculture Minister Columba López reported that more than 177,000 residents of Michoacán are working in the government’s reforestation/employment program called Sembrando Vida (Sowing Life). She said the government is investing almost 2.2 billion pesos (US $117.9 million) in the program in Michoacán this year.

María Luisa Albores, director of the Mexican Food Security agency (Segalmex), reported that the government has purchased more than 63,000 tonnes of corn directly from some 2,400 small-scale farmers in Michoacán.

Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena reported that the government is investing 168.2 million pesos (US $9 million) in “sustainable forestry” projects in Michoacán.

Energy Minister Luz Elena González reported that more than 1,200 electricity projects have been completed in Michoacán, increasing electricity coverage to 99.99% of homes in the state. She said that 508 million pesos (US $27.2 million) were invested in the projects.

Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez reported that more than 2.46 million tourists visited Michoacán between January and August. She said tourist numbers increased 10.1% compared to the same period of last year. She said that tourism-related spending injected more than US $186 million into the Michoacán economy between January and August.

Infrastructure, Communications and Transport Minister Jesús Esteva reported that the government is upgrading 411 kilometers of highway in Michoacán. He said that the government and the private sector are investing more than 41 billion pesos (US $2.2 billion) in six highway projects in the state.

Welfare Minister Leticia Ramírez reported that the government is spending more than 30.4 billion pesos (US $1.6 billion) on welfare and social programs in Michoacán in 2026. She said that more than 1 million Michoacán residents benefit from the programs, which include pension schemes, educational scholarships and the distribution of fertilizer to farmers.

Education Minister Mario Delgado reported that over 795,000 students in Michoacán receive government scholarships. He said that primary school, middle school, high school and university students all receive monetary assistance. He said that the scholarships are funded with an investment of 5.7 billion pesos (around US $306 million).

IMSS Bienestar director Alejandro Svarch reported that a new hospital focused on the treatment of addictions had opened in Apatzingán. He also reported that a mental health center had opened in Huetamo. The combined investment in the two projects was 76.1 million pesos (US $3.6 million).

118 billion pesos in investment planned for Plan Michoacán by 2030

Presenting Plan Michoacán on Nov. 9, 2025, Sheinbaum described it as a “comprehensive strategy” and told reporters that it was based on 12 central tenets and included “more than 100 actions.”

Her presentation on Wednesday showed that there are, in fact, more than 2,500 Plan Michoacán “actions,” 1,680 of which have been “completed.” Sheinbaum said that represented progress of 67%.

She also said that 118 billion pesos (US $6.3 billion) is slated to be invested in Plan Michoacán between 2025 and 2030, the final year of her six-year term. That amount is more than double the 57-billion-peso investment that was originally announced.

Sheinbaum said that 72.43 billion pesos has already been spent on the plan. That amount represents 61% of the projected total.

Sheinbaum said that Plan Michoacán involves “very intense work” that is coordinated by the Interior Ministry. She also said that all of the federal government ministries have a “permanent presence” in Michoacán, one of 23 Mexican states governed by the Morena party.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Tourists, traffic and turtles, oh my!
World.content:
Let me be the first to officially welcome you to tourist season in Puerto Vallarta! It’s the time of year when local entertainment ramps up, traffic jams up, and the checkout lines at Costco pile up.

But we may get a little help with traffic this season with the opening of the new Amado Nervo Bridge. It’s not just car traffic, but sea turtle traffic, too. Puerto Vallarta is in the thick of hatching season, when the newborn tortuguitas stumble their way from their nests to the sea by the hundreds, and you can help them on their journey.

And everyone is hoping for a more tranquil winter than last, when, on Feb. 22, members of the Jalisco New Generation cartel blocked traffic and burned cars and OXXO stores in the downtown area. The aftereffects of which have changed perceptions of safety here and abroad.

Read on to learn about how the city is working to restore tourist confidence and attract new visitors, the opening of a new commuter bridge, and sea turtle season.

Vallarta works to restore tourist confidence

Puerto Vallarta is working to revive tourism and attract new visitors amidst a backdrop of increased public perception of insecurity. According to the National Urban Public Safety survey, Vallartenses’ perception of insecurity has more than doubled since last year, rising from 24.7% in September 2025 to 53.6% in September 2026. While significantly up since this time last year, locals’ perception of insecurity has actually decreased since June, when it peaked at 65.4%.

The survey measures public perception of insecurity and doesn’t reflect actual crime rates. Puerto Vallarta remains one of the safer places to travel compared to other tourist destinations, and experiences less theft and violent crime than most U.S. cities of the same size. Also, the U.S. State Department, known for being expeditious about issuing travel warnings, has no current restrictions on travel to Vallarta.

But perception is everything, so the Vallarta tourism industry is working hard to win back traveler confidence and attract new visitors. This fall, representatives from the Puerto Vallarta Tourism Trust toured western states, hosting seminars for high-performing travel advisors in Arizona, Colorado and Utah, and welcomed tourism representatives from the U.S., Canada and other parts of Mexico to Vallarta. They even traveled to Poland, which will have direct weekly flights to Vallarta starting in December.

Despite February’s unrest, Puerto Vallarta remains one of the top destinations for vacationers in the world and is among the Top 10 global destinations for the Thanksgiving holiday, according to a recent survey by Allianz Partners. And if the traffic and Costco lines are any indication, we’ll have a healthy tourist season this year.

Amado Nervo Bridge opening

Here’s hoping a new commuter bridge between Banderas Bay and Puerto Vallarta will ease traffic on the busy Highway 200. The new Amado Nervo Bridge officially opened to cars on Oct. 28th. The bridge is located east of the main tourist corridor, connecting the towns of San Vicente and Ixtapa and surrounding communities, all of which previously had to use the 200 to get from one municipality to the next.

Local transportation officials estimate the bridge will cut as much as 40 minutes from the commute and ease congestion on Highway 200, especially between Mezcales and the Puerto Vallarta airport. The bridge is two kilometers long with three lanes in each direction and a bike lane. It’s a bit out of the way of the normal tourist route, but will hopefully direct more local traffic eastward and make traveling along the 200 smoother.

Turtles take to the sea

Hundreds of thousands of baby sea turtles are making their journey to the sea along Puerto Vallarta’s beaches. November is one of the best months to see them during the height of hatching season.

In Vallarta, a collaborative network of local community groups, grassroots non-profits, university researchers, government agencies, and beachfront resorts runs sea turtle camps along the coast. These camps protect eggs and ensure as many hatchlings as possible reach the sea. When mother turtles come ashore at night to dig nests and lay their eggs, the next morning conservationists remove them and place the eggs into manmade nests at the camps. This helps protect the eggs from predators and poachers. Not all nests are moved; camps only have capacity to protect so many. But still, they manage to save and release more than 150,000 baby turtles each year.

Turtle camps can be found at various spots along the coast of Banderas Bay, including the south end of Varadero beach in front of the Vidanta resort, Playa Holi in front of La Isla Mall, and Boca de Tomates turtle camp north of Bocanegra in the Marina. (Boca de Tomates took a beating with recent storms and could use support to rebuild.)

Camps often invite the public to witness and help with baby turtle releases. There are few things more precious and inspiring in nature than watching a baby sea turtle stumble its way into the surf. Crowds cheer and gasp as the little guys earnestly follow their instincts into the water, only to be washed back onto the sand time and time again until they finally make it out. I highly recommend you try to see a release when you visit.

Debbie Slobe is a writer and communications strategist based in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco. She blogs at Mexpatmama.com and is a senior program director at Resource Media. Find her on Instagram and Facebook.

World.title: 38th Morelia Music Festival kicks off next week, highlighting artists from Asia
World.content:
The historic city of Morelia, Michoacán, is gearing up to host the 38th edition of the “Miguel Bernal Jiménez” Music Festival, which will take place from Nov. 13 to 22.

Featuring Asia as a guest region, the festival will feature representatives from China, Japan, India, Thailand, South Korea and Indonesia, in addition to the participation of artists and musical groups from 13 countries.

“It’s a must-see show,” head of the event Verónica Bernal told news outlet Crónica in an interview.

The festival will take place in different locations across the city, including cultural and religious landmarks like the Morelia Cultural Center, the Clavijero Cultural Center, the Roses Conservatory, the Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe and more.

The opening concert will feature the National Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Ludwig Carrasco, with violinist Yesong Sophie Lee as soloist. The performance will take place on Nov. 13 at 8 p.m. at the Teatro Morelos, one of the event’s primary venues.

The inaugural program includes music by Tan Dun, winner of an Academy Award and a Grammy for the soundtrack to the 2000 film “Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon”, in addition to the performance of El Chueco, a famous 20th-century ballet composed by the Mexican composer Miguel Bernal Jiménez, whose legacy gives this festival its name.

#musitecamx #ballet #guillermokeysarenas #miguelbernaljimenez #compositormexicano ♬ original sound – Fonoteca Nacional de México @fonotecanacional 𝙀𝙡 𝙘𝙝𝙪𝙚𝙘𝙤 es un ballet que utiliza elementos populares y religiosos para contar la historia de un niño paralítico que le teme al mundo exterior y que, tras soñar que supera sus miedos, despierta para disfrutar las procesiones que desfilan frente a la puerta de su casa. El argumento es del bailarín y coreógrafo Guillermo Keys-Arenas, que encargó la música al compositor Miguel Bernal Jiménez, y la obra se estrenó en el Teatro de Bellas Artes en 1951. Sin embargo, con el tiempo la música se independizó de la puesta en escena y es considerada por algunos la mejor partitura del compositor. Bernal Jiménez falleció el 26 de julio de 1956 pero su legado sigue vivo a través de su música, que la Fonoteca Nacional difunde a través de Musiteca.mx. Encuentra la grabación competa en el link denuestra biografía. Fotografía: Caracterización de el Chueco. Guillermo Keys-Arenas, Heterofonía, núm. 114-115, enero-diciembre de 1996, p. 87. México, INBA, Cenidim #FonotecaNacional

Miguel Bernal Jiménez (1910–1956) was an organist, researcher and teacher, originally from Morelia. He was a prominent figure in 20th-century Mexican sacred music and a pioneer in the research of music from the era of New Spain.

According to Festival Director Bernal, other events will also feature works by the composer.

Among the most anticipated performances is Carnaval Barroco by the French ensemble Le Poème Harmonique, which combines music, theater, dance and acrobatics. The show will be part of the celebrations marking 200 years of diplomatic relations between Mexico and France.

Additionally, violinist Lidia Baich and pianist Donka Angatscheva will commemorate the 125th anniversary of the resumption of diplomatic relations between Mexico and Austria.

Bernal said that nearly half of the activities will be free of charge, with a program that includes masterclasses, children’s performances and the traditional floral carpets of Patamban. Tickets can be purchased at a discount (through Nov. 6) here.

With reports from Excélsior and Mi Morelia

World.title: Will Pope Leo XIV visit Mexico in 2027?
World.content:
A potential visit by Pope Leo XIV to Mexico in 2027 caused confusion after statements by Mexican and Vatican officials were interpreted by Mexican media as confirmation of the trip. However, no official visit to the country has been announced.

The misunderstanding arose during a recent press conference by María Montserrat Alvarado, new Prefect of the Vatican Dicastery for Communication, in which she said that the pontiff would visit Our Lady of Guadalupe — a reference that was interpreted as an allusion to the Basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City.

Later on Tuesday, when asked about the matter during a press conference, Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada said that she had no confirmation of the visit. Still, she added that if it were to take place, it would be in 2027 on the occasion of the Guadalupan Jubilee Year.

“That is surely one of the reasons [of the Pope’s visit], and it will happen next year. We need to look at the dates, and we will provide an update right away,” she said.

The Guadalupan Jubilee Year began on Oct. 12 and is linked to the 50th anniversary of the consecration of the new Basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City.

Noticing the confusion, Televisa’s Vatican correspondent Valentina Alazraki clarified Wednesday morning that the Vatican’s spokesperson was referring to the Parish of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Casavalle, Uruguay.

#Actualización | La jefa del Gobierno capitalino, Clara Brugada, calificó como una buena noticia la visita que realizaría el papa León XIV a México. Sin embargo, momentos después se aclaró que en realidad se trata de la parroquia de la Virgen de Guadalupe en Uruguay. 👇 https://t.co/4cDfTySBYR — MVS Noticias (@MVSNoticias) November 3, 2026

“According to Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni, Montse Alvarado was not referring to the Basilica of the Virgin of Guadalupe in Mexico City, but rather to the parish in Casavalle, Uruguay. Therefore, there was no confirmation of a papal visit to Mexico,” Alazraki wrote on her X account.

In a later post, Alazraki said that according to several Vatican sources, “it is very clear that Pope Leo does indeed want to go to Mexico” and visit the Basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City.

However, “there is nothing concrete, neither regarding the date nor the program. There is only the intention,” she stated.

Confusion over the Pope’s visit to Mexico comes days before his upcoming Apostolic Journey to Latin America, which will include visits to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru between Nov. 6 and 17.

With reports from El Sol de México

World.title: In Pomuch, to honor the dead is to preen them
World.content:
There are few places across the world where the dead are as ever-present as they are in Pomuch, a town in the municipality of Hecelchakán, in the southern state of Campeche.

Every Día de Muertos, the deceased are prepared for their return in a bittersweet process. While welcoming those who have left is cause for celebration, it is also a reminder that they cannot stay with us all year round.

In the words of Marisol Yam, the process is “very mystical, very intimate,” and “a way of loving the people who are no longer here.”

Marisol, or Mari for short, is a 29-year-old woman who has spent her entire life knowing this way of drawing close to the dead in Pomuch. For those unacquainted with this reality, the process might seem crazy. However, for Mari, it’s part of the commitments that exist with her family.

“For as long as I can remember, my grandparents always took us to the cemetery to visit our great-grandparents and a young cousin who passed away before his time,” Mari says. “To me, that was normal. Going to the cemetery to clean my great-grandparents, accompanying my grandmother to bring the candle, the flowers and the tablecloth, was normal.”

To be loved is to be taken care of

The people of Pomuch have a unique way of celebrating their ancestors.

With the utmost care and affection, families begin making preparations a few weeks before the Day of the Dead; they tell their deceased family members that it is time to start getting ready for the celebration, and an unexpected scene unfolds in Pomuch’s cemetery.

Under the loving hands of their families, the dead finally return to celebrate the union between both worlds. The bones that now rest in small carved wooden boxes — or ossuaries — acquire new life with each cleaning and feel that they have not been forgotten.

Preparing the bones for celebration

Among the graves, skulls and ribs begin to appear, delicately removed from their ossuaries so that the cloth in which they are wrapped — often decorated by a family member — can be changed.

With the devotion of someone dressing a loved one, each household wraps the bones in lace and embroidered tablecloths, taking care not to seal the lids so the bones can catch a bit of air. In this revered tradition, death is merely another form of presence, and the bones, trapped between two worlds, still need the air to “breathe.”

“The family will decide what kind of tablecloth to put on (with little angels, flowers, their name, a character), whether they will sing to them, pray to them, if the whole family will go with the children or just mom and dad, if you want to tell them about your life and how you’ve been doing since they left. If you had them in life, you still have them in death. The only difference is that they can no longer see you, but they can hear you,” Mari explains.

She goes on to say, “Cleaning them before Oct. 30 is an absolute must, because Oct. 31 is the celebration for the children who are no longer with us, and Nov. 1 is for the adults. There is a belief that if you don’t go clean them, they become forgotten souls — souls whose families didn’t care or bother to prepare them for their celebration. On Nov. 1, they go out for a walk and are free to come visit us.”

When is the grave opened for the first time?

Although this ceremony takes place every year on the Day of the Dead, it does not happen immediately after a loved one passes away.

Mari says that “when a person dies, three years must pass before the family can exhume their remains.” She explains that for the cleaning process to be done properly, human remains must be reduced to bones, and the body must be completely decomposed.

“If after three years the body hasn’t decomposed,” Mari says, “they rebury it for as long as they deem necessary depending on its condition. There are families that sometimes take four or five years to exhume the remains. This can happen if the person who passed away took a lot of medication.”

The initial exhumation process

That first time they are taken out to transition from burial to ossuary is one of the most important moments for commemorating the family member’s life and cleaning their remains.

“The first turning point is when they come out. They open a wall of the vault to pull out the casket (some families pay the gravedigger or a mason to do it). Some people take them out at the exact time they passed away; others wait until the whole family is present,” Mari says. “And when they open the casket, if only bones remain, they begin cleaning them one by one — using a brush or a cloth — and place them one by one into a box similar to a shoebox, but slightly wider and taller.”

At that point, “They arrange the entire skeleton,” marking the “first moment of the tradition of cleaning them every year.”

Not only on the Day of the Dead

According to Mari, while the cleaning for the reception of the dead cannot be missed, it is not the only date when ancestors can be celebrated, spoken with and remembered. Throughout the year, each family decides how often they want to clean their loved one’s remains and on what dates to do so.

“The family decides when to go clean them: Do they visit for their birthday? They decide. Do they visit for a wedding anniversary? They might bring them flowers or candles. They can bring an object, a photo or introduce new members of the family to them.”

Celebrations outside the cemetery

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Campeche Turismo Mx (@campecheturismomx)

As with all major celebrations, the commemoration is not confined to the cemetery. Just as altars are set up in other parts of Mexico, homes in Pomuch are filled with banquets for loved ones who are no longer here.

“My grandmother would always wake us up at 6 or 7 in the morning to set the table, buy ingredients and get ready.”

Mari recalls how she experienced the Day of the Dead as a child, and how it is lived in her home today: “In my house, when my little cousin is coming, we decorate with balloons and buy him a toy because that’s what he likes. We buy bread, fruit and set out water, hot chocolate, candied coconut, candied squash, candied plum and candied nance. It’s our little offering for him. He’s coming to eat.

“My dad puts food on the table for him at 11 in the morning, and when we are about to eat, he takes it away and says to him: ‘We are going to eat now; I hope you enjoyed the food we prepared for you today. You are welcome to come back whenever you like. Excuse us while we eat. If you’d like to join us, we left something on the table for you.’ My mom prepares food, making sure it’s yard chicken — the kind raised at home that you bought as a chick, and you decide if you’re going to slaughter it for those dates.”

A lifelong commitment of love

What might seem unsettling to an outsider is, for Marisol Yam and the families of Pomuch, the ultimate expression of love. It is a lifelong commitment that transforms a cold grave into a living, breathing dialogue.

Whether introducing a new baby to a great-grandparent’s bones or buying a toy for a cousin who left too soon, this tradition ensures that to be dead is still to be taken care of.

Lydia Leija is a linguist, journalist and visual storyteller. She has directed three feature films, and her audiovisual work has been featured in national and international media. She’s been part of National Geographic, Muy Interesante and Cosmopolitan.

World.title: Querétaro-Irapuato train line now 25% complete
World.content:
The 102-kilometer Querétaro-Irapuato train line is 25% complete one year into its construction, according to the Agency for Trains and Integrated Public Transportation (ATTRAPI).

The US $5.3 billion project, which broke ground in September 2025, is being developed in Mexico’s Bajío region, which hosts global manufacturing, agribusiness and technology companies. Once complete, the route is expected to benefit up to 2 million people.

On Saturday, President Claudia Sheinbaum inspected construction of the new train line, which is part of a federal plan to lay 2,500 km (reduced from 3,000) of tracks for passenger and freight services by 2030, at an estimated cost of 700 billion pesos (almost US $37.2 billion).

“The construction of trains is driving employment and economic development in the country,” Sheinbaum said on Saturday. “So, congratulations to those who are with us today, to the companies that are building, to the workers, to the governor of Querétaro, who has been a great help and to the governor of Guanajuato,” she added.

“We belong to different political parties, but that has nothing to do with it when we work together for the good of Mexico.”

The train line will have five stations once complete: Apaseo el Grande, Celaya, Cortazar/Villagrán, Salamanca and Irapuato. As part of the project, 10 viaducts, a box tunnel and 13 roads are being built, creating an expected 3,365 direct and 5,700 indirect jobs throughout construction.

The multinational transportation company Alstom is manufacturing the trains in Hidalgo, each one measuring 100 meters long and capable of being coupled together if required, according to the head of ATTRAPI’s construction unit, Efraín Deschamps Gutiérrez de Velasco.

Querétaro Governor Mauricio Kuri González and Guanajuato Governor Libia Dennise García Muñoz Ledo, both of the opposition National Action Party (PAN), thanked the president for spearheading the railroad, which is expected to enhance connectivity between Mexico City and the Bajío region, generate employment opportunities and spur economic development.

The Querétaro-Irapuato train line will eventually connect with the Mexico City-Querétaro train line, which is currently between 32% and 35% complete, Sheinbaum said during an official tour of the work site on Monday.

With reports from El Universal and Debate

World.title: How might the results of today’s midterm elections in the United States impact Mexico?
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump could make greater security-related demands on Mexico after the U.S. midterm elections, according to a Mexico City-based public affairs and political risk consultancy.

All 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives and 35 of 100 seats in the U.S. Senate are on the line in today’s midterms. The Republican Party currently holds majorities in both the House and the Senate, but control of one or both chambers could change in early 2027 when newly elected lawmakers take office.

In a report titled “México y Estados Unidos. Entre la revisión del T-MEC y el impacto de las elecciones intermedias” (Mexico and the United States: Between the USMCA Review and the Impact of the Midterm Elections), Integralia Consultores says that the U.S. midterms “will modify counterweights on Trump, but won’t necessarily reduce pressure on Mexico.”

“A Democratic majority in one or both chambers would lead to increased investigations and oversight of the executive branch, intensifying internal political confrontation. Faced with greater domestic constraints, Trump might focus more attention on foreign policy to build his legacy,” the consultancy writes in the executive summary of its report.

“The fight against drug trafficking and organized crime — which enjoys greater bipartisan consensus than other international issues — could take on greater prominence and lead to new demands on Mexico,” Integralia says.

To date, President Claudia Sheinbaum has maintained a respectful relationship with Trump, even as the U.S. government pressures Mexico on a range of issues, including trade, security and immigration. Her administration has taken some steps that have been interpreted as attempts to appease the Trump administration — such as increasing tariffs on imports from China and sending scores of organized crime figures to the U.S. — but Sheinbaum has remained a steadfast defender of Mexican sovereignty and hasn’t shied away from denouncing what she sees as U.S. meddling in Mexican affairs.

What demands could Trump make on Mexico?

According to Integralia, “[a] Trump with more internal constraints due to a Democratic majority [in Congress] could dedicate more attention” to the international fight against drug trafficking, stepping up demands on Mexico for “cooperation, extraditions and actions against criminal organizations.”

“New threats of unilateral [U.S.] actions [in Mexico] can’t be ruled out,” adds the consultancy.

The Mexican government already cooperates closely with the Trump administration on security issues, but is steadfastly opposed to U.S. action on Mexican soil. Sheinbaum has denounced the Central Intelligence Agency’s alleged participation in a drug lab raid in Chihuahua in April without the authorization or knowledge of her administration.

Her government has sent more than 90 organized crime figures to the United States to face justice, while security authorities have arrested more than 70,000 people for allegedly committing high-impact crimes since she took office in October 2024. In the same period, authorities have seized over 36,000 firearms and almost 570 tonnes of narcotics, and dismantled close to 2,800 clandestine drug laboratories.

Despite the progress in combating crime and violence — homicides declined in every state in the first nine months of 2026 — the Trump administration has continued to pressure Mexico to do more to combat drug trafficking, and the U.S. president himself has periodically threatened unilateral military action against cartels in Mexico.

A continuation of such threats, as Integralia says is possible, would certainly not be a surprise.

Will the midterm results affect USMCA negotiations?

According to Integralia, the United States trade negotiations with Mexico “will move forward regardless of the electoral result.”

“Trump will retain broad authority to maintain or modify tariffs and push for stricter regional content requirements,” the consultancy says.

“However,” Integralia adds, “Republican defeats in states affected by the tariffs could increase pressure within the party to moderate some trade measures and avoid further political costs leading up to 2028,” when the next U.S. presidential election will be held.

In ongoing trade talks with the United States, Mexico is aiming to negotiate a reduction — if not the total elimination — of U.S. tariffs on Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles. The dialogue is taking place after the Trump administration announced in July that it had decided against renewing the USMCA free trade pact for an additional 16 years to 2042. The three-way agreement remains in effect, but is currently subject to annual reviews.

Both Sheinbaum and Trump said last month that Mexico and the U.S. were “very close” to reaching a trade deal. Such an agreement could improve the prospects of the Trump administration agreeing to a 16-year renewal of the USMCA, although Washington and Ottawa would also need to resolve their trade differences.

The U.S. government has many concerns about the USMCA and its trade relationships with its neighbors, including ones related to trade deficits, energy policy and China.

How could the US midterm results affect Trump’s deportation agenda?

According to Integralia, immigration policy will remain a priority for Trump, “regardless of the makeup of the [U.S.] Congress.”

However, Democratic Party control of Congress “could increase oversight of deportations, ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] operations and the treatment of migrants” by the Trump administration, the consultancy says.

“… Mexico will continue facing pressure to contain migration flows and receive deportees,” Integralia says.

During the second Trump administration, Mexico has received Mexican deportees as well as nationals of other countries. Meanwhile, data indicates that illegal crossings into the United States from Mexico have fallen sharply during Trump’s second term.

A Democratic Party-controlled Congress that increases oversight of ICE and the treatment of immigrants in the U.S. would be a welcome development for the Mexican government, which has filed complaints with prosecutor’s offices in the U.S. regarding the deaths of Mexican citizens in the custody of ICE or during ICE operations.

Eighteen Mexicans have died in ICE custody or ICE operations during Trump’s second term, including Emiliano Andrade Covarrubias, who passed away in the Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo, Texas, last month after he was allegedly denied medication he needed to control his health problems, including diabetes.

On numerous occasions, Sheinbaum has expressed her opposition to Trump’s aggressive deportation agenda, and said in July she disagreed with his call for continued immigration traffic stops.

“If there is a person who committed a crime, he or she must be pursued. But migration in itself shouldn’t be criminalized,” she said on July 16.

World.title: Mérida Marathon 2027 Guide for US Runners
World.content:
MEXICO · SPORTS GUIDE

Key Facts What is happening Sunday, 10 January 2027, Monumento a la Patria, Paseo de Montejo, Mérida; marathon, half, 10K and 3K walk.

Why it matters Certified route, pre-dawn start, and organisers expect 8,000 runners in the city’s 485th anniversary year.

The numbers Marathon entry is MXN 690 (about US$37) to 15 November, then MXN 750 (about US$40); 1,300 places.

What to watch Official call: marathon start 5:15 a.m.; local press: 5:00 a.m. Kit pick-up venue is not set.

Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 71.4 points (October 2026 edition).

The Mérida Marathon is a pre-dawn race through the colonial centre of the Yucatán capital. Entry is open to visitors, and the marathon fee rises on 16 November.

Why the Mérida Marathon 2027 Matters to US Runners

The Mérida Marathon 2027 takes place on Sunday, 10 January 2027, in Mérida, the capital of Yucatán state on Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula. The official name is Marat’hon de Mérida, and it forms part of the city’s 485th anniversary celebrations.

Organisers expect 8,000 runners across four events, up from about 6,000 last year. By 21 August 2026, 2,377 people had registered, and 55 percent of them came from other Mexican states.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

For US runners, the race offers a certified course, a January date and a historic city centre. Mérida keeps a clock only 1 hour behind New York, which helps with jet lag.

The marathon is limited to 1,300 places, which makes it smaller than the big marathons in Mexico City or Monterrey. Early registration matters, because the fee rises and places can run out.

Distances, Start Times and Time Limits

All events start and finish at the Monumento a la Patria on Paseo de Montejo, in central Mérida. The marathon is listed at 5:15 a.m. in the official call.

All times are local. The half marathon starts at 5:25 a.m., the 10K at 5:35 a.m. and the walk at 5:45 a.m.

Yucatán stays on UTC-6 all year, so Mérida is 1 hour behind New York in January. The 5:15 a.m. marathon start is 6:15 a.m. Eastern and 3:15 a.m. Pacific.

Local press listed the marathon start as 5:00 a.m. in August and September. The official call from the city government says 5:15 a.m., so treat the call as the safer guide.

The time limit is 6 hours for the marathon and 3 hours 15 minutes for the half marathon. It is 1 hour 45 minutes for the 10K and 1 hour for the walk.

Marathon runners must pass kilometre 30 within 4 hours 30 minutes of the start. Slower runners may be stopped there so that roads can reopen.

Race services, including the finish area, medical care, hydration and bag check, end by 12:00 noon. Runners who finish late may find that road closures have lifted and services have closed.

The Course and the Weather

The official call says prizes require the route certified by AIMS, the international marathon association, World Athletics and the Mexican athletics body. No elevation profile was confirmed for this guide.

Whether the race counts as a Boston Marathon qualifier was not confirmed. If you need a qualifying time, ask the Boston Athletic Association first.

The pre-dawn start means most of the race is run before the day’s heat builds. No weather forecast exists this far ahead, so check it the week before and pack for both cool and warm conditions.

How to Enter and What It Costs

The city government set four price periods, and the third runs until Sunday, 15 November 2026. In it, the marathon and half marathon each cost MXN 690 (about US$37).

The 10K costs MXN 400 (about US$21) and the 3K walk MXN 300 (about US$16). From Monday, 16 November 2026, the marathon and half marathon rise to MXN 750 (about US$40).

The 10K rises to MXN 450 (about US$24) from 16 November, and the walk stays at MXN 300 (about US$16). Dollar values use the Banco de México FIX rate of 3 November 2026, MXN 18.76 per US$1.

Entry is online at marathonmerida.dashport.run, which the city’s own page says is operated independently of the city government. You can also register in person at shops named in the official call and at the city sports office on Calle 65.

Places are capped at 1,300 for the marathon, 2,800 for the half marathon, 3,200 for the 10K and 700 for the walk. Registration is personal, so enter your own details and keep the confirmation.

You must prove your age with a copy of a photo ID, such as a passport, and sign a liability waiver. The minimum age is 18 for the marathon, half marathon and 10K, and 6 for the walk.

Use only the official city page and the platform it links, because entry scams spread around popular races. Whether the marathon has sold out was not checked in the sources read for this guide.

Kit Pick-Up and Race Morning

Kit pick-up is on Saturday, 9 January 2027, from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., and the venue has not been set. You must bring a valid photo ID and a printed, signed waiver.

Pick-up is in a single window, and runners who miss it lose the rights that come with their entry. Someone else may collect a kit with your signed receipt and copies of both photo IDs.

The kit holds a commemorative shirt, a disposable timing chip, your bib and a finisher medal. Marathon and half marathon entrants also receive a finisher towel.

The medal is awarded only to those who cross the line within the time limit. Plan your hotel so that you can reach the Paseo de Montejo start area before the gates close.

Prizes and Categories

The prize purse is MXN 949,000 (about US$50,600) in total. The overall winners of the men’s and women’s marathons each receive MXN 90,000 (about US$4,800).

Second and third place in each marathon receive MXN 25,000 (about US$1,300) and MXN 20,000 (about US$1,100). Prizes for the other distances are listed in the official call.

Age categories run from the open class, ages 18 to 29, through sub-master, master, veteran and veteran-plus for ages 60 and over. A mixed wheelchair class is offered in the marathon.

The official call applies the same rules and prices to every runner, with no separate foreign category. The registration platform could not be read for live availability on 4 November 2026.

Getting to Mérida

Manuel Crescencio Rejón International Airport serves Mérida. No flight routes were checked for this guide, so ask airlines about nonstop service from your home airport.

The start area on Paseo de Montejo is in the historic centre, so staying in the centre makes the early morning easier. Hotel prices for race weekend had not been published, so book early.

Expect road closures around the course, as in the 2026 edition, although the 2027 list had not been published. Ask your hotel about the closures and about taxi pick-up points on race morning.

Use hotel taxis or ride-share apps for the pre-dawn trip, and agree a pick-up point for the way back. Keep your phone charged and carry a copy of your passport.

Safety and Costs for Visitors

The State Department rates Yucatán Level 1, Exercise Normal Precautions, and names Mérida as a tourist area. Its Mexico advisory was last issued on 6 September 2024 and was read on 4 November 2026.

Quintana Roo, the neighbouring state with Cancún, is rated Level 2 for crime. Mérida’s rating is lower, but street theft can occur in any city, so keep valuables out of sight.

Mexico’s emergency number is 911, and US citizens can reach consular help at 1-844-528-6611 from the United States. Check the State Department’s Mexico page for passport and tourist permit rules before you fly.

Race costs are entry, flights and a hotel. Only the entry prices are confirmed here, and no hotel or flight price was available.

What It Means for You

For a US runner, the Mérida Marathon 2027 is a January race in a Level 1 state, with entry near US$37. The fee rises on 16 November, so deciding this month saves money.

Enter only through the official city page and platform, and print your waiver before you travel. Book a refundable hotel until you know your entry is confirmed.

Pack for both a cool start and a warm finish, because no forecast exists yet. Read the State Department advisory again before you fly, because levels can change.

What Is Not Known

The marathon start time is listed as 5:15 a.m. in the official call and as 5:00 a.m. in some press. The kit pick-up venue and the final course map had not been announced.

Whether the marathon has sold out, and whether the route is flat or counts as a Boston qualifier, was not confirmed. Hotel prices, flight prices and race-morning shuttles were also unpublished.

The State Department advisory dates from September 2024, so check it for newer advice. Weather for 10 January 2027 cannot be forecast yet.

Connected Coverage

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Mérida Marathon 2027?

It is on Sunday, 10 January 2027, and the marathon starts at 5:15 a.m. local time under the official call. That is 6:15 a.m. Eastern.

How much does the Mérida Marathon cost?

Marathon entry is MXN 690 (about US$37) until Sunday, 15 November 2026, then MXN 750 (about US$40) to 3 January 2027. The 10K costs MXN 400 (about US$21) until 15 November.

Can foreign runners enter the Mérida Marathon?

Yes, the official call is open to all runners who meet its rules. You need photo ID, a signed waiver and, for the marathon, a place within the 1,300-runner cap.

Is Mérida safe for US visitors?

The State Department rates Yucatán Level 1, Exercise Normal Precautions, and lists Mérida as a tourist area. Use normal city precautions and plan your pre-dawn transport.

Sources: City of Mérida, official call for Marat’hon de Mérida 2027; City of Mérida, official marathon page; US State Department, Mexico travel advisory (Yucatán); Banco de México, FIX exchange rate of 3 November 2026.

World.title: Caribbean Series 2027 Hermosillo Guide
World.content:
MEXICO · SPORTS GUIDE

Key Facts What is happening Monday, 1 February 2027, to Sunday, 7 February 2027, at Estadio Fernando Valenzuela, Hermosillo, Mexico.

Why it matters Four winter-league champions and a guest team compete, with a pitch clock planned for the first time.

The numbers Season-ticket carnets run from MXN 6,800 (about US$362) to MXN 25,450 (about US$1,357).

What to watch Public sale, single-game prices, game times and a US broadcaster are not yet announced.

Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 71.4 points (October 2026 edition).

The Caribbean Series comes to northern Mexico for a seven-day baseball tournament in February 2027. Dates and venue are set, but only season-ticket holders can buy so far.

Why the Caribbean Series 2027 Matters to US Fans

The Caribbean Series 2027 will be played in Hermosillo, in northwest Mexico, from Monday, 1 February 2027, to Sunday, 7 February 2027. The Caribbean professional baseball confederation (CBPC) and the Hermosillo organising committee announced the dates on 25 June 2026.

It is the yearly tournament that pits the winter-league champions of the Caribbean region against each other. Many of those players also work in US baseball, from the minor leagues to the majors.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

For US readers, Hermosillo keeps the same clock as Arizona all year. Fans from the southwest can reach the city in a day.

Mexico hosts the series for the third year in a row after Mexicali in 2025 and Guadalajara in 2026. Miami hosted in 2023 and 2024.

Who Is Playing

Each country sends the champion of its main winter league. Mexico, Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic and Venezuela are the four members named for 2027.

A fifth, guest team completes the field, and the guest country had not been named when this guide was written. The winter leagues finish in December and January, so the actual clubs are not yet known.

Venezuela is named again for 2027 after missing 2026, when the series moved from Caracas to Guadalajara. Its champion has not been decided, because the winter league is still under way.

The host club is the Naranjeros de Hermosillo, who play at this ballpark in the Mexican Pacific League. Mexico’s entry is the champion of its winter league, not necessarily the home team.

Schedule and Format

The round-robin phase runs from Monday, 1 February 2027, to Friday, 5 February 2027, with two games a day. Semifinals follow on Saturday, 6 February 2027.

The third-place game and the final are both on Sunday, 7 February 2027. Game start times had not been published when this guide was written.

Sonora does not use daylight saving time and stays on UTC-7 all year. In February that puts Hermosillo 2 hours behind New York and 1 hour ahead of Los Angeles.

A 7 p.m. game in Hermosillo would begin at 9 p.m. Eastern. Treat that as an example only until real times are published.

The organisers and the CBPC have said this will be the first Caribbean Series played with a pitch clock. The rule is meant to shorten games and keep the tournament moving.

The Ballpark in Hermosillo

Games are played at Estadio Fernando Valenzuela, which opened in 2013 as Estadio Sonora and hosted that year’s Caribbean Series. It was renamed in December 2023 for the Mexican pitcher Fernando Valenzuela, a former Los Angeles Dodgers star.

No official capacity figure was confirmed for this guide. Organisers say the stadium is being upgraded for the tournament.

No details of the work have been published. Check the seller and the organisers for seating maps before you choose a section.

How to Buy Tickets

The first sale is a presale limited to season-ticket holders of the Naranjeros who have paid their 2026-27 carnet in full. It opened on 18 September 2026, and seat protection ended on Friday, 16 October.

Rates: Banco de México FIX of 3 November 2026, MXN 18.76 per US$1. The carnet covers every game, from MXN 6,800 (about US$362) to MXN 25,450 (about US$1,357).

Preferente costs MXN 9,900 (about US$528), Central Preferente MXN 12,750 (about US$680) and Platea MXN 16,200 (about US$864). Paying in full gets 10 percent off, so Lateral falls to MXN 6,120 (about US$326).

Holders can buy at the Naranjeros stores in Plaza Girasol and Plaza Dila. They can also buy online on Boletomovil, using the code from their email.

No general-public sale date had been announced when this guide was written. The organisers say they will publish the conditions for later sale stages and any single-game tickets.

Last year’s tournament in Guadalajara sold single-game tickets from MXN 390 (about US$21) to MXN 5,500 (about US$293), only online through Boletomovil. That is context, not a price for 2027.

Buy only from the Naranjeros stores or from the platform the organisers name. Tickets offered by strangers on social media are a common source of fake entries.

How to Watch in the US

No US broadcaster or stream for the 2027 series had been announced on 4 November 2026. The CBPC and the organising committee are the first places to look.

The 2026 series in Guadalajara was announced for live English coverage of all 13 games on MLB Network. Rights can change each year, so treat that only as a place to look first.

Check the schedule on the organisers’ channels in January. Fans abroad should also expect that some games may be offered only on regional streams.

Getting to Hermosillo

Hermosillo International Airport serves the city, and American Airlines lists fares to Phoenix, Dallas, Los Angeles and Las Vegas, among others. Its page did not say which routes are nonstop.

Confirm nonstop service with the airline before you book, and reserve early because the tournament may fill rooms. Hotel prices for the week had not been published.

Driving from Arizona is possible through Nogales on Federal Highway 15. The State Department tells its own staff to use that road only in daylight, citing carjackings and shootings.

If you drive, carry a full tank, tell family your plan and avoid unnecessary stops. Many visitors prefer to fly and use a hotel taxi or a ride-share app inside the city.

Safety and Costs for Visitors

The State Department rates Sonora Level 3, Reconsider Travel, because of crime and kidnapping. Its page, last issued on 6 September 2024, was read on 4 November 2026.

The same advisory lists Hermosillo, Bahia de Kino and Puerto Penasco as tourist areas open to US government staff under its rules. It also bars government staff from travelling between cities after dark.

Stay in the central hotel and stadium districts, and plan your ride home before the last game ends. Do not walk long distances at night or leave valuables in a parked car.

Check the State Department’s Mexico page for entry rules, including the passport and tourist permit, before you travel. Carry a passport copy and keep the original in the hotel safe.

Beyond the carnet prices, no ticket, hotel or transport cost for the series had been confirmed. Budget only after single-game prices are published.

What It Means for You

For a US baseball fan, the Caribbean Series 2027 is a chance to see winter-league champions close to the border. It also means a trip to a Level 3 state, so the safety steps matter.

If you want a seat, ask the Naranjeros or the organisers when tickets reach the public, and check the platform weekly. Do not book a non-refundable trip until you hold tickets.

Watch the winter leagues in December and January to learn which clubs qualify. Read the State Department advisory again shortly before you fly, because levels can change.

What Is Not Known

The date of the general public sale, the single-game prices and the seller for those tickets were not announced. Game start times and the guest country were also unpublished.

The four champions will be decided in the winter leagues, so no team list exists yet. The pitch clock is announced by organisers, and the rule details are unpublished.

The scale of the stadium works, its capacity and any seating changes are unknown. The State Department page dates from September 2024, so check it for newer advice.

Connected Coverage

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Caribbean Series 2027?

It runs from Monday, 1 February 2027, to Sunday, 7 February 2027, in Hermosillo, Mexico. The final and the third-place game are on 7 February.

Where can I buy Caribbean Series 2027 tickets?

A season-ticket presale is open only to Naranjeros carnet holders through their stores and Boletomovil. No public sale date or seller has been announced.

How can I watch the Caribbean Series 2027 in the US?

No US broadcaster has been announced. The 2026 series was announced for live English coverage on MLB Network.

Is Hermosillo safe for US visitors?

The State Department rates Sonora Level 3, Reconsider Travel, with tourist areas of Hermosillo open to its staff. Avoid night driving between cities and plan rides in advance.

Sources: Confederación de Béisbol Profesional del Caribe (CBPC) and the Hermosillo 2027 organising committee, dates and format announced 25 June 2026; Naranjeros de Hermosillo, carnet presale terms and prices, 18 September 2026 (Boletomovil); US State Department, Mexico travel advisory (Sonora); Banco de México, FIX exchange rate of 3 November 2026 (banxico.org.mx).

COLOMBIA · MUSIC

Key Facts What is happening Tuboleta lists four singer duels at El Corazón de Bogotá arena on Saturday, 28 November 2026, at 18:00.

Doors and age Doors open at 17:00, the minimum age is 18, and the special guest is Pastor López Jr.

Prices First-stage tickets run from COP 188,000 to COP 880,000 (about US$58 to US$272), service included.

Who is who Eventos Sírvalo Pues S.A.S. is the responsible company; Tuboleta is a Colombian ticket seller.

Not confirmed Only Tuboleta lists the show; the arena’s own events page did not show it on 4 November.

La Última del Año, a year-end popular music show, is listed at El Corazón de Bogotá arena on Saturday, 28 November 2026. Tuboleta sells tickets from COP 188,000 (about US$58).

What the Night Is

The ticket page describes the night as a popular-music concert and calls it the best way to close the year. It lists four duels, which it calls mano a mano, Spanish for hand to hand.

The first duel pairs Jhonny Rivera with Jhon Alex Castaño. The second pairs Andariego with El Charrito Negro.

The third duel pairs Luisito Muñoz with Andrés Franco, known as El Agropecuario. The fourth pairs La Banda del Aventurero with Los Legendarios.

Pastor López Jr appears as special guest. The page does not give a running order or a set length, and the line-up may change.

Eventos Sírvalo Pues S.A.S. is the responsible company named on the page. The page does not describe the style of music beyond calling it popular music.

Dates, Times and Tickets

The concert is on Saturday, 28 November 2026, with doors at 17:00 and the show at 18:00. The minimum age is 18.

Presales ran in late September for customers of the Movistar Total phone plan and for fans of Sírvalo Pues. The first general stage opened on Monday, 28 September 2026, and runs until sold out.

Prices in the first stage include the service charge. Palco Invitados Especiales costs COP 880,000 (about US$272), and Palco Alfombra Roja costs COP 855,000 (about US$264).

Palco Diamante costs COP 780,000 (about US$241), and Palco Oro costs COP 630,000 (about US$195). Palco Plata costs COP 500,000 (about US$155), and Palco Bronce costs COP 380,000 (about US$117).

Tribuna Fan Sur costs COP 495,000 (about US$153). Piso 2 costs COP 327,000 (about US$101), or COP 295,000 (about US$91) with a partial view.

Piso 3 costs COP 270,000 (about US$83), and Piso 3 sectors with partial or no view cost COP 188,000 (about US$58). The page lists no later-stage prices, so costs may rise once the first stage sells out.

Buyers may purchase up to six tickets per transaction. Web, call-centre and point-of-sale purchases carry an extra delivery fee shown before payment.

Buyers who pay with an international card collect their tickets at the box office, and only the cardholder may do so. Ask Tuboleta how this works before you travel.

El Corazón de Bogotá and Getting There

The arena’s website gives the address as Diagonal 61C number 26-35 in Bogotá. The ticket page also calls the venue Movistar Arena, and its sector rules use that name.

The arena says visitors can use the TransMilenio station called Corazón de Bogotá. Bus routes 599, 59B, 142 and F410 run along Calle 63.

Routes T11, T26, T163, 191, 599, H608 and H631 run along Carrera 30. Check route numbers on the day, because they can change.

Partner car parks are at the El Campín stadium, north and south, and at the Palacio de los Deportes. For some events the arena runs free buses, and prices depend on each car park.

The arena has more than 100 free bicycle spaces, so bring your own lock. It also lists two Tembici bike-share stations, one beside the skate park and one at El Campín.

For taxis and ride apps, tell the driver you are going to El Corazón de Bogotá. The arena says organised access points drop visitors near the main entrances.

Entry Rules for the Concert

Sectors 206, 214, 306 and 314 are alcohol-free, with no sale or consumption of alcohol. Sectors 201, 219, 301 and 319 may have limited views, and the buyer accepts this at purchase.

Visibly pregnant women may not enter, following the recommendations of the authorities. Guests with reduced mobility should tell Tuboleta when buying and tell staff on the day.

The page says nothing about bag rules. Times and line-up may change for operational, weather or official reasons.

Entry Rules and Safety for US Visitors

The State Department says US citizens need no visa for stays of 90 days or fewer. The passport must be valid on entry and for the whole stay.

Colombia’s migration authority describes Check-Mig, an online trip pre-registration, to be filled in from 72 hours to one hour before travel. Its page lists the form as required when minors leave Colombia, so check whether it applies.

The department rates Colombia Level 3, Reconsider Travel, in an advisory dated 17 April 2025, citing crime, terrorism, civil unrest and kidnapping. Its Level 4 areas include Arauca, Norte de Santander and the Venezuelan border region.

What It Means for You

A US visitor can fit this night into a late-November Bogotá stay, but the show is a Spanish-language, adults-only event. Buy only through Tuboleta, and never pay a stranger for a ticket file.

World.title: Belize Population and Ethnic Groups Explained
World.content:
BELIZE · POPULATION

Key Facts What is happening Belize counted 397,483 people in its 2022 census, up 23% since 2010, and estimates 418,982 for mid-2026.

Why it matters English is official, but 54.0% of people speak Spanish and 49.0% speak Kriol, an English-based creole.

The numbers Mestizo 51.7%, Creole 25.2%, Maya about 10% to 11%, Garifuna 4.0%; 57.8% of people live in rural areas.

Who is who Mestizo means mixed Spanish and Maya roots; Creole, African and British roots; Garifuna, African and Indigenous Caribbean roots.

What to watch Watch the 2022 census tables on birthplace and migration, and Stann Creek and Cayo, growing 40% and 32%.

What it means for you English is official and 2 Belize dollars are fixed at US$1, which makes Belize easy for Americans.

Belize is a small, young and mixed country where English, Kriol and Spanish share the streets. This guide explains who lives there, where they live and how the groups fit together.

Belize population stood at 397,483 people in the 2022 census, which makes it one of the smaller countries in the Americas. It is also very mixed, with Mestizo, Creole, Maya, Garifuna, Mennonite and East Indian communities.

This guide covers who lives in Belize, what they speak and where they live, as of November 2026. Related reading: the Rio Times Belize page, Belize Explained 2026, the culture pillar, the politics pillar and Moving to Belize.
