We send a confirmation link first, and the same address then receives The Rio Times Brief, our daily briefing. Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

Belize Population in Numbers

The Statistical Institute of Belize, the government statistics office, counted 397,483 people in the census of 2022. That is 75,060 more than the 322,424 counted in 2010, a rise of about 23%.

The same office published a mid-year estimate of 418,982 people for July 2026. The World Bank, which uses its own method, shows 422,924 people for 2025 and annual growth of 1.4%.

Women outnumber men slightly, with 201,789 women and 195,695 men in 2022. Growth averaged about 1.8% a year from 2010 to 2022, calculated from the two census counts.

People in 2022: 397,483, up from 322,424 in 2010, 248,916 in 2000 and 145,353 in 1980.

397,483, up from 322,424 in 2010, 248,916 in 2000 and 145,353 in 1980. Urban and rural: 42.2% urban and 57.8% rural in 2022.

42.2% urban and 57.8% rural in 2022. Median age: 25 years in 2022, up from 21 in 2010.

25 years in 2022, up from 21 in 2010. Born abroad: 11.5% of residents in 2022; 87.8% were born in Belize.

RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Belize is a young country that is ageing. The median age rose from 21 in 2010 to 25 in 2022, while people aged 65 and over are 5.2%.

The World Bank puts fertility at 2.0 children per woman in 2024, near the level that keeps a population steady. Average household size fell from 4.0 people in 2010 to 3.6 in 2022.

Ethnic Groups of Belize

Belize has no official ethnic quota, but the census asks people which group they belong to. In 2022 the statistics office reported 51.7% Mestizo, 25.2% Creole, 4.0% Garifuna and 1.5% East Indian.

For the Maya it gives two numbers, 11.2% in its census infographic and 9.8% on its key-findings page. The Maya share is therefore best read as roughly 10% to 11%.

Mestizo is the biggest group and has grown from 33.1% in 1980 to 51.7% in 2022. The Creole share fell from 39.7% in 1980 to 21.1% in 2010, then rose to 25.2% in 2022.

Mestizo: people of mixed Spanish and Maya ancestry; the largest group, living across the country but mostly in the north and in Cayo.

people of mixed Spanish and Maya ancestry; the largest group, living across the country but mostly in the north and in Cayo. Creole: people of mixed African and British descent; about two-thirds live in Belize City, on the coast.

people of mixed African and British descent; about two-thirds live in Belize City, on the coast. Maya: Belize’s Indigenous people, in three groups, Q’eqchi’ (Ketchi), Mopan and Yucatec; Toledo district in the south is the heartland.

Belize’s Indigenous people, in three groups, Q’eqchi’ (Ketchi), Mopan and Yucatec; Toledo district in the south is the heartland. Garifuna: descendants of Africans and Indigenous Caribbean people, centred on Dangriga and the southern coast.

descendants of Africans and Indigenous Caribbean people, centred on Dangriga and the southern coast. East Indian and Mennonite: East Indians descend from indentured labourers; Mennonite farmers, mostly German-speaking, began arriving from Canada and Mexico in 1958.

The Mestizo share grew in two waves, first with Caste War refugees from Yucatan, Mexico, in the mid-1800s. Refugees and migrants from Central America followed in the 1980s.

Garifuna people mark 19 November each year as Settlement Day, a public holiday that remembers their arrival at Dangriga in 1832. UNESCO, the UN culture agency, lists the language, dance and music of the Garifuna as intangible heritage of humanity.

Languages and Religion

English is the only official language and the language of schools, courts and government. The 2022 census counted 278,390 English speakers, 199,393 Spanish speakers and 180,792 Kriol speakers.

Kriol, an English-based creole language, is spoken by 49.0% of people, and by 72.9% in Belize District. Spanish is spoken by 54.0%, and by 82.5% in Corozal and 83.6% in Orange Walk.

English: 278,390 speakers, 75.5% as the statistics office shows it; 85.8% in Belize District and 79.8% in Cayo.

278,390 speakers, 75.5% as the statistics office shows it; 85.8% in Belize District and 79.8% in Cayo. Spanish: 199,393 speakers, 54.0%; highest in Orange Walk and Corozal in the north.

199,393 speakers, 54.0%; highest in Orange Walk and Corozal in the north. Kriol: 180,792 speakers, 49.0%; strongest in Belize District, at 72.9%.

180,792 speakers, 49.0%; strongest in Belize District, at 72.9%. Q’eqchi’ (Ketchi): 23,315 speakers, 6.3%; about half of Toledo district speaks it.

23,315 speakers, 6.3%; about half of Toledo district speaks it. Mopan Maya: 14,479 speakers, 3.9%; most live in Stann Creek and Toledo.

14,479 speakers, 3.9%; most live in Stann Creek and Toledo. Others: smaller groups speak German, Garifuna, Yucatec Maya and Chinese.

Many people speak two or three of these languages, so the shares add up to more than 100%. The census does not measure how well people read or write each one.

The 2022 census found Roman Catholics at 31.8%, people with no religion at 31.0% and Protestants at 29.8%. Other faiths made up the remaining 6.3%.

Catholics were 61.7% of the population in 1980 and 40.1% in 2010. The share with no religion doubled from 15.5% in 2010 to 31.0% in 2022.

Where Belizeans Live and Where They Come From

Belize has six districts, and the largest is Belize District, with 113,630 people in 2022, or 28.6% of the country. Cayo follows with 99,105, then Orange Walk with 54,152, Stann Creek with 48,162, Corozal with 45,310 and Toledo with 37,124.

Every district grew between 2010 and 2022, led by Stann Creek at 40% and Cayo at 32%. Toledo grew 21%, Belize District 19%, Orange Walk 18% and Corozal 10%.

Belize District: Belize City, the largest city, with the most Creole residents.

Belize City, the largest city, with the most Creole residents. Cayo: the capital Belmopan, San Ignacio and the Mennonite farms of Spanish Lookout; fast growing.

the capital Belmopan, San Ignacio and the Mennonite farms of Spanish Lookout; fast growing. Orange Walk and Corozal: the north, with a Spanish-speaking Mestizo majority.

the north, with a Spanish-speaking Mestizo majority. Stann Creek: Dangriga, Hopkins and Placencia, home to the Garifuna and the fastest-growing district.

Dangriga, Hopkins and Placencia, home to the Garifuna and the fastest-growing district. Toledo: the most Maya district, in the far south, with the smallest population.

Belize is both a destination and a source of migrants. The 2022 census found 11.5% of residents born abroad, though the published tables do not rank the home countries.

Many Belizeans live abroad, above all in the United States. The World Bank counts US$123.8 million of remittances, money sent home by workers abroad, in 2025, up from US$121.5 million in 2024.

How the Groups Live Together

Mestizo people form a bare majority at 51.7%, so every other group is a minority. Creole, Maya, Garifuna, East Indian and other communities together make up almost half of the country.

Languages and religion cut across these lines, so a Creole family may speak Spanish and a Mestizo family may be Protestant. Most people speak more than one language.

Tensions exist over land, especially in Toledo, where Maya communities have long sought title to customary lands. In October 2015 a regional appeal court, the Caribbean Court of Justice, found Belize had failed to protect Maya customary land rights.

What It Means for US Readers

Belize is easy for Americans to visit because English is official. The Belize dollar is also pegged at 2 to US$1, so prices convert at a glance.

For retirees, remote workers and investors, the map shows how the coast, the Spanish-speaking north and the Maya south differ. Services, land rules and community life differ too.

For US companies, about 419,000 people is a small market. World Bank data put GDP per head at US$7,865 in 2025.

What Is Not Known

The home countries of the 11.5% born abroad are not confirmed, because no country-of-birth table was found. The size of the Belizean community in the United States could not be retrieved.

The statistics office gives the Maya share as 11.2% in one release and 9.8% in another. The census results used here are labelled preliminary, so final figures may differ.

The share of Mennonites is not given as a separate figure in the documents checked. No current count of undocumented migrants or refugees was found.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people live in Belize?

The 2022 census counted 397,483 people. The statistics office estimates 418,982 for mid-2026.

What is the biggest ethnic group in Belize?

Mestizo people, of mixed Spanish and Maya descent, are the largest group at 51.7% in the 2022 census. Creole people follow at 25.2%, then Maya at roughly 10% to 11% and Garifuna at 4.0%.

What languages are spoken in Belize?

English is the official language and 278,390 people speak it. Spanish (199,393 speakers) and Kriol (180,792) are also widely spoken, plus Maya languages, Garifuna and German.

What religion is most common in Belize?

Roman Catholics are the largest group at 31.8% in 2022, just ahead of people with no religion at 31.0%. Protestants are 29.8%.

Who are the Garifuna of Belize?

The Garifuna are a people of African and Indigenous Caribbean descent. They make up 4.0% of Belizeans and celebrate Settlement Day each 19 November.

Is Belize growing or shrinking?

Belize is growing. The census showed a 23% rise between 2010 and 2022, and the World Bank puts growth at 1.4% in 2025.

Sources: Statistical Institute of Belize, Census 2022 preliminary results; Statistical Institute of Belize, languages spoken, 2022 census; Statistical Institute of Belize, 2022 census key findings (released 8 April 2024); Statistical Institute of Belize, mid-year population estimate (July 2026); World Bank, population, growth, age, fertility, remittances and GDP per head for Belize; UNESCO, Garifuna language, dance and music; Central Bank of Belize, exchange rate; Caribbean Court of Justice, Maya Leaders Alliance v Attorney General (30 October 2015) (all accessed 4 November 2026).

World.title: Suriname History Explained, From Origins to 2026
World.content:
SURINAME · HISTORY

Key Facts What is happening Jennifer Geerlings-Simons became Suriname’s first woman president on 16 July 2025, fifty years after independence from the Netherlands.

Why it matters Dutch rule, slavery and contract labour made Suriname a very mixed society, and a 1980 coup still shapes its politics.

The numbers Dutch rule began in 1667 and ended on 25 November 1975. Slavery ended on 1 July 1863.

Who is who Maroons descend from enslaved people who escaped into the forest; Hindustani and Javanese families descend from Asian contract workers.

What to watch First oil from the US$10.5 billion GranMorgu offshore project is expected in 2028, so watch for production milestones.

What it means for you A Houston oil company, APA Corporation, held half of the biggest oil project at its 2024 decision, linking this history to US investors.

Suriname is a small country on South America’s northern coast whose people came from four continents. This guide walks through its history, from the first inhabitants to independence, a coup, civil war and oil.

Suriname history is the story of a small country shaped by Indigenous peoples, Dutch planters, enslaved Africans and Asian contract workers. It became independent on 25 November 1975 and now expects its first offshore oil in 2028.

This guide follows that past in order, as of November 2026. More sits on the Rio Times Suriname page, in Suriname Explained 2026, the culture pillar and the politics pillar.

Suriname History in Brief

The list below gives the turning points, and the sections after it give the detail. Each date was checked against official or archive records.

Before 1651: Indigenous peoples live along the coast and in the southern forests.

Indigenous peoples live along the coast and in the southern forests. 1651 and 1667: British planters found the first lasting colony, and a Dutch fleet seizes it in 1667.

British planters found the first lasting colony, and a Dutch fleet seizes it in 1667. 1760 to 1767: the colonial government signs peace treaties with three Maroon peoples who had escaped slavery.

the colonial government signs peace treaties with three Maroon peoples who had escaped slavery. 1 July 1863: slavery is abolished, followed by ten years of state supervision of freed people.

slavery is abolished, followed by ten years of state supervision of freed people. 1853 to 1939: contract workers arrive from China, British India and Java.

contract workers arrive from China, British India and Java. 25 November 1975: Suriname becomes independent after self-government from 1954.

Suriname becomes independent after self-government from 1954. 1980 to 1991: a coup, the killings of December 1982, a war in the interior and the return of elections.

a coup, the killings of December 1982, a war in the interior and the return of elections. 2010 to 2025: Bouterse is elected president, Chan Santokhi follows in 2020, and Geerlings-Simons in 2025.

Indigenous Peoples and the Dutch Colony

Indigenous peoples lived in the land now called Suriname long before any European ship arrived. Their descendants still live along the rivers and in the southern forests, and they press the state for land rights.

The first lasting European settlement came in 1651, founded by British planters with enslaved people. In 1667 a Dutch fleet seized the colony, and the Netherlands kept it in exchange for New Amsterdam, now New York.

From 1683 a company called the Society of Suriname ran the colony as a plantation economy. UNESCO, the UN culture agency, dates the street grid of Paramaribo to that year and Fort Zeelandia to 1667.

Slavery, Maroons and Contract Workers

The plantations ran on the forced labour of enslaved Africans, and many escaped into the forest. Those who settled in the interior became the Maroons, who built societies of their own.

Colonial authorities signed peace treaties with the Ndyuka in 1760, the Saamaka in 1762 and the Matawai in 1767. The treaties let the Maroons live in the interior and keep their own governance, religion and culture.

The Netherlands abolished slavery in Suriname on 1 July 1863, but freed people stayed under state supervision for ten years. The day is remembered each year as Keti Koti.

Planters then recruited contract workers, first from China and Madeira from 1853. About 34,000 more came from British India between 1873 and 1916, and about 33,000 from Java between 1890 and 1939.

Many stayed after their contracts ended, and their descendants are today’s Hindustani (Indian-descended) and Javanese communities. They live beside Chinese, Creole (of mixed African and European descent) and Maroon communities in one small country.

Independence, Coup and the Interior War

Suriname gained universal suffrage in 1948 and self-government within the Dutch kingdom in 1954. The US company Alcoa had begun mining bauxite, the ore of aluminium, in 1916.

In the 1960s the Afobaka dam on the Suriname River was built to power an aluminium smelter. The Nieuwe Instituut, a Dutch design institute, says its reservoir flooded about 43 villages of Saramaka and Ndyuka Maroons.

Suriname became independent from the Netherlands on 25 November 1975, with Johan Ferrier as president and Henck Arron as prime minister. On 25 February 1980 army officers led by Dési Bouterse overthrew Arron’s government.

In December 1982 soldiers abducted 16 government critics, including lawyers and journalists, and killed 15 at a fortress in Paramaribo. A trial over the killings began in 2007 and ended with a conviction in 2019.

From 1986 the Jungle Commando, a Maroon rebel group led by Ronnie Brunswijk, fought the army in the interior. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights found that state agents killed at least 39 people at Moiwana village on 29 November 1986.

The Court, a regional human rights tribunal, ruled against Suriname on 15 June 2005. It counted at least 200 civilians, mostly Maroons, killed in army operations in 1986 and 1987.

Elections, Bouterse and the Road to Oil

Civilian government returned after elections in November 1987, but the army seized power again in December 1990. Ronald Venetiaan became president after the 1991 elections.

Bouterse returned as an elected leader and was chosen president in 2010 and again in 2015. He had led the 1980 coup, and the case over the 1982 killings stayed open until 2019.

On 29 November 2019 a military court sentenced Bouterse to 20 years for the December 1982 killings. He denied the charges, and he died in December 2024 at the age of 79.

Chan Santokhi was chosen president by parliament in July 2020. In the elections of May 2025 no party won a majority, and parliament chose Jennifer Geerlings-Simons on 6 July 2025.

Geerlings-Simons leads the National Democratic Party and was sworn in on 16 July 2025 as the first woman president. The World Bank counts about 640,000 people in Suriname in 2025.

On 1 October 2024 TotalEnergies, a French oil company, approved the US$10.5 billion GranMorgu offshore project, with first oil expected in 2028. APA Corporation, a Houston oil company, held 50% then, and Staatsolie, the state oil company, announced an option for 20%.

The Dutch government apologised for its role in slavery on 19 December 2022, and King Willem-Alexander did so on 1 July 2023. He visited Suriname from 1 to 3 December 2025, the first visit by a Dutch head of state in 47 years.

UNESCO describes Paramaribo’s historic centre as mainly wooden buildings that blend Dutch and other European styles with local influences. The same mixing shows in the communities who share the country today.

What It Means for US Readers

Suriname’s past explains a present that US investors follow, because APA Corporation held half of GranMorgu in 2024. Oil money is expected from 2028, in a country that depends on a single large project.

The history also shows why the army, old leaders and the Dutch link still matter in politics. Travellers will find Paramaribo’s historic centre, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2002, but should check the State Department advisory before booking.

First oil is still about two years away. Any revenue forecast for Suriname therefore remains a projection until the offshore platform starts producing.

What Is Not Known

The total number of Africans brought to Suriname is not settled, and the counts of Indian and Javanese workers are estimates. The ethnic shares of the latest census were not re-checked for this guide.

The legal status of the December 1982 case after Bouterse’s death was not confirmed. The terms of any Dutch programme on the legacy of slavery had not been published in the documents checked.

Staatsolie’s final stake in GranMorgu was not confirmed, and no official start date beyond the 2028 target is known. No prediction market on Suriname with real trading was found for this guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

When did Suriname become independent?

Suriname became independent from the Netherlands on 25 November 1975. Johan Ferrier was its first president and Henck Arron its first prime minister.

Who ruled Suriname before independence?

The Dutch ruled Suriname from 1667, after taking it from the English. In 1954 it gained self-government within the Dutch kingdom.

When was slavery abolished in Suriname?

Slavery ended on 1 July 1863. Freed people had to work under state supervision for ten more years.

Who are the Maroons of Suriname?

Maroons are descendants of Africans who escaped slavery and built their own communities in the interior. They signed peace treaties with the colonial government in 1760, 1762 and 1767.

What happened in Suriname in 1980?

Army officers led by Dési Bouterse overthrew the elected government on 25 February 1980. In December 1982, 15 government critics were killed at a fortress in Paramaribo.

Who is the president of Suriname in 2026?

Jennifer Geerlings-Simons of the National Democratic Party has been president since 16 July 2025. She is the first woman to hold the office.

When will Suriname produce offshore oil?

TotalEnergies and APA Corporation expect first oil from the GranMorgu project in 2028. The project costs about US$10.5 billion and targets 220,000 barrels a day.

Sources: TotalEnergies, GranMorgu final investment decision (1 October 2024); World Bank, population of Suriname (2025); UNESCO, Historic Inner City of Paramaribo (World Heritage, 2002); Government of the Netherlands, apology for slavery (19 December 2022); Royal House of the Netherlands, state visit to Suriname (1 to 3 December 2025); Inter-American Court of Human Rights, Moiwana Community v. Suriname (judgment of 15 June 2005); Nieuwe Instituut, Afobaka dam (all accessed 4 November 2026).

World.title: Salsa Star Jerry Rivera Plays Lima 12 Feb
World.content:
PERU · CONCERT GUIDE

Key Facts What is happening Salsa singer Jerry Rivera plays Costa 21, Lima, on Friday, 12 February 2027, from 9 p.m.

Why it matters Rivera is a romantic salsa star, and the date falls two days before Valentine’s Day.

The numbers S/142 to S/330 (about US$41 to US$95), fee included, central bank rate 3.46.

Who is who Teleticket is the official seller, and Concerts Sports AEI10 is the organiser.

What to watch No opener or doors time yet; sales are online only, with a virtual queue.

Power Index Peru ranks 5th of 14 in Peru ranks 5th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 54.7 points (October 2026 edition).

What it means for you No US visa under 90 days; passport valid six months; buy only on Teleticket.

A Puerto Rican salsa star returns to Lima in February, and tickets are on sale now. The date, venue and seller are all listed on the official ticket page.

Salsa singer Jerry Rivera plays Costa 21 in Lima on Friday, 12 February 2027. Teleticket, the official seller, says the show may begin at 9 p.m. local time.

Rivera is a Puerto Rican singer known for romantic salsa, a smooth style built on love songs and a danceable beat. For US fans, the Jerry Rivera Lima concert means a passport, a flight and some planning for late night transport.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Why This Show Matters to US Fans

Puerto Rico is a US territory, and its people are US citizens, so Rivera’s career sits close to American Latino audiences. Salsa romántica has long drawn large crowds in Latino communities across the United States.

The organiser’s text calls Rivera one of the biggest names in salsa and promises a night of nostalgia and rhythm. It names five hits: “Amores como el nuestro”, “Qué hay de malo”, “Cara de niño”, “Casi un hechizo” and “Cuenta conmigo”.

We never share your email.

The show falls on Friday, 12 February 2027, two days before Valentine’s Day on Sunday, 14 February 2027. The organiser describes it as a single night in Lima, so there is no second date to fall back on.

Schedule and Start Time

Teleticket lists one Lima show, on Friday, 12 February 2027, at Costa 21 in the San Miguel district. Its event page says the show may begin at 9 p.m. and last about two hours.

Lima keeps the same clock all year and does not change for daylight saving time. In February the United States is on standard time, so 9 p.m. in Lima is 9 p.m. in New York.

That start is 8 p.m. in Chicago and 6 p.m. in Los Angeles on the night of the show. Teleticket words it as the time the event may begin, so treat 9 p.m. as a guide.

No opening act, doors time or set length has been published for the Jerry Rivera Lima concert. Teleticket also says entry after the time printed on the ticket is subject to the organiser’s rules.

How to Buy Tickets Safely

Teleticket is the official seller for the Lima show, and it sells tickets only on its website. Each customer may buy at most six tickets.

A presale on 22 and 23 October gave 15% off with Interbank, a Peruvian bank, on 5,700 tickets. General sale began on Saturday, 24 October and runs until the show or until each zone sells out.

These are the general sale prices on the Teleticket page, with the service fee included. They are listed below in soles and in US dollars.

Platinum, numbered seats: S/330 (about US$95)

VIP, numbered seats: S/259 (about US$75)

General: S/142 (about US$41)

Conversions use 3.46 soles per US dollar, the interbank rate of Peru’s central bank on 2 November (100 soles is about US$29). A US card may add a foreign transaction fee on top of the ticket price.

Sales use a virtual queue, where fans wait online and receive a random place in line when sales open. Teleticket also warns that its seat map is only a reference and may change for technical or logistical reasons.

The organiser recommends the show for adults aged 18 and over, and children aged five and older may enter with an adult. Both need a ticket for the same zone and must sit together.

Teleticket says it takes no responsibility for tickets bought outside its official channels, so skip resellers and social media sellers. Keep the confirmation email, because the e-ticket can be downloaded from two days before the show.

Getting to Costa 21

Costa 21 is a concert venue on the Costa Verde, the coastal road below Lima’s cliffs, in the San Miguel district. Teleticket gives its address as Costa Verde s/n, San Miguel, with no street number.

Teleticket says you must show a ticket or e-ticket to enter, and it states that re-entry is not allowed. No access plan, parking arrangement or shuttle service has been published for this night.

Lima’s Jorge Chávez International Airport is in neighbouring Callao, so allow extra time to cross the city to your hotel. Ask your hotel to arrange a taxi back after the show, and save its address on your phone.

The State Department advises app-based or pre-arranged taxis, because travellers have been robbed or assaulted after hailing unknown taxis on the street. It also says the risk of crime increases at night.

Safety and Costs for Visitors

The State Department says US citizens need no tourist visa for stays of 90 days or less in Peru. Officials set the permitted stay on arrival, and overstays bring fines that must be paid before departure.

Your passport must be valid for at least six months after you enter Peru and have one blank page. Make sure immigration records your entry, because a missing record can block your exit.

The State Department rates Peru Level 2, exercise increased caution, because of crime, civil unrest and the risk of kidnapping. Its advisory page showed a May 2025 issue date when it was read on 4 November 2026.

It says petty theft, muggings and carjackings are common, sometimes in daylight, and that demonstrations can shut roads without warning. Lima and Callao are not on its list of areas to avoid.

Peru’s medical emergency number is 113 and the national police number is 105. Tap water is unsafe to drink in many areas, so choose sealed bottled water.

The ticket is the main fixed cost, from about US$41 to US$95 including the Teleticket fee. No price for flights, hotels or taxis in February 2027 was confirmed for this guide.

The State Department says most private hospitals ask for payment in advance, and it recommends travel insurance. It also says you must declare cash above US$10,000 when you enter or leave Peru.

What It Means for You

For a US fan, the Jerry Rivera Lima concert is a chance to hear a Puerto Rican salsa classic in South America. It also means a long flight, a passport check and a late night in a large city.

Buy only through Teleticket, and check its event page before you book flights. That page is the first place where a change of date, time or venue should appear.

Budget for a ticket priced in soles, a possible card fee and a taxi back after the show. Check the State Department advice again shortly before you fly, because advisories can change.

What Is Not Known

The doors time, the opening act, the guest list and the length of the set have not been published. Teleticket says only that the show may begin at 9 p.m.

Live availability by zone was not visible when this guide was written, so any zone may already be sold out. Access rules, parking and the list of banned items for this show are also unpublished.

Prices on the Teleticket page can change, and the presale prices have ended. The State Department advisory shows a May 2025 date, so check it for newer advice before you fly.

Connected Coverage

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Jerry Rivera concert in Lima?

It is on Friday, 12 February 2027, at Costa 21 in San Miguel. Teleticket says it may begin at 9 p.m., which is also 9 p.m. US Eastern.

Where can I buy official tickets?

Teleticket is the official online seller. General prices run from S/142 to S/330 (about US$41 to US$95), and buying from strangers risks fake tickets.

Do US citizens need a visa to go to Lima?

No visa is needed for tourist stays under 90 days, the State Department says. Your passport must be valid for six months from your entry date.

How do I get to Costa 21?

Costa 21 is on the Costa Verde in San Miguel. Taxis booked by app or through your hotel are the simplest option, and no shuttle plan has been published.

World.title: Honduran Migrant Caravan Heads to US Amid Midterm Elections
World.content:
Dozens of people left northern Honduras yesterday in a caravan bound for the United States, hoping the congressional elections will weaken U.S. President Donald Trump, who has maintained a crackdown on irregular migration. The Hondurans set out on foot from San Pedro Sula, many carrying backpacks or pulling rolling bags, on the same day as the pivotal elections in which Republicans and Democrats are vying for control of Congress.

“Trump is on his way out in these elections. That’s why we’re taking the risk. Here in Honduras, we have nothing left,” Jimena Morazán, 47, who is traveling with five family members, said. In Honduras, 61% of the country’s 11.2 million people live in poverty, and the homicide rate stands at 24 per 100,000 residents, three times the global average, according to official figures.

This is the third caravan of dozens of migrants to leave Honduras since September. Salvadorans, Guatemalans, Nicaraguans and Mexicans joined the previous groups along the route toward the southern U.S. border. Salvadorans also plan to leave the capital, San Salvador, on Wednesday aboard two buses to join the Hondurans at the Guatemala-Mexico border.

“We found out on social media that a caravan was leaving, and I decided to go with my family,” explained Jesús Carías, 30. Accompanied by his wife and three young children, he acknowledged that the journey would be “complicated.” “We’re putting ourselves in God’s hands and will see what they decide over there,” added Carías, who will be making his fourth attempt to enter the United States.

“While they’re going through the election process, we’ll be on our way. We have faith that we’ll arrive while they’re busy with that,” Beverly Medina, 39, who is traveling with her three-year-old daughter, said.

The Trump administration warned Thursday that it would revoke the visas of people organizing these caravans, which are largely coordinated through TikTok and WhatsApp. The U.S. Embassy in Tegucigalpa said on X that the caravans “have no chance of entering” U.S. territory.

Trump has made combating irregular immigration a central pillar of his domestic policy, conducting raids across the country and enforcing a policy of zero admissions at the southern border. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced last week that it had revoked the immigration status of 2.2 million foreign nationals since January 2025, in addition to restricting work permits.

World.title: Four Days of Rough Surf Ahead for Costa Rica’s Pacific Beaches
World.content:
If you’re planning on going to the Pacific coast this week, expect rough surf and storms every day. Waves could reach 2.7 meters (8.9 feet) in the North and Central Pacific today and Thursday. On Friday and Saturday, the biggest swell shifts to the South Pacific. Costa Rica has been under a nationwide green alert since yesterday and green is the first step on the color-coded emergency scale. It means authorities expect enough rain to watch rivers and hillsides closely, not that an emergency is under way.

Most waves will run 1.4 to 2.2 meters (4.6 to 7.2 feet), with sets up to 2.7 meters (8.9 feet), according to the University of Costa Rica’s marine research center, CIMAR. A low-pressure system near the Pacific coast and westerly winds are driving the swell. Today and Thursday, the roughest water hits the North Pacific, the Gulf of Nicoya and the Central Pacific. That covers beaches from Guanacaste down through Jacó and Manuel Antonio. On Friday and Saturday, it moves to the South Pacific, including Dominical, Uvita and the Osa Peninsula.

Bigger surf matters because it strengthens rip currents. More water piles onto the beach, and it has to rush back out to sea somewhere. Swim only where there are lifeguards and stay out of the water where red flags are posted. Many beaches have no lifeguards, so ask locally before you go in. If a current pulls you out, don’t fight it. Swim parallel to the shore until you’re free, then head back in.

If you have a boat tour, fishing trip or water taxi booked, check with your operator. The National Emergency Commission (CNE) asked small fishing and tour boats to take extra care, so trips may be delayed or rescheduled. The rain is heaviest in the same places. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) expects the biggest totals in the Central Pacific, the South Pacific and the Nicoya Peninsula, with coastal storms starting before dawn.

Today, expect coastal downpours and thunderstorms this morning and again at night along the Pacific, with scattered rain in the afternoon. Highs reach about 31 C (88 F) in Quepos and Liberia. In San José, expect morning and evening fog, on-and-off rain and temperatures from 18 to 24 C (65 to 75 F). The Caribbean and the Northern Zone should stay mostly dry in the morning, with afternoon showers and storms in the mountains.

The IMN expects the unsettled weather to last through Sunday. Late in the week, westerly winds could bring slightly cooler temperatures to the Pacific. Don’t cross a swollen river or a flooded road, on foot or by car. Rivers can rise fast after storms upstream, even when it isn’t raining where you are. CNE President Alejandro Picado said that if it starts raining and rivers begin to rise, people should get to shelter.

Take extra care on mountain roads and trails in national parks. Rain, fog and wind can bring down trees and loosen slopes, and the ground in parts of the country is still wet from mid-October’s flooding. Yesterday morning, falling rocks damaged two vehicles on Route 32 between San José and the Caribbean but thankfully, no one was hurt.

Watch for loose roofing, signs, power lines and trees in gusty storms, as you did during last weekend’s strong winds. Alert levels can change quickly, so check the IMN and CNE before you travel.

World.title: Democrats Win Congress but Costa Rica’s US Tariff Stays
World.content:
Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections. The result hands President Donald Trump a divided government for his final two years in office. It does not lower the 12.5% duty Washington charges on most Costa Rican goods. The US trade office imposed that duty under a 1974 law that gives the decision to the executive branch.

The Associated Press called the Senate for Democrats late Tuesday after the party flipped several Republican seats. In Texas, James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown unseated Sen. Jon Husted, and in North Carolina former Gov. Roy Cooper won the seat Thom Tillis is leaving.

NBC News and CBS News projected that Democrats will also hold a majority in the House. The new Congress is seated in January. Trump told The New York Times he was “absolutely willing to accept” the results and said, “We’ll work with the Democrats.” He also posted an image of his campaign hat bearing the word “VETO.” On Fox News, he said Democrats were “really not in control.”

Exit polls cited by CBS News put his approval among midterm voters at 38%. Costa Rica’s current rate comes from a Section 301 investigation the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) opened on March 12 into 60 economies. On June 2, the agency concluded that Costa Rica had failed to impose and enforce a ban on imports of goods made with forced labor.

The 12.5% rate took effect on July 24. It replaced the 10% surcharge Costa Rica had paid since April 2025. The USTR set two tiers. Economies with no forced-labor import ban pay 12.5%, and those with a ban that is weakly enforced pay 10%. The action has no expiration date and stays in place unless the agency amends it.

Coffee, pineapple, bananas, orange juice, plant cuttings, fruit and vegetable seeds and certain refined sugars are excluded, according to the Ministry of Foreign Trade (Comex). Textiles and apparel entering duty-free under the CAFTA-DR trade agreement are also exempt. Because Section 301 places the decision with the president and the USTR, a Democratic majority cannot repeal the duty by voting. A bill limiting it would need Trump’s signature, or two-thirds of both chambers to override a veto.

What Democrats gain is oversight: hearings, subpoenas and leverage over spending bills. Those tools can raise the political cost of trade measures without removing them. The same limits apply to the other US decisions that weigh most on Costa Rica. Visa rules, immigration enforcement and deportation flights are all set by the executive branch.

So are entry requirements such as the health declaration for US-bound air travelers, which took effect at 10:59 p.m. Costa Rica time Tuesday. That leaves Costa Rica’s own case before the USTR as the more direct route. On July 6, Comex asked the agency in written comments to drop the 12.5% rate and keep the market access Costa Rica negotiated under CAFTA-DR. The higher rate took effect 18 days later.

The government has since issued Decree 45941-H-MTSS-COMEX, published Sept. 28. It orders Comex and the Ministry of Labor and Social Security to create an official public list of goods at risk of being made with forced labor, and importers must check their purchases against it. The two ministries have 60 calendar days from the decree’s entry into force to set the parameters for the first list. The USTR has not said whether the measure would change Costa Rica’s tier.

That work now falls to new leadership at Comex. Arianna Arce Camacho is serving as interim Foreign Trade Minister after Indiana Trejos was removed on Oct. 28. That was the same day President Laura Fernández announced that Costa Rica would not pursue membership in the CPTPP. First Vice President Francisco Gamboa signed both orders while Fernández was in Europe. They were published in La Gaceta on Tuesday.

For now, the duty remains in place and Congress changes hands in January. Any change to Costa Rica’s rate will depend on how Washington’s trade office judges the measures the country is now building. As the analysts consulted before the vote expected, that decision still sits with the White House rather than Capitol Hill.

World.title: Djokovic Rallies in Paris to Keep ATP Finals Hopes Alive
World.content:
Novak Djokovic came from a set down to beat Valentin Vacherot 6-7 (5), 7-5, 6-1 in the first round of the Paris Masters on Tuesday. At 39, the Serbian became the oldest player to win a match in the tournament’s history. The win keeps alive his bid to reach the ATP Finals in Turin, Italy. He now faces Australia’s Rinky Hijikata in the second round.

It was no routine opener for a seven-time Paris champion. Djokovic, seeded 10th and without a first-round bye, drew the hottest player on the indoor swing. Vacherot of Monaco won the Swiss Indoors title in Basel on Sunday, and he beat Djokovic in the Shanghai Masters semifinals last year on the way to his first Masters 1000 title.

Vacherot hit 22 aces to Djokovic’s six and took the first set in a tiebreak. He broke in the opening game of the second set to lead 2-0, putting Djokovic a set and a break down. Djokovic broke back for 2-2. Serving at 4-4, he saved three break points that would have let Vacherot serve for the match, then broke again to level at one set apiece.

Both players took medical timeouts during the second set. Djokovic received treatment on his right shoulder, and Vacherot had his left ankle strapped. The deciding set was one-sided. Djokovic broke at the start, built a 3-0 lead and closed it out 6-1 on his second match point with a two-handed backhand winner down the line. The match lasted more than two and a half hours.

Djokovic said the speed of the court made Vacherot’s serve especially hard to handle. “His second serves are faster than my first serves, so it’s very tough to play a guy in these conditions, which are really, really fast,” he said. “For a set and a half, I had difficulty reading his serve,” Djokovic added. “Even if I guessed right, it was coming with some speed.”

The stakes in Paris go beyond one match. Djokovic arrived 11th in the race to Turin after a loss in Basel last week, and the Paris Masters is the last Masters 1000 event of the season. With Jannik Sinner injured and out for the rest of the year, ninth place in the race is the final qualifying spot for the eight-player ATP Finals, which run Nov. 15-22.

By the race math, Djokovic needs to reach at least the semifinals in Paris to stay in contention, and only the title would guarantee his place. Spain’s Rafael Jódar, who opened his Paris campaign with a win over Alejandro Tabilo, holds ninth place. Djokovic played down the Turin chase after the win. Asked whether qualifying was his main motivation in Paris, he said no, and that he is taking the tournament one match at a time.

That is a shift from last month, when he called Turin his goal after winning the title in Beijing and took a wildcard into Basel to chase points. His season has swung between those highs and setbacks such as his early US Open exit against Argentina’s Mariano Navone. His path in Paris does not get easier. Australia’s Alex de Minaur, seeded eighth, could wait in the third round, and top seed Alexander Zverev, who clinched the year-end No. 1 ranking in Shanghai, is the projected quarterfinal opponent.

Hijikata reached the second round by beating Italy’s Luciano Darderi. Whether or not Djokovic reaches Turin, the Australian Open in January looms as his next major test, at the Grand Slam he has won a record 10 times.

World.title: What JetBlue’s Multi-Billion Dollar Debt Means for Costa Rica Flights
World.content:
JetBlue Airways, one of the main carriers linking Costa Rica with the United States, is under mounting financial pressure, and how that resolves could reshape low-fare service to San José and Liberia. The New York-based airline has posted operating losses for six consecutive years and reported about $8.4 billion in debt as of Sept. 30.

In late October, a group of senior creditors, including holders of about $2 billion in notes due 2031, hired investment bank PJT Partners and law firm Akin, The Wall Street Journal reported. Those notes had fallen to about 42 cents on the dollar, down from near 80 cents earlier in the month.

JetBlue shares hit an all-time low on Oct. 26, hours before the company released its third-quarter results. S&P Global Ratings cut the airline’s credit rating to CCC+ in June, deeper into junk territory, citing the surge in jet fuel prices tied to the conflict in the Middle East. Fitch made the same downgrade in April.

The quarterly report showed revenue up 21% to $2.8 billion on steady demand and higher fares. The net loss, however, widened to $257 million from $143 million a year earlier, as fuel averaged $3.91 a gallon, up 57%.

JetBlue ended September with $2.2 billion in liquidity, including an undrawn $600 million credit facility, and expects operating margins to improve year over year in the fourth quarter. It still forecasts a full-year adjusted operating margin of between negative 4.5% and negative 6.5%.

Chief Executive Joanna Geraghty said the airline remains on track to reach sustained operating profitability in 2027. She told Reuters on Oct. 27 that JetBlue is not in talks with its creditors and is not considering a debt restructuring. In an April memo to employees, she said the company was not considering bankruptcy in 2026.

Merger speculation predates the latest turmoil. In March, Semafor reported that JetBlue had hired advisers to explore a sale, with United, Alaska and Southwest among the possible partners. JetBlue said at the time that it was focused on its JetForward turnaround plan.

United is the carrier most often named as a buyer. The two airlines already cooperate through their Blue Sky partnership, which lets travelers earn and redeem points across both carriers and is set to give United slots for up to seven daily round trips at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport as early as 2027. JetBlue’s Fort Lauderdale base would also give a buyer a South Florida gateway to the Caribbean and Latin America.

United Chief Executive Scott Kirby has rejected the idea. At an investor conference in May, he said, “The last thing I’m going to do is buy a route network that loses money.” Asked about JetBlue on United’s Oct. 21 earnings call, he said he had nothing new to add. Any deal involving a major U.S. airline would also face antitrust review.

JetBlue has served Costa Rica since March 2009, when it launched a daily Orlando to San José flight, and added New York to Liberia service in 2012. It now connects Fort Lauderdale and New York with both San José and Liberia, and runs seasonal flights between Boston and Liberia.

The airline ended its Orlando to San José route on July 8, citing higher fuel costs and a focus on its Fort Lauderdale hub. The Costa Rica Tourism Board (ICT) confirmed that cut on May 20, less than three weeks after Spirit Airlines ceased all operations, which removed another low-fare option between the two countries.

The outcome for those routes depends on how JetBlue’s situation is resolved. A United acquisition could bring consolidation on overlapping routes, since United already flies to San José and Liberia from hubs including Newark and Houston. A larger United presence in Fort Lauderdale, however, could help preserve or expand South Florida service.

A restructuring that kept JetBlue independent would likely produce a smaller network, and seasonal leisure routes are often among the first to be cut in such cases. A combination with Alaska or Southwest would involve less overlap on the New York routes that feed Liberia. Guanacaste has the most at stake.

Hotels and tour operators in the province rely heavily on direct flights into Liberia from the U.S. Northeast, and the December-to-April high season is about to begin. For now, JetBlue continues to operate normally and has not announced further changes to its Costa Rica service. Airlines that file for Chapter 11 protection typically keep flying and honor tickets and loyalty points during the process, though that is not guaranteed.

World.title: Your 2027 Marchamo Is Lower if You Drive a Private Car
World.content:
If you drive a private car, your 2027 marchamo is probably a little cheaper than last year’s. The National Insurance Institute (INS) puts the average for a private car at ₡208,359 (about $459), down ₡9,347 (about $21), or 4.3%. INS based that average on a 2018 model. Almost all of the saving comes from vehicle property tax, which drops from ₡167,100 to ₡156,054 for that car. Property tax makes up about 59% of the marchamo, so it is the first number worth checking.

Other vehicles pay more as taxis see the steepest rise, 19.87%, to ₡341,355 (about $752). Most of that, 89%, comes from a higher fee that taxi owners pay to Aresep, the public services regulator. Buses go up 16.32%, to ₡387,185 (about $853), and motorcycles rise 3.9%, to ₡130,556 (about $288). In both cases the main driver is mandatory insurance, which rose because those vehicles are involved in so many serious crashes.

Your property tax usually falls a little each year because the Finance Ministry lowers your vehicle’s taxable value as it ages. For cars, it spreads that loss over a 15-year useful life, counted from the model year. Sometimes the ministry’s value is still higher than what your car would actually sell for. If so, you can ask for a review. Start by looking up the fiscal value on the ministry’s AutoGestión page with your plate number.

To file online, sign in to the Oficina Virtual (OVi) in TRIBU-CR, the ministry’s tax platform. Open the Expediente section and choose the review of the fiscal value for Marchamo 2027. Explain why the value is too high and attach evidence such as listings for comparable vehicles and photos of your own. Add a signed request and submit it. The ministry reviews the case and issues a decision.

Setting up an OVi account online requires a current, new-format identity card. If yours won’t register, or you prefer to do it in person, you can file at the tax office closest to your fiscal address. The ministry has not published a deadline for reviews or said how long a decision takes. The Dec. 31 payment deadline doesn’t move, so file early. Ask the tax office whether to pay the current amount while your review is pending.

Paying after Dec. 31 costs more, and each part of the marchamo carries its own charge. Unpaid property tax builds interest at 10.67% a year from the deadline. On the average private car, that is roughly ₡1,390 (about $3) for every month you are late. Mandatory insurance is charged at the Central Bank’s basic passive rate, a benchmark deposit rate, plus five percentage points, prorated by the day. Unpaid municipal parking-meter charges add 2% a month, for up to 12 months. Traffic fines included in your total carry a surcharge of 36% a year.

The bigger risk is on the road. Driving without a current marchamo after Dec. 31 can bring fines under the Traffic Law, and your vehicle can be taken off the road. You can check your total at marchamo.grupoins.com or in the INS Móvil app before you pay. For the new 10-year windshield sticker, the emailed proof of payment and the optional insurance box to watch for, see our guide to paying your 2027 marchamo.

World.title: Forbes Picks Costa Rica’s Rancho Pacifico to Beat the Crowds
World.content:
A Forbes travel feature published Oct. 26 names Rancho Pacifico, an adults-only resort in the rainforest above Uvita on Costa Rica’s southern Pacific coast, as one of its picks for travelers who want to avoid the crowds by going in the shoulder season. The piece, by Forbes contributor Wendy Altschuler, argues that time is the real luxury on any trip and that the weeks between a destination’s busy and quiet periods often bring lower prices, more availability and shorter lines. Costa Rica shares the list with the English countryside, Montana, Lake Tahoe and Mexico’s Chichen Itza.

Altschuler pitches the property as a couples retreat built around slowing down rather than following a packed itinerary. She describes coffee on a private balcony surrounded by rainforest, with more birdsong than a visitor can identify. Early mornings, she writes, bring sightings of blue morpho butterflies, yellow-throated toucans and white-faced capuchin monkeys. Guests can also hike to a waterfall on the property with an onsite naturalist.

The feature praises the food, prepared by experienced chefs, and a warm, attentive staff. It also highlights shared spaces designed for time with other guests or quiet moments as a couple, along with the Pacific sunsets that are one of the resort’s main draws. The resort sits about 600 meters (2,000 feet) up a mountainside, reached by a steep 3-kilometer (2-mile) road from Uvita, on 101 hectares (250 acres) of private rainforest. It holds two Michelin Keys, and the Michelin Guide lists room for a maximum of 20 guests, all over 18.

According to the Michelin listing, the drive takes about 45 minutes from the Quepos airport or roughly three and a half hours from the international airport outside San José. Beyond the resort, Forbes points readers to three national parks. Marino Ballena, known for its whale-tail sandbar, sits on the coast just below Uvita, Manuel Antonio National Park lies to the north, and Corcovado is on the Osa Peninsula to the south, where visitors must enter with a certified guide. The feature also recommends a horseback ride on the beach.

Shoulder season works a little differently in Costa Rica. The high season runs roughly from December through Easter week, while the green season, from about May through November, brings thinner crowds and often lower rates. On the southern Pacific coast, the heaviest rain usually falls in September and October, though mornings are often dry. Altschuler notes that destinations with wet and dry seasons take more planning so the weather does not get in the way of activities.

The feature adds to a run of Forbes coverage of Costa Rica this year, including a September piece on La Fortuna’s turn toward Costa Rican fine dining and the country’s selection as Best Nature Destination at the Forbes Travel Awards in March.

World.title: Costa Rica Researchers Study Pollution Exposure in Ostional Sea Turtles
World.content:
Researchers are examining olive ridley sea turtles at Ostional for exposure to antibiotic-resistance genes as part of a broader investigation into marine pollution. Details released yesterday describe an initial sampling visit conducted in March. The team collected noninvasive samples to establish a starting point for future conservation decisions. No test results were released.

Ostional is known for its arribadas, mass nesting events when thousands of turtles come ashore to lay eggs. The protected area includes Ostional, Nosara, Pelada and Guiones beaches in Guanacaste, along with surrounding marine habitat. The investigation focuses on pollution associated with farming, livestock operations and pharmaceutical use that can reach the ocean through waterways and runoff. Its broader scope includes heavy metals and seabirds, with bird sampling planned for the Gulf of Nicoya.

Scientists from several disciplines are participating in the project, which aims to improve understanding of pollution exposure in marine wildlife and help guide conservation efforts. For people visiting Ostional, existing wildlife protections remain central to the experience. Visitors must enter with a local guide during arribadas, and nighttime flash photography is prohibited. Visitors should also ask their guide before using a flashlight because light can disrupt nesting turtles.

The refuge prohibits vehicles on the beach, horseback riding on the sand, bonfires and pets in protected areas. Those rules help protect the nesting habitat that makes Ostional one of Costa Rica’s best-known wildlife destinations.

World.title: Prime Minister engages Commonwealth leaders on affordability and climate financing
World.content:
Prime Minister engages Commonwealth leaders on affordability and climate financing

By Zoila Palma: Prime Minister John Briceño is engaging with fellow Commonwealth leaders during the 2026 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda, where discussions are focused on issues affecting member countries, including affordability and climate financing.

The engagements provide an opportunity for the PM to exchange perspectives with other heads of government and discuss shared development challenges facing Belize and other Commonwealth nations.

Through these discussions, Belize is seeking to strengthen international partnerships and explore solutions to common challenges, particularly those related to economic pressures, climate financing, and sustainable development.

World.title: Belize represented at World Travel Market in London
World.content:
Belize represented at World Travel Market in London

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Tourism Board (BTB) is joined by 9 industry partners at this year’s World Travel Market (WTM) London, taking place November 3–5.

Participating industry partners include: Muy’Ono Resorts, Best Western Plus Belize Biltmore Plaza, Sunbreeze Hotel and Suites, The Belize Collection, S & L Travel and Tours, Lamanai Outpost Lodge, K’in Resort, Darah Travel Services, and the Belize Hotel Association.

This event brings together destinations, exhibitors, and buyers, attracting more than 46,000 attendees from around the world.

“Belize’s participation reinforces its presence on the global tourism stage and creates valuable opportunities to strengthen its position in various international markets,” the BTB said.

World.title: “We need more people to sue”: Dickie Bradley takes aim at unlawful police detention
World.content:
“We need more people to sue”: Dickie Bradley takes aim at unlawful police detention

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Thousands of residents are now living under extraordinary police powers for the next 30 days. But attorney Richard “Dickie” Bradley says the Constitution has not been switched off.

In an interview with Channel 5, Bradley said the state of emergency allows police to restrict certain freedoms, but residents still have legal protections.

“Although a state of emergency restricts certain rights, it does not wash away your rights. The law still applies,” Bradley said.

He did not hold back on the police. Bradley accused the department of having no respect for the law, pointing to Section 5(3) of the Constitution, which deals with the rights of people who are arrested or detained.

“Can you tell me they have five lawyers and don’t know Section 5(3) of the Constitution?” he asked.

Bradley said the courts have already ruled against unlawful police detentions and ordered compensation for those locked up. His message to the public was direct.

“We need more people to sue,” he said.

The state of emergency covers Southside Belize City and parts of the Belize and Cayo Districts, following a week of deadly violence that included the murder of four men on the Coastal Highway.

World.title: “Rosado must go now”: Panton demands immediate removal of Police Commissioner
World.content:
“Rosado must go now”: Panton demands immediate removal of Police Commissioner

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Opposition is doubling down on its demand for Commissioner of Police Dr. Richard Rosado to step aside.

Opposition Leader Tracy Panton has renewed her call for his removal, this time as police use emergency powers under the state of emergency in Southside Belize City and parts of the Belize and Cayo Districts.

Panton said the UDP wants accountable leadership at the top of the force and accused the Commissioner of falling short on several fronts.

Among her concerns are low morale within the department, alleged conflicts of interest involving his office and the political directorate, detentions she described as seemingly illegal and unconstitutional, and a failure to hold rogue officers accountable.

She also said Rosado has not earned the trust and respect of marginalized communities.

“The UDP calls for the immediate removal of the current police commissioner, Dr. Richard Rosado, as a first step to bolstering the public trust and confidence in effective policing. Dr. Richard Rosado must go and he must go now,” Panton said.

It is the second time in days that Panton has called for Rosado’s exit. Neither the Commissioner nor the Ministry of National Security has publicly responded.

World.title: UDP Leader disagrees with former PM Barrow’s outlook that PUP will win again
World.content:
UDP Leader disagrees with former PM Barrow’s outlook that PUP will win again

By Zoila Palma: Recently, former Prime Minister Dean Barrow indicated that from the look of things, the PUP is leading to secure a 3rd term in office.

“Well, if he does run the way things are going, it looks like he will win again. And that’s why I come back to my point that he will win despite the fact that if you look at things objectively, you might say he has no business winning again, too much is happening within the PUP. But on the other hand, for whatever reasons, and this is not any kind of a criticism of my party, and certainly not of the leadership of my party,” Barrow said.

He also said that UDP Leader Tracy Panton is making every effort to lead the UDP.

“I believe Mrs. Tracy Panton is making every effort to lead from the front, but for all sorts of objective reasons, We have not yet gelled as a as a proper, forceful opposition. So, one of the prices that we’re paying for that is that indeed, if the good Mr Briceno decides he would run again as things now stand, he will win again,” Barrow explained.

But, during Tuesday’s UDP press conference, Panton said that she disagrees with that outlook.

“I absolutely do not agree with that premise, and my colleagues on my left will tell you we are actively on the ground and everywhere. Every part of this country that I travel to-every village, every town, every city-the people, no matter what part of the social stature they come from, say the same thing: enough is enough is enough, and it is time for the UDP to get back to governing this country. If I’m going to bet, I will bet on the people,” Panton said.

World.title: Woman leaves bike on verandah, returns hours later to find it gone
World.content:
Woman leaves bike on verandah, returns hours later to find it gone

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A man from Santa Martha Village has been charged with theft after a bicycle was taken from a home in Orange Walk Town.

Eustaquio Pott was formally charged on Tuesday, November 3, by Orange Walk police.

According to the report, a self employed woman from the Otro Benque area left her green 26 inch Hurricane beach cruiser unlocked on her front verandah on October 24 when she went to work at 5:20am. The bicycle is valued at $420.

When she returned around 11:00am, it was gone.

She checked footage from the six surveillance cameras installed at the front of her house and recognized the man who took it as Pott, whom she has known for more than a year. She reported the matter to police and requested court action.

Police later recovered the bicycle after it was handed over by another man, who gave a statement. A scenes of crime technician photographed the bicycle, and the camera footage was retrieved.

On Monday, November 2, a police officer on patrol saw Pott standing in front of Nubes Shop on Palmar Road and arrested him. He was taken to the Orange Walk Police Station.

The next day, police obtained a warrant and formally charged him with theft. He remained silent when cautioned.

World.title: Leader of the Opposition says Bukele’s measures are “draconian”
World.content:
Leader of the Opposition says Bukele’s measures are “draconian”

By Zoila Palma: During the UDP’s Tuesday’s press conference, Leader of the Opposition Tracy Panton expressed concerns about Belize’s hopes to learn from El Salvador’s crime fighting strategy.

“The reason the UDP felt very compelled to be here this morning to offer proposals for consideration is because the government is bankrupt of ideas. Their first response is to engage in an unconstitutional, illegal measure that has been taken to the Appeal Court that says we cannot use SOEs as a crime prevention strategy. And while the Commissioner sought to make reference to the Constitution to say it’s constitutionally sound, if you read the provisions of Section 18(b) of the Constitution of Belize, it certainly does not, in my view, provide for this SOE to be deemed constitutional,” Panton said.

With reference to Belize seeking to learn from El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele’s strategy, Panton said that those measures are “draconian.”

“Well, I don’t know what the Minister hopes to glean from President Bukele. It’s widely known that the measures that he has used are draconian. But Bukele has said something critically important, and I want you to bear with me. He said if a government is unable to arrest crime in its community, it is because the government is criminals themselves,” Panton added.

World.title: Woman summoned after 5 Sisters Patio and Lounge stays open too late
World.content:
Woman summoned after 5 Sisters Patio and Lounge stays open too late

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 26 year old woman from San Jose Village, Orange Walk District, has been summoned to court after police found the lounge she runs open after its permitted hours.

Laureny Tzul, who is self employed, was summoned for the offence of contravening the condition of a licence.

According to police, around 1:10am on Sunday, November 1, two officers on duty in San Jose Village noticed disco lights at 5 Sisters Patio and Lounge and went to check.

At the counter, they met Tzul, who told them she was in charge of the establishment. She handed over a publican special licence issued by the Orange Walk District Liquor Licensing Board in February 2026.

The licence requires the business to close between midnight and 10:00am on regular days. On Sundays, Christmas and Good Friday, it must close from 1:00pm to 3:00pm and from 11:00pm until 9:00am the next day.

Police say the licence holders were not present. Tzul explained that she runs the business and planned to get the liquor licence in her own name.

She was warned for summons and appeared at the Orange Walk Police Station on Tuesday, November 3, where she was formally summoned. She is to appear in the Orange Walk Magistrate’s Court on Monday, November 9, at 9:00am.

World.title: Phillips regrets House outburst, says Mckenzie insulted his deceased mother
World.content:
Manchester North Western Member of Parliament (MP) Mikael Phillips

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Manchester North Western Member of Parliament (MP) Mikael Phillips has apologised for his use of an expletive during Tuesday’s confrontation at Gordon House, while accusing Government MP Desmond McKenzie of making an offensive remark about his deceased mother.

Phillips, in a statement Wednesday, said he regretted his response to the exchange but insisted that accounts of the incident circulated by Deputy Leader of Government Business Robert Nesta Morgan were “inaccurate and misleading”.

According to Phillips, he was standing with two other Opposition MPs discussing the circumstances surrounding the premature adjournment of the House of Representatives when the speaker exited the chamber.

He alleged that shortly after the speaker left, McKenzie, the MP for Kingston Western, verbally attacked him.

“As soon as the speaker left, the Member of Parliament for Kingston Western, Desmond McKenzie, verbally attacked me, making an offensive reference to my deceased mother. He then repeated the offence,” Phillips explained.

The Opposition MP acknowledged that he became angry and responded with an expletive, describing his reaction as inappropriate.

“My reaction was inappropriate, and I regret that I allowed myself to respond in that manner. I sincerely apologise to the Jamaican people,” he said.

However, he rejected Morgan’s claim that he pushed Opposition Leader Mark Golding during the confrontation, maintaining that Golding was not involved in the incident.

READ: Opposition, not Gov’t, responsible for ‘unparliamentary behaviour’ in House — Morgan

Phillips also said that although two Government MPs intervened, he did not physically touch either of them.

Questioning Morgan’s account, Phillips argued that the deputy leader of government business was not in the immediate vicinity when the incident occurred.

“It is deeply irresponsible for a Member of Parliament, particularly one entrusted with a leadership role in the House, to circulate an account that is so fundamentally at odds with what actually occurred. Mr Morgan should withdraw his false and malicious claims immediately,” Phillips said.

The Manchester North Western MP also linked the confrontation to growing tensions in Parliament, accusing the Government of repeatedly seeking to curtail debate and restrict the Opposition’s participation in parliamentary proceedings.

He argued that efforts to limit members’ opportunities to speak and debate have contributed to an increasingly strained atmosphere in the House and undermined parliamentary order.

“The right of elected representatives to speak, question and debate is fundamental to our parliamentary democracy. When those rights are repeatedly frustrated, it undermines the proper functioning of Parliament and contributes to an atmosphere of unnecessary tension,” he said.

Phillips maintained that Parliament should remain a place where differing views can be expressed freely and respectfully, while acknowledging that all MPs have a responsibility to uphold order and decorum.

He called for restraint from both sides of the House and urged the Government to respect the rights of elected representatives to perform their parliamentary duties without unnecessary obstruction.

World.title: ‘We will not be bullied’: Golding clarifies events leading to parliamentary uproar
World.content:
PNP President Mark Golding Photo: Karl Mclarty

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Opposition Leader Mark Golding has provided an account of the events that led to Tuesday’s parliamentary uproar, explaining that the Opposition’s protest was triggered by what he described as the Government’s abuse of parliamentary procedures to shut down debate on a censure motion concerning Jamaica’s position on Cuba.

Golding said the confrontation followed the Government’s decision to bring the debate to an early close without allowing the Opposition an opportunity to contribute to the motion it had tabled.

Opposition Member of Parliament (MP) Anthony Hylton opened the debate before Leader of Government Business Floyd Green responded. However, Golding said Speaker Juliet Holness subsequently allowed the Government to move to end the debate without giving him or other Opposition members an opportunity to speak.

“Anthony Hylton MP opened the debate on our censure motion in regard to the Government’s deception in the House the week before on the matter of Cuba. Minister Floyd Green then responded in the censure motion debate. The speaker, however, allowed a blatant abuse of power by the Government, letting them move a motion to bring an early close to that debate without letting me or anyone else on our side speak on our own motion,” Golding said in a video posted to his social media on Wednesday.

He questioned the fairness of the decision, noting that Opposition members were also prevented from challenging the move after their microphones were switched off.

“Mek that make sense? We weren’t allowed to speak on the motion that we had brought. Then we were prevented by the speaker from questioning that decision to bring it to an early close as she shut off our mics. We have a right to speak and we all stood up in protest,” he said.

Golding also explained the circumstances surrounding his exchange with the speaker, saying he had to raise his voice to be heard because his microphone was off and there was considerable noise in the chamber.

“So I raised my voice to make the point to the speaker that she has a duty under the standing orders to take into account the interests of the minority in this situation. I had to speak loudly to be heard because the speaker wouldn’t turn on my mic and there was a lot of noise in the room. I didn’t say anything rude or use any inappropriate language in making that point,” he said.

He said Opposition members maintained their protest rather than allow the sitting to continue without being given an opportunity to speak, prompting the speaker to adjourn the House.

“We will not be bullied,” Golding said.

Tensions escalated further after the formal proceedings had ended, with a confrontation between Manchester North Western MP Mikael Phillips and Government MP Desmond McKenzie, which was captured on video.

In condemning the conduct of Opposition MPs, Deputy Leader of Government Business Robert Nesta Morgan said McKenzie intervened to urge Phillips to show respect towards the speaker, prompting Phillips to respond with a series of expletives before advancing aggressively towards him. Morgan said Phillips had to be restrained by several members of the House.

READ: WATCH: House in turmoil over Cuba censure motion

In an additional release, the Opposition sought to outline its objections to the handling of the censure motion, accusing the Government of manipulating the House’s Standing Orders to avoid accountability over Jamaica’s abstention from a United Nations resolution calling for an end to the United States embargo against Cuba.

The Opposition said it had expected the motion, tabled by Hylton on Tuesday, to be debated at the next sitting, as Standing Orders prohibit debate on a motion on the same day it is tabled.

However, it said Green moved to suspend the Standing Orders and proceed immediately to which Opposition MP Phillip Paulwell objected, citing the procedural breach and the absence of the prime minister during debate on a censure motion against the Government.

According to the Opposition, the speaker ruled that the Standing Orders, including the notice requirement, be suspended, allowing Hylton to open the debate, followed by Green.

The Opposition said that when its members prepared to contribute, Green moved to close the debate without further contributions. It objected, citing Standing Order 38(2), which bars the early closure of a debate where doing so would oppress the minority.

Golding then called for a division, which the speaker acknowledged, but no vote was taken amid the disorder in the chamber. The sitting was subsequently adjourned, leaving the censure motion unfinished.

Golding said the Government could not be allowed to use parliamentary procedures to prevent scrutiny of an issue of national importance.

“The censure motion stands, and every Opposition voice must be given the opportunity to be heard,” he said.

Hylton also accused the Government of seeking to avoid accountability, saying: “The Government misled the House on Cuba. It then tried to bury the consequences. We will not rest until accountability is delivered.”

The Opposition maintained that the dispute goes beyond parliamentary procedure, arguing that it concerns democratic accountability and the public’s right to know about decisions affecting Jamaica’s international standing and reputation.

It further contended that the Government’s handling of the Cuba vote had damaged Brand Jamaica and reiterated its demand that the censure debate resume at the next sitting, with all members allowed to contribute.

READ: Shift in policy

World.title: Opposition, not Gov’t, responsible for ‘unparliamentary behaviour’ in House — Morgan
World.content:
Deputy Leader of Government Business Robert Nesta Morgan.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Deputy Leader of Government Business Robert Nesta Morgan has condemned the conduct of Opposition Members of Parliament (MPs) during Tuesday’s sitting of the House of Representatives, singling out Manchester North Western MP Mikael Phillips over an expletive-laden confrontation with Government MP Desmond McKenzie.

The incident occurred shortly after the House was adjourned following heated exchanges during debate on a motion seeking to censure the Government over Jamaica’s decision to abstain from a United Nations resolution calling for an end to the United States embargo on Cuba.

According to Morgan, tensions escalated after Phillips verbally confronted House Speaker Juliet Holness. Morgan said McKenzie intervened and urged Phillips to show respect towards the speaker, prompting Phillips to respond with a series of expletives before moving aggressively towards McKenzie.

Morgan said Phillips had to be restrained by several members of the House.

He also referenced video footage of the incident, which he said showed Phillips making apparent physical contact with Opposition Leader Mark Golding as he moved towards McKenzie.

READ: WATCH: House in turmoil over Cuba censure motion

In a statement on Wednesday, condemning the conduct of Opposition members, Morgan criticised comments allegedly made towards the speaker during the sitting.

“We wish to decry the unparliamentary behaviour of several members of the Opposition, both during the sitting of the House, as we were carrying out the nation’s business, and after. Particularly the leader of the Opposition, who made unparliamentary comments to the speaker, Angela Brown Burke, who also made unparliamentary comments off mic, but especially Mikael Phillips, who moved aggressively towards Member of Parliament from West Kingston, Desmond McKenzie, and had to be restrained by several members of the House based on his behaviour.

“We are representatives of the people. Our duty is to go to Parliament and conduct the business of the country and the people of Jamaica in a respectful and professional manner,” Morgan said.

He said the Government would not condone the conduct displayed by Opposition members, arguing that it reflected poorly on Parliament and set a negative example for the public.

“Our side, that is the Government side, will not tolerate, condone or support the type of behaviour that we saw today [Tuesday] in Parliament from the Opposition. It sets a bad example to everyone who is observing what is happening in the House,” Morgan said.

“We do not want it to be said that all parliamentarians or the Parliament is behaving in this manner. The distinction must be made that the behaviour was of the Opposition and not the Government side. A behaviour that we condemn, a behaviour that we reject and a behaviour that we will constantly speak and act against,” he added.

The confrontation followed an increasingly contentious sitting of the House, during which Opposition members protested after Leader of Government Business Floyd Green called for debate on the censure motion to be brought to an end.

The motion, brought by Opposition MP Anthony Hylton, challenged the Government’s decision to abstain from the October 28 United Nations General Assembly resolution on the US embargo against Cuba. The abstention marked the first time Jamaica had not supported the resolution since it was introduced in 1992.
