World.title: Hard truths
World.content:
TUFTON... we must obtain more value from the investments we have already made (Photo: JIS)

THE latest review of Jamaica’s public health sector presents a mixed bag of progress and troubling setbacks, with improvements in infrastructure and staffing overshadowed by soaring medicine costs, weaknesses in primary health care, and persistently high maternal and neonatal deaths.

Most alarming is the finding that complications from non-communicable diseases (NCDs) account for nearly four in every five deaths in Jamaica, while too many patients are turning up at hospitals with conditions already at an advanced stage.

The findings are contained in the Jamaica Health Public Expenditure Review, prepared by the World Bank at the request of the Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ) and the Ministry of Health and Wellness, covering the years 2016 to 2022.

Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton, who presented aspects of the report, along with the Government’s response, to Parliament on Tuesday, did not shy away from the findings, describing the review as “candid” and declaring that the Government accepts its conclusions.

“The review asks how much Jamaica spends on health, how well that money is spent, and what results it buys for our people,” Tufton explained.

He noted that the review measures Jamaica’s progress against the World Bank’s 2017 review, and compares the island’s performance with countries of similar demographic profiles.

He told Parliament that NCDs cause close to 80 per cent of deaths, maternal and neonatal mortality remain too high, and Jamaica’s per capita health expenditure is still below that of comparable countries, including Brazil, Grenada, Guyana, St Lucia, Dominica, Suriname, and Colombia.

Too much of the country’s health care spending, he acknowledged, is also being channelled into expensive late-stage hospital care, while medicine costs have risen rapidly.

“We need more nurses and more doctors in our health centres. And our service level agreements with the regional health authorities are not yet used to their full potential to hold the system accountable,” Tufton acknowledged.

According to the minister, “None of these findings comes as a surprise to the ministry. They validate the internal assessment that the ministry itself undertook, which led to the development of Vision for Health 2030, our 10-year strategic plan.

“That assessment told us that a health system built for acute and infectious disease must be reoriented towards prevention, primary healthcare and the management of chronic illness; that our workforce must grow and be deployed where it is needed most; that our facilities need sustained investment and maintenance; and that we need stronger governance and accountability for results,” said Tufton.

He posited that, working independently, the bank has reached the same conclusions.

“That tells us that we have diagnosed the problem correctly and that we are on the right road,” he said before reminding of the steps the ministry has taken over the past 10 years to address each of the bank’s findings.

“The ministry has not waited. Over the past decade we have acted on each of these fronts,” said Tufton.

On the matter of prevention, he reminded of the ‘Jamaica Moves’ programme launched in 2017 to tackle physical inactivity, poor diet, and the risk factors for NCDs. He also reminded of the ‘Know Your Numbers’ campaign, which encourages Jamaicans to have annual health checks and understand what he values mean for their health status.

On primary care, Tufton said the health and wellness ministry adopted the Primary Health Care Policy and, through the Health Systems Strengthening Programme, with support from the Inter-American Development Bank and the European Union, was upgrading health centres into comprehensive facilities. These include the Greater Portmore Health Centre, and redeveloping Spanish Town Hospital.

“On mothers and children, the Programme for the Reduction of Maternal and Child Mortality strengthened high-dependency and neonatal care in our hospitals; and the Western Child and Adolescent Hospital in Montego Bay, a gift of the People’s Republic of China, will be the first hospital of its kind in the English-speaking Caribbean,” said Tufton.

“On infrastructure, we have rehabilitated the Cornwall Regional Hospital and, following Hurricane Melissa, we are working with the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority to rebuild the Black River, Falmouth, and Noel Holmes hospitals to a more resilient standard,” he added.

Tufton told the Parliament that the National Health Fund (NHF) integrated the NHF Card and the Jamaica Drugs for the Elderly Programme in 2020, simplifying access for patients.

Regarding human resources, he said “The review rightly identifies people as the foundation of any health system.” He said the ministry is focused on training more health care workers, retaining those already employed, and deploying them to primary care and underserved communities.

Tufton argued that the review records real progress, and he asked his fellow lawmakers to note it. He also stressed that Jamaica stands out in the region for the priority it places on health, highlighting that by 2021/22 the ministry’s spending had reached 16 per cent of central government expenditure, a larger share than almost every other Caribbean country.

Tufton also pointed out that the burden on households has fallen as the Government now finances 68 per cent of current health spending, up from below 40 per cent in 2012. He said out-of-pocket payments have fallen to 15 per cent, below the international threshold of 20 per cent.

He also cited investment in health facilities, sharing that capital spending more than doubled in real terms between 2015/16 and 2019/20, while spending on the maintenance and upgrading of facilities rose by 150 per cent.

Additionally, Tufton noted that more Jamaicans were getting their medicines, with NHF prescriptions rising from 1.5 million to 2.7 million, enrolment growing by 86 per cent, and prescription fill rates growing from 85 to 92 per cent.

Tufton said the health workforce has grown, with 1,996 posts for medical officers established since 2016.

“Of note is that there has been a 30 per cent increase in doctors in primary care, in keeping with the reform of primary health care, moving from 338 in 2023 to 432 in 2025.

Arguing that the World Bank’s central message is that money alone is not enough, Tufton said, “We must obtain more value from the investments we have already made”.

Opposition spokesman on health Dr Alfred Dawes latched on to that point, telling Tufton, “As I listened the minister’s presentation, it just drives home the point that we have been making — spending more money on health does not equate to better health care.”

World.title: Utility cables hobble SPARK project
World.content:
President of Greenwood Citizens Association Trevor Burnett, Jr indicates a section of unfinished road in his community.

GREENWOOD, St James — Utility cables have emerged as the latest obstacle delaying the completion of a Shared Prosperity through Accelerated Improvement to Our Road Network (SPARK) project in Greenwood, St James.

Contractors have been unable to complete the rehabilitation of just under one-mile of road leading into the community as they await relocation of the underground wires.

“The reason why the Greenwood project has not been completed is that there are some telecommunications cables that are there. We have made requests to the telecommunications company that is responsible for those cables to move them,” minister without portfolio in the Ministry of Economic Growth and Job Creation Robert Morgan, told the Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

He has responsibility for works.

“We can’t move them because if we move them, then they might get damaged and a large portion of the area would be without telecommunications services,” the minister added.

The Greenwood road is among several in St James earmarked for rehabilitation under the government’s $45-billion SPARK programme. However while other roads — including some on which work began later — have seen varying levels of completion, the Greenwood project remains unfinished.

The incomplete section stretches approximately half-a-kilometre from the community’s entrance off the highway to a section of Greenwood Avenue.

“We are really trying to work with the telecommunications company to remove those cables — I think some of them are fibre-optic cables — so we can finish the road,” Morgan continued.

Work began on the road late last year but the project has been plagued by delays, which the minister acknowledged. While most of the repairs have been done and drainage installed, the last portion has lagged for about six months. China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), the contractor undertaking the project, has completed approximately 90 per cent of the work.

“I know the residents have been challenged. Because initially we had a water line issue where we had to instal new pipes and now that the road is pretty much paved that little section there is a challenge to the residents; so we are working on it,” Morgan assured.

For now, sections of the unfinished road remain open for drainage works, with caution signs placed in the area to alert motorists and pedestrians to potential hazards.

President of the Greenwood Citizens’ Association Trevor Burnett, Jr said he had been given a similar explanation for the delay.

“CHEC came out, I think August 1st, and said they were going to put in a new drain so that we don’t have any more flooding and as they started to dig, Flow cables and fibres underground started to be impacted,” he shared.

“We got Flow involved and so we are waiting on Flow now to complete their leg. They are supposed to move the fibre from underground, temporarily, and put it on poles so that CHEC can get to install the drain,” Burnett, Jr added.

Already concerned about the delay, the association president said he is also worried that there may be additional challenges ahead if the relevant parties fail to properly coordinate their work.

“After they remove the underground cables and put them on the post and CHEC completes their road paving, will Flow have to dig up the road again in order to bury back their fibre?” he asked.

“We need to know if they can work in conjunction with each other. My thought process is that Flow or CHEC would have put in some pipes alongside the drain so that Flow can just insert their fibres inside of it and we have a smooth sailing going forward,” Burnett, Jr explained.

He said he has been seeking answers but had yet to receive any substantial response.

Meanwhile, residents continue to contend with the inconvenience caused by the unfinished project.

“When it rains, it’s horrible, it’s flooded and you can’t get in and out most of the time. Pedestrians have to be using alternative routes, we have to be creating detour roads for pedestrians to go in and out of the community,” Burnett, Jr said.

He said CHEC had placed marl on the road as a temporary measure. However, the recent dry spell has turned the area into a dust bowl for those travelling through the community.

Residents said the situation continued to disrupt their daily lives and urgently needs to be addressed.

“When it rains it’s a problem and when it’s dry, it’s a dust nuisance; every day I have a cold,” complained Madge-Neil Burnett, who owns Greenwood Plaza.

She said the conditions have also affected her business.

“My thing them spoil up. Some of them we clean and sell [but] a lot of it we have to throw them away,” she lamented.

World.title: Masicka brings it home with Forever 1NE
World.content:
Minister of Culture and Entertainment Olivia “Babsy” Grange is out to support Masicka at the launch of his upcoming Forever 1NE concert held at D’Ferrano Restaurant & Lounge Rooftop on Monday night. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Portmore, his birthplace and the community that helped shape his journey, will take centre stage in a defining moment for Masicka when he brings his Forever 1NE music festival to Caymanas Park on December 19.

For the dancehall star, the occasion represents more than the staging of a major concert; it is an opportunity to give back to the place he calls home, while demonstrating the possibilities that open up when Jamaican artistes take ownership of their success and create opportunities on their own terms.

“This a mi place, Portmore; yah so mi birth, so dis a history,” Masicka declared at Monday night’s official media launch at D’Ferrano Restaurant & Lounge Rooftop, where sponsors, government officials, music industry stakeholders, and fans gathered to celebrate the undertaking.

The entertainer, who has spent more than a decade establishing himself as one of dancehall’s leading voices, was visibly at home as he addressed the gathering, expressing gratitude to the team working behind the scenes to bring the festival to fruition.

“Big up mi team, because this wouldn’t possible without dem; dem work hard. It’s a great feeling to host this in the community weh mi come from. With everything weh mi achieve inna mi career, me feel like a di right place to give back to,” he said.

It is a sentiment that resonates beyond the festivities planned for December. Portmore has long been said to be a breeding ground for Jamaican musical talent, and Masicka’s return as an internationally recognised act, now leading his own festival, is a moment of considerable significance for the municipality.

Minister of state in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade and Member of Parliament for St Catherine East Central Alando Terrelonge captured that pride in his address, welcoming the entertainer back to the community that helped shape his career.

“The truth is that we always say home is where the heart is, but tonight, home is where music is, and Masicka, I want to say welcome home,” Terrelonge said. “For years Portmore has been the incubator for Jamaica’s rawest, most undeniable talent. It is the community that shaped Masicka’s career, and to see him return to Portmore as an international headliner, commanding his own festival for the first time in his hometown, it fills every single Portmore resident with pride.”

Terrelonge praised Masicka as a master lyricist and storyteller whose career reflects patience, dedication. and growth. He also highlighted the potential benefits of the festival for the surrounding community, including increased commercial activity, job creation, and greater tourism visibility.

For him, December 19 represents an opportunity to celebrate not only Masicka’s achievements, but also the ability of Jamaican artistes to headline major productions at home.

“It’s celebrating a homecoming and proving that when possible, our own Jamaican musicians can headline their own concerts,” he said.

Dominic Bell, communications manager at J Wray & Nephew, which is partnering with the festival through Magnum Tonic Wine, pointed to the work behind Masicka’s success and the significance of the moment for the genre.

“Magnum’s Forever 1NE music festival will provide the manifestation of over 15 years of hard work from Masicka, garnering local and international acclaim,” Bell said. “As a lover of dancehall, this is exactly what the culture needs right now.”

Minister of Culture and Sport Olivia “Babsy” Grange, in welcoming the Forever 1NE initiative, commended Masicka for his discipline and for remaining focused on his music.

“I want to congratulate him for the example that he has been setting, the focus on the music. Him not ‘chatty chatty’ and run up him mouth and get himself into problems, him focus on him music, and that is what I admire so much about him,” Grange said.

She added that artistes have an important role to play in creating opportunities for the wider music industry, noting that Masicka and his team were taking that responsibility seriously through the festival.

“Music is entertainment, but it’s also a business,” she said, encouraging fans to support the artiste while reminding him of the responsibility that comes with their continued backing.

Minister of State in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce Delano Seiveright said the festival could help reinforce the municipality’s importance beyond its reputation as a residential community.

“Masicka is a game-changer and he is showing us what game-changing looks like,” Seiveright said. “Portmore is important to us. Over 200,000 people live in Portmore. It’s not just a residential community, it’s a place for business, a place for retail, and it’s going to become a place again for major events.”

Caymanas Park, the festival venue, is central to that ambition. Gary Peart, of Supreme Ventures, operators of Caymanas Park, said the property was poised to broaden its identity beyond horse racing and establish itself as a major entertainment destination.

“Everybody sees Caymanas as horse racing, the reality is that it’s going to be the biggest entertainment place in Jamaica,” Peart said, inviting patrons to witness a different side of the venue when Forever 1NE takes place.

Chief executive officer of Main Event Entertainment Group Solomon Sharpe, himself a Portmore native, said considerable work was already under way to deliver a production worthy of the occasion.

“We really want to put on a good production. Masicka is the biggest, baddest thing around town, and at Main Event we will try our best to keep up with him,” Sharpe said.

He disclosed that the team had already conducted six or seven site visits and reworked the venue layout several times, with an extensive range of production elements being considered.

The scale of the preparations is matched by a line-up designed to bring together some of dancehall and reggae’s distinctive voices. Joining Masicka on December 19 will be Dexta Daps, Shaneil Muir, and I Wayne, with additional surprise guests expected to make appearances.

And while the night’s full musical offering remains under wraps, those at Monday’s launch received a brief preview of what Masicka has in store. His performance was short but powerful, offering a taste of the commanding stage presence that has helped propel him to the forefront of the genre.

Masicka promised that the December staging would be anything but ordinary.

“December 19 nah go normal. Me and mi musical bredda dem ago create a pandemonium,” he declared.

World.title: FREIGHT FEARS
World.content:
CARIBBEAN businesses are pressing the United States to permanently exempt the region from maritime fees that could send freight costs soaring by as much as 60 per cent, fearing that concessions secured last year could be reversed as Washington continues its trade negotiations with China.

The charges, intended to curb China’s dominance in shipbuilding and maritime logistics, have also placed Caribbean trade in the firing line, given the region’s reliance on Chinesebuilt vessels to transport goods to and from the United States.

Washington suspended the wider measures last November as part of a trade agreement with Beijing and is now considering a further two-month extension until January 9, 2027. The Caricom Private Sector Organisation (CPSO), however, wants the separate exemptions secured for Caribbean shipping in April 2025 made permanent, removing the risk of future policy changes driving up costs along some of the region’s busiest trade routes.

In an October 29 submission to the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR), the CPSO and its US Business Council argued that the original fees could have increased freight costs between Florida and Caribbean ports by 50 to 60 per cent, potentially eroding the competitiveness of imports and disrupting supply chains on which regional businesses depend.

The organisation, which represents more than 6,250 firms across Caricom, maintains that the proposed charges of approximately US$1 million per vessel entry, as initially proposed in February 2025, would disproportionately affect Caribbean shipping, where smaller vessels make frequent trips between islands and US ports, carrying considerably less cargo than the large container ships operating on major international routes.

More than 90 per cent of the region’s merchandise trade moves by sea.

The exemptions subsequently granted by Washington largely shielded the region from those charges, covering qualifying smaller vessels, short-sea voyages of less than 2,000 nautical miles into continental US ports and certain specialised cargo ships.

However, the CPSO is now seeking to close gaps in the existing arrangements, particularly differences in how the US measures treat Chinesebuilt vessels and shipping companies owned or operated by Chinese interests.

The US measures are divided into two main categories: Annex I, which targets Chinese shipping operators, and Annex II, which applies to Chinese-built vessels regardless of ownership. While Annex II provides exemptions for smaller vessels and shortsea services, those same protections are absent from Annex I, potentially leaving some Caribbean shipping services exposed to fees because of who owns or operates the vessels.

The organisation wants those provisions aligned, alongside permanent exemptions for vessels already serving the Caribbean, including Chinese-built ships, and protection for regional transshipment hubs.

The concern is compounded by the Caribbean’s dependence on a shrinking pool of shipping lines, leaving some countries particularly vulnerable to any withdrawal or reduction in service.

According to the CPSO, the number of carriers providing consistent service to Caricom has fallen from more than 15 over the past two decades to just five, with some member states regularly served by only two or three lines.

Each of the five principal carriers operates at least one Chinese-built vessel, while many of the ships serving the region are specifically designed to navigate shallow ports and handle cargo at facilities with limited unloading equipment.

Replacing those vessels would be difficult, particularly as comparable American-built ships are not readily available. The CPSO warned that imposing additional charges could force carriers to reconsider their sailing schedules and routes, threatening the flow of food, manufacturing inputs and other essential goods.

The organisation said the exemptions secured in April 2025 have so far helped preserve those services, with no regular shipping line withdrawing from a Caricom port as a result of the measures and, to its knowledge, no carrier imposing a surcharge to recover the US maritime fees.

The CPSO also drew on Jamaica’s experience following Hurricane Melissa, which struck the island on October 28, 2025, to highlight the importance of maintaining reliable shipping routes during periods of disaster and recovery.

It reasoned that relief supplies, food and reconstruction materials continued arriving from Florida on the same short-sea vessels that would otherwise have been exposed to the charges, allowing shipments to reach the island without the additional costs associated with the US measures.

The organisation added that with reconstruction activity continuing across Jamaica, the reliability of those services remains important to businesses importing building materials, machinery and equipment needed to restore damaged properties and operations.

The implications also extend to the tourism sector, where hotels and other businesses depend on regular shipments of food, beverages, furnishings and supplies, much of which moves through Florida ports.

CPSO is also making the case that permanently exempting Caribbean shipping would protect American commercial interests, given the United States’ dominant position as a supplier to the region.

Figures cited from the US Census Bureau show that merchandise trade between the United States and the 15 Caricom member states reached US$30.1 billion in 2025, with American exports totalling US$18.6 billion against imports of US$11.6 billion.

That left Washington with a trade surplus of approximately US$7 billion, continuing a longstanding pattern in which the US sells substantially more goods to Caricom than it purchases from the region.

American suppliers account for a significant share of Caribbean imports, including food, agricultural products, industrial inputs and consumer goods, with much of that trade moving through PortMiami, Port Everglades and the Port of Palm Beach.

The CPSO argued that higher shipping costs could weaken the competitiveness of those products, encouraging Caribbean importers to turn to alternative suppliers and potentially eroding the US share of a market it has dominated for decades.

Manufacturers dependent on imported raw materials would also face pressure on production costs, while distributors and retailers could be forced to absorb higher freight expenses or pass them on to consumers.

The organisation further cautioned that some goods move through US ports more than once during processing and distribution, meaning charges imposed on individual vessel entries could compound costs along the same supply chain.

Energy exports present another concern, particularly shipments of crude oil, liquefied natural gas, ammonia and methanol from Guyana, Trinidad and Tobago and other regional producers.

Many of those operations involve US investment and specialised vessels, including Chinese-built tonnage. Depending on contractual arrangements, additional freight costs could either reduce exporters’ margins or increase prices to buyers, weakening the competitiveness of regional energy products.

Despite its objections to the proposed fees, the CPSO maintains its support for Washington’s efforts to rebuild its shipbuilding and maritime industries, arguing that closer US-Caribbean cooperation would offer a more practical approach than imposing restrictions on existing shipping services.

It has proposed partnerships that could eventually introduce American-built vessels to Caribbean routes as US shipbuilding capacity develops, along with advance consultation on any policy changes affecting regional shipping.

The organisation is also seeking an explicit exemption for shipping to and from the Caribbean Basin, preferably backed by US legislation, to ensure that the region’s treatment is no longer dependent on temporary suspensions or negotiations between Washington and Beijing.

The CPSO argues that such an arrangement would protect established supply chains and give shipping operators, importers and investors greater certainty when making commercial decisions, while preserving a trading relationship valued at more than US$30 billion annually.

World.title: Green: There will be adequate supplies of eggs, poultry and vegetables for Christmas
World.content:
Green says they expect supplies of most vegetables and fruits to be adequate during the Christmas period. (Photos: Naphtali Junior and Garfield Robinson)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Despite a persistent drought and the lingering effects of Hurricane Melissa, Agriculture Minister Floyd Green has reiterated that there will be adequate supplies of chicken meat, eggs and vegetables for the Christmas period.

“Our assessment is that, despite the severity of the drought and the significant impact it has had on production, Jamaica is positioned to have adequate supplies across most of our major food lines for the Christmas period. There will be tighter availability in some individual commodities, but the overall production outlook is encouraging,” said Green.

He gave the assurance Tuesday while making a ministerial statement in the House of Representatives.

Green noted that poultry remains one of the most important sources of protein for Jamaican households, especially during Christmas. He said the poultry industry has made a significant recovery.

“This is particularly noteworthy when we recall the impact of Hurricane Melissa, which resulted in the loss of approximately 700,000 broilers and 400,000 layers,” he said.

The minister shared that for the period November 14 to December 26, broiler meat production is forecast at approximately 22.3 million kilogrammes.

“That would be approximately 30 per cent above the hurricane-affected Christmas period of 2025 and close to the levels recorded in 2024,” said Green. He highlighted that weekly broiler production is expected to peak at approximately 3.5 million kilogrammes during the week ending December 12.

“Based on the current forecast, we therefore expect Jamaica to have adequate supplies of locally produced chicken for Christmas,” he added.

In terms of eggs, the minister said the recovery in egg production has also been significant, although it is important to recognise that this recovery is not yet complete.

“For November and December, egg production is forecast at approximately 38.1 million eggs, with approximately 20.1 million eggs projected for December alone. That represents approximately 650,000 eggs per day during December,” Green said.

This would place Christmas egg production at approximately 2024 levels and significantly above the hurricane-affected levels of 2025. But, Green cautioned that the national layer flock remains below its earlier level, a situation that could result in some tightness in the egg market during periods of peak demand.

Green also assured that based on the latest production forecasts, field observations and planting activity, “We expect supplies of most vegetables and fruits to be adequate during the Christmas period.”

However, this is contingent on weather conditions remaining favourable, and the country not experiencing a major adverse event.

Green pointed to encouraging signs across a number of commodities, with field assessments indicating increasing supplies of cabbage, lettuce, cucumber, string beans, plummy tomato and sweet pepper, driven by increased planting activity following localised rainfall. Additionally, sweet potato and yellow yam are expected to have relatively stable supplies into the Christmas period. And supplies of escallion have been increasing and are expected to continue improving into January.

The minister said cucumber supplies are expected to improve, while increased supplies of tomato are anticipated during December.

“We are also projecting increased availability of hot pepper during December. For cabbage, increased supplies are expected as current plantings mature, while additional interventions are being undertaken in vegetable production to support availability through the Christmas period,” he said.

Despite being upbeat, Green cautioned that the severity of the drought that has affected the country this year must be put into context.

“This was no ordinary dry spell. The conditions Jamaica has been experiencing are unlike a normal drought cycle. We have been affected by exceptionally dry conditions which significantly disrupted our usual rainfall patterns. What made the situation particularly concerning was its timing. Jamaica was experiencing worsening drought conditions during what should have been our wet season,” he said.

Notably, rainfall across the island in September and October was below the 30-year average.

“That is significant because water availability is critical to agricultural production. Water sources were under pressure. Rainfall was significantly below normal and farmers were trying to establish and maintain crops through one of the most difficult dry periods we have faced,” Green noted.

World.title: Midterms : 5 points que l’Europe doit surveiller après l’écrasante victoire des démocrates face à Trump
World.content:
Ces résultats impliquent probablement de futures enquêtes sur la guerre en Iran, le fonctionnement du FBI et, bien sûr, les business de la famille Trump. Pour se faire une idée de leur magnitude sur le plan politique : c'est comme si vous aviez le scandale du Whitewater de Bill Clinton et la première procédure de destitution contre Donald Trump réunis, avec en prime l'affaire Iran-Contra pour pimenter le tout.

Quel sera l'impact de ces bouleversements politiques majeurs sur l'Europe ? Des prix de l'énergie à la guerre en Ukraine, l'avenir du continent dépend en grande partie de ce qui se passe à Washington. Voici cinq points à surveiller.

L'Europe risque de faire les frais de la frustration de Trump

Certains observateurs chevronnés estiment que cela n’est pas seulement possible, mais hautement probable. "Nous devons nous préparer non pas à des relations transatlantiques plus harmonieuses, mais à plus d’animosité et à encore davantage d'exigences de la part de Trump envers l’Europe", a averti Wolfgang Ischinger, un diplomate allemand expérimenté qui a présidé pendant de longues années la Conférence de Munich sur la sécurité.

Les démocrates auront davantage d'occasions de s'opposer à Donald Trump via des procédures budgétaires et en se montrant plus fermes lors des auditions de contrôle et des enquêtes. Ils commenceront probablement aussi à imposer des conditions plus strictes aux projets de loi souhaités par la Maison-Blanche.

Mais le président américain dispose d’une marge de manœuvre constitutionnelle considérable en matière de politique étrangère, de diplomatie et de sécurité nationale — ainsi qu’en matière de politique commerciale. Et Donald Trump s’en est ouvertement emparé en recourant à des décrets et en mettant au point des stratégies juridiques inédites et controversées pour contourner le Congrès.

“[Trump] est à la tête des forces armées. Il a la main sur les droits de douane et les accords commerciaux. Il dispose d’une tribune influente. Même si les démocrates remportent les deux chambres, il peut opposer son veto aux projets de loi”, a énuméré Phil Gordon, ex-conseiller à la sécurité nationale de l’ancienne vice-présidente Kamala Harris, auprès de Brussels Playbook.

World.title: Mélenchon a-t-il déjà son ticket pour le second tour ?
World.content:
La France insoumise s’est réjouie de la défaite de Donald Trump lors des élections de mi-mandat aux Etats-Unis, y voyant la possibilité de “faire reculer l’extrême droite”. Toute coïncidence avec la situation française n’est pas fortuite, alors que le scénario d’un second tour opposant Marine Le Pen à Jean-Luc Mélenchon devient de plus en plus probable, sondage après sondage. Pourquoi les Insoumis se sentent-ils pousser des ailes ? Ont-ils raison d’y croire ? Cela oblige-t-il les candidats de la droite et du centre à redéfinir leur stratégie ? Anthony Lattier en discute avec Victor Goury-Laffont, journaliste à POLITICO, et Marcelo Wesfreid, directeur adjoint de la rédaction.

World.title: Metsola tells MEPs not to rely on AI when drafting laws
World.content:
“No matter how AI may be used in a parliament, the responsibility is still [with] those who are elected,” she said.

Secretary-General Alessandro Chiocchetti said at the same event that Parliament is building its own AI tool for sensitive work, hosted on its internal infrastructure.

As POLITICO reported in July, commercial AI models, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Meta’s Llama, can still be used for less sensitive tasks.

Parliament officials have warned of a surge in AI-written amendments, including some that reference laws that don't exist. Chiocchetti cited the case of an MEP who turned to AI for legal advice and got a wrong answer. “Our jurists took two days just to prove ChatGPT wrong,” he said.

The administration will submit new guidelines on using AI to senior leaders “very soon,” Chiocchetti said. Existing guidelines for staff date from 2024.

“Basically it boils down to three things: be open about using artificial intelligence, meaning if they use it, they have to say it as the rules require; never put sensitive material into a public tool; and check everything before it leaves your desk because it is your name on it,” Chiocchetti said.

He added he wants to use AI to help sort through thousands of amendments. But the drafting and consideration of laws need to remain with MEPs, as “the risk is indeed that we delegate the political debate to a chatbot.”

“Every text we vote has to be one that people wrote, checked, and are willing to defend. Anyone reading a new regulation should be able to find out who decided and hold them responsible.”

World.title: Fridge hacks also hit French blood banks
World.content:
The incident appears linked to a fresh wave of cyberattacks on supermarket refrigerators across Europe, which forced stores to throw out spoiled food. That wave came just weeks after French supermarkets were first hit by a cyberattack that also hit refrigerators.

French media reports said refrigeration company Coolworld is the supplier to EFS. The company said in a statement that it's aware of the incident and that it "concerns a component supplied by a third-party provider and not directly controlled by Coolworld." It said only a "limited number" of its units were affected.

In the attacks on supermarkets, refrigerator defrost settings were manipulated so the coolers reached very high temperatures, mirroring the EFS’s experiences. The blood stored in the affected equipment, which included plasma bags for transfusions, has been “transferred or secured,” the EFS said.

French digital minister Anne Le Hénanff said in the country's Senate today that the recent attacks on the country's refrigerators "have directly targeted our economy and our supply chain."

"I would even go so far as to say that, beyond that, their objective may potentially be to undermine the unity of our country and to create anxiety among the population," she said.

Emile Marzolf contributed to this report.

World.title: Talks underway for Trump-Xi-Putin meeting, China says
World.content:
Mao did not elaborate on which topics the leaders would cover if they convene, amid fears in Europe that talks on ending the war in Ukraine could take place without Kyiv or European capitals at the table.

Trump last month indicated interest in discussing “denuclearization” in a trilateral meeting, but “not so much” Ukraine. China hasn’t commented on what would be on the agenda, although German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said Xi rejected the idea of discussing Ukraine in that format when both leaders spoke last week. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that such a meeting would be “appropriate and very useful,” but did not elaborate on a potential agenda.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed concern over a potential trilateral meeting, “I really don’t want this to be a ‘Yalta – 2, 3, 4,’ when there is a redistribution of influence,” Zelenskyy told reporters in late October, referring to the 1945 talks between the U.S., British and Soviet leaders to discuss the future of postwar Germany.

“Europe must and wants to play a role in this process,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Tuesday alongside Zelenskyy in Berlin. “Key elements of a peaceful solution — whether regarding sanctions or the security architecture — can only be resolved with us Europeans. And everyone involved knows that very well.”

World.title: Als Weidel noch gegen Sexismus kämpfte
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Ein gigantisches Datenleck enthüllt das verborgene Innenleben der AfD. Mehr als 400.000 interne E-Mails zeigen, wie der Bundestagsabgeordnete Markus Frohnmaier brisante Informationen für das syrische Assad-Regime sammelt. Gleichzeitig offenbaren die Leaks, wie die heutige Parteichefin Alice Weidel intern vehement gegen sexistische Wahlplakate kämpfte – und damit krachend scheiterte.

Die Recherchen von Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler bringen weitere brisante Personalien ans Licht. So versuchte die AfD einst, ein Mitglied wegen mutmaßlich rassistischer Äußerungen auszuschließen – heute sitzt er als Verfassungsrichter in Bayern. In Nordrhein-Westfalen eskaliert derweil der parteiinterne Machtkampf um Landeschef Martin Vincentz bis hin zu einer Strafanzeige wegen Untreue.

Aktuelle Brisanz birgt zudem eine geplante Bundestagsveranstaltung Frohnmaiers, die eine neutrale „Schweiz des Ostens“ propagiert. Dass ausgerechnet Julia Mendel, eine ehemalige Sprecherin des ukrainischen Präsidenten, auf dem Podium sitzt, sorgt für Entsetzen und wirft die Frage auf, wie die Partei ihre außenpolitische Agenda in der Praxis vorantreibt.

Den Artikel von Frederik Schindler bei WELT zum Machtkampf in der NRW-AfD gibt’s hier.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.

World.title: Pistorius verteidigt Bevorzugung der deutschen Industrie bei Rüstungsausgaben
World.content:
Der Streit verdeutlicht ein Problem für Europas Ambitionen. Die EU-Staaten wollen stärkere Streitkräfte aufbauen und dafür mehr gemeinsam beschaffen, doch die Regierungen sind auch bestrebt, Arbeitsplätze und Fabriken im eigenen Land zu schützen.

Das zeigen auch die Zahlen. 2025 gaben die EU-Länder 115 Milliarden Euro für militärische Ausrüstung aus. Laut der Europäischen Verteidigungsagentur entfielen 24 Prozent dieser Ausgaben auf gemeinsame Beschaffungen.

Brüssel möchte, dass dieser Anteil bis 2030 mindestens 40 Prozent erreicht. Die EU hat das mit 150 Milliarden Euro dotierte SAFE-Programm für Waffenkredite ins Leben gerufen, um Länder zu bewegen, Waffen gemeinsam statt einzeln zu kaufen.

Doch Regierungen zögern oft, große Rüstungsaufträge an Unternehmen in anderen Ländern zu vergeben. Die polnische Regierung erklärte, sie wolle 89 Prozent der fast 44 Milliarden Euro, die sie aus dem SAFE-Fonds erhält, für die heimische Industrie ausgeben.

Pistorius verteidigte diesen Ansatz. Regierungen hätten auch eine Verantwortung dafür, ihre Volkswirtschaften und Industrien zu schützen.

„Ich würde daher die Kritik in Ihrer Frage zurückweisen“, sagte er zu Strack-Zimmermann. „Und wenn es Kritik zu üben gibt, dann sollte sie sich nicht gegen Deutschland richten, sondern gegen buchstäblich alle Europäer mit einer Rüstungsindustrie.“

Dieser Artikel erschien zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO.

World.title: Brazil: Santa Claus School celebrates graduation at Christ the Redeemer
World.content:
Christmas came early to Rio de Janeiro on Tuesday, when 55 graduates of the Escola de Papai Noel do Brasil gathered beneath Christ the Redeemer to mark the end of their training. Dressed in red suits and white beards, the new Santas sang carols as they rode the Corcovado mountain railway to the statue, then climbed the final steps for a ceremony that included a blessing and the presentation of diplomas.

 

The free course, open to men aged 50 and over with naturally white or grey hair and beards, runs for a month of Tuesday afternoon classes covering acting, improvisation, diction, posture, make-up, costume and beard care, plus Brazilian Sign Language. It was founded in 1993 by the actors Limachem Cherem and Conrado Freitas, with the costume designer Fátima Tavares Cherem, in the basement of Cherem's house in Vila Isabel.

More than 1,000 Santas have passed through the school in 33 years, along with about 300 Noeletes, its female equivalent. Many graduates are retirees earning extra income at shopping centres, hospitals and parties; some, such as the lorry driver Marinezio Teixeira de Oliveira, come back for a second certificate.

World.title: Just six climate actions could save 1.6 million lives a year, WHO says
World.content:
Climate change exposes growing populations to its effects and the resulting health risks. An estimated 3.6 billion people live in areas that make them highly susceptible to climate change and its impact on health.

 

Implementing six climate and health interventions could prevent 1.6 million deaths every year – around one in every 40 deaths – and generate trillions of dollars in economic and fiscal benefits, according to a new World Health Organization (WHO) report published on Wednesday.

“The climate crisis is a health crisis, but much of the harm it causes can be prevented with tools we already have,” said Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General.

The six actions are heat-health warning systems; climate-resilient drinking-water services; basic sanitation, hygiene and handwashing facilities; cleaner household fuels and technologies for cooking and heating and more effective fossil fuel pricing policies.

“Scaling up proven, affordable actions could save millions of lives, with the greatest gains in the countries that need them most,” Tedros said. “As governments prepare for the next round of climate negotiations, protecting health must be at the centre of climate action.”

Without additional intervention, selected climate-related health risks such as undernutrition, malaria, diarrhoea and heat stress are estimated to cause 250,000 premature deaths per year between 2030 and 2050.

By 2050, climate change could also expose an estimated additional 500 million people worldwide to vectors that transmit climate-sensitive diseases, the report noted.

Related Climate change should be declared health emergency as health risks can no longer be ignored

What are the measures?

The interventions target different climate-related health risks, ranging from extreme heat and air pollution to infectious diseases and unsafe water.

WHO wants to see heat-health warning systems that alert populations to dangerously high temperatures and trigger responses such as promoting hydration, providing cooling facilities and reaching out to vulnerable groups.

On top of that, resilient sources of clean water to prevent shortages and contamination during extreme weather events, as well as access to basic hygiene services, should be ensured to reduce exposure to waterborne pathogens.

Switching to cleaner energy would reduce indoor air pollutants and greenhouse gas emissions and can prevent deaths and illnesses linked to respiratory infections and chronic non-communicable diseases, including stroke, ischaemic heart disease, lung cancer and asthma, WHO said.

WHO is also calling on governments to introduce more efficient fossil fuel pricing policies by ensuring the price reflects fossil fuel impact on health, climate and the environment.

According to the report, phasing out fossil fuels delivers the largest health benefits, preventing more than one million premature deaths annually from non-communicable diseases, including stroke, ischaemic heart disease, lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma, as well as road traffic accidents, while generating US$5.4 trillion in fiscal benefits each year.

The other five measures, on average, every US$1 invested is estimated to generate US$24.8 in benefits, according to the WHO. Returns are expected to be even greater in low- and middle-income countries, helping to reduce health and economic inequalities.

World.title: As maritime threats grow, France pushes to strengthen Europe's naval power
World.content:
From attacks on commercial ships in the Red Sea to Russia’s escalating strikes on maritime vessels in the Black Sea, critical maritime corridors have once again emerged as major geopolitical flashpoints.

 

Against a backdrop of growing uncertainty over the transatlantic defence partnership, Europe is striving to strengthen its naval capabilities and strategic autonomy.

With the second-largest exclusive economic zone (EEZ) in the world, France is at the forefront of these efforts. This week, international delegations are flocking to Euronaval, the world's largest marine and naval defence trade show (3-6 November) near Paris.

Sailors are aboard a submarine awaiting the arrival of French President Emmanuel Macron at the nuclear submarine navy base of Ile Longue in Crozon, France, Monday 2 March, 202 Yoan Valat via AP Photo

France renews its military fleet

Speaking at the opening of this year's Euronaval edition, France's Defence Minister Catherine Vautrin stressed that the country was renewing its "attack submarines, frigates and support vessels."

"We are preparing for our future aircraft carrier, the France Libre, and the SNLE 3G (third-generation nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine), which will replace the current generation of submarines responsible for maintaining the continuous at-sea deterrence of our nuclear deterrent", she added.

The Charles De Gaulle, the French aircraft carrier, is docked in the French Navy base of Toulon, southern France, Wednesday, 9 November 2022. Eric Gaillard via AP Photo

France is the only European country to operate a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier and boasts one of the continent’s most balanced submarine fleets. It is also the world's second-largest arms exporter, trailing behind the United States.

In March, French President Emmanuel Macron delivered a landmark speech from a ballistic-missile submarine base in north-western France, which captured global audiences. He pledged to increase the country's nuclear warhead stockpile for the first time since 1992 and that he would not flinch if the country’s “vital interests” were threatened.

Since September 2025, France has intensified its efforts to tackle Russia's shadow fleet, which Moscow uses to evade Western sanctions on its energy sector. Authorities have intercepted and boarded at least six tankers suspected of belonging to the shadow fleet, amid concerns over irregular or fraudulent flag registrations.

Domestic and European companies favoured

On Tuesday, the French government signed a new agreement to build a domestic ecosystem of drone manufacturers that can rapidly respond to the navy’s operational needs. This comes as unmanned and autonomous naval systems have taken centre stage at this year's edition of Euronaval.

"One of the major revolutions of our time is the naval drone. It incorporates artificial intelligence and allows us to achieve more at a lower cost and over a greater distance", François Watteau, Director of the Naval Combat Programme Management Unit at the French Directorate General of Armaments (DGA) told Euronews.

France prioritises domestic and European companies in its defence procurement, with 92% of the Ministry of the Armed Forces' suppliers based domestically in 2024.

According to Watteau, France has "always had a strong navy", but it has been significantly bolstered over the past year.

"This is due to the military programming laws [which lay out spending for 2024-2030], as well as its maritime armament drive, which has led to greater budgets and a strengthened national interest in naval equipment."

French Navy Vice-Admiral Éric Chaperon, now naval advisor to Thales, told Euronews that this year marked a strategic turning point, "in previous years, we would showcase new products and technologies that we were working on, but which were still some way off. Given the current geopolitical context, however, it is clear that navies have become much more focused on the near future and what can be delivered immediately."

The French state is a stakeholder in Thales, a major French defence and technology group, which has extensive contracts with the country's armed forces and European defence and space programmes.

Despite this, other defence companies have criticised what they describe as a monopoly of French "success stories."

"There are favoured companies, the industry leaders, the big players such as Naval Group and Thales in France. These major companies employ thousands of people and tend to capture most of the market", Martin Serrault, Director General of Sillinger, a French manufacturer specialising in domestically produced inflatable boats for defence purposes, told Euronews.

French helicopter pilot checks his helicopter prior a take off aboard the French navy frigate Normandie keep watch as the vessel patrols in a Norwegian fjord, 6 March 2024. Thibault Camus via AP Photo

The future of France's defence plans hinges on the country's upcoming elections. At present, the government has proposed upping France's 2027 defence budget to €63.4 billion, an increase of approximately €6.5 billion (11.4%) compared with 2026.

A number of presidential candidates are expected to attend this year's Euronaval edition, with left-wing candidate Raphaël Glucksmann participating on Wednesday, while conservative figures Edouard Philippe and Bruno Retailleau, as well as the far-right's Marine Le Pen are scheduled to appear on Thursday.

"Protecting our fellow citizens and protecting France are absolutely vital priorities", Guillaume Merveilleux du Vignaux, Director of the Euronaval summit told Euronews.

"National defence is inherently a political matter. It is not solely the responsibility of the military, but requires the commitment of the entire nation and all its citizens, starting with the country's foremost representative, the President", added du Vignaux.

World.title: WHO backs trials for two new vaccines against Ebola outbreak
World.content:
The World Health Organization (WHO) has backed clinical trials for two new Ebola vaccine candidates as health workers battle an outbreak in several African countries that has killed more than 5,300 people.

 

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare Ebola variant for which no vaccine has been approved.

“Today WHO expert groups are recommending adding two vaccine candidates to the trial that had been developed specifically for the Bundibugyo virus,” WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told reporters during a press conference in Geneva on Wednesday.

The two vaccine candidates are being developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India and Moderna. The trial will be led by the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)’s National Institute for Biomedical Research, with support from international partners, including WHO.

“Vaccines are powerful tools, but they're not substitutes for the proven measures that can save lives now,” Tedros added, citing early care, contact tracing, isolation, safe and dignified burials, and trusted engagement with communities.

The outbreak, which began in the DRC in May, has infected more than 10,000 people, with a fatality rate of over 50%, according to the country’s latest data from 31 October, making it the fastest-growing and most widespread Ebola epidemic on record.

Cases have also been reported in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda, although the DRC remains the epicentre and the hardest-hit country with 5,103 deaths reported.

In response, some countries, including Ghana and the United States, have introduced travel restrictions on travellers arriving from the DRC.

The WHO chief condemned these measures and recommended against them.

“We call on countries that have imposed travel restrictions to lift them. Such restrictions punish countries for doing the right thing, create disincentives for transparency and harm the response,” he said.

This position is shared by the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), which, since the beginning of the outbreak, has said that travel restrictions should not be used as a primary public health tool during outbreaks.

World.title: Grand Voyager in Copenhagen: cycling, culture and Nordic cuisine
World.content:
Copenhagen, Denmark’s capital, is known for its colourful architecture, rich cultural heritage and relaxed way of life. It’s a city where historic landmarks and modern Scandinavian design sit together.

 

One of the best ways to discover the city is with a local guide. In this episode of Grand Voyager, Lilly joins Therese from Copenhagen by Mie to explore the Danish capital, learning about its history, traditions and distinctive character.

Art is an important part of Danish culture. At the National Gallery of Denmark, Lilly explores the country’s artistic heritage, discovering works from Danish masters alongside contemporary art.

Cycling is one of the most popular ways to get around in Copenhagen, with dedicated cycle lanes and a city built around two wheels. To experience this for herself, Lilly joins a cycling tour before visiting the Happiness Museum. Here, she meets the team to discover why Denmark is often associated with happiness and how the Danish concept of hygge influences everyday life.

Copenhagen is also known for its contemporary architecture and waterfront neighbourhoods. In the district of Nordhavn, Lilly checks into Hotel Frihavnen, a boutique hotel surrounded by modern buildings, independent cafés and harbour views.

Food is at the heart of Danish culture, with a strong emphasis on tradition, quality and local ingredients. At Epicurus, Lilly discovers a creative approach to Nordic cuisine, where seasonal ingredients meet French culinary techniques. The restaurant also combines its dining experience with an intimate jazz atmosphere.

To finish her journey, Lilly visits Tivoli Gardens, which first opened its gates in 1843. With its landscaped gardens, amusement rides and lively atmosphere, it remains one of Copenhagen’s best-known attractions.

With its rich cultural heritage, celebrated food scene, cycling culture and distinctive approach to wellbeing, Copenhagen offers visitors a fascinating mix of experiences and plenty to discover.

World.title: UK: Police arrest Palestine Action supporters outside Supreme Court
World.content:
Footage shows demonstrators lying on the pavement, with groups of officers lifting them and carrying them to a waiting police van, while others continued holding placards. Police said 25 people had been detained on suspicion of supporting a proscribed organisation under the Terrorism Act, with further arrests expected.

 

The legal challenge was brought by Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori, who is seeking to overturn the group's designation as a terrorist organisation. The court heard that it was the first of 98 proscribed groups banned solely for causing serious property damage, rather than advocating violence against people.

More than 4,000 arrests have been made under the ban, including 325 outside the US embassy on 31 October. Charges linked to the prohibition could be affected if the appeal succeeds.

World.title: UK parliament risks 'catastrophic failure' after renovation delay
World.content:
The continuous delay of Britain's centuries-old parliament major restoration project puts it at risk of a major failure, members of the UK parliament warned on Wednesday.

 

Crumbling masonry, ageing electrics, frequent leaks and high asbestos levels are just some of the problems threatening the integrity of the UK's parliament building, parts of which are over 900 years old.

The UNESCO World Heritage site requires billions of pounds to be renovated, but members of parliament have been unable to decide on how to proceed.

This indecisiveness has led to spiralling costs and risks causing a "catastrophic failure" that would harm the UK's "morale and reputation", according to the parliament's public accounts committee.

"A lack of action risks, for instance, the chamber being plunged into darkness during the state opening of parliament," said chair Geoffrey Clifton-Brown MP, referencing when the monarch comes to the lower House of Commons to read out the government's legislation plans.

"Consider the impact of global rolling news footage of Notre Dame-like flames licking out of the building's roof, resulting in the destruction of our heritage, or worse, injuries or loss of life. These are not notional possibilities, but real and rising risks," he added.

The building, originally built in the eleventh century, has already suffered two fires that destroyed the royal apartments in 1512 and a larger one that destroyed the majority of the palace in 1834.

MPs delaying renovation since 2018

Parliamentarians first voted to move out of the central London site in 2018 to allow extensive repairs. But there has since been disagreement about whether this should go ahead.

Both houses are expected to hold a series of votes on this restoration plan later this year to choose how deep the renovation should be carried out.

The current options include a "full decant" costing up to £15.6 billion (€18.7 billion) and lasting up to 24 years, where both houses leave for much of the works.

A partial decant called "enhanced maintenance and improvement plus", where no more than 30 per cent of staff would stay on site at any one time, is projected to cost £39 billion (€46.8 billion) and take up to 61 years.

Current timescales predict that work will start in 2032.

In its report, the committee warned that the weekly cost of maintenance on the parliamentary estate is expected to grow from the current £1.5 million (€1.8 million) to £2 million (€2.4 million) in the coming years.

Each year the programme is delayed will add £420 million (€504 million) to the lifetime costs of delivering the scheme, it added.

World.title: French blood banks targeted by refrigerator cyberattack
World.content:
A cyberattack had attempted to destroy blood plasma by raising the temperatures in cold storage facilities past the boiling point.

Blood banks in France were included among cyberattacks that hit refrigeration systems in several European countries on Sunday and Monday, French authorities said on Wednesday.

The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said that a "cybersecurity incident "targeted a refrigeration service provider affecting control systems at three cold storage sites for plasma and blood samples.

The cyberattack attempted to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but it was warded off before any damage could be done. The plasma in the affected refrigerators was transferred or secured, the EFS said.

"No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost," the EFS said in a statement, adding that its distribution operations were not interrupted.

Hackers try and make blood boil

The cyberattack was first reported on Wednesday by the French weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaine, which said the temperatures had been programmed to reach a boiling 110 C (230 F), rather than -30 Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit).

"Monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the anomalies, allowing staff to take action to ensure that no blood products or samples were compromised," the EFS said.

France's cybersecurity agency and Health Ministry said an investigation is underway, but did not indicate who could have been responsible.

The Health Ministry said Wednesday that remote access to the affected refrigerators was disabled, and credited monitoring and alarm systems with ensuring the safety of blood supplies.

Coolworld, the company supplying the refrigeration equipment, said the vulnerability was related to a component from a "third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld's direct control."

European supermarkets targeted by cyberattacks

On Sunday and Monday, a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at supermarkets in several European countries, including France and Germany, destroying large quantities of frozen food.

It was reminiscent of a similar attack three weeks ago targeting refrigeration systems at dozens of French supermarkets.

The attacks have cost supermarkets millions of euros in wasted food.

On Wednesday, Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize said it expects the cyberattack in October to reduce quarterly sales by as much as €250 million ($281 million).

"While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations," CEO Franz Muller said.

World.title: Neo-Nazi NSU attacks exposed 15 years ago
World.content:
Many questions still surround the National Socialist Underground whose existence was revealed by neo-Nazi terrorist Beate Zschäpe on November 4, 2011. How has German society reacted to its crimes? Has justice been done?

Halit Yozgat was the NSU's ninth murder victim. He was killed at point-blank range on April 6, 2006, in Kassel, in the German state of Hesse. Before him, eight other men with immigrant backgrounds had also been shot point-blank since September 2000. The tenth and final victim that did not fit this pattern: she was a woman. Police officer Michèle Kiesewetter was killed on April 25, 2007, in Heilbronn, in the German state of Baden-Württemberg.

Four and a half years after Kiesewetter's death, the identities of those behind the mysterious series of murders finally came to light. On November 4, 2011, Beate Zschäpe, who was later sentenced to a long prison sentence, revealed the existence of the National Socialist Underground (NSU). The group also included Uwe Böhnhardt and Uwe Mundlos, who were found dead in a burned-out RV on the same day.

The two men are believed to have taken their own lives following a failed bank robbery in the eastern German city of Eisenach, under circumstances that have never been fully clarified. In a macabre confession video that Zschäpe sent to the media, they boasted that they had shot and killed nine men on racist grounds.

Second NSU trial ends with suspended sentence

One of the many unanswered questions is why Michèle Kiesewetter was also killed. No definitive answers were provided either in the first NSU trial before a Munich court, which lasted from 2013 to 2018, or in numerous parliamentary investigative committees.

A woman who helped Beate Tschäpe received a suspended sentence Image: Sebastian Kahnert/dpa/picture alliance

Fifteen years after the neo-Nazi terrorist group was exposed, the families of the murder victims are increasingly losing hope that any new information will come to light. One such opportunity was the trial of Susann Eminger — who was sentenced in July 2026 by a court in Dresden, in the state of Saxony, to two years' probation for supporting the terrorist group.

Eminger helped her friend Beate Zschäpe assume a different identity during doctor's visits and when dealing with the police by letting Zschäpe use her health insurance card and ID card. However, the court was unable to prove that she was aware of the series of murders committed by the NSU.

Nonetheless, relatives of the murder victims and the survivors of a bombing carried out by the NSU in Cologne, in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia, think the verdict beggars belief: "Ten people were executed in cold blood, and countless others were injured in bombings," said Michalina Boulgarides, whose father, Theodoros, was shot dead in Munich on June 15, 2005.

The NSU murdered 9 men of immigrant background and one woman Image: Norbert Försterling/Polizei-Handout/dpa/picture alliance

"When will the victims get justice?" asked Boulgarides, in response to the suspended sentence handed down to Susann Eminger in the second — and likely final — NSU trial. Her husband, André, had received a two-and-a-half-year prison sentence in 2018 in the first criminal trial against the terrorist group, but he was required to serve only two-thirds of it. That, too, has outraged the victims' families.

The sentence for neo-Nazi Ralf Wohlleben, who had been sentenced to ten years in prison for aiding and abetting murder in the first NSU trial, also ended in May 2026. This means that Beate Zschäpe remains the only person convicted in connection to the NSU who is still incarcerated; she is likely to remain behind bars until 2035. All other investigations by the Federal Prosecutor's Office against suspected NSU supporters have been dropped.

A national NSU documentation center to be established in Nuremberg

While legal proceedings appear to be largely concluded, the broader societal debate surrounding the unprecedented series of murders and attacks carried out by right-wing terrorists continues. Two key projects, however, are making slow progress: the national memorial center planned for Nuremberg (Bavaria) and the memorial on Keupstraße in Cologne.

Nuremberg is an obvious choice for a national documentation center for the victims of racism and right-wing extremism. It was here where the NSU murdered its first victim, Enver Şimşek, a florist, followed by two others. Another man was badly injured here in what is believed to be the first NSU bombing.

Florist Enver Şimşek was the NSU's first murder victim Image: Bernd Thissen/dpa/picture alliance

What's more, Nuremberg also played a major role during the Nazi era, where Adolf Hitler held propaganda-laden Nazi Party rallies featuring mass marches and speeches.

The German Bundestag has been considering the idea of an NSU Documentation Center since 2024. However, plans for a swift implementation fell by the wayside because the governing coalition at the time, led by Chancellor Olaf Scholz (SPD), collapsed prematurely. The project is now set to be completed by 2030.

A response from the federal government to a parliamentary inquiry from the environmentalist Green Party provides initial details: Just under €9 million ($10 million) has been earmarked to create the central memorial site under the leadership of the Federal Agency for Civic Education (BpB).

How far has Germany come in 15 years?

Things are further along in the city of Chemnitz, in the eastern German state of Saxony. A documentation center on the NSU complex has been in operation in the city since 2025, the year in which it was European Capital of Culture. The title of the exhibition, "Open Trial," speaks to its broad, ambitious approach as a space for education, research and events.

Gamze Kubaşık gave a speech at the opening. Her father, Mehmet, was shot and killed by the NSU in Dortmund on April 4, 2006. In fact, Chemnitz was where the terrorists Zschäpe, Mundlos and Böhnhardt had been in hiding for years. "This is also where they planned my father's murder," said Gamze Kubaşık, highlighting the significance of the location. "The support they received from the local neo-Nazi scene enabled them to carry out their schemes and reinforced their ideology."

The executive directors of the Chemnitz-based organization, Nora Krzywinski and Esther Gerstenberg, believe a national memorial and documentation center dedicated to the NSU complex is necessary. "However, it cannot replace the work being done at the actual sites of terror and to address the social conditions that gave rise to it," they emphasized in their response to a written inquiry from DW.

The NSU documentation center in Chemnitz opened in 2025 Image: NSU-Dokumentationszentrum/Mark Frost

The guiding concept for the exhibition, explained Krzywinski and Gerstenberg, is to highlight the perspectives of those affected and to link remembrance with an examination of the persistence of racism and the responsibility of the state and society. "That is why we do not view our work as a substitute for a national memorial site but rather as part of an integrated system that connects sustained local, regional and national efforts to remember and come to terms with the past in a lasting way."

While efforts to address the multifaceted NSU complex in Chemnitz have already taken concrete form, the residents of Keupstrasse in Cologne are still waiting for the promised memorial to the 22 people injured in the June 9, 2004, bomb attack. According to media reports, however, construction cannot begin until 2030 at the earliest, because old buildings around the planned site must first be demolished and new ones erected.

This means that it will take more than a quarter-century until a memorial honoring the victims of the NSU bombing on Keupstrasse can be erected where it took place. Meanwhile, 15 years after the NSU exposed itself, the German Bundestag has agreed to hold a debate. It is titled: "Commemorating the victims, living up to our responsibilities and taking today's threats seriously."

The text was originally written in German.

World.title: Kosovo: Protests and outrage after a woman was killed despite repeatedly seeking assistance from the authorities
World.content:
Despite reporting her husband to the police and pleading for protection, Arlinda Zekaj was brutally murdered. Now, thousands in Kosovo are protesting what they say is a dramatic failure of state institutions.

Arlinda Zekaj repeatedly asked the Kosovo police for protection. They believed she was exaggerating.

On October 25, the 49-year-old once again reported her husband to the police. This time, he was arrested. But Zekaj also asked the police for additional protection — this time against her husband's family. But to no avail.

The police drove Arlinda Zekaj home, where her killer was waiting. At 8:58 p.m., Zekaj got out of the squad car. A short time later, the police received an emergency call. When officers arrived at Zekaj's house at 9:10 p.m., they found only her body.

The 49-year-old had been brutally murdered in her bedroom with an axe. By that time, the alleged perpetrator — her brother-in-law, Albert Sylaj — had fled.

Protests across Kosovo

The murder, which took place in the village of Vitomirica near the city of Peja in western Kosovo, has sparked numerous public protests and demonstrations involving thousands of people across the country.

This was the eighth femicide in Kosovo this year — and apparently the most brutal.

More so than almost any other femicide in the country in recent years, Zekaj's death showed that one of the things that made her killing possible was the fact that police and prosecutors ignored the victim's pleas for help .

Ministers refuse to resign

One of the first protests took place the following day, on October 26, when a group of feminists emptied buckets of red paint on steps outside the seat of Kosovo's government in the capital, Pristina.

"The state killed Arlinda," read a banner the activists hung at the entrance to the building.

In the days that followed and on November 1, public anger brought thousands of people onto streets across the country. Many carried photographs of murdered women. One slogan appeared again and again: "The government has blood on its hands."

The protesters are demanding that charges be brought against the police officers and prosecutors responsible for handling the Zekaj case.

They are also calling for the resignation of Interior Minister Xhelal Svecla and Justice Minister Donika Gervalla, whom Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti appointed national coordinator for protection against domestic violence in March.

Both Svecla and Gervalla have so far rejected calls to step down.

'They won't be able to sleep; the flames will consume them' reads a large banner at a demonstration in Pristina, the capital of Kosovo, on October 28 Image: Vjosa Cerkini/DW

For his part, however, Kurti acknowledged that certain Kosovo state institutions had "failed."

A murder foretold

In many ways, this was a murder foretold.

As far back as the summer, Arlinda Zekaj had reported her husband to the police for making threats against her. A court in Peja subsequently issued a protection order, granted her temporary custody of their son and gave her the right to remain in the family home.

The protection order allowed her husband to continue living in the same house, provided he did not come within two meters (about 6.5 feet) of her. Outside the home, he was required to keep a distance of at least 20 meters.

Zekaj had decided against moving to a women's shelter because she wanted to continue living in her own home with her son.

Even after the protection order was issued, she repeatedly made complaints to the police, among other things about threats from her brother-in-law Albert Sylaj.

Three days before the killing, on October 22, Zekaj reported that members of her husband's family, including Sylaj, were in her home against her wishes. According to her account, he threatened her with the words: "Leave or I'll kill you."

Nevertheless, Sylaj was questioned only as a witness in the case against Zekaj's husband.

Police arrested him near Peja on October 27. He is now under investigation for murder.

'A collapse of the state and society in relation to women'

Since 2010, 55 women in Kosovo have been killed by partners or family members, often after years of documented abuse and ignored complaints.

In recent years, successive Kosovo governments have adopted a number of laws and regulations aimed at better combating violence against women.

These measures include the possibility of life sentences for perpetrators in femicide cases.

Activists argue, however, that the authorities responsible for enforcing these measures — including police, social services, prosecutors and courts — have failed to implement them consistently and in a coordinated manner.

Relations of Arlinda Zekaj, who was murdered in her home at the end of October, took part in a protest on October 28. One of the placards reads 'Mom, I love you very much' and shows a photo of the victim and her son Image: Vjosa Cerkini/DW

Writing in an article for the news portal Nacionale, lawyer Njomeza Zejnullahu said that "After every murder, we hear the same word: failure. 'The institutions have failed.' I disagree. Failure is when something happens once, when a system that normally works breaks down at one point. When the cases keep repeating themselves, when the victims are almost always women and each of them had previously knocked on the door of an institution, it is no longer a failure. It is a collapse of the state and society in relation to women in general."

What needs to change?

In the aftermath of Arlinda Zekaj's killing, several senior police officers from Peja and the surrounding area have been suspended. A prosecutor who had handled Zekaj's complaints has also been suspended.

For the protesters in Kosovo, however, this is not nearly enough.

"All those involved within the chain of responsibility must not only be removed from office but also criminally prosecuted for failing to fulfil their official duties," said Liridona Sijarina, a political scientist and feminist activist with Kosovo's Kolektivi Feminist (Feminist Collective).

"That includes not only police officers, prosecutors and judges, but also Mayor of Peja Gazmend Muhaxheri and, ultimately, government ministers," she told DW.

Sijarina went on to say that feminist activists are also calling on the Interior Ministry to create a dedicated unit that would treat women's safety as a matter of national security and focus specifically on preventing femicides.

She also said that the government should make its draft legislation on affordable social housing a top political priority and ensure that women who have experienced domestic violence are eligible for social housing.

"In our view," said Sijarina, "the behavior of the institutions so far has deepened women's distrust of the state and, as a result, allowed violence against them to escalate. The government now has the opportunity to show whether it truly takes women's lives seriously by clearly responding to our demands."

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Gold for Palestine: Meet junior karate champ Mariam Bsharat
World.content:
The occupied West Bank is not an obvious breeding ground for sporting success. But Mariam Bsharat, 17, has beaten the odds to become a karate world champion and is making a new life in Germany.

"After the referee lifted my hand to show I'm now a two-time world champion, it was a very overwhelming feeling," Mariam Bsharat said. "Making history once is something, but making it twice is really something else. I felt very happy and I felt a big relief. Only I know how many sacrifices I made and how many hardships I needed to overcome."
