The 70-year-old said she no longer “felt comfortable” with the requirement for European central bankers to be neutral in an increasingly polarised world, but has not given detailed reasons for her departure.

Reuters reported three weeks ago that the World Economic Forum, the Davos-based think tank, was lining her up as its next chair.

World.title: Anger after Maastricht university stops Jewish students’ meeting
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The University of Maastricht has been accused of “encouraging intimidation” after it cancelled a meeting by a Jewish students’ organisation at an hour’s notice because of protests outside the event.

Organisers said 12 students were due to attend a lecture by social sciences professor Eli Sapir titled Three Years after October 7, referring to the terrorist attacks by Hamas in Israel that triggered the destruction of Gaza.

The event was relocated at short notice after pro-Palestinian groups posted social media messages calling on people to demonstrate at the venue.

Protest group Maastricht Students for Palestine denounced the meeting as “Zionist propaganda” in an Instagram post, adding: “Bring your friends, something to cover your face, and some pots and spoons or drums to make some noise.”

University authorities decided to call off the event an hour before it was due to start after demonstrators appeared outside the new venue, even though the organisers said they were not acting aggressively.

In a statement, the university blamed pro-Israeli and pro-Palestinian groups for stoking tensions by appealing to their supporters to travel to Maastricht.

It said: “Because of online appeals by both supporters and opponents of the meeting with the aim of mobilising large numbers of people, the University could not guarantee its safety.”

But the organisers, the Jewish students’ union IJAR and campaign group StandWithUs Nederland, reacted furiously, accusing the university of “a systematic suppression of Jewish student life on campus”.

StandWithUs director Claudia van Zanten said: “I am absolutely furious that a small gathering of Jewish students was cancelled just before it was due to begin, without any legal justification whatsoever.

“By cancelling this lecture, the university is rewarding and encouraging intimidation.”

The group said it was considering taking further action against the university.

World.title: “Joy and relief”: Americans in the Netherlands react to midterms
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

US Democrats in the Netherlands are rejoicing at the results of the US midterm elections, which saw the party take back control of both the Senate and House of Representatives in a landslide victory.

The victory was widely expected by pollsters and attributed largely to the Trump administration’s war on Iran, which has driven up inflation and the cost of living. Hundreds of formerly Republican state and local seats were lost, some for the first time in decades.

Chad Lykins, a spokesperson for Democrats Abroad Netherlands, a campaign group helping people vote from overseas (despite the mounting obstacles), told Dutch News he was “thrilled” by the result.

“Republicans tried to limit our right to vote and I think that actually motivated people both domestically and abroad to turn in their ballot and vote Democrat,” he said.

“Voters rejected Republicans’ incompetence, corruption, and violence and chose a positive vision focused on affordability, good governance, and a sane foreign policy.”

Greg Shapiro, a US-Dutch comedian who hosted an election night event in Amsterdam on Tuesday, said he felt “joy and relief” and also expressed surprise at Trump’s initial acceptance of the results.

“I was predicting that the current Republican Congress would refuse to certify the election results, and I hope I’m wrong about that too,” he said.

“We all have a long enough memory to realise that Americans are stupid enough to elect Donald Trump twice. But for now, it’s nice that so many qualified candidates seem to have won.”

Impact on US expats

Shapiro also said the results “matter to every US expat in the Netherlands” as the Dutch public is so well informed on US political affairs that it shapes how they see their American neighbours.

“Dutch people know more about the details of American democracy than over half of America. The fact that American voters occasionally act responsibly is palpably reassuring for every Dutch person I talk to.”

“Are Dutch people going to allow me to ‘doe normaal’? Or are they going to lecture me about everything wrong with my birth country’s domestic and foreign policy?”

Another US citizen, Amsterdam-based reporter Sabine Waldeck, told Dutch News that since leaving her home country she cares more about US politics than ever, that “distance makes the heart grow fonder” and that the inability to do much beyond voting when living abroad while her friends and family remain there is hard.

“Right now, the US is run by a tyrannical fascistic government,” she said, and the outcome “gives me hope”.

Sharon Comiteau, an 86-year-old US Amsterdam resident, told us the result “is the only way we can survive”.

“I’m jumping for joy,” she said. “I’m proud of America for the first time in a long time.”

Opportunity for Dutch politics?

Shapiro said the Dutch government is “absolutely going to benefit from this election result.”

“There will now be checks and balances against the Project 2025 White House. There will now be so-called guard rails, which existed during Trump’s first term. This makes Trump a lot less dangerous on the world stage,” he said.

“Dutch politicians can perhaps afford to stop licking Trump‘s boots and make public alliances with the new Democratic power centre in Congress.”

With Washington being extremely divided, some analysts see an opportunity to begin dealing with individual US states.

Ian Kenny, director of the John Adams Institute in Amsterdam, told news programme EenVandaag: “There is an entire country behind the White House.

“There are 50 different states with their own culture. If you do business with individual states, you create more opportunities for yourself.”

World.title: Court upholds ban on heritage group’s bid for former Nazi bunker
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Dutch state was entitled to block a heritage organisation’s attempt to buy a former wartime bunker outside The Hague because it breached the strict bidding conditions, a court has ruled.

The non-profit organisation, Stichting BOEi, was one of two bidders for the building in Wassenaar that was built as a hideout by the Nazi governor Arthur Seyss-Inquart during the war.

The Dutch government’s real estate agency Rijksvastgoedbedrijf put the building up for sale last year after the defence ministry said it was no longer needed.

Strict conditions were attached to the sale to protect “the cultural-historical value of the complex” and prevent it being exploited by commercial owners. The rules restrict the use of the site to a museum or centre for culture or education.

The decision leaves Jeroen de Wilde, a local property developer who reportedly plans to turn the building into a music studio, as the only bidder.

The state excluded Stichting BOEi from the bidding after it sent WhatsApp messages to De Wilde asking about a possible collaboration.

Ban “reasonable”

Stichting BOEi sought an injunction from a judge in The Hague to lift the ban, but the court said the exclusion by Rijksvastgoedbedrijf was “reasonable”.

The court said the approach breached the rules in the bid book that prohibited contact between potential buyers after they had submitted their bids.

BOEi, which submitted a higher bid than De Wilde’s, was also accused of breaking antitrust rules by discussing the price with the rival bidder. The organisation’s lawyers have insisted it made no direct contact with De Wilde.

BOEi also allegedly breached confidentiality rules by presenting details of the plans at a community meeting last year.

Disguised as farmhouse

The bunker on the Clingendael estate, which was disguised as a Dutch farmhouse, was commissioned by Seyss-Inquart, the Nazi-appointed Reich Commissioner of the Netherlands, in 1942 but never actually used.

The interior was lined with thick concrete walls and had two “chimneys” to conceal anti-aircraft guns, as well as a bedroom, a kitchen and an office.

After the war it became known as Commandopost Clingendael and was used as a communications and crisis centre by the Dutch government.

Seyss-Inquart was executed in 1946 following his conviction for war crimes at the Nuremberg trials.

World.title: Nitrogen law falls short for farmers but may help housebuilding
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The cabinet has announced its new nitrogen law and received criticism from farmers, relief from builders, and skepticism from environmentalists.

Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen presented the law on Tuesday, which is an update of the plan already announced in June. Its core points are that farmers must cut nitrogen emissions by 42% to 46% by 2035 (compared to 2019 levels), and the industry and transport sector must cut its own by 50%.

Nitrogen from manure on farms and exhaust fumes is destroying the environment, which has led to courts blocking building permits amid the housing crisis.

Provinces have until September 2028 to draw strict zones around vulnerable nature areas, where farms will eventually be able to keep no more than 1.5 cows per hectare. The cabinet has set aside €9 billion to support affected farmers.

Ger Koopmans, chairman of the largest farmers’ organisation LTO, said the package was “less bad on important points” but that “fundamental objections” remained, broadcaster NOS reported.

LTO says farmers still don’t know how much they need to cut. Van Essen rejected an alternative plan from farmers’ groups last month.

At present, almost any building project that emits any amount of nitrogen needs a nature permit. Construction industry body Bouwend Nederland said the law creates “room to build homes and roads again”. Greenpeace accused the cabinet of ignoring the 2025 court ruling it won against the state.

The minority cabinet needs opposition votes to pass the law. The centre-left alliance Pro has backed the plans so far.

World.title: VodafoneZiggo wants staff to spend three days a week in office
World.content:
Telecoms provider VodafoneZiggo has told its staff to spend at least three days a week in the office or leave the company.

The firm plans to step up its minimum attendance requirement from two days a week as it moves towards “the next phase of hybrid working”.

Employees who are unable or unwilling to meet the new contract terms will be able to leave through a temporary severance deal if the company’s works council approves the plan, a spokesman said.

“This regulation will be available through the month of January and is voluntary,” the company said.

VodafoneZiggo is the latest Dutch company to compel its staff to spend more time in the office as firms move away from the working patterns that were established during the pandemic.

Last week a court ruled that Amsterdam-based travel website Booking could require employees to be in the office for 40% of their working hours, or two days a week for full-time staff.

Booking’s works council had objected to the plan because of the impact on staff’s work-life balances and the cost of commuting, but the judge said that asking employees to travel to work twice a week was “very normal”.

ABN Amro bank also said during collective bargaining talks this year that it wants its staff to spend at least half their contracted hours in the office, replacing a flexible arrangement introduced in 2020.

Polish political leaders have reacted to the results of Tuesday’s US midterm elections, in which the Democrats won control of both houses of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republicans. The outcome received a positive reaction from Poland’s ruling coalition, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk declaring that “democracy won”. The response was more muted from the right-wing opposition and the office of conservative President Karol Nawrocki, who is a Trump ally. 🚨 🇺🇸 Tusk gives Trump some great advice. But will the US president listen? Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk urged the US president to seek compromises after the Republicans' defeat and not to rely on vetoes as his main way of governing. Trump had earlier threatened to become… pic.twitter.com/s3E6G5zIQT — NEXTA (@nexta_tv) November 4, 2026 Tusk addressed the election results on Wednesday afternoon local time at a press conference alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš. “Today, democracy won in America,” said a smiling Tusk. “I love democracy; it is a beautiful thing.” “As President Donald Trump himself said just after the election, the Democrats did a good job, and I really could not agree more with him this time,” added Tusk. “I hope that the result will stabilise the situation also in our region.” Although the United States remains Poland’s most important security partner, Tusk’s government – a broad, pro-EU coalition that ranges from left to centre right – has at times had uneasy relations with the Trump administration. It has been critical of Trump’s conciliatory approach towards Russia, his often tough stance on Ukraine, as well as his pursuit of US control over Greenland. Meanwhile, the head of the parliamentary caucus of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, Zbigniew Konwiński, told broadcaster Polsat News that “personally, I was happy with the Democrats’ victory”. “We know how Donald Trump behaves, how volatile he is in his political declarations, how he can sometimes put Ukraine in a more difficult position than Russia, so I would rather look for the positives in what happened,” said Konwiński. “If we look at recent years, the more Democrats, the stronger the Democrats, the better for Poland,” he added. .@Konwinski_PO: Cieszę się z wygranej Demokratów w USA, bo to lepszy scenariusz dla Polski. @marcinfijolek pic.twitter.com/gJ3TnlMn0l — Graffiti_PN (@Graffiti_PN) November 4, 2026 The speaker of Poland’s parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is also the leader of one of KO’s junior coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), has clashed with the US ambassador to Poland twice this year over Czarzasty’s criticism of Trump. Today, Czarzasty shared and commented on a social media post by Trump, published in the wake of the Democrats’ victory, in which the US president showed an image of his signature red cap with the word “VETO” on it. “Where have I heard this before?” wrote Czarzasty, referring to the fact that Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills passed by parliament, where Tusk’s coalition has a majority. Czarzasty then went on to list a series of characteristics that he suggested both Trump and Nawrocki share, including “arrogance”, “lack of respect for women”, a “suspicious past”, “transactional exploitation of their position”, and “admiration for politicians with fascist tendencies”. Skąd ja to znam? Arogancja. Buta. Nieuzasadniona pewność siebie. Brak szacunku dla kobiet ( a to popchnę jakąś dwojga nazwisk, a to zakpię prymitywnie). Dziwna przeszłość. Instrumentalne traktowanie dziennikarzy. Pieniądze za spotkania. Transakcyjne wykorzystywanie funkcji.… pic.twitter.com/ryT2BMOZb2 — Włodzimierz Czarzasty 📚📖 (@wlodekczarzasty) November 4, 2026 Nawrocki has closely aligned himself with Trump. During last year’s Polish presidential election campaign, Trump invited Nawrocki for a private meeting at the White House. His then-homeland security secretary, Kristi Noem, visited Poland to endorse Nawrocki. Nawrocki himself has not thus far commented on Tuesday’s midterm election results. However, Marcin Przydacz, the head of the president’s International Policy Bureau, did address the issue in a social media post. “As predicted, in the US midterm elections voters decided on change,” wrote Przydacz. “Poland will continue its good cooperation with the US, because it is our ally, and collaboration is in our mutual interest.” Przydacz also added that the results were “a reminder for Tusk” that “no government lasts forever”. In Poland, too, “the moment will come when voters will decide on change – and it might be quite soon”, added Przydacz, in a nod to next year’s Polish parliamentary elections. Zgodnie z przewidywaniami w wyborach połówkowych w USA wyborcy zdecydowali o zmianie. Wcześniej wygrywali Republikanie, dziś Demokraci. Polska będzie kontynuować dobrą współpracę z USA, bo jest to nasz sojusznik, a kooperacja jest w naszym wspólnym interesie. O tym, kto sprawuje… — Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 4, 2026 Tusk’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, meanwhile, used the US election results to revive his long-running feud with Elon Musk, who is no longer part of the Trump administration but donated enormous amounts of money to support the Republicans agead of the midterms. Last year, Musk and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio criticised Sikorski after he suggested that Musk had threatened Ukraine. In a post on his social media platform, X, Musk told Sikorski to “be quiet, small man”. On Wednesday, Tusk shared a screenshot of a tweet he had published last year, after Musk left the Trump administration, in which Sikorski wrote: “See, big man, politics is harder than you thought.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: International Commission of Jurists criticises takeover of Polish constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) has criticised the takeover of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) by a group of government-backed judges. It says that the move “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”. However, the ICJ, a Swiss-based NGO led by judges, lawyers and academics from around the world, also chastised Poland’s opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, for his role in the crisis around the TK, in particular his refusal to swear in judges elected by parliament. 🚨#Poland’s constitutional crisis must be resolved through the rule of law. The ICJ urges all authorities to respect judicial independence, follow lawful procedures, and comply with European court rulings. 🔗More information: https://t.co/NWmca9mpUx — ICJ (@ICJ_org) November 3, 2026 On Friday, eight judges who were elected to the TK this year by the government’s parliamentary majority effectively took over the tribunal. They announced that the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to properly fulfil their duties. Meanwhile, large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the grounds. Święczkowski denounced the takeover of the court as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the rule of the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence. Nawrocki, who is also aligned with PiS, has likewise denounced the actions of the government-backed judges. In the early hours of Saturday, he dramatically forced his way into the court, where he clashed physically and verbally with the judges who had taken over the TK. During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court. The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026 In a statement on Tuesday, the ICJ expressed regret that the latest developments have “deepened the crisis over the tribunal”. It called on Polish “state institutions to seek solutions…that comply fully with the rule of law, including the principle of the independence of the judiciary”. The ICJ’s secretary-general, Santiago Canton, noted that Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of the eight TK judges elected by parliament this year. That “violates international standards and is contrary to the interim measures indicated by the European Court of Human Rights”, said Canton. In May, the ECHR issued an interim order for all judges elected by parliament to be allowed to serve on the court. However, that has been ignored by Nawrocki and Święczkowski, who argued that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. The ICJ also noted that the roots of the crisis at the TK date back a decade, to the time when the PiS government took actions – including unlawfully appointing judges to the tribunal – that rendered the court illegitimate. “At the same time,” continued Canton, “the suspension of the president and vice-president of the tribunal without a fair and appropriate procedure established by law, carried out with the involvement of the police, contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary.” In its statement, the ICJ added that “criminal and disciplinary proceedings must respect all the guarantees of a fair trial and must never be used as a means to change [a court’s] composition”. Later on Tuesday, after the ICJ had issued its statement, the eight government-backed judges held their first general assembly, at which they moved forward with disciplinary proceedings against Święczkowski and Sochański. The justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, has also submitted six requests to the TK to lift Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution so that he can face charges for a range of alleged crimes relating to both his time as chief justice and his previous role as a senior prosecutor under the PiS government. Skierowałem do Trybunału Konstytucyjnego kolejny, szósty już wniosek o uchylenie immunitetu Bogdanowi Święczkowskiemu, dołączając go do pięciu wniosków przekazanych w piątek. Dzisiejsza sprawa dotyczy zakupu systemu szpiegowskiego Hermes w czasie, gdy pełnił funkcję Prokuratora… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 3, 2026 The takeover of the TK has also stirred controversy among Polish legal experts. The issue has even caused an unprecedented split at the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a well-respected NGO. On Saturday, the HFPC’s management board issued a statement, signed by its president, Maciej Nowicki, saying that it “sees no clear legal basis” for the actions taken on Friday by the government-backed judges to suspend Święczkowski and take control of the tribunal. It warned that the situation “set a dangerous precedent” and “does not contribute to fixing the tribunal”. However, HFPC also made clear that the crisis at the court dates back a decade and reiterated its view that Nawrocki “has no right to block or invalidate the election [of judges] by parliament”. That statement prompted six of the eight members of HFPC’s council – a separate body from the management board – to resign. Those to depart included a former chief justice of the TK, Andrzej Rzepliński, and a former deputy human rights commissioner, Hanna Machińska. Machińska announced their resignation in a social media post. She said that the reason for her decision had been the management board’s statement, “with which I disagree”. Speaking later to broadcaster TVN, Machińska said that “we believe that the legal basis [for the TK takeover] was clearly defined”. Poland’s government, including Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has also argued that the takeover of the tribunal was necessary to ensure that legally appointed judges can take up their seats and that the court’s legitimacy can be restored. However, on Tuesday evening, Tusk shifted to a more conciliatory tone, offering to hold a one-on-one meeting with Nawrocki to discuss the crisis around the Constitutional Tribunal and “try to find solutions that will protect Poland from any political upheaval” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Disputed Polish constitutional court holds first meeting after takeover by government-backed judges
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The group of eight government-backed judges who last week took control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) have held a meeting at which they made a number of key decisions, including moving forward with disciplinary proceedings against the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski. However, the situation is mired in controversy and uncertainty. Święczkowski and the opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, do not recognise the judges who are now claiming control of the court, describing their actions as a “coup d’état”. Meanwhile, there are doubts as to whether today’s general assembly even had a valid quorum, given that the chief justice and six other judges appointed under the former government did not attend. PILNE: Zgromadzenie Ogólne Sędziów TK przyjęło, że kworum to osiem osóbhttps://t.co/SYEf9Ead3L — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 3, 2026 The meeting was called by Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who on Friday declared that Święczkowski and the deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to fulfil their duties. Korwin-Piotrowska said that she herself, as the longest-serving judge on the court, was taking control. Large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the court. However, Nawrocki himself did enter the premises, where he clashed physically and verbally with Korwin-Piotrowska. For a general assembly of the TK to be valid, two thirds of the court’s judges need to be present. Normally, given that the tribunal has 15 positions, that would mean at least 10 judges being present. However, only eight judges attended today’s meeting. They were all appointed to the TK by the government’s parliamentary majority this year. But Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of them, meaning that their legal status has become disputed. The TK’s seven other judges, including Święczkowski and Sochański, were all appointed to the court under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under its political control, including by unlawfully appointing three judges. None of them attended Tuesday’s general assembly. Nevertheless, the eight judges present at the meeting, which was broadcast live for the first time in the TK’s history, decided that a quorum had been reached. They did so on the basis that three of the TK’s judges were not authorised to attend: Święczkowski and Sochański, because they are suspended, and Jarosław Wyrembak, because he inherited his position from one of PiS’s unlawfully appointed judges. That meant only 12 judges were authorised to attend, and two thirds of that number is eight, meaning that a quorum had been reached. Zgromadzenie Ogólne TK: JEST KWORUM! 👏 Według przedstawionej interpretacji liczy się je od 12 uprawnionych osób. 2/3 × 12 = 8. Prawo i matematyka.👏 pic.twitter.com/77v2ep9HbT — Pani Prezes 👠 (@PaniNaSzpilkach) November 3, 2026 Once that issue was agreed, the eight judges present proceeded to decide upon a number of key issues. First, they adopted a draft budget for the TK for 2027, something that Święczkowski had been unable to achieve, which was used as an argument for his ousting. Second, they drew lots to decide which of the TK’s judges would sit on disciplinary panels for Święczkowski and Sochański in relation to their suspension from the court. However, some legal experts have expressed doubt as to whether a legal quorum was established at today’s meeting. Ryszard Piotrowski, a prominent constitutional scholar, called the meeting “illegal”, reports news website Onet. Przemysław Rosati, the president of the Supreme Bar Council, also expressed his doubts. Obniżenie progu kworum na skutek zawieszenia prezesa i wiceprezesa otwiera puszkę Pandory. To jest mechanizm, który pozwala dowolnie obniżać kworum na Zgromadzeniu Ogólnym TK – wystarczy, że prezes zawiesi 10 sędziów i będzie mógł na Zgromadzeniu podejmować decyzję w trzy osoby.… — Marcin Matczak (@wsamraz) November 3, 2026 Święczkowski himself rejected the legitimacy of what he called a “social gathering”, saying that Korwin-Piotrowska is a “usurper” who has no right to call a general assembly at all, reported Polsat News. Shortly before the meeting at the TK, Nawrocki also met with the prime minister, Donald Tusk, for the first time since the crisis at the court broke out last Friday. They had convened at the presidential palace for a meeting of the National Security Council that Nawrocki had called before the TK crisis. During public remarks broadcast before the confidential meeting got underway, Nawrocki accused the government of “illegally taking over the Constitutional Tribunal”. He added that Tusk “bears full responsibility for…all these illegal actions”. Grubo! Karol Nawrocki do Tuska: „Pełną odpowiedzialność za wszystkie nielegalne działa w Trybunale Konstytucyjnym ponosi jeden człowiek, który jest obecny – premier Donald Tusk” pic.twitter.com/WMPnWTZIKt — chrzanik (@chrzanikx) November 3, 2026 Tusk and his government have argued that the source of the crisis is, in fact, Nawrocki’s refusal to swear in judges appointed by parliament, as he is required to do, and then Święczkowski’s resultant refusal to accept those judges onto the court. They also note that the TK has not been legitimate for a decade, since PiS unlawfully appointed judges and brought the court under its political influence. Speaking to broadcaster TVN on Tuesday before the general assembly, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said that the actions being undertaken by Korwin-Piotrowska are the only way “to rebuild the independence of the tribunal”. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland had the second-highest household electricity prices in the European Union in the first half of 2026 after adjusting for differences in the cost of living, new Eurostat data show. Prices in Poland were also among the fastest-rising in the bloc. Poland’s relatively high electricity costs reflect the country’s continued reliance on coal, which results in EU charges for carbon emissions, and its taxes and levies, which make up the largest share of household electricity bills anywhere in the EU. In nominal terms, Polish households paid €29.99 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh) for electricity in the first half of 2026. This was the seventh-highest price among the EU’s 27 member states and above the bloc-wide average of €28.32. Ireland (€38.71 per 100 kWh) had the highest prices, followed by Germany (€36.18) and Belgium (€35.75). The lowest costs were recorded in Hungary (€11.39), Malta (€12.68) and Bulgaria (€13.41). However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in the cost of living, Poland ranked second in the EU, at 41.12 PPS per 100 kWh. Only Romania had higher prices, at 46.89 PPS. The lowest prices when measured in PPS were recorded in Malta (13.75), Hungary (14.7) and Luxembourg (15.47). Poland’s electricity prices, in PPS terms, rose by 10.7% compared with the second half of 2025, which was the second-biggest increase in the EU after Finland. They were also up 17.6% compared to the first half of 2025, the fourth-largest rise in the bloc. One reason why electricity prices in Poland remain high is the country’s continued reliance on coal, which last year generated just over half of power, by far the highest proportion in the EU. Almost all coal used in Polish power plants is mined domestically and is among the most expensive in the world to extract. Additionally, burning it also produces high carbon emissions, which power generators must pay for under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS). These costs contribute to the high taxes and levies included in household electricity bills, which accounted for 39% of the final price in Poland in the first half of 2026. This was the highest share in the EU, ahead of Germany (23.6%) and well above the bloc-wide average of 18.6%. “In Poland, only one-third of our electricity generation is carbon-free. We have to pay for the rest – often dearly,” noted Polish energy journalist Jakub Wiech, commenting on the data. Without taxes and levies, the nominal price of electricity in Poland would have been just under €16 per 100 kWh, below the EU average of €20.27. However, Bartłomiej Orzeł of the Project Tempo think tank notes that electricity prices in Poland would, in fact, be even higher were it not for the huge state subsidies paid to support the unprofitable coal mining sector, which amount to billions of zloty a year but also shield end consumers from the full cost of extracting coal. He told news website Interia that mines actually sell coal to power stations at a price below the cost of extraction. Poland will from next month be the last remaining EU country still mining hard coal, after the Czech Republic – the only other producer – announced the closure of its last mine https://t.co/0sfMDQb19N — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026 According to Wiech, the high tax burden also reflects the costs of transforming Poland’s energy sector while continuing to support coal-fired power stations and the state budget. He says Poland needs “on the one hand, to fund the accelerated but delayed transformation and modernisation of the electricity sector; on the other hand, to maintain the fleet of coal-fired power stations; and thirdly, to contribute to the state budget”, which is struggling with persistently high deficits. Wiech expects, however, that politicians will come under pressure to reduce electricity bills ahead of next year’s parliamentary election. He says they may be tempted to “interfere with electricity bills” and that “it is therefore quite likely that certain charges (e.g. the distribution charge) will be reduced in 2027”. Komisja Europejska wrzuciła dane o cenach prądu za I półrocze 2026 roku i – boy, oh, boy – niesamowita jest to lektura. Na początek mocne uderzenie: w ujęciu standardu siły nabywczej polskie gospodarstwa domowe mają drugie najwyższe ceny prądu w całej Unii Europejskiej.… pic.twitter.com/yKvt5251i7 — Jakub Wiech (@jakubwiech) November 1, 2026 Energy prices and the wider energy transition have already become increasingly politicised this year, with the right-wing opposition criticising EU climate policies. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, recently called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from ETS, claiming that it treats “Poles as a cash machine for the absurd leftist climate policy of the EU”. Opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has twice attempted to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policy, but in both cases his proposals were rejected by the more pro-EU government’s majority in parliament. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 However, when PiS was in power from 2015 to 2023, it recognised the need to move Poland away from coal and towards a mix of renewables and nuclear. Solar energy installations boomed under the PiS government, and the overall share of renewables in the energy mix rose from around 9% in 2015 to a record 29% in 2024. The current government has continued with PiS’s plans to shift towards nuclear and renwables. This year, Poland’s first offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea began generating electricity, with a number of other offshore projects set to follow. Poland’s national energy and climate plan, approved in June, envisages coal accounting for 0-5% of the energy mix by 2040. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). World.title: Polish journalist held at Ukraine border and handed three-year entry ban
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A prominent Polish journalist and commentator, Łukasz Warzecha, has been prevented from entering Ukraine and handed a three-year ban on crossing into the country. Warzecha, who is primarily associated with right-wing weekly Do Rzeczy, says he was told that the decision had been made for “security reasons”. Polish journalist Łukasz Warzecha was travelling to Kyiv on a study visit jointly organised by Poland’s @MieroszewskiPL Centre and the Ukrainian Institute @UA_Institute an institution affiliated with Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry. According to head of @MieroszewskiPL Dr Łukasz… https://t.co/Tawp2hEJ5u — Sławomir Dębski (@SlawomirDebski) November 2, 2026 Warzecha had been due to join a study visit to Ukraine for Polish journalists organised by the Mieroszewski Centre, a Polish state institution, and the Ukraine Institute, a Ukrainian public body affiliated with the foreign ministry. The head of the Mieroszewski Centre, Łukasz Adamski, revealed that the list of journalists attending the tour had been agreed between the two organisers and forwarded to the relevant Ukrainian state authorities, who previously raised no objection. However, on Monday afternoon, Warzecha announced on social media that he had been held at the Ukrainian border and told to wait in a room. The journalist remained there for over seven hours before being informed that he was banned from entering Ukraine for three years. Proszę państwa, oto miś. Miś jest bardzo grzeczny dziś. pic.twitter.com/aVEUnkGhM7 — Łukasz Warzecha (@lkwarzecha) November 3, 2026 Adamski revealed that his organisation had sought to intervene with the foreign ministries of both countries, but to no avail. Warzecha said on social media that he had been told the decision, which was issued by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), was made due to “security reasons”. Adamski commented that, while he “recognises Ukraine’s sovereign right to decide whom to grant entry…restricting journalists’ work on state security grounds…creates fertile ground for unfriendly commentary”. At the time of writing, there had been no comment from the SBU regarding its decision to issue an entry ban against Warzecha. In his journalistic work, Warzecha has at times been critical of Ukraine, for example over its honouring of historical nationalist figures, and has called for a reduction in social benefits given to Ukrainian refugees in Poland. However, those views are within the Polish mainstream. Warzecha has also voiced support for Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. In February 2023, on the first anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion, he expressed satisfaction that Ukraine defended itself so effectively. However, Do Rzeczy, with which Warzecha has been associated for around a decade, has taken a tougher position on Ukraine. In 2024, its front cover warned of the “Ukrainisation of Poland”, a phrase often used by the far right to warn against the growing presence and influence of Ukrainians. OKŁADKA "Do Rzeczy" nr 35: Ukrainizacja Polski. Raport "Do Rzeczy" o groźnym procesie pic.twitter.com/SUYy1GhIat — DoRzeczy (@DoRzeczy_pl) August 25, 2024 Speaking to Do Rzeczy after the ban against him was issued, Warzecha said he had “wanted to confront my own views with open-minded politicians and opinion leaders in Ukraine. Unfortunately I was not given the opportunity to do so”. Ukraine’s decision was criticised by Andrzej Śliwka, an MP from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party. He asked if Warzecha had been banned “because he dared to criticise Ukrainian corruption, the confrontational policy toward Poland, and the distortion of history”. “One can agree with editor Warzecha or not, but such a decision demands explanations and a firm response from Polish authorities,” wrote Śliwka. At the time of writing, Poland’s government had not commented on the case. Polski dziennikarz, red. Łukasz Warzecha, otrzymuje od ukraińskich służb trzyletni zakaz wjazdu na Ukrainę. Dlaczego? Czy dlatego, że odważył się krytykować ukraińską korupcję, konfrontacyjną politykę wobec Polski i zakłamywanie historii? Można zgadzać się z red. Warzechą albo… https://t.co/JvuhLL9O8F — Andrzej Śliwka 🇵🇱 (@SliwkaAndrzej) November 2, 2026 Adamski said that the visit to Ukraine had been arranged specifically with the aim of “representing diverse editorial perspectives”. The Mieroszewski Centre last month arranged a similar visit for Ukrainian journalists to Poland. The aim was “to enable Polish journalists to gain direct knowledge of the situation in Ukraine, engage in conversations with representatives of various communities, and achieve a better understanding of the challenges facing Ukrainian society”, wrote Adamski. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support. However, there have also been regular tensions between the two countries, in particular over their difficult shared histories. This year has seen the two sides clash over the unresolved issue of large-scale massacres during World War Two. World.title: Polish ambassador to UN becomes third envoy to resign amid crisis over constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s ambassador to the United Nations, Krzysztof Szczerski, has resigned, becoming the third Polish ambassador to do so since a government-backed move by a group of judges to take control of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw. All three of the departing ambassadors were previously aides or advisers to former President Andrzej Duda, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. They have criticised the attempt to oust the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed to the court under PiS. Following the resignations of Poland’s Ambassadors to China and Romania, Prof. Krzysztof Szczerski, Poland’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, has also submitted his resignation. All three are senior state officials and experienced diplomats who have served at the… — Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 2, 2026 On Monday afternoon, foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór announced that Szczerski had “submitted a request to shorten his diplomatic mission at the UN”, where he has served as ambassador since 2021. Szczerski’s resignation followed those of Jakub Kumoch, Poland’s ambassador to China, and Paweł Soloch, the Polish envoy to Romania, who quit their posts on Friday and Saturday, respectively. While Szczerski has not yet commented on the reasons for his departure, Kumoch and Soloch made clear that their decisions were motivated by Friday’s move to suspend Święczkowski from the TK. Soloch wrote that the “attempt to unlawfully take over the Constitutional Tribunal” left him with “no possibility of continuing to serve as ambassador”. Kumoch said his decision was a “matter of conscience”, as “there are certain things I cannot explain abroad without losing face, and I have no intention of speaking ill of Poland”. There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice. Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026 Szczerski previously served as a member of the European Parliament for PIS. In 2015, he joined the chancellery of PiS-aligned President Duda, later becoming the head of his cabinet and then head of his International Policy Bureau. Kumoch was a member of Duda’s National Development Council, an advisory body to the president, before serving as ambassador to Switzerland, Turkey, and then China. Soloch was the head of Duda’s National Security Bureau from 2015 to 2022. On Monday, after Szczerski’s resignation, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski suggested that the three ambassadors had quit at the urging of the current president, Karol Nawrocki, who is also aligned with PiS. Sikorski sardonically suggested that, in contrast to Polish ambassadors who quit in 1981 over the imposition of martial law despite “risking vengeance from the communist regime”, the newly resigned trio “will surely be handsomely rewarded for their heroic deeds”. The developments are part of a much broader fallout from the crisis around the TK, which began on Friday evening when large numbers of riot police appeared outside the court. It soon transpired that a group of eight judges appointed by parliament to the TK this year – but five of whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in – had entered the court and declared that Święczkowski had been suspended from his position for failing to fulfil his duties. Święczkowski, who before becoming a TK judge previously served as a member of the former PiS government, declared their actions unlawful and an attempted “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the six other justices appointed when PiS was in government. Święczkowski has also been supported by Nawrocki, who dramatically entered the court in the early hours of Saturday morning, clashing physically and verbally with the self-proclaimed acting head of the court, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska. During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court. The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026 The developments have created an unprecedented situation at the TK. However, the court has been in crisis since 2015, when Duda and the then-PiS government – which came to power that year – unlawfully rejected three judges appointed by the former parliament and replaced them with three of their own. The current government, a broad coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, does not recognise the TK due to those illegitimate judges and has ignored its rulings since replacing PiS in power in December 2023. This year, Tusk’s coalition began appointing judges to fill vacancies on the court. It has condemned Nawrocki and Święczkowski for refusing to accept those judges, saying that their actions are unlawful. Given those circumstances, Tusk and his government have argued that tough action is necessary to restore the legitimacy of the TK. On Saturday evening, Tusk gave an address to the nation declaring that there can be “no compromise” over the rule of law. "On some issues, there can be no compromise," declared Prime Minister @donaldtusk in an address to the nation on the crisis around the constitutional court. He condemned the actions of President Karol Nawrocki, accusing him of "intimidating judges" https://t.co/RPyt87mcFO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026 However, a number of legal experts – including many who were highly critical of PiS’s policies towards the TK and other courts – have expressed doubts over the manner in which Korwin-Piotrowska and her colleagues have sought to take control of the tribunal. Further developments are expected on Tuesday, when Korwin-Piotrowska has called a general assembly of the tribunal. However, it is uncertain that she will obtain the necessary quorum of 10 judges normally required for the assembly to be valid. While the eight judges appointed by the ruling coalition this year are all expected to attend, those appointed under the PiS government appear likely not to. World.title: Poland launches operation along Russian border in response to reports of planned sabotage
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish police have launched a special operation to secure the area along the border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad after receiving information that acts of sabotage may take place there in the coming days. The operation – which has involved sending additional officers, including counter-terrorism forces, to the northeastern Podlasie and Warmia-Masuria provinces – was first reported by broadcaster RMF and confirmed by the national police chief, Marek Boroń. “Police are putting security measures in place around the Kaliningrad region in anticipation of possible incidents that could lead to acts of sabotage,” he told RMF. “This is based on information we also have from external security services.” “We are responsible for ensuring the safety of the citizens living there, as well as for facilities and any situations that may pose a threat to society,” he added, noting that the police were coordinating their operation with the army, border guard and security services. RMF reports, based on unnamed sources, that Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW) and agencies from unnamed allied countries last week issued a warning that sabotage activities could take place on the Polish-Russian border, potentially including border violations by armed groups. In a separate statement, the national police headquarters told RMF that the ongoing operation is “directly related to the situation taking place in our country today, that is, acts of sabotage…and the actions of eastern services”. That was a reference to the activities of Russia and its ally Belarus, which have in recent years carried out a series of acts of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” against Poland and other countries in the region. A spokeswoman for the police headquarters, Katarzyna Nowak, told broadcaster TVN that they were unable to provide any further information on the nature of the operation as the details are confidential. W Komendzie Głównej Policji powstał sztab operacji specjalnej prowadzonej w Warmińsko-Mazurskiem i na Podlasiu przez policję przy współpracy wojska, straży granicznej i służb specjalnych – mówi dziennikarzowi RMF FM Krzysztofowi Zasadzie szef KGP Marek Boroń. Chodzi o działania… — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) November 2, 2026 On Thursday last week, the deputy police commander, Tomasz Michułka, issued an order for officers to be on “full readiness” between 2 and 8 November due to the “operational situation across the country”. Some had interpreted that order as related to the situation around the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw, where riot police were called in on Friday to secure the court amid protests against an attempt by a group of government-backed judges to take control of the TK. However, on Friday night, the police issued a statement “emphatically denying” that the order had anything to do with the situation at the TK. They said that it was, in fact, “related to the current threats regarding acts of sabotage and subversion”. The following day, Boroń himself wrote to police officers confirming that Thursday’s order had been issued in response to “attempts to destabilise our country by foreign intelligence services from the east”. List Komendanta Głównego Policji do funkcjonariuszy pic.twitter.com/3jTMdme1bz — Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) November 1, 2026 Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism identified Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe. Those operations have included an arson attack that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and an attempt to derail a train. In September this year, a Russian military helicopter crossed the border from Kaliningrad and remained in Polish airspace for around 42 seconds before returning. In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload entered Polish airspace from Ukraine before landing in a field in eastern Poland. The Polish government has regularly warned in recent months that Moscow is planning further provocations against eastern NATO member states, including potential border violations. World.title: First Asian hornet nest in Poland eliminated but experts warn more to appear next year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s first-ever nest of Asian hornets, an invasive species seen as a particular threat because it preys on honeybees, has been eliminated. But scientists who have studied the colony say that it is likely more will be found next year. Since arriving in France in 2004, Asian hornets, which are indigenous to Southeast Asia, have gradually spread to other European countries. The first confirmed nest to be found in Poland was sighted in a tree in the village of Wielka Wieś near Kraków in mid-October, with individual hornets also being spotted at the apiary of the city’s AGH University of Science and Technology. The nest was removed last week and sent to be studied by a team of scientists at Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Paweł Migdał, from the university’s faculty of biology and animal science, told PAP that the nest was “fairly large” considering the Polish climate, containing around 1,000 workers and several dozen queens and males. The scientists’ assessment of the nest revealed that it contained eggs and larvae, indicating that the hornets inhabiting it were still feeding, he added. “I think we’ll find more of these nests,” Migdał told PAP. “They’re often built in the treetops, which means they’re invisible until the leaves fall in the autumn.” Young queens had already left the nest to establish new ones after overwintering, and have greater chances of surviving the longer and warmer the Polish autumn is, he explained. They seek shelter in warm, dry places, such as underground or in storage areas. With queens measuring 30mm and males about 24mm, Asian hornets, also known as the yellow-legged hornet, are smaller than the European variety, and no more dangerous to humans than European hornets or wasps. The major concern over their arrival relates to their tendency to seek out beehives and prey on honeybees. “Besides killing honeybees, their presence also causes bees in apiaries to stop working,” explained Migdał. “With the European hornet, the bees recognise the threat but, in a sense, continue working. However, the yellow-legged hornet presents a completely new threat to them.” The number of bee colonies in Poland has risen 54% over the last decade to reach two million, thanks in part to a state programme supporting beekeepers. Bees' value to the ecosystem as pollinators is estimated to be worth 5bn zloty (€1.1bn) https://t.co/ElISOc2o2T — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 30, 2022 The scale of the species’ invasiveness is shown by the fact that it releases an average of 150 young queens from its nest, and sometimes even 500 – each of which can potentially create its own nest – while European hornets release just 50, Migdał pointed out. The location of the first nest found in Poland surprised scientists as the closest previously known was in Opava, around 150 km away in the Czech Republic. The hornets therefore probably travelled in a vehicle, although Migdał noted a potential concern that other populations might be found between the two sites.
