World.title: Frank Sinatra & Friends Live Show Brings Las Vegas Classics to Prague
World.content:
Fans of Frank Sinatra and the golden age of Las Vegas entertainment will have a chance to relive the era this Christmas.

The Frank Sinatra & Friends Live Show will arrive in Prague on December 29, bringing its tribute to the legendary Rat Pack to O2 Universum.



Originally created to mark the 100th anniversary of Frank Sinatra’s birth, the international production features Stephen Triffitt, George Daniel Long and Mark Adams, three performers known for their portrayals of Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin and Sammy Davis Jr.

All three previously starred in the acclaimed The Rat Pack Live from Las Vegas, performing for nearly a decade in London’s West End. Their careers have also taken them to stages alongside prestigious orchestras, including the BBC Concert Orchestra, the London Symphony Orchestra and the Amsterdam Metropole Orchestra.

The trio has since taken the show around the world, recreating the music, humour and spontaneous stage chemistry that made the original Rat Pack one of the most celebrated entertainment acts of its time.

The Prague performance will feature more than just the three leading artists. They will be joined by the Golddiggers, a trio of singers and dancers whose costumes and choreography add a classic Las Vegas revue atmosphere to the production. The show will also feature a special appearance by Nancy Sinatra.

The programme includes classics such as Fly Me to the Moon, My Way, New York, New York, Strangers in the Night and more.

Combining live music, comedy and theatrical performances, the production aims to recreate the atmosphere of the Las Vegas stages that defined an era of popular entertainment.

World.title: Beyond the Usual Order: 7 Prague Restaurants to Try on Bolt Food
World.content:
We all have one. The order you place without thinking. Same app, same five restaurants, same Thursday night. It is comfortable, it is reliable, and if we are honest, it is getting a little boring.

Prague’s food scene runs far deeper than the places that sit at the top of your feed. Tucked into Nusle side streets, Dejvice corners and the quieter end of Libeň are small kitchens with loyal regulars, big personalities and dishes worth crossing the river for.

The good news? You don’t have to cross the river. They deliver.

So as the evenings get darker and the sofa gets more convincing, we asked Bolt Food to point us towards the city’s hidden gems. Here are seven places worth adding to your rotation, from an Aussie pub in Vinohrady to a half-metre pizza you will want to share (or not).

1. The Down Under, Vinohrady

For when you miss home (or just miss a proper pie).

On Vinohradská street sits what bills itself as Prague’s only Australian restaurant. The menu reads like a trip home: a whole section of beef, chicken and vegetarian pies, a chicken parmy, a proper schnitty, fish and chips and, for the curious, a bag of “Skippy’s” kangaroo jerky. Wash it down with something from the Aussie bottled beer list.

Can’t make it in? The pub classics travel well. A pie with a side of gravy and the match on your own TV is a very respectable Sunday.

What to order: the Melbourne Pie, the most popular pie on the menu, with gravy on the side. Or the chicken parmy if you’re properly hungry.

2. Pizza Bici, Dejvice

For when you want a pizza with a story

During lockdown, half of Prague learned to bake sourdough bread. Pavel Petřík went for sourdough pizza instead. A few years, many pop-ups and one very customised electric cargo bike later (yes, it carries a pizza oven that runs hotter than 500°C), Pizza Bici has a permanent home on Na Hutích in Dejvice.

The shop is decorated with vintage bike parts, and the sourdough dough is the star. The menu is short and built for takeaway, with picks like the Marinara Sprint, a Mortadella & Pistachio and the spicy Diavola Express.

What to order: the Mortadella & Pistachio for something different, the Diavola Express if you like heat.

3. Pizza Napoletana, Podolí

For flatmate nights and office Fridays

Yes, a second pizza place. But this one comes with a measuring tape. Near the Žluté lázně riverside, Pizza Napoletana bakes proper Neapolitan pies with San Marzano tomatoes and Sabelli mozzarella, plus its party trick: pizza by the half metre.

The mezzo metro pizzas are built for sharing (in theory). The Margherita D.O.P. comes with buffalo mozzarella, the Parma version with cured ham and rocket, and the Carciofara is a little wild, with artichoke cream, salsiccia, pistachios and crispy potato. Prefer your own pizza? The classic 32 cm range covers everything from marinara to quattro formaggi.

What to order: one half-metre pizza for the table, and a slice of torta caprese for whoever wins the last piece.

4. Alambre, Nusle

For when Tex-Mex just won’t cut it

If you have ever lived somewhere with a serious taco scene, you know the difference between Mexican food and “Mexican-style” food. Alambre, on náměstí Bratří Synků in Nusle, is firmly in the first camp: modern, casual and easy to love.

The menu leans into the dishes taco lovers actually crave: tacos al pastor, loaded nachos, quesadillas and the house namesake, Alambre Camarón. The real headliner, though, is the birria de res quesadilla.

What to order: birria quesadilla, no debate. Add tacos al pastor if you are feeding two.

5. Tahini, Nusle

For the hummus purists

Supermarket hummus is fine. Then you try the real thing and there is no going back. Tahini on Nuselská street calls itself the home of legendary hummus, with Israeli roots and, lately, an Indian twist on the menu too.

Start with the classic hummus plates, topped with anything from falafel and chicken shawarma to sabich or a full shakshuka. Feeling adventurous? Check the daily specials, which have included mezze spreads and hummus with lamb kebab.

What to order: Hummus & Sabich, or Hummus & Shakshuka on a slow weekend morning.

6. Hadog Burgers, Libeň

For proper American-style burgers

Out on Sokolovská, far from the burger joints of the centre, Hadog has quietly built a loyal following. Expect 200 g beef patties, melted cheese and sauces with a kick, like the Chipotle burger with smoked cheese, bacon, BBQ sauce and chipotle mayo.

Smash fans should head straight for the Smash Juicy Lucy, one of the most popular picks on the menu. Any burger can come in a gluten-free bun or with a Beyond Meat patty, so nobody gets left out of burger night.

What to order: the Smash Juicy Lucy, or the Chipotle burger if you like it smoky.

7. Bento Café & Bistro, Holešovice

For when you can’t decide which Asian cuisine you’re craving

Small room, fresh flowers on the tables, big portions. Bento Café & Bistro in Holešovice is the kind of neighbourhood spot locals tend to keep to themselves.

The menu hops across Asia, from Vietnamese bun nem to udon noodles and a red curry ramen that regulars rave about.

It is exactly what you want on a grey November evening: something warm, something fresh and a little bit of everything. Don’t skip the homemade passion fruit lemonade.

What to order: red curry ramen on a cold night, bun nem when you want something lighter.

Your new rotation, sorted

An Aussie pie in Vinohrady, sourdough from a cargo-bike pizzaiolo, birria in Nusle and ramen in Holešovice. Prague tastes a lot more interesting once you look past the usual suspects.

All seven are available on Bolt Food, so the only thing you need to explore is the app. Open Bolt Food, search for any of the names above and try something new this week. Your Thursday-night order will forgive you.

Ordering more than once a week? Then Bolt Plus is worth a look. Members get free delivery from Bolt Food partner restaurants marked with a “+” in the app, on orders over 170 CZK (delivery discount up to 45 CZK), with no promo codes to type in.

The membership covers your rides too, with cashback on every trip and up to three free cancellations a month. And the first month is free, so you can test it on your new hidden gems before deciding.

World.title: Your Next Weekend Away: A Renovated Neoclassical Spa Hotel in Františkovy Lázně
World.content:
The hotel, housed in a 1918 Neoclassical building, has renovated its rooms, restaurant and wellness facilities.

Františkovy Lázně, one of the Czech Republic’s best-known spa towns, is offering visitors a renovated accommodation option following an extensive refurbishment of the five-star Harvey Spa Hotel.



Located in the town’s park zone in western Bohemia, the hotel occupies a Neoclassical building dating back to 1918. The recent renovation covered all 105 rooms, as well as the lobby, corridors and restaurant, updating the interiors while retaining the building’s historic character.

The hotel is situated next to the town’s central park, within walking distance of its main colonnades and mineral springs. Glauber I Spring, one of the town’s traditional drinking cure springs, is located in the nearby park by Swan Lake.

Spa treatments and wellness facilities

The hotel offers a range of spa treatments, massages and wellness services, alongside a relaxation pool, sauna and fitness centre. Guests can combine traditional spa procedures with recreational facilities during both short stays and longer wellness programmes.

The property also features a restaurant and BAR 222, which has been renovated as part of the wider refurbishment.

Františkovy Lázně has a long history as a European spa destination, attracting visitors with its mineral springs and therapeutic treatments for more than 200 years. In 2021, the town became part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing Great Spa Towns of Europe, together with ten other historic spa towns across seven countries.

Its compact centre, historic colonnades and landscaped parks make it suitable for visitors looking to explore the town on foot. The surrounding region also offers opportunities for walking and excursions beyond the spa centre.

Staying at Harvey Spa Hotel

The hotel has 105 air-conditioned rooms, all refurbished as part of the renovation. You can book your room directly here.

Its location directly beside the central park also means guests can reach the town’s main spa attractions on foot, while the hotel’s five-star facilities make it possible to combine accommodation with spa treatments and wellness services during the same stay.

World.title: Christmas Charity Market Brings Gifts and Flavours from 50 Countries to Prague
World.content:
One of Prague’s best-known international Christmas events will return this November, bringing gifts, food and traditions from nearly 50 countries under one roof.

The DSA International Christmas Charity Market 2026 will take place on Saturday, November 21, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at the Hilton Prague Atrium.



Organised by the Diplomatic Spouses Association (DSA) together with Prague’s international diplomatic community, the annual event allows visitors to shop for Christmas gifts while supporting Czech charities.

Stalls representing almost 50 countries will offer a wide range of products, including traditional sweets and spices, gourmet food, handicrafts, toys, glassware, porcelain, cosmetics, fashion accessories and Christmas gifts.

The market is held under the patronage of First Lady Eva Pavlová and regularly attracts thousands of visitors.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by DSA Prague (@dsa_prague)

Shopping for a Good Cause

The event also serves as one of the DSA’s main fundraising initiatives. Money raised through the market, together with donations and sponsorship, is distributed to Czech charitable organisations.

Earlier this year, the association awarded a total of CZK 1.32 million to 16 Czech charities during its Grant Award Ceremony in June.

According to Jana Muranska, President of the Diplomatic Spouses Association, the event is intended to bring together Prague’s international community while supporting organisations working across the Czech Republic.

“The Christmas Charity Market is about much more than Christmas shopping,” Muranska said. “It brings together people from across the world in a spirit of friendship, generosity and solidarity.”

World.title: “The Art of James Cameron” to Open at Prague’s Municipal House in April 2027
World.content:
An exhibition dedicated to filmmaker James Cameron will open at Prague’s Municipal House (Obecní dům) on April 29, 2027, bringing more than 300 items from the director’s archive to the Czech capital.

Titled The Art of James Cameron, the exhibition will run until October 3, presenting original drawings, paintings, film props, costumes and photographs connected to the Canadian director’s career.



Visitors will also see examples of 3D technologies developed or adapted for his films, alongside multimedia installations and audio commentary in which Cameron discusses his artistic development.

The collection will cover several decades of his work, from early sketches and storyboards to the technical innovations behind some of Hollywood’s biggest productions, including The Terminator, Aliens, Titanic and the Avatar films.

Although Cameron is widely recognised for pushing the technical boundaries of cinema, the exhibition will focus on his work as an artist and illustrator.

His creative process often began with pencil and paper, with early sketchbooks filled with imaginary creatures, futuristic machines and visions of distant worlds.

The exhibition will also explore recurring themes in his films, including the threat of nuclear catastrophe and the risks posed by rapid advances in artificial intelligence.

Cameron made his feature-film debut in 1981 with the action horror film Piranha II. His breakthrough came three years later with The Terminator, followed by Aliens in 1986. He continued to explore science fiction with The Abyss (1989), which follows a team investigating an underwater encounter with an unknown form of life.

His biggest success at the time came with Titanic (1997). The film won 11 Academy Awards and became one of the highest-grossing productions in cinema history, earning approximately $1.85 billion worldwide.

World.title: Prague Music Week Brings Czech and International Music Names to Prague
World.content:
From November 4 to 6, Výstaviště Praha will become a hub for musicians, industry professionals, and fans interested in everything happening both on and off the stage.

The fourth edition of Prague Music Week—themed “Women Shaping the Industry”—will feature keynote interviews with Aneta Langerová and Jana Kirschner, as well as discussions with local artists such as Lenny, Jiří Burian, Eva Saija Burešová, Klára Vytisková, and Ventolin.



A newly confirmed guest is singer Ben Cristovao, who will join a panel addressing the surge of AI-generated music.

International guests include renowned PR expert Fiona Bloom, Sziget Festival Operations Director Ádám Kiss, diversity, equity, and inclusion specialist Brechje Merckx, and representatives from Spotify.

Will also join: Finnish music industry professional Maija Talvisto; Christine Osazuwa—founder of Measure of Music and an expert in music data and analytics; Vasja Veber, co-founder of the leading analytics platform Viberate; Kristina Janušauskaitė, Executive Director of the IFPI European Office.

The event will offer practical workshops, speed-meeting sessions, opportunities to receive feedback on one’s own work, a technology expo, industry awards, informal gatherings, and space for forging new collaborations.

Tickets for the festival portion of the program are available for purchase via the GoOut and NFCtron networks.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Prague Music Week (@praguemusicweek)

Conference tickets can be obtained via a voluntary contribution through the NFCtron platform. More information is available at www.praguemusicweek.cz.

Prague Music Week will feature an Expo spanning 2,000 m², showcasing companies and products that are driving the music industry forward.

Throughout the day, attendees can combine conference sessions with exploring new innovations, participating in hands-on activities, and connecting with exhibitors.

The Expo will also include an “Experience Lab,” where visitors can try out new skills and discover the technologies used in producing music events.

World.title: German Rock Legends Scorpions to Play Prague’s O2 Arena in 2027
World.content:
One of the most successful hard rock bands of all time will perform on June 9, 2027, at Prague’s O2 arena.

Fans can look forward to an evening filled with unforgettable hits, iconic guitar riffs, and the electrifying energy that has defined the Scorpions for over six decades.

Led by charismatic frontman Klaus Meine, the band will revisit tracks that have left an indelible mark on the history of rock music, including “Rock You Like a Hurricane,” “Still Loving You,” and the timeless ballad “Wind of Change.”



In 2027, the Scorpions will embark on another extensive world tour titled “Love, Peace & Rock’n’Roll,” following up on their successful “60th Anniversary – Coming Home” anniversary concerts.

The schedule includes approximately thirty performances across three continents—ranging from European festivals and arena shows (including stops in their native Germany) to dates in North and Latin America.

The Scorpions rank among the most significant and influential rock bands in music history. Formed in 1965 in Hanover, Germany, the group has built a global reputation over the course of an extraordinary career, thanks to their unmistakable sound, high-energy live shows, and an ability to connect with audiences across generations. They have sold over 100 million records and performed countless times on the world’s biggest stages.

Their major breakthrough arrived in the 1980s with the albums Blackout and Love at First Sting, which catapulted the band into the global rock elite. It was during this period that hits such as “No One Like You,” “Rock You Like a Hurricane,” and “Big City Nights” emerged—songs that remain an essential part of their live repertoire to this day.

The Scorpions also gained fame for their emotive ballads, most notably “Still Loving You” and “Send Me an Angel.”

A truly special place in their discography is held by the song “Wind of Change,” which became a symbol of the political and social changes at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s.

Inspired by the atmosphere at the end of the Cold War, the song remains one of the most famous rock ballads of all time.

World.title: Sherlock Holmes Exhibition Lets Visitors Play Detective in Prague
World.content:
Visitors can test historical investigative techniques, examine crime scenes and follow clues at a new interactive Sherlock Holmes exhibition in central Prague.

The exhibition, located on the third floor of the Bílá labuť department store, covers more than 2,000 square metres and features over 200 exhibits.

Rather than simply moving between display cases, visitors take on the role of an investigator and work through a series of tasks inspired by the methods used by detectives more than a century ago.



Each visitor receives a detective’s notebook to record observations and clues. The notebook guides them through the exhibition as they investigate evidence, solve puzzles and gradually build their own picture of the case.

One section focuses on the history of criminal investigation around the turn of the 20th century. It includes authentic objects loaned by the Police Museum, ranging from historical fingerprinting equipment and tools used by safecrackers to more disturbing evidence connected with violent crimes.

The exhibition also explores the development of forensic science. Visitors can make footprint impressions, examine insects found at a crime scene, send messages by telegraph and learn how investigators studied bullets and other evidence. Several interactive stations test whether visitors can identify clues and apply the techniques used by detectives of the period.

The literary side of the exhibition looks at the life and work of Arthur Conan Doyle. Visitors can see early editions of the Sherlock Holmes stories and learn more about the author behind one of literature’s most enduring fictional detectives.

A reconstruction of Holmes’s famous Baker Street apartment is among the main attractions. The exhibition then moves into a series of crime scenes where visitors search for evidence and attempt to connect the clues. Some puzzles draw on well-known Sherlock Holmes stories, while others require close attention to details hidden throughout the exhibition.

Period newspapers are also part of the investigation, and visitors are encouraged to look carefully: a coded message may be concealed within the reports.

The final section examines Sherlock Holmes’s lasting influence on popular culture, including books, comics, films and television adaptations. Vintage Sherlock Holmes comic books are also on display.

A scavenger hunt for younger visitors has been added for the current school year, with children asked to find objects hidden throughout the exhibition. The format also works well for school groups, which can divide into smaller teams and compare their discoveries.

Visitors are allowed to take photographs without flash. A full visit typically takes between 90 minutes and two hours, and booking a timed entry is recommended.

Opening hours: Daily from 9 a.m. to 8:30 p.m.

Duration: The exhibition is scheduled to run at least until January 10, 2027.

Admission: Adult tickets start at 380 CZK, while family tickets start at 980 CZK.

World.title: Ancient Roman treasure lost in WWII found hiding in Hungarian museum collection after 80 years
World.content:
An ancient bronze of Apollo that vanished during the Second World War and was feared lost forever went back on display at the Hungarian National Museum on Wednesday, 80 years after it was last seen.

The statue’s return to public view is a detective story in itself. It resurfaced recently in the museum’s modern-age mixed collection, where it had been entered in the 1961 inventory book as a “pharmacy figurine” of unknown origin from the mid-19th century. It took the museum’s conservators and archaeologists to establish its true identity — that of the Apollo bronze believed lost in the war, the museum told MTI on Wednesday.

The work is one of the museum’s earliest pieces, acquired before 1825. Its first scholarly publication appeared in 1894, tracing it probably to Pecs, the site of the Roman town of Sopianae. Before the war it was a fixture and highlight of the archaeological exhibitions; amid the post-war disorder of the museum’s collections it slipped into the modern-age holdings, where its age and origin went unidentified for decades.

The 56-centimetre figure depicts a naked youth in a pose invoking contrapposto, the compositional principle of mature classical sculpture. Its striking eyes were covered in silver sheet, and they still seem to glow against the dark bronze of the face. Its eye modelling, stockier proportions and deeply grooved hair point to a date in the second half of the 2nd century AD, the Antonine period.

The hollow, thin-walled casting was made by ancient bronzesmiths using the indirect lost-wax process — body parts cast separately, then joined by soldering. Curiously, while the front has suffered aggressive pitting corrosion, the back survived the centuries in almost pristine condition.

In Greek mythology, Apollo is the most complex of gods, embodying order, radiant intellect and moral purity. This figure follows the Apollo Citharoedus type, the kithara-singing Apollo popular since the Hellenistic age: the raised left arm once held the instrument, the lowered right hand the plectrum. Apollo’s stringed instrument stood for mathematical precision and the triumph of civilisation over untamed Dionysian wildness.

Medium-sized bronzes are rarities, their production prohibitively expensive in antiquity. The newly identified work once graced a representative space — perhaps a garden or a fountain — of a Roman town house or country villa.

The Apollo can be seen for a month from Nov 4 in Room 6 of the museum’s permanent archaeological exhibition “On the Border of East and West“, as part of the Treasure of the Month series of small exhibitions.

World.title: Revolut abruptly withdraws important service in Hungary – Here’s what happens to your money
World.content:
Revolut has unexpectedly announced the withdrawal of its commodity trading services in Hungary, leaving local customers unable to purchase precious metals through the fintech platform. The change takes effect on Wednesday, 4 November, and reportedly comes without any prior warning to users.

What happens to existing investments?

According to Revb, a portal specialising in Revolut-related developments, the decision exclusively affects Hungarian customers. The service, which has been available for years, allowed users to trade commodities, including gold, silver and other precious metals, directly through the Revolut app.

Under the new measures, customers will no longer be able to place buy orders or increase their existing commodity positions. New users will also be prevented from registering for the service in Hungary. However, existing investors will have time to manage their holdings. Revolut customers who currently own commodities can sell their investments through the app until 4 January 2027.

The fintech company has also confirmed that selling fees associated with commodity transactions will be waived throughout this period, giving customers an opportunity to liquidate their holdings without incurring additional charges.

The affected commodities include gold (XAU), silver (XAG), palladium (XPD) and platinum (XPT). Although the buying option may still appear in the application, reports indicate that transactions are failing when users attempt to complete purchases.

No official explanation for the withdrawal

Revolut has not yet provided an official explanation for its decision to discontinue commodity trading services in Hungary. The investment service was previously provided to Hungarian customers by Revolut Ltd, which operates under the supervision of the UK’s financial regulator.

The announcement has raised questions among users, particularly given the lack of advance notice and the fact that the measure appears to be limited to Hungary rather than affecting the platform’s international customer base.

Another service disappears from the Hungarian market

The latest development follows Revolut’s previous withdrawal of cryptocurrency services from Hungary in December 2025, which was linked to regulatory requirements at the time. Although Hungary subsequently eased its cryptocurrency regulatory framework, Revolut has not resumed its crypto services in the country.

The company has reportedly indicated that another service will soon become available on its platform, although further details have yet to be disclosed. For Hungarian customers holding precious metals through Revolut, the immediate priority is to review their existing positions and decide whether to sell them before the 4 January 2027 deadline.

World.title: Police seize evidence at Hungary’s Foreign Ministry in pandemic ventilator probe
World.content:
The National Bureau of Investigation has seized evidence from Hungary’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs in connection with controversial ventilator purchases made during the Covid-19 pandemic. Foreign Minister Anita Orbán called the move an important step in the investigation into the nearly HUF 300 billion (EUR 0.8 billion) procurement programme carried out under former minister Péter Szijjártó.

“An important development: the National Bureau of Investigation has seized evidence related to the ventilator purchases at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs,” Orbán announced on Facebook on Wednesday.

The seizure follows an internal investigation by the ministry and a criminal complaint filed by Orbán in August. The complaint concerns healthcare equipment purchases made in March and April 2020, when Szijjártó was foreign minister and Hungary was operating under emergency powers during the pandemic.

Nearly HUF 300 billion spent on ventilators

In spring 2020, the Foreign Ministry purchased 16,853 ventilators, accounting for the vast majority of the 19,002 devices bought by the Hungarian state during the pandemic. The ministry spent close to HUF 300 billion on ventilators and other medical supplies, including protective equipment, PCR tests and medicines.

Many of the ventilators were never used in hospitals, and a significant number have reportedly remained in storage. The purchases also attracted scrutiny because of the companies involved and the large sums paid to intermediaries.

According to the ministry’s internal review, serious irregularities were identified concerning the quantity, price and usability of the equipment, as well as the financial justification for the expenditure.

Orbán has said the findings raised suspicions of mismanagement causing particularly significant financial damage to the state, alongside other potential criminal offences. The ministry also said that incomplete documentation initially made it difficult to reconstruct the decisions behind the purchases. Investigators managed to recover missing electronic files and restore parts of the records.

Two suspects detained in October

These development comes after prosecutors sought the detention of two suspects in connection with the ventilator procurement case in late October. A court ordered their detention.

According to the prosecution, one suspect was responsible for the accounting of a network of companies involved in the transactions. The other is suspected of withdrawing part of the money in cash from a foreign company’s bank account and may have acted as the network’s contact with the former Foreign Ministry.

The National Bureau of Investigation’s seizure of evidence at the ministry marks another step in efforts to establish what happened during the procurement process and whether anyone bears criminal responsibility. The investigation is ongoing, and the seizure of evidence does not in itself establish the guilt of any individual.

World.title: Winter is knocking on the door: widespread frost to hit Hungary
World.content:
Hungary is bracing for a taste of winter as a flow of cold, dry air brings widespread overnight frost, falling temperatures and increasingly clear skies. Meteorologists are warning that freezing conditions could affect almost the entire country from Thursday, 5 November, with particularly cold weather expected in frost-prone areas.

Temperatures to drop below freezing nationwide

According to meteorologist László Molnár, eastern air currents will bring below-average, winter-like temperatures across Europe, with Hungary facing widespread frost in the coming days. Following recent rainfall of between 3 and 10 millimetres associated with a Mediterranean cyclone, the weather is expected to turn significantly drier. Rain is unlikely, while persistent morning fog will also become less frequent.

Wednesday, 4 November, will remain relatively mild, with daytime temperatures reaching 8-13°C and overnight lows between 0°C and 5°C. However, colder conditions will arrive from Thursday, as northern and eastern air currents bring increasingly chilly air into the Carpathian Basin.

Daytime temperatures will remain largely unchanged initially, although maximum readings will frequently stay below 10°C. Overnight temperatures are expected to fall to between 0°C and -5°C across much of Hungary. In areas particularly prone to frost, temperatures could plunge to -6°C or -7°C, with some forecasts suggesting localised lows of -8°C over the weekend.

Protect your sensitive plants from winter’s bite

The approaching cold spell has prompted warnings for gardeners to bring vulnerable plants indoors before temperatures drop below freezing. Geraniums, balcony plants, young oleanders, citrus trees, bougainvillea and myrtle are among the species particularly susceptible to frost damage, writes Időkép.hu.

Geraniums should have their shoots trimmed before being moved to a cool, bright indoor location for the winter. Plants can also be sheltered in conservatories, garages or other suitable spaces. Gardeners should additionally protect frost-sensitive roots in outdoor flowerbeds. Mulch, fallen leaves or bark can provide insulation for perennial plants and shrubs, including young rose bushes.

Rain and milder temperatures expected next week

A change in the weather is forecast for Monday, 9 November, when a small weather system passing north of Hungary could bring rain to several regions. Cloudier skies should also prevent overnight temperatures from falling below freezing.

A stronger cyclone developing near the Iberian Peninsula could influence Hungary’s weather around 11-12 November, bringing substantial rainfall and a temporary rise in temperatures. Southern Hungary could experience daytime highs of 12-17°C. A more pronounced cold front is expected around 13 November, although meteorologists currently consider a return of severe frosts unlikely.

World.title: Why 4 November is a day of mourning in Hungary: 70 years since Soviet tanks crushed the 1956 revolution
World.content:
Hungary is marking one of the darkest days in its modern history on Wednesday, 4 November. Exactly 70 years ago, Soviet troops launched a full-scale military assault to crush the 1956 Revolution and freedom fight, ending the country’s brief hope of breaking free from communist rule.

The anniversary is being observed across Hungary, with memorial ceremonies, wreath-laying events and a national flag lowered to half-mast. This year’s commemorations also coincide with the publication of long-awaited communist-era state security records, commonly known as the agent files.

What happened on 4 November 1956?

The Hungarian Revolution began on 23 October 1956 with peaceful demonstrations against the communist dictatorship and Soviet occupation. The protests soon escalated into an armed uprising, as Hungarians demanded political freedom, national independence and the withdrawal of Soviet troops.

On 1 November, Prime Minister Imre Nagy declared Hungary’s neutrality and announced its withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact. He also appealed to the international community for help.

The Soviet Union responded with a massive military operation. At dawn on 4 November, Soviet forces launched Operation Whirlwind, attacking Budapest, other major cities and key military installations. Nagy’s appeal was broadcast on Hungarian radio at 5:20 AM, informing the country and the world that Soviet troops had intervened.

Despite fierce resistance, the vastly superior Soviet forces gradually crushed the uprising. Fighting continued in parts of Budapest for days, with the last pockets of resistance defeated around 11 November.

Photo: MTI

Thousands killed, followed by brutal reprisals

The human cost was devastating. According to a January 1957 report by Hungary’s Central Statistical Office, 2,652 people were killed and 19,226 injured between 23 October 1956 and 16 January 1957. Budapest alone accounted for 2,045 deaths and 16,700 injuries.

The Soviet military also suffered casualties: an official 1991 statistic recorded 669 Soviet soldiers killed and 51 missing.

The defeat was followed by a wave of reprisals. Former Prime Minister Imre Nagy, Defence Minister Pál Maléter and journalist Miklós Gimes were executed on 16 June 1958 after a show trial. Depending on the source, between 220 and 340 people were executed for their involvement in the revolution, while thousands more received prison sentences or were interned. Around 200,000 Hungarians fled the country.

Photo: MTI

Hungary remembers its fallen

The Hungarian government officially designated 4 November a National Day of Mourning. The national flag is lowered to half-mast, and ceremonies are held to honour those who died during the revolution and the subsequent reprisals.

On Wednesday morning, a military ceremony took place in Kossuth Square in front of Parliament, where the national flag was raised and then lowered to half-mast. A black mourning flag was also displayed on the Parliament building.

Government representatives laid wreaths at the 301 Plot in Budapest’s New Public Cemetery, where many victims of the communist reprisals are buried. Further commemorations are taking place at memorial sites in the capital and in cities across the country.

The anniversary also marks the publication of communist-era state security records, giving the public access to files that have been the subject of longstanding debate. The release is a separate, but significant, part of this year’s 70th-anniversary events.

World.title: Tisza MP reveals Orbán government’s extraordinary promises to Chinese battery manufacturer CATL
World.content:
The former Hungarian government pledged extensive financial incentives, housing support, expedited immigration procedures and infrastructure development to Chinese battery giant CATL as part of its plans for a major factory in Debrecen. Newly disclosed details of a 2022 investment declaration have shed further light on the scale of commitments made by the Orbán administration.

Thousands of foreign workers and rental homes

Zsolt Tárkányi, State Secretary at the Ministry of Transport and Investment and a Tisza Party MP representing Debrecen, published further excerpts from the document on Facebook, highlighting promises that could have significantly expanded the Chinese company’s operations in Hungary. According to the declaration, CATL provided the government with annual estimates of its non-EU workforce requirements between June 2022 and December 2029.

The figures reportedly started at 42 workers, approached 2,000 by the summer of 2023 and exceeded 6,000 by the end of 2024. The company expected to require between 4,000 and 5,000 non-EU employees in 2025. Following the completion of construction, the projected permanent workforce was expected to stabilise at between 1,000 and 2,000 from 2027 onwards.

The Orbán government pledged to prioritise visa and work permit applications, with dedicated officials helping Chinese and other third-country nationals navigate immigration procedures. The local municipality also committed to working with the state to develop thousands of rental homes for CATL employees. Tárkányi criticised the proposal, arguing that the previous government had not shown comparable willingness to introduce housing programmes for Hungarian public sector workers.

Public money for training and infrastructure

The investment declaration outlined substantial financial support. Previously disclosed provisions included non-refundable grants covering up to 25 per cent of innovation project costs, energy efficiency tax incentives worth up to EUR 15 million over six years, and training subsidies covering half of eligible costs, capped at EUR 2 million.

The government also considered reducing local business taxes and providing municipal support of up to EUR 200,000. Training subsidies could additionally reach EUR 5,000 per employee. Infrastructure commitments were another key element. The government agreed to examine railway modernisation and electrification, while road and rail developments connected to the investment were expected to be financed by Hungarian taxpayers.

Potential expansion beyond Debrecen

The declaration also envisaged identifying suitable plots of land exceeding 100 hectares within a 50-kilometre radius of Debrecen for possible additional CATL factories. The municipality was expected to acquire land from private owners, prepare and consolidate the plots at its own expense, and subsequently sell them to CATL. The company would not be required to pay any additional fees or costs beyond the purchase price of the land.

However, the declaration was non-binding. Individual projects and subsidies would have required further agreements and, where applicable, approval from the Hungarian government, CATL or the European Commission. CATL announced its Debrecen investment in 2022. The first production unit, part of a planned three-phase development, has since received environmental and operational permits, with trial production reportedly beginning in September. The full project, however, remains unfinished.

World.title: Hungary opens communist-era secret police files – But does a name in the database mean someone was an informer?
World.content:
Hungarians can now search a new online database to find out whether their relatives were listed in the communist-era state security records. The launch of Nyitottaktak.hu on 4 November fulfils a major campaign promise by Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government, but historians warn that finding someone’s name does not automatically mean they worked as an informer.

The website, available at nyitottaktak.hu, gives the public access to digitised copies of three types of documents preserved by the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security Services (ÁBTL). The records relate to people who appeared in the communist regime’s state security databases before the 1989–1990 democratic transition.

The launch took place on 4 November, the anniversary of the Soviet crackdown on the 1956 Hungarian Revolution. It marks a major step towards opening the so-called agent files, a long-standing demand that successive governments failed to fulfil after the regime change.

What can you find in the database?

The website is a searchable database rather than a simple list of names. Users can look up relatives, acquaintances or former colleagues, including by name, date of birth and address.

Three types of historical records are currently available:

Magnetic tape records: These contain the so-called H database, a network register with the names and basic details of approximately 55,000 people who appeared in the state security system. The information can include their code name, recruitment file number, workplace and other personal details. However, the database is incomplete and does not contain the actual reports or photographs.

These contain the so-called H database, a network register with the names and basic details of approximately 55,000 people who appeared in the state security system. The information can include their code name, recruitment file number, workplace and other personal details. However, the database is incomplete and does not contain the actual reports or photographs. B-registers: These recruitment registers, dating from 1957 to 1962, contain around 25,000 names and record people for whom state security files were opened.

These recruitment registers, dating from 1957 to 1962, contain around 25,000 names and record people for whom state security files were opened. Form 6 index cards: These provide more detailed information, including personal data, occupation, workplace, recruitment date and the grounds on which someone was recruited. They may also indicate how long a person remained in the state security records and which officer handled their recruitment.

However, there is an important distinction between appearing in these records and actually working as an informer.

Does a name in the files mean someone was an agent?

Not necessarily. The commonly used term agent files can be misleading, as the documents cover several different categories of people who came to the attention of the communist state security services.

Some were recruited and actively provided information, while others resisted recruitment attempts, never submitted reports or supplied information considered useless by the authorities. Some people were simply registered because they were of interest to the services.

According to Telex’s summary, the more precise term is therefore network member. Even a Form 6 card does not automatically prove that someone actively collaborated with the state security services.

The actual reports written by informers about the people they monitored will not be published in the database. The authorities say this is necessary to protect the victims of surveillance, whose personal information and private lives should not be exposed. Those affected and their relatives can, however, request access to relevant documents from the archives.

More than 9,000 recruitment files to follow in February

The publication process is not yet complete. The fourth and potentially most revealing category, the individual recruitment files, is scheduled to become available by 25 February 2027.

The archives hold more than 9,000 such files, some running to dozens or even hundreds of pages. They could reveal how individuals were approached and recruited, whether they were pressured or blackmailed, what kind of work they carried out and how their involvement with the state security services ended.

Preparing these documents takes considerably longer because they must be digitised and checked, with protected personal information removed. The process involves approximately one million pages of material.

A long-awaited step towards confronting Hungary’s past

Opening the files has been a political demand for decades. The Fidesz-KDNP government repeatedly rejected proposals to make the records public, while Magyar promised during his political campaign that his government would finally open them.

The government has also established an independent, interdisciplinary panel of historians, sociologists, psychologists and other specialists to help address the social consequences of publication. Its work is intended to support families and communities as they confront potentially difficult discoveries about their past.

World.title: Three Hungarian restaurants named among the world’s Top 100
World.content:
Three Hungarian restaurants have earned a place in the Luxury Lifestyle Awards’ 2026 TOP 100 Restaurants of the World selection, bringing international attention to the country’s culinary scene.

Three Hungarian restaurants awarded

Budapest’s VIRTU Restaurant, ISSEI and Tortuga have all been included in the prestigious list, which recognises establishments for their gastronomic achievements, service quality, distinctive atmosphere and overall dining experience, writes vince.hu.

Located on the 28th floor of the MOL Campus, VIRTU offers a contemporary interpretation of Hungarian cuisine. Chef Levente Lendvai and his team combine familiar Hungarian flavours and traditional ingredients with modern techniques, creative approaches and refined presentation.

The restaurant’s appeal also extends beyond its menu. Its elegant interior, attentive service and panoramic views of the Hungarian capital contribute to an experience that places it among the internationally recognised venues in this year’s selection.

Among the world elite

VIRTU shares the list with several celebrated restaurants from around the world, including Bangkok’s Sühring, which holds three Michelin stars, and Madrid’s Coque and Rome’s Il Pagliaccio, both awarded two Michelin stars. The selection also features Blue by Alain Ducasse in Bangkok, associated with the renowned French chef.

Lendvai said the recognition came as a surprise and was particularly meaningful given the company VIRTU found itself in. He noted that he had long followed the work of several restaurants included in the selection. “It is an honour to be part of such a prestigious international field. It is also a huge motivation for further development,” the chef said.

What is the Luxury Lifestyle Awards?

The Luxury Lifestyle Awards is an international awards programme that recognises leading businesses in the luxury sector. World.title: EU Hails Montenegro’s Progress – Regrets Stagnation in Much of Balkans
World.content:
The European Commission’s annual Enlargement Package, its report on the progress of EU candidate countries, on Wednesday introduced accession roadmaps for Montenegro and Albania, while criticising a lack of progress towards EU integration in other Western Balkan countries.

“Membership is moving closer for countries that deliver. For the first time, we introduce roadmaps for accession negotiations with Montenegro, Albania, Moldova and Ukraine,” Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, said during the launch in Brussels.

“Montenegro is the closest to the finish line with a clear path to signing the accession treaty by next summer,” Kallas added.

Marta Kos, European Commissioner for Enlargement, highlighted that, “for the first time since 2011, when the EU closed accession negotiations with Croatia, we are in a position to close accession negotiations with another candidate country”, referring to Montenegro, adding: “The country has already closed 21 negotiating chapters; 14 to go.”

Albania’s Prime Minister, Edi Rama, praised the report, describing it as “another step forward toward the historic goal of uniting with Europe.

“This assessment does not diminish the significance or the urgency of the challenges in the country’s daily life – issues that have received, continue to receive, and will continue to receive the full attention of myself, the government, and the parliamentary majority. On the contrary, the high praise in today’s report motivates us to do even more and to perform even better,” he said.

Serbia was described as having a high level of alignment with EU laws but Kos warned that, “in Serbia, we have seen backsliding across the fundamentals. The new government will have the chance to reverse the course”, referencing recent elections that ousted the long-ruling Serbian Progressive Party.

The country had “made further steps backwards on fundamental rights, in particular in the freedom of expression, public administration, and academic freedom” she noted.

Bosnia and Herzegovina made no progress in key areas of EU integration, including the judiciary, the fight against corruption, media freedom and the economy, while its visa policy has regressed, the Commission said.

The report, covering September 2025 to September 2026, described Bosnia’s growing political instability, weak institutions and state capture, noting that most of the recommendations from last year remain unimplemented.

The Commission also urged Bosnia to align its visa policy with the EU, warning that visa-free arrangements with seven countries could increase irregular migration risks.

North Macedonia was also criticised for failure on EU-related reforms, singling out the lack of progress in fighting corruption, media freedom and judicial independence, while noting that constitutional changes required to advance accession negotiations remain untouched.

Bulgaria has blocked North Macedonia’s EU accession path over disputes concerning history, language and national identity. Although Sofia formally lifted its veto in 2022 following a French-brokered compromise, North Macedonia’s commitment to include Bulgarians among its constitutive peoples in its Constitution remains unfulfilled, leaving the country’s accession process effectively stalled.

In Kosovo, an almost two-year institutional blockade halted the implementation of EU-related reforms, and the country has made only limited progress in key areas, with political instability, a lack of judicial independence, and shortcomings in the fight against corruption.

Kos noted that “Kosovo has recently intensified the implementation of the reform agenda. The EU has welcomed the election of the new president and we hope that the renewed institutional stability will enable Kosovo to progress”. Because of the two-year political crisis, Kosovo risks losing more than 40 million euros in EU growth plan funds after missing the June 2026 implementation deadline.

The Commission’s 2026 Turkey Report painted a bleak picture. It said that “democratic backsliding continued, particularly in the areas of political pluralism, integrity of electoral process, the rule of law and local governance”, amid intensified judicial pressure on opposition politicians and parties.

The report highlighted the continued detention and prosecution of opposition politicians in Turkey, including Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, the annulment of the opposition Republican People’s Party’s 2023 congress, and government pressure on independent media and critics.

Turkey started EU accession negotiations in 2005, but its membership bid has been practically frozen amid international deadlocks and democratic backsliding.

World.title: Greek American Becomes First Openly Gay US Senator
World.content:
Chris Pappas. Photo: Chris Pappas/Facebook

Greek-American Chris Pappas, a Democratic Party candidate, made history as the first openly gay man elected to the US Senate, representing New Hampshire. “Tonight is a victory for everyone,” he wrote on X on November 4.

“For the last 579 days, we’ve taken this campaign to every corner of New Hampshire. Every one of those days has brought me closer to the people who make this state so special,” he added in another post.

Pappas, 46, was elected in the US midterms on November 3 with 56.20 per cent of votes cast, defeating Republican rival John Sununu in the New England state.

The US midterms have turned into a rout for President Donald Trump’s Republicans who lost control of both houses of Congress amid massive swings to the Democrats triggered partly by discontent over rising prices and the Iran war.

Pappas has served in the House of Representatives as a Democrat since 2019.

Born and raised in Manchester, he is of Greek descent, with roots in Livadi, a village in Thessaly. His paternal great-grandfather arrived in New Hampshire in the early 20th century.

“I stand on the shoulders of my ancestors who came to this country to build a life. They started a small business over 100 years ago and I am the recipient of their journey, their struggle, and their hard work,” he said in an interview on Greek TV on November 2.

“I am also blessed that they have bequeathed to me their traditions, their faith, and their involvement in the local community here. And so I think about their example every day. And I try to show the best of what Hellenism represents and the best of what my ancestors reflected throughout their lives and their journey,” he added.

Papas attended Manchester Central High School, and, after graduation in 1998, studied at Harvard College. He then worked in his family’s 106-year-old restaurant in New Hampshire.

Before serving in Congress, he represented District 4 on the New Hampshire Executive Council. When he was elected to the US House in 2018, he became New Hampshire’s first openly gay member of Congress.

His page for his candidacy reported that in Congress he fought for tax cuts for working families and small businesses, and for “cracking down on predatory companies that target veterans and pollute our water, and standing up to Big Pharma to lower drug costs”.

Pappas is married to his husband, Vann.

World.title: Kosovo Identifies Three More Wartime Missing Persons
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip



Excavations in the village of Kalluder in Zubin Potok of a mass grave, July 30, 2026. Photo: BIRN

Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti confirmed on Tuesday that three more victims of enforced disappearance during the Kosovo 1998-99 war were identified following DNA analysis carried out in the Hague.Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti confirmed on Tuesday that three more victims of enforced disappearance during the Kosovo 1998-99 war were identified following DNA analysis carried out in the Hague.

“Following initial identifications from remains exhumed in Kalluder and Jabuke (villages near Zubin Potok in north Kosovo), the Government Commission on Missing Persons has received new DNA reports confirming the identities of Adem (Fazli) Ademi, Fatmir (Bajram) Fazlija and Ali (Islam) Haliti,” Kurti wrote on Facebook.

Kurti said the families had been notified. The three men were amongst missing Kosovo Albanian intellectuals “who were abducted by Serbian armed forces in April 1999 and subsequently subjected to enforced disappearance”, Kurti explained.

He added that the effort to find missing persons “goes hand-in-hand with the ongoing pursuit of accountability for war crimes – crimes that continue to be denied and concealed, while relevant documents and archives remain classified or sealed, and the perpetrators of genocide are glorified”.

Excavations conducted by Kosovo authorities in August 2026 in the villages of Kalluder and Jabuke in Zubin Potok, discovered human remains believed to belong to at least 23 people. The excavation process in these two villages began on July 28, 2026, and lasted for four weeks.

Three suspects are currently under investigation and in custody in connection with this case, suspected of committing war crimes against the civilian population.

Around 1,600 people remain missing from the Kosovo war.

According to a report by the Institute for Crimes Committed During the War in Kosovo, IKKL, at least 13,227 people were killed, subjected to enforced disappearance or died as a result of the war between January 1, 1998, and December 31, 2000.

The publication of this list marks the first phase of the IKKL’s institutional database, which was developed to document the human toll of the war and serve as a reliable resource for institutions and researchers.

World.title: Crackdown on Serbian Alta Bank Plunges Russians into Financial Uncertainty
World.content:
Alta Bank thrived during the rule of SNS and former President Aleksandar Vucic.

In 2025, for example, Serbia’s state-owned electricity company, Elektroprivreda Srbije, EPS, changed its payment arrangements, directing Belgrade residents to pay their electricity bills into Alta Bank accounts. And shortly before last month’s election, Vucic launched a podcast on his YouTube channel featuring Alta Bank as a sponsor.

On Monday, the bank’s owner, Davor Macura, was detained on suspicion of illegally withdrawing nearly 385 million euros.

The bank’s clients, many of them Russians, have been locked out of their accounts.

Olga, who opened her Alta Bank account in November 2024, said that she and her partner could no longer access their money and had received no information directly from the bank.

“The worst thing is the bank didn’t give us any information, no email, no message about the situation,” she said.

Serbia’s Deposit Insurance Agency said it would begin reimbursing insured deposits of up to 50,000 euros per depositor within seven working days, after the Commercial Court in Belgrade on Tuesday opened bankruptcy proceedings against Alta Bank. The agency appointed state-owned Banka Postanksa stedionica to handle the payments.

In the meantime, the lives and livelihoods of many in Serbia’s Russian community have been turned upside down.

“We used it for everything – salary and savings,” said Olga’s partner, Eugene, who described Alta Bank as the default banking option for Russians who moved to Serbia.

Like Ekaterina, Ivan had also sold his Moscow apartment last month. He transferred some 180,000 euros to his Alta Bank account, which he had opened in December 2023, with the intention of buying a property in Serbia.

“Insurance will give me back 50,000 euros, but it’s less than a third,” he said.

Ivan said the bank had provided no information since its closure, while its branches were closed and its mobile application and website were inaccessible, leaving him unable even to obtain an account statement.

“I’m very happy I took some money out on Thursday to pay my rent and food, but before the end of the year my wallet will be empty,” he told BIRN.

According to Popovic, the Deposit Insurance Agency will pay out compensation for deposits up to 50,000 euros. For deposits above that amount, the creditor will “join the queue” for the bank’s bankruptcy or liquidation estate.

“This procedure can take a long time, measured in years, and payouts are usually made in installments, following successful sales of bank assets.”

‘Cash Only’

World.title: Scapegoats? Accused Shooters in 1992 Sarajevo Execution Protest Innocence
World.content:
BIRN cannot corroborate either man’s account of what happened in Veliki Park on April 22, 1992.

It is a fact, however, that the witnesses in the trial of Vikic and his three co-accused offered contradictory accounts.

One protected witness, a member of Matic’s unit identified only as Witness A, told the court he watched Herenda shoot all eight prisoners from a range of just two metres, though he did not initially tell this to investigators.

Amir Medjic, a reservist in Vikic’s unit guarding Police House, also said Herenda was the sole shooter.

But they differ on how the shootings unfolded.

Witness A put Herenda forcing the prisoners out of a van and shooting them as they climbed a wall; Medjic had them arriving on foot with escorts, whom Herenda sent away after a word from a State Security official.

Other witnesses placed Herenda nearby, but did not say he fired. Two members of Vikic’s unit and its secretary said they had heard that the killers were either Matic’s men or those of Jusuf ‘Juka’ Prazina, another wartime commander; a Novi Grad shift chief said he heard Matic pulled the trigger. None of them actually saw it happen

Jusic, Herenda and a witness from Prazina’s unit each describe four or more shooters, in stark contrast to those who say Herenda acted alone. The appeals panel wrote that many witnesses identified Herenda and Jusic as the killers, yet none of the testimony cited identified Jusic as opening fire.

Individual testimonies have also shifted.

Witness F made several statements to prosecutors between 2006 and 2016, then told the court they were untrue and that he signed them under pressure. The trial chamber itself noted that for many prosecution witnesses it could not tell what they had seen from what they had heard.

A claim that Herenda confessed to the executions rests on two former officers of the intelligence service AID: Edin Garaplija, sentenced to 13 years for abducting Herenda in June 1996, months after the war had ended, and trying to kill him; and a convicted colleague identified in the trial as Witness L.

The abduction came amid a power struggle inside the AID, the successor to the wartime Bosnian State Security Service, as a new leadership moved against alleged rivals.

Interrogated and tortured by the AID officers for four days, Herenda said he never confessed. Yet the trial chamber cited both accounts, by Garaplija and Witness L, when it concluded that the evidence pointed to Herenda as the killer.

Oleg Cavka, a former war crimes prosecutor at the Bosnian Prosecutor’s Office, also said Herenda admitted being “involved”, when Cavka interviewed him in the Netherlands in May 2015. Herenda disputed this, saying he told Cavka only that he had been present, not that he took part. The court judgement cited no record of the interview and Cavka declined to comment for this story.

World.title: Low Presidential Election Turnout Suggests Bulgarians are Giving up on Politics
World.content:
When the government-backed candidate, Iliana Iotova, won the recent presidential elections in Bulgaria, that was not a surprise. A more unexpected aspect of the vote was the record low turnout.

On November 1, Iotova won 57.6 per cent of votes cast in a runoff against the pro-EU opposition candidate, Andrey Gyurov, on 39.5 per cent. But only 29.1 per cent of all eligible voters bothered to cast ballots.

Even that was an improvement on the first round of voting on October 25, when the figure was 22.98 per cent. This means less than 2 million citizens were engaged in total. By contrast, turnout in the elections in 2021 was 40.5 per cent, and, in 2016, 56.28 per cent.

The poor turnout may have benefited Iotova, who served as Vice President from 2016 to 2026 to Rumen Radev, and then Acting President after Radev stepped down to chase a majority in the parliament.

World.title: Seven Arrested in International Investment Fraud Crackdown in Balkans
World.content:
Kosovo police and Europol during the raids against an international investment fraud scheme, November 3, 2026. Photo: Kosovo Police

The European Union Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation, Eurojust, announced on Tuesday that seven persons were arrested in an international action against investment fraud in an action conducted with the EU police agency Europol that also involved Germany, Cyprus, Finland, Albania, Kosovo, North Macedonia and Israel.

“Authorities, supported by Eurojust and Europol, have taken action against a criminal network running an investment fraud scheme, leading to the shutdown of over 100 servers and seven arrests,” Eurojust announced. According to Europol, extradition to Germany is being considered for the arrested.

The operation started in 2022 after a German couple reported that they had been victims of a fraud scheme after they invested savings but could not withdraw their profits from the online platform they had used.

Europol explained that, “led by the German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor’s Office (Staatsanwaltschaft Itzehoe), the operation targeted a company suspected of supplying fraudulent trading websites to criminal groups. The entity is connected to call centre operators who allegedly persuaded victims to hand over their savings. Investigators estimate losses exceeding EUR 4 million.”

Kosovo police announced on Facebook that after raiding five locations, three suspects were arrested in Kosovo. “M.P., I.H., and F.Z., [were arrested] on suspicion of committing the criminal offences of participating in or organising an organised criminal group, fraud, unauthorised computer access and computer fraud”. Police announced that “cars, mobile phones, computers and other electronic devices that may serve as evidence in criminal proceedings” were seized.

This is not the first time the international operation has made arrests in this case.

In May 2025, Eurojust announced that one suspect had been arrested in Cyprus after “an organised criminal group (OCG) operating globally defrauded more than 100 victims of over EUR 3 million through a fake online investment platform”.

In September 2022, Eurojust announced that two suspects had been arrested after raids in 12 locations. “With the support of Eurojust, authorities in Finland, Germany, Belgium and Latvia have succeeded in striking a blow against the operators of various fraudulent online investment platforms that have defrauded victims from 11 different countries out of several million euros,” it said.

World.title: Serbia Detains Police Officials Over Abuse of Position, Torture, Allegations
World.content:
The Higher Court in Belgrade on Tuesday ordered 30 days of detention for the head of the Criminal Police Directorate, Marko Kricak, and the head of the Crime Suppression Service, Bosko Sekulovic.

They are charged with abuse of official position, while Kricak is also charged with mistreatment and torture, both linked to a murder in a Belgrade restaurant in May.

Detention was ordered to prevent them influencing witnesses. However, the Higher Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade said it would complain about the court’s decision and demand that detention be ordered both due to the potential to influence witnesses and to prevent any repeat of the criminal offence within a short period of time, as earlier proposed by the prosecution.

Kricak and Sekulovic were arrested on Sunday, a week after parliamentary elections in which the long-ruling Serbian Progressive Party lost power after 14 years.

Belgrade’s chief prosecutor, Nenad Stefanovic, insisted on Monday that the arrests “have nothing to do with electoral processes or the results of the parliamentary elections”.

Kricak and Sekulovic are suspected of abusing their official positions and of “failing to perform their official duty” during their handling of the case of the murder of A.N. in “27” Belgrade’s restaurant on May 12, the Higher Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade said on Tuesday.

Their actions between May 12 and June 3 allegedly caused damage and also violated the rights of the former head of the Belgrade Police Department, Veselin Milic.

Milic was arrested on May 15 under suspicion that he had assisted an offender in the murder and had failed to report the crime. In June, the Higher Prosecutor’s Office dropped part of the complaint relating to assisting an offender after the commission of a crime.

The prosecution said on Tuesday that Sekulovic had drafted a criminal complaint that also named Milic, even though he knew that Milic had left the restaurant before the murder took place. Kricak allegedly gave verbal approval to Sekulovic to submit the criminal complaint, despite being aware of its contents.

On May 21, police found a dead body in a metal drum buried near the town of Indjija. Five days later, it was confirmed that it belonged to A.N. Media have reported that the victim was a gangland figure.

Kricak was also suspected of having used force against those suspected of being involved in the murder.

“Additionally, there are grounds for suspicion that Marko K. on May 16, 2026 … abused the victim N.L. while performing his official duties, in such a way that he, together with unidentified police officers, first struck him with open hands and closed fists in the head area, and placed a hood over his head, suffocating him,” the prosecution’s press release said.

Furthermore, Kricak is suspected of removing the victim’s socks and of beating him on the soles of his feet and back with a belt.

During the massive anti-government protests in Serbia in the last two years, some protesters have claimed that Kricak used force against them. One female detainee, Nikolina Sindjelic, said in August 2025 that Kricak had threatened her with rape. He has not been prosecuted over these allegations.

World.title: Women in Croatia Will Now Need to Wait Longer to Retire
World.content:
November the 4th, 2026 – Women in Croatia will now need to wait longer to retire, with new rules coming into force as of January the 1st, 2027.

As of January the 1st 2027, the conditions for women to take regular and early pensions are changing. Index reports that women in Croatia will have to be three months older than this year, and for early retirement, the required pensionable service is also increasing, according to data from the Croatian Pension Insurance Institute (HZMO). For a regular pension next year, women in Croatia will have to be at least 64 years and three months old and have 15 years of pensionable service. In 2026, the requirement is 64 years of age and at least 15 years of service.

stricter rules for early retirement

The changes also apply to those hoping to begin drawing their pensions earlier. Women will have to be three months older than they did this year in order to retire. This year, for early retirement, at least 59 years of age and 34 years of service are required. This means that from the beginning of next year both conditions increase by three months.

when will men and women be equalised?

The age limit for women is gradually increasing every year. In 2028, women will need to be 64 years and six months of age in order to claim their regular pension, and in 2029, they’ll need to be 64 years and nine months of age. From the 1st of January 2030, the conditions are completely equalised. Both women and men will then need 65 years of age and at least 15 years of pensionable service for a regular old-age pension. For early retirement from 2030 the requirement of at least 60 years of age and 35 years of pensionable service will apply to both genders.

Taking an early pension also means a lower initial pension amount. Under the current law, the pension is reduced by 0.2 percent for each month of earlier departure in relation to the prescribed age for a regular old-age pension. This means that the reduction amounts to 2.4 percent for one year of earlier retirement, or a maximum of 12 percent for five years. However, from the beginning of 2026 the reduction is abolished after the recipient of the early pension reaches the age of 70.

who can retire early?

Special conditions apply to long-term insured persons. They can acquire the right to their regular pension at the age of 60 and with 41 years of insurance service in actual duration. This possibility applies to women and men who meet the prescribed conditions, and it differs from an earlier pension. Women who have already fulfilled the conditions for a pension under earlier regulations do not automatically lose the acquired right because the age limit additionally increases at the beginning of next year.

World.title: Croatian Tourist Board – London and Advent Launch Winter Campaign
World.content:
November the 4th, 2026 – The Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ) has officially kicked off its winter campaign, showcasing Advent up and down the country in London.

This very influential London fair brings together more than 4,000 exhibitors from 180 countries, and Croatia is presenting its offer with the participation of more than 30 domestic co-exhibitors. Zrinka Gabelica Toplek reports for Poslovni that the Croatian National Tourist Board is currently showcasing a very intensive winter promotion campaign and preparations for the next tourist year. Key activities include appearance at one of the world’s largest tourism fairs, WTM London, which is currently going on, as well as the launch of the first national campaign for Advent events.

The Croatian delegation is led by the Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina and HTZ director Kristjan Staničić, who will hold meetings with leading British and global partners, including airlines and tour operators such as EasyJet Holidays, British Airways, Jet2Holidays and the ABTA association. “WTM London as one of the world’s leading tourism business gatherings enables us to have direct contacts with key partners. It’s also an opportunity to open new possibilities for Croatian destinations, and in that context it is important to further encourage interest in travel in the pre-season and post-season, with a quality offer and an appropriate price-quality ratio,” revealed HTZ director Kristjan Staničić, emphasising the strategic importance of this appearance for positioning Croatia as a year-round destination.

The promotional appearance in London relies on a new visual identity of the stand and multimedia content with John Malkovich, along with the presentation of domestic wines in cooperation with the Croatian Chamber of Economy (HGK). At the beginning of November, the first national Advent campaign for Croatia is also starting across 11 European markets, with the aim of promoting festive and overall winter programmes in Zagreb, Varaždin, Osijek, Opatija and other cities.

World.title: Pula Among the Top 10 Most Affordable Global Air Destinations
World.content:
November the 4th, 2026 – Gorgeous Pula has been ranked among the top 10 most affordable global air destinations.

When planning their trips, people are increasingly guided by expected changes in transport costs, and not only by accommodation and other services. Marin Penavic reports for Poslovni that the Istrian coastal city of Pula has found itself among the ten most affordable world tourist destinations for 2027, according to the ranking published by the wildly popular flight search engine Skyscanner.

pula took seventh place

The Croatian city took seventh place, and one of the key reasons highlighted is the expected drop in air ticket prices. According to Skyscanner’s estimates, the average price of flights to Pula should be around 20 percent lower than this year. In first place on the list is Bilbao in Spain, where the largest drop in air ticket prices is expected – as much as 66 percent compared to 2026. It is followed by Polish Wroclaw with an estimated cheapening of 47 percent, while French Bordeaux is in third place, with flight prices that should be 34 percent lower.

In addition to Pula, among the ten destinations that could be particularly interesting to travellers in 2027 due to more affordable air tickets are also Zurich, Ancona, Rhodes, Carcassonne, Fez and Krabi. Skyscanner’s list thus suggests that the price of transport could play an important role in the choice of destinations during the coming year. Lower flight prices could boost demand for cities that have so far been less accessible or more expensive to visit, and among them is Pula.

pula’s competitiveness

The inclusion of Pula among the ten most affordable destinations is particularly interesting for Croatian tourism, since accessibility by air directly affects the international competitiveness of the destination. At the same time, Skyscanner’s findings show how travellers, when planning their trips, can increasingly be guided by expected changes in transport costs, and not only by the prices of accommodation and other services at the destination.
