The government is also introducing a new approach to assessing industrial capacity. The Ministry of Industry and Construction has approved a methodology that will assess each proposed project against market demand, the capacity utilization of existing enterprises and the availability of resources.

The findings will be taken into account when granting incentives and refining government support measures.

A new industrial cluster model is also being introduced to strengthen cooperation between manufacturers, support the production of finished goods and bring small and medium-sized businesses into supply chains around major industrial enterprises.

New approaches to geological exploration

Kazakhstan is also introducing new technologies to improve geological exploration. For the first time, the country has launched state geological mapping at a scale of 1:50,000.

Over the next three years, the government plans to implement 20 projects covering approximately 100,000 square kilometers.

Alongside conventional exploration methods, specialists are using Ionic Leach technology to identify concealed mineral deposits, as well as artificial intelligence, satellite data and unmanned aerial vehicles.

Preliminary results have identified seven promising sites. Areas confirmed to have potential are expected to be prepared for auction next year, Nalybayev said.

The government is also integrating approximately 4.8 million records of primary geological information into the Unified Subsoil Use Platform. The integration is expected to improve access to existing geological data and support the search for new deposits.

By combining geological exploration with investment in domestic processing and manufacturing, Kazakhstan aims to strengthen its position in critical materials supply chains and develop industries that produce higher-value goods.

World.title: Tokayev Meets Network School Founder, Welcomes Launch of Kazakhstan Branch
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with Balaji Srinivasan, founder of Network School, to discuss cooperation in technology, education and innovation, reported the presidential press service on Nov. 4.

Tokayev praised Network School’s contribution to the development of Kazakhstan’s technology ecosystem and expressed readiness to strengthen cooperation with the organization.

He said Kazakhstan is investing in education, science and digital skills to prepare a new generation of technology leaders.

In this context, Tokayev spoke about the People’s Construction initiative, announced in his recent address, saying it would help create a lasting legacy for future generations. The program envisages large-scale construction of social infrastructure, including schools, universities and healthcare facilities.

President Tokayev welcomed the launch of Network School Kazakhstan in Astana and the organization’s interest in expanding partnerships with Kazakh universities, startups and technology companies.

Tokayev also thanked Srinivasan for his investment support for the Astana AI Film Festival. In turn, Srinivasan highlighted Kazakhstan’s ability to combine advanced technological solutions with traditional sectors of the economy. He presented Network School Kazakhstan’s priorities, which include promoting digital solutions, developing human capital and creating an environment conducive to innovation.

World.title: Kazakhstan and China Build Digital Bridge for Data Economy
World.content:
Access to reliable data gives businesses a competitive advantage when they develop AI tools, build digital services or enter new markets. Kazakhstan and China are working to make that resource easier to use securely across borders.

China and Kazakhstan deepened their cooperation in the data economy at the Global Data Ecosystem Conference 2026 (GDEC 2026) in Shanghai on Oct. 30–31. Kazakhstan participated as the Special Invited International Partner, a sign of the growing importance of data cooperation in relations between the two countries. At the opening session, Kazakhstan’s Bureau of National Statistics outlined the country’s approach to building a data market. The Bureau is part of the Agency for Strategic Planning and Reforms, which oversees the development of the data economy.

On Oct. 31, Astana Data Exchange (ADX) and Shanghai Data Exchange (SDE) began to work on their first joint listing of data products so that data providers could offer them on both platforms. Industry associations, state-owned enterprises and private firms in finance and IT also joined a broader initiative on data markets, research on the digital economy and smart city projects.

The cooperation fits a broader agenda discussed by Presidents Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Xi Jinping in Shanghai in July, when digital technologies and AI were identified as areas for closer ties. At the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, Tokayev proposed the Kazakhstan–China Digital Bridge Initiative to expand digital trade and connect the two countries’ digital economies. For Kazakhstan, the proposal builds on its record as a digital state. The country is now turning to the economic use of the data its industries and public institutions generate.

If Kazakhstan and China connect their national data exchanges under rules both sides trust, other countries could use the same approach to share data securely and transparently.

From digital government to a data economy

This cooperation follows years of digitization in Kazakhstan, particularly in public services and banking. More than 90% of public services are available online, and the country ranked 24th among 193 countries in the 2024 UN E-Government Development Index. In 2025, 98.3% of personal payments and transfers were cashless.

The Digital Qazaqstan strategy builds on that experience and sets out how the country plans to develop its data economy through 2029. It calls for wider use of AI across industries and for government agencies to use data when making decisions. The Law on Artificial Intelligence establishes rules for developing and using AI systems.

Under Kazakhstan’s Digital Code, in force since July 2026, organizations can exchange data products through registered platforms. Providers set the terms of use, and the products must exclude personal data that could identify individuals.

As part of a broader effort to treat data as an economic asset, Kazakhstan has adopted a method for valuing data products held by public agencies and state-owned enterprises.

China took an early lead in building a market for such assets when it recognized data as a factor of production in 2019. It has since set rules for using data, built a network of exchanges and introduced a national system for registering data rights. Its National Data Administration supports the development of industry datasets for training AI models.

A digital bridge between these markets would give Kazakhstan and China a stronger basis for joint work on AI. With agreed rules for secure access, researchers and businesses could draw on data from both countries to train models and build digital services for a wider market.

A digital bridge in practice

One example of this digital bridge is the partnership between Astana Data Exchange and Shanghai Data Exchange. Their 2025 strategic cooperation agreement laid the groundwork for the joint listing. ADX, one of the platforms on Kazakhstan’s national register under the Digital Code, helps organizations list, find and exchange data products.

SDE is a leading hub for cross-border data exchange, connecting international providers with buyers in China and helping Chinese firms bring their data products to markets abroad. In 2026, it became one of three institutions designated to register data rights under China’s national system.

Eleven international providers, including KoDATA, are preparing to list products on ADX. Their products cover business information, finance, shipping and logistics, research and AI. The partnership could also help Kazakhstani providers offer data products and services in China, including market analysis based on aggregated, anonymized records. A data service could show a Chinese exporter where household appliances sell best in Kazakhstan without sharing individual sales receipts.

China’s experience with data assets suggests a next step for the partnership. The exchanges could agree on how to value data products and register rights in them. Banks could then assess whether those rights can serve as collateral. In shared data spaces, partners could agree on who may use sensitive records. Confidential computing could let them analyze those records together while keeping the underlying data private.

What this means for trade and investment

Secure data exchange could help Kazakhstan and China expand trade and investment. Bilateral trade reached $48.7 billion in 2025, according to Chinese customs figures. As their data markets develop, sharing verified records could help the two countries reach their $100 billion target by speeding up border checks and customs clearance.

An importer could verify a supplier’s registration, a shipment’s origin or a product certificate. A Chinese exporter could check a Kazakhstani distributor’s trading history before offering credit. A retailer choosing a site for a store in Almaty could use aggregated mobility data to compare foot traffic across neighborhoods.

A global network of data exchanges could widen access while leaving providers in control of who may use their data and for what purpose. If those terms are clear and enforceable across borders, more countries could use shared data to build their own AI tools and digital services and expand trade and investment.

Lu Yong is the Executive Director of Shanghai Data Service Provider Association and the Chief Expert of Shanghai Data Exchange. Sarsen Zhanabekov is CEO of Astana Data Exchange.

World.title: Kazakhstan Eyes 2035 Completion for First Two Nuclear Power Plants
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan expects its first two nuclear power plants to be completed by 2035, with construction of the Balkhash plant involving a Russian-led consortium headed by Rosatom and negotiations underway with China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) over the second plant, known as Moyinkum, Minister of Energy Erlan Akkenzhenov said at a Nov. 4 government briefing.

According to Akkenzhenov, discussions with CNNC are ongoing and cover the terms of the agreement, project parameters and construction timeline.

“The parameters of the project are currently being discussed, including the terms of the deal and the timeline. We believe that the projects should be completed by 2035,” he told journalists.

The minister said the Balkhash plant would be implemented with the participation of the Russian consortium, while cooperation with CNNC is being explored for the Moyinkum project.

Responsibility for nuclear energy projects was initially held by the Ministry of Energy but was later transferred to the newly established Agency for Atomic Energy. Akkenzhenov noted that the agency is now responsible for the projects.

Meanwhile, Kazakhstan plans to establish a strategic uranium reserve by the end of 2027, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin said on Nov. 3. The reserve is intended to supply three nuclear power plants planned in the country, involving Russia’s Rosatom and China’s CNNC.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Complete Construction of Three New Airports by End of 2026
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to complete construction of three new airports in Zaisan, Katon-Karagai and Kenderli by the end of 2026 as part of efforts to expand the country’s aviation infrastructure and strengthen its transit potential, First Deputy Prime Minister Nurlan Nalybayev said at a Nov. 4 government press conference.

Nalybayev also added that the government is also working to modernize existing airports and improve air navigation systems. Construction and modernization work is underway at Almaty and Urdzhar airports, while a second runway is being built in Shymkent. In August, Pavlodar Airport’s runway was reconstructed and Arkalyk Airport was restored.

Kazakhstan is also upgrading its air navigation system using international equipment and standards.

New routes and cargo capacity

The country is expanding its international air connections. The first flight on the Almaty-Tokyo route is scheduled for Nov. 30, while new routes to Vienna, New York, Milan and other cities are planned for 2027.

Kazakhstan is also developing a national cargo airline, Air Cargo, which is expected to operate a fleet of 10 aircraft.

The first aircraft is expected to arrive in November 2026, followed by a second in March 2027. The carrier will operate in the international air freight market as part of the government’s efforts to strengthen Kazakhstan’s position in global cargo transportation.

Fueling facilities and cargo terminals are also being modernized and connected to road and railway networks to support multimodal transportation.

The government is working to digitize the transport sector through the integration of information systems into the unified E-Kolik intelligent platform. The system is expected to enable fully paperless documentation, shorten the processing time for transport documents and improve transparency in cargo flows.

Kazakhstan’s transit ambitions

The airport projects form part of a broader effort to develop Kazakhstan’s transport and logistics infrastructure and improve connections between international markets. The government has identified several key transport hubs where free economic zone arrangements have been introduced. Modernization of fuel facilities and cargo terminals, alongside better road and railway connections, is expected to support the development of multimodal freight services.

The expansion of airport capacity, international routes and cargo operations is intended to strengthen Kazakhstan’s role as a regional aviation and logistics hub.

World.title: Tokayev’s ‘Build! Once Again – Build!’ Initiative Takes Shape Across Kazakhstan With $14.3 Billion Plan
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is preparing for a nationwide construction drive that will direct nearly 6.5 trillion tenge (US$14.3 billion) toward infrastructure development through 2029, as President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev calls for a new phase of economic modernization built around tangible improvements in people’s lives.

The initiative, known as Khalyktyq Qurylys, or the People’s Construction program, will cover roads, airports, railway stations, power plants, hospitals, schools, rehabilitation centers, sports facilities and other public infrastructure across the country. Tokayev has designated 2027 as the Year of Nationwide Large-Scale Construction.

First Deputy Prime Minister Nurlan Nalybayev announced the funding plans at a Nov. 4 government press conference on the development of Kazakhstan’s real economy. He said the National Fund would provide resources for social, transport and engineering infrastructure projects across all regions by the end of 2029.

The initiative is already moving forward. According to Nalybayev, 262 projects worth a combined 1.5 trillion tenge (US$3.3 billion) have been approved through the Infrastructure Development Fund. A significant share of the funding is earmarked for social infrastructure.

Hospitals, schools and public facilities

The approved project pipeline covers several sectors, with healthcare, education, culture, sports and utilities among the priorities.

Healthcare projects account for 344 billion tenge (US$758 million) and include the construction of hospitals, outpatient clinics, perinatal centers and maternity hospitals. Another 266 billion tenge (US$586 million) is allocated to culture, tourism and sports, with 23 facilities planned, including sports complexes, cultural centers and theaters.

Education projects will receive 101 billion tenge (US$223 million) for the construction of 28 facilities, including schools and multifunctional complexes.

Transport infrastructure accounts for 369 billion tenge (US$813 million) across 48 projects, including road reconstruction and the construction of new roads and bridges. A further 284 billion tenge (US$626 million) is earmarked for 55 water supply and wastewater facilities, including main pipelines, treatment plants, protective dams and reservoirs. Another 136 billion tenge (US$300 million) will support 67 projects to develop heating and gas supply systems.

“This is not just plans on paper. A total of 497 billion tenge (US$1.1 billion) has already been allocated for the implementation of these 122 projects. I would particularly like to emphasize that all 6.5 trillion tenge (US$14.3 billion) allocated for infrastructure modernization will be under strict government oversight,” he said.

The government also plans to establish a state commission to oversee the People’s Construction program and ensure public monitoring of how the funds are spent. It will include representatives of government agencies, members of the Kurultai and the People’s Council, public figures, activists, volunteers and journalists.

Nalybayev also said the construction program would rely on domestic building materials and production capacity.

Investment and domestic industry

The infrastructure drive is also expected to create opportunities for Kazakh businesses and manufacturers.

At a separate meeting of the Board of Directors of Samruk Kazyna, chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov on Nov. 4, the fund reviewed progress on 69 major investment projects with a combined value of 43.8 trillion tenge (US$96.5 billion). The largest share of investment is directed toward the oil and gas industry, petrochemicals and conventional power generation, alongside gas transportation, energy infrastructure, transport and communications.

Construction and installation work is underway on 44 projects, while the remaining initiatives are at different stages of implementation.

The fund reported that purchases from Kazakh companies reached approximately 1.4 trillion tenge (US$3.1 billion) in the first nine months of the year, a 45% increase compared with the same period last year. Offtake contracts with domestic producers amounted to 73 billion tenge (US$161 million).

Among the projects launched in October was a 380-kilometer fiber-optic communication line connecting Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan. The link is expected to expand international data exchange and strengthen digital connectivity between the two countries.

Samruk Kazyna is also continuing construction of social facilities. Several major healthcare projects in Astana, Turkistan and Petropavlovsk are scheduled for completion in 2027 and 2028. Other initiatives cover inclusive sports, rehabilitation, education and culture.

Transport corridors and road modernization

Transport remains another major focus of the government’s infrastructure plans, as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its position as a transit and logistics hub in Eurasia.

Rail freight transit through Kazakhstan increased by 15% to 33.8 million tons, Nalybayev said. The government is also modernizing 37 automobile border crossing points, with completion scheduled by the end of 2027.

The Aral-Caspian highway, construction of which officially began in August 2026, is expected to reduce cargo delivery times to three days. The project is scheduled for completion by the end of 2028. Preparations are also underway to expand the Kokshetau-Petropavlovsk highway, with construction expected to begin in the first half of 2027.

The government is placing particular emphasis on road quality and accountability in the construction sector. A working group led by Nalybayev has been established to review international practices and develop proposals to improve road construction standards and strengthen the responsibility of all parties involved.

Along international road corridors, Kazakhstan currently has 1,465 roadside service facilities. A total of 221 facilities have been built over the past three years, including service complexes with fuel stations, hotels, shops and vehicle maintenance services.

Construction sector growth

The new program comes as Kazakhstan’s construction industry continues to expand. Construction work reached 7.8 trillion tenge (US$17.2 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, up 11.5% compared with the same period last year. More than 20 million square meters of housing are expected to be commissioned nationwide by the end of the year.

The broader economy has also recorded growth in infrastructure-related sectors. Kazakhstan’s gross domestic product grew by 6.5% in 2025, with construction expanding by 17.5% and transport and warehousing by 19.4%, according to the Bureau of National Statistics.

The government says the People’s Construction program is intended to turn this momentum into visible changes across the country. Over the next few years, the results will be measured not only by investment figures and completed projects, but also by the roads people travel, the schools and hospitals they use, and the utilities that serve their communities.

World.title: AI Bubble: Global Investors Seek AI’s Real Enterprise Value at Hong Kong’s Cyberport Forum
World.content:
HONG KONG — The term “bubble” was not a whispered fear but a baseline for discussion at the Nov. 4 Cyberport Venture and Capital Forum, where participants focused on winning the next competitive cycle in AI. As artificial intelligence valuations soar to unprecedented heights, venture capitalists are shifting their focus from the marketing noise of .ai domain names to the harder realities of monetization, scaling bottlenecks, and a shifting geopolitical landscape in which China and the United States (U.S.) are locked in a high-stakes race for dominance.

For Ganesh Rengaswamy, founding managing partner at Quona Capital, the current atmosphere feels hauntingly familiar, yet fundamentally different from the dot-com era.

“Yes, of course we are in a bubble, but great transformation also comes out of the bubble,” Rengaswamy noted.

He pointed out that while modern capital deployment features “a couple of more zeros,” the foundational stack of AI: compute, cloud, models, and tooling, remains in flux. Unlike the early internet, where protocols and browsers stabilized quickly, the AI industry is still searching for its definitive architecture.

“Human beings don’t like that change; we don’t like this rapid transformation. How do we break through that and find real value? It’s tough, and I think we’re all going through that experience,” Rengaswamy added.

AI bubble: are we living it?

The sheer volume of venture capital currently in the market is historically unprecedented. Christine Keung, an advisor at Capital6 and former Bridgewater associate, suggested that the market is in a state where it remains “unclear if the public markets can withstand” the massive private valuations assigned to “hot” companies like Anthropic.

Keung highlighted a growing divide: a “Cambrian explosion” of small businesses empowered by AI, contrasted against a shrinking pool of “venture-backable” companies capable of returning the massive funds now managed by institutional investors.

“Our funds are getting bigger, which means the hurdle in which we need to return those funds increases substantially. It is only a bubble if the markets can’t absorb it… right now the bubble actually hasn’t burst yet,” she said.

Jeremy Dalton, an advisor to FOV Ventures, issued a stern warning to founders: the era of AI as a mere marketing term is over.

“Stop buying .ai domain names,” Dalton said.

He cited a recent Deloitte report showing that only a quarter of business leaders have successfully pushed even 40% of their AI pilots into production. According to Dalton, the disconnect between “hype” and “utility” is the primary driver of current turbulence.

Michael Phillips, executive managing director at Alumni Ventures, echoed the need for resilience, emphasizing that “investing through the bubbles” is the only way to catch the next generation of breakout leaders. The focus has shifted to companies that leverage existing AI layers to create tangible profit and efficiency, rather than those simply burning capital on research.

A multipolar race: China and the democratization of AI

The discussion inevitably turned to a profound geopolitical shift. For the first time in modern tech history, the U.S. faces an unchallenged rival in China. This is not just a race for better Large Language Models (LLMs), but a battle for “physical AI” — the integration of intelligence into manufacturing and robotics.

“China has always had an advantage with physical AI,” Keung noted, pointing out the country’s lead in manufacturing.

Panelists also highlighted that China is leading the charge in open-source models, which may ultimately do more to democratize AI than the proprietary ecosystems of Silicon Valley giants. The “DeepSeek moment,”a reference to recent Chinese AI breakthroughs, served as a reality check, proving that the monopoly on high-end innovation has ended.

Rengaswamy observed that the world has moved toward a bipolar reality.

“China and the U.S. are much more polarized. The world is not able to follow a linear or user-driven technology evolution in this transformation,” he said, noting that this creates significant uncertainty.

However, the rise of Chinese open-source initiatives was seen by some as a positive force for global equity.

“It opened up the market. It allowed for a view towards a path of democratization. My hope is that it will lead us on a positive path towards getting AI into the hands of every individual globally,” Keung said.

She compared the current lack of international alignment on AI safety to previous debates over human rights during peak globalization.

“What’s happening right now in our labor economies isn’t new,” she said, grounding the disruption in the historical context of the Industrial Revolution.

“It just feels scary because we’re living in it,” she added.

And they are living that reality firsthand. The panelists also discussed AI’s impact on their work and it was less about dramatic predictions of replacement but more about pragmatic, daily applications: speeding up research, testing ideas, and dealing with an expanding volume of machine-generated material.

“I have six to eight hour conversations with AI regularly… to code solutions. To do that would have cost hundreds of thousands of dollars without it,” Dalton said.

While it has enabled 24-hour research cycles, a new skepticism has emerged. Rengaswamy admitted that while AI has cut his team’s “time to do work” by two-thirds, his own “time to review” has tripled as he filters through AI-generated “slock.”

“Every single deck, every single memo I look at, it takes me probably five minutes to know if it’s done on AI or not. And that just turns me off,” Rengaswamy said.

World.title: ‘Some European leaders don’t want to be photographed with you’ – Georgian PM’s visit to Brussels: what happened
World.content:
Georgia’s Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze took part in the second EU summit, organised by Euronews in Brussels. The summit focused on the prospects for EU enlargement, candidate countries’ integration into the bloc, and the political and economic challenges involved.

At the summit, Kobakhidze invited European Commission representatives to hold open, public debates on democracy, the rule of law, human rights, the economy and transparency.

He said the assessments in the European Commission’s forthcoming report did not reflect reality and described the report as politicised. Kobakhidze said the Georgian government was ready to discuss all contentious issues in public, but claimed that the European side was unwilling to engage in dialogue.

Kobakhidze made these remarks a day before the European Commission published its 2026 annual enlargement report. The report assesses the progress candidate countries have made towards EU membership against criteria including: Democratic institutions and elections;

The rule of law and judicial independence;

Human rights and media freedom;

The fight against corruption;

Economic conditions and reforms;

Progress towards closer integration with the European Union.

What Irakli Kobakhidze said

The prime minister said the Georgian government disagreed with the assessments in the European Commission’s report and believed that issues concerning the country should be open to public debate.

“We criticise European bureaucrats. We are inviting European Commission representatives to take part in a public discussion, a public debate, because we believe that everything in the report does not reflect reality. But let’s debate it. Let’s hold a public debate with European Commission representatives. This is a politicised report,” Kobakhidze said.

He said the European Commission’s report drew on assessments by experts, but the Georgian government disagreed with their conclusions. According to the prime minister, Georgia is one of the most democratic countries among the EU candidates. He also claimed that the country upholds the rule of law and human rights and enjoys high rates of economic growth.

Kobakhidze said the Georgian government was proposing talks with EU representatives, but insisted that they should take place in public rather than behind closed doors. He said the public had a right to know which issues the two sides were discussing and what arguments each was putting forward.

Kobakhidze said the government was confident in its position and believed its decisions served to protect the country’s sovereignty and build a more developed, democratic and transparent state.

Speaking about relations with the European Union, the prime minister said Georgia could not change its behaviour without dialogue. If the European side had concerns about Georgian laws or specific government decisions, he said, it should raise them directly with the Georgian authorities.

“If anyone wants to change Georgia’s behaviour, they should talk to us. But the problem is that they do not talk to us. They are not ready to engage in dialogue,” Kobakhidze said.

The prime minister said Georgia had its own values, which he claimed were in line with those of the European Union. He listed sovereignty, democracy, the rule of law and judicial independence among them.

Kobakhidze also drew a comparison with the Soviet era, saying relations with Europe should not be based on one side giving orders to the other.

“We were part of the Soviet Union for 70 years. I was young at the time, and this is what happened: whatever Moscow said, Georgia had to do. That was not an appropriate approach in a democratic society. Europe needs to adopt a different approach, and we are optimistic that attitudes will change. We are not puppets,” the prime minister said.

Speaking about the attitude of European countries towards Georgia, Kobakhidze also referred to protests in France. He called on EU representatives to apply a consistent and unified approach when assessing Georgia’s laws and government actions.

The prime minister nevertheless expressed optimism that the EU’s attitude towards Georgia would change and that both sides would reconsider the current course of their relations.

At the summit, journalist Maria Tadeo asked Irakli Kobakhidze about the Georgian government’s attempt to ban five opposition parties.

“We have a very good example: Ukraine and Moldova. They have banned political parties and are much further ahead than we are. So we intend to catch up with them,” Kobakhidze replied.

Asked whether this could create problems if he wanted to continue talks with the EU, Kobakhidze said he was inviting “European bureaucrats to provide legal comments”.

“The case is before the Constitutional Court of Georgia. We have asked the court to rule on the constitutionality of certain political parties. This is a legal matter. We are inviting European bureaucrats to provide legal comments. But no one is offering legal comments; they are only making political statements. In doing so, they are interfering with Georgia’s independent judiciary, which goes against European standards,” Kobakhidze retorted.

Maria Tadeo also asked Kobakhidze about his relations with European leaders. In particular, she raised the widely held view that some European leaders would not want to be photographed with him. Kobakhidze replied that he had photographs with all of them.

Comment

According to Rikard Jozwiak, editor of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Europe bureau, the EU’s 2026 enlargement report says the Georgian authorities have taken no steps to improve democracy or protect fundamental rights in the country.

Jozwiak says these problems prompted the European Union to suspend visa-free travel for holders of Georgian diplomatic passports. He warns that this also puts the country’s visa-free regime as a whole at risk.

The report also repeats last year’s assessment that Georgia remains an EU candidate “in name only” and continues to turn down the benefits that come with candidate status and the pre-accession process.

What is the Euronews EU Enlargement Summit?

The Euronews EU Enlargement Summit is an international political event organised by the European media outlet Euronews in Brussels. It was first held in 2025.

Its main purpose is to discuss the prospects for EU enlargement: how the process of admitting new member states should move forward and what political, economic and democratic reforms this requires.

The summit brings together representatives of EU institutions, leaders of EU member states, presidents and prime ministers of candidate countries, members of the European Parliament, and political and economic experts.

Discussions cover candidate countries’ progress, EU enlargement policy, security, democracy and economic cooperation. The event is broadcast on television and digital platforms.

However, this is not an official EU summit or a formal negotiating format organised by EU institutions. Rather, it is a high-level international forum for discussion.

Euronews EU Enlargement Summit

World.title: Foreigners face higher costs and stricter requirements to obtain residency in Armenia
World.content:
Armenia’s new residency application rules

From 1 November, foreigners in Armenia have had to apply for residency permits entirely online. The government has also increased the state fees applicants must pay.

A temporary residence permit now costs 150,000 drams ($418), up from 105,000 drams ($293). A permanent residence permit now costs 250,000 drams ($698), compared with 135,000 drams ($377) previously. Applicants will not receive a refund if the authorities reject their application.

The Migration and Citizenship Service says the number of people seeking residence permits in Armenia has recently increased.

For example, Armenia granted residence permits to 10,561 foreigners in the first half of 2026, compared with 6,656 during the same period in 2025. That represents a 59% increase. Russian citizens make up the largest group among those who received temporary or permanent residence permits.

Analyst Artem Yerkanyan believes that Armenia is regulating the inflow of foreign nationals in line with its own interests.

He explains that making it harder to obtain residency clearly shows that the country is shifting its priorities from quantity to quality.

However, he sees no reason to believe that Armenia will stop attracting people relocating from abroad, particularly from Russia.

“For the overwhelming majority of Russian relocants, this reform will not be a life-changing ordeal. They will be able to adapt easily to the new conditions,” Yerkanyan said, pointing to the rules that apply within the Eurasian Economic Union.

Russia leads the EAEU, whose members include Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia. The union operates a customs framework that guarantees the free movement of labour, goods, services and capital.

Foreign nationals can obtain temporary residency if they have grounds to stay in Armenia for at least one year. These include studying, employment, family circumstances, business activities, Armenian ancestry or other grounds recognised by law.

Foreigners can qualify for permanent residency if they are married to an Armenian citizen, have a close relative who holds Armenian citizenship or have a close relative with special residency status. However, applicants must also have accommodation and sufficient means of subsistence, and must have lived in Armenia for at least three years. Applicants of Armenian ancestry or those who run a business in the country can also qualify for permanent residency.

Special residency status will no longer be granted: what is changing?

The changes, which took effect on 1 November, affect not only state fees but also the eligibility criteria for residency and the procedures for processing applications.

The Interior Ministry says temporary residence permits will now be valid for up to one year, while permanent residence permits will last five years.

The grounds for obtaining permanent residency include:

Armenian ethnicity;

making investments in Armenia;

providing exceptional services to the country;

having family ties or running a business in Armenia, subject to additional legal requirements.

From now on, Armenia will have only two types of residency status: temporary and permanent.

The authorities will no longer grant special residency status. However, those who already hold it will retain all their rights and obligations until their status expires.

Until 1 November 2026, Armenia also granted a special residency status valid for 10 years. The prime minister awarded it to foreign nationals of Armenian descent, as well as foreigners engaged in economic or cultural activities in Armenia. They received a special Armenian passport that allowed them to enter and live in Armenia without an entry visa. People with special residency status enjoyed the same rights and freedoms as Armenian citizens and had the same obligations. The only exception was that they could not vote. They were also exempt from compulsory military service in the Armenian Armed Forces.

Applicants must now submit residence permit applications through a single online platform. The authorities will make decisions within 30 days.

“EAEU regulations will remain in force” – deputy interior minister

Armenia’s Deputy Interior Minister Armen Ghazaryan said that citizens of Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) member states remain subject to special rules. These reflect the union’s principle of free movement of labour.

As a result, EAEU citizens do not need special permits to work in another member state.

“This provision remains in force. Throughout their employment in Armenia, citizens of EAEU member states – for example, Russia or Kyrgyzstan – are considered to be legally residing in the country.”

According to Ghazaryan, once EAEU citizens obtain a document confirming the legality of their stay in Armenia, they enjoy the same rights as other foreign nationals legally residing in the country.

The document confirming their legal stay costs 30,000 drams ($83).

The deputy minister stressed the importance of digitising procedures for granting residency on the basis of employment or education. He noted that study ranks second among the reasons foreign nationals apply for residency in Armenia. Employment accounts for the largest number of applications.

He also said the government plans to introduce a new type of visa – a work visa – to make it easier for people to enter Armenia. It will complement the existing visa categories: visitor, official, diplomatic and transit visas.

Comment

Analyst Artem Yerkanyan notes that the changes which took effect on 1 November will primarily affect foreigners engaged in economic activities in Armenia.

He points out that, previously, a foreign national could obtain residency by registering as an individual entrepreneur and paying minimal tax. Under the new rules, applicants will have to:

“Invest a more substantial amount in their business – either maintain a bank account balance of at least 1 million drams ($2,793) or provide proof of turnover over the previous 60 days;

In addition, if a foreign national is a co-founder of a limited liability company, its registered capital must amount to at least 2 million drams ($5,586).”

As for Russian citizens, the expert noted that they will continue to benefit from the privileges available to citizens of EAEU member states. In particular, Russians can stay in Armenia for 180 days a year without restrictions.

“Moreover, if they take up employment in Armenia under an employment contract, they will no longer need additional permits. They will only have to pay the fees and taxes required by law,” he added.

Yerkanyan believes that Russian relocants will be able to adapt to the new rules after the necessary consultations.

“They should approach these changes with understanding, as they reflect Armenia’s national interests. Armenia is not the only country reforming its legislation. Kazakhstan, for example, has taken a similar path, and its rules are considerably stricter.”

According to Yerkanyan, the changes to the residency application process reflect both Armenia’s transition to biometric passports and its efforts to liberalise the visa regime with the European Union. In other words, the EU has driven these changes through its requirements.

He believes countries around the world are now seeking to attract migrants who are “law-abiding, economically active, competent and well-educated”:

“In this respect, Armenia is in a fairly advantageous position, because the migrants arriving here – Russians, as well as Indians and Iranians – are not ‘problematic’ migrants.”

In his view, Europe, by contrast, faces serious threats from the arrival of “problematic” migrants. However, he stresses that Armenia should also approach migration with greater caution.

“Until recently, the Russians arriving in Armenia were self-sufficient IT specialists. But if Russia does announce mobilisation, less affluent people may try to move to Armenia. They are more likely to create additional problems for the country than to contribute to the state budget.”

Armenia’s new residency application rules

World.title: Georgia’s new amendments to Election Code: how will they affect right to challenge election results?
World.content:
The Georgian government is proposing amendments to the Election Code that would significantly affect the procedures for counting votes and challenging election results, the powers of the election administration, and the registration rules for local and international election observer organisations.

The bill was introduced in parliament on 28 October.

What will change

Election results will no longer be compiled at district level

Until now, Georgia has had three tiers of election commissions:

Precinct commissions , which operate at polling stations and count the votes cast at each station separately;

, which operate at polling stations and count the votes cast at each station separately; District commissions , which collect and consolidate data from the precinct commissions in their respective districts;

, which collect and consolidate data from the precinct commissions in their respective districts; The Central Election Commission (CEC), which compiles the overall results based on data from the district commissions.

Under the proposed changes, polling station protocols will go directly to the CEC, which will compile the results itself.

The final results protocol can only be challenged on specific grounds

Under the amendments, a challenge to the results protocol will only be admissible if:

It omits or incorrectly records data from precinct election commissions;

It omits, incompletely records or incorrectly reflects the results of final court rulings concerning violations of election law.

The amendments also specify that “a claim filed with a court in violation of the requirements of this paragraph will not be admitted for consideration”.

If a court does accept a claim, it will only be able to examine the specific circumstances defined by law.

District commissions will no longer have to conduct random recounts after elections

Until now, district commissions had to randomly select five polling stations and recount their votes within six days of the end of an election.

The amendments abolish this requirement.

The bill’s authors argue that, at polling stations equipped with electronic voting machines, officials count the votes after printing out the results. At stations without such machines, they digitise ballot papers within two days and publish them online. They say this makes additional random recounts unnecessary.

The deadline for finalising election results will be cut from 26 days to 15

Previously, the CEC had 26 days to finalise the results of parliamentary elections, Tbilisi City Council elections and the Tbilisi mayoral election. It had 15 days to finalise the results of local government elections and mayoral races in other municipalities.

Under the new rules, the CEC will have to finalise the results of all elections within two weeks of election day – no later than the 15th day.

Any court proceedings challenging election protocols must also conclude within this period.

The explanatory note accompanying the bill says that 14 days are sufficient to challenge results before district commissions and in court.

“Accordingly, by the 15th day, final protocols that have entered into force will already be in place, while the additional 11 days only prolong the process,” it says.

Winners will have less time to submit campaign spending reports to the Audit Office

An electoral subject – a party or bloc – that preliminary results show has secured the legally required number of votes will have to submit a full report on its election spending to the Audit Office within five days.

Previously, parties had 12 days to submit these reports.

If a party that wins an election fails to submit its report on time or violates the law, the Audit Office will issue a written warning and demand that it rectify the problem. If the violation is serious and could have affected the election results, the CEC will be able, on the Audit Office’s recommendation, to apply to the court and finalise the results without counting the votes cast for that party.

Broadcasters will no longer be able to reallocate unused political advertising slots to other parties

Under the new bill, the final second of every political television  must display the name and number of the electoral subject. Broadcasters will not be allowed to air political s that fail to meet this requirement.

Previously, broadcasters and publications could reallocate advertising time or space to another electoral subject if a party or bloc declined to use its allocated slot.

The amendments will prohibit this practice.

The bill’s explanatory note says the change will help prevent broadcasters from allocating political advertising time beyond the limits set by law.

“This effectively removes the right to challenge election results”

Nona Kurdovanidze, director of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), believes the amendments would effectively remove the possibility of challenging election results.

The lawyer points in particular to the new rules governing challenges to the CEC’s final results protocol. She says that, had these rules applied during the 2024 parliamentary elections, it would not even have been formally possible to challenge violations of ballot secrecy. Consequently, the Tetritskaro court precedent would never have been established.

The Tetritskaro precedent concerns events during Georgia’s parliamentary elections on 26 October 2024.

Voters marked a circle next to their preferred party’s number on the ballot paper. They then placed the ballot inside a special frame envelope and fed it into an electronic vote-counting machine. The ballot papers were printed on thin paper, so the marker ink showed through on the reverse side. As a result, anyone could see how a voter had cast their ballot when they inserted it into the machine.

GYLA subsequently launched legal proceedings over the breach of ballot secrecy, seeking to annul the results at every polling station that used electronic voting technology.

On 4 November, Vladimir Khuchua, a judge at the Tetritskaro District Court (Tetritskaro is a town in southern Georgia), upheld GYLA’s claim and annulled the results at 30 polling stations in two electoral districts. This was the first time a court had confirmed a breach of ballot secrecy during the 2024 elections. However, on 7 November, the Tbilisi Court of Appeal overturned the ruling.

Amendments to Georgia’s Election Code

World.title: Georgia’s ruling party founder Ivanishvili again named press freedom predator
World.content:
Illustration by Reporters Without Borders (RSF)

Bidzina Ivanishvili, the oligarch, founder and honorary chairman of Georgia‘s ruling party, who is widely regarded as the country’s de facto ruler, has once again been included in the annual list of “Press Freedom Predators” compiled by the international organisation Reporters Without Borders (RSF).

The 2026 list features 33 “predators”, including politicians, businesspeople and companies, accused of harassing journalists and media outlets over the course of the year.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and Nicaraguan leader Daniel Ortega remain permanent fixtures on the list. It also includes the presidents of Azerbaijan, Belarus and Turkey — Ilham Aliyev, Alexander Lukashenko and Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

“What do they have in common? The same hatred of press freedom. Their methods differ, but their goals are the same: to silence independent voices and trample on freedom of information. Killings, prison sentences, discrediting campaigns, propaganda, the use of troll armies… Any means are considered acceptable to silence opponents. This is an ironic ranking that nevertheless illustrates the diversity and brutality of the strategies used against journalism,” RSF wrote.

US President Donald Trump was also added to the list of “predators” in 2026 over his attacks on the media.

“Since the beginning of his second term, attacks on the press have increasingly gone beyond rhetoric and general government policy, escalating into physical restrictions on journalists,” the organisation’s report said.

The list is divided into five categories according to the type of persecution faced by media outlets in each country: political pressure, threats to safety, legal pressure, economic pressure and social pressure.

Bidzina Ivanishvili is included in the economic category, while Ilham Aliyev is listed in the political category.

In the economic category — which includes those who “financially strangle media outlets” — Ivanishvili is joined by technology giants Alphabet and Meta, French billionaire Vincent Bolloré, head of a pro-Kremlin propaganda organisation Vladimir Tabak, and Kenyan President William Ruto.

RSF on Bidzina Ivanishvili

The RSF report describes Ivanishvili as a billionaire oligarch, former prime minister and founder of the Georgian Dream party.

“He remains the real power behind Georgia’s government. His business empire and network of influence allow him to exercise tight control over the country’s media landscape, particularly through the pro-government television channels Imedi and Rustavi 2,” RSF said in its profile of Ivanishvili.

According to the profile, under his influence, the country’s economic resources and state institutions are used to restrict independent media through financial pressure, repressive laws, censorship and legal prosecution.

Independent journalists are stigmatised, intimidated and silenced.

The following incidents of pressure on the press were documented in Georgia during 2026:

Mzia Amaglobeli, a prominent figure in independent journalism, remained in custody after the Supreme Court rejected an application for her early release.

New repressive laws were adopted, introducing criminal liability for receiving certain forms of foreign funding, thereby threatening the existence of independent media outlets and the NGOs supporting them.

The Communications Commission was allegedly manipulated to punish television channels seeking to hold the authorities accountable, particularly Formula TV and TV Pirveli. The restrictions went as far as prohibiting them from using certain critical expressions about the authorities.

There was a growing trend of legal proceedings and sanctions against journalists, alongside restrictions on their parliamentary accreditation.

Ivanishvili’s profile also quotes remarks he made in 2024:

“…Human rights and freedom of thought and expression are protected; we have a sound judiciary, the media are independent, and businesses are inviolable — a country where people live freely and no longer fear political persecution.”

The following year, in 2025, Ivanishvili was included in the “Press Freedom Predators” list for the first time.

Georgian Dream’s reaction

The Georgian Dream party attributed Bidzina Ivanishvili’s inclusion in the “Press Freedom Predators” list to the machinations of the “global war party” — a mysterious, supposedly all-powerful organisation that the Georgian government blames for all its troubles.

Georgian Dream’s official position is that Ivanishvili’s inclusion in the list is “nothing more than the price that the honorary chairman of Georgian Dream, the figure with the greatest political — and not only political — authority in Georgia, is paying at great personal risk for refusing to sacrifice our country’s peace, national interests and sovereignty to serve the interests of the global war party”

Background

Over the past two years, the work of independent media in Georgia has been restricted in several ways. The authorities have tightened legislation, physical and legal pressure on journalists has intensified, and financial difficulties have threatened the survival of several independent and regional media outlets.

The main restrictions include:

Restrictions on foreign funding: The Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence, adopted in 2024, required media outlets and organisations receiving foreign funding to undergo special registration. An additional law adopted in 2025 made government approval mandatory for receiving foreign grants.

Expanded powers for the regulator: Amendments to the Law on Broadcasting gave the Communications Commission greater powers to interfere in the operations and content of media outlets. The commission has repeatedly used these powers to fine broadcasters critical of the government.

Persecution and intimidation of journalists: Physical attacks, threats, detentions and legal proceedings against journalists have become more frequent. Four journalists are currently in prison, three convicted on criminal charges and one on administrative charges.

Restrictions on court reporting: Legislative amendments have restricted the right to film and report on court hearings. Over the past year, filming has been banned not only in courtrooms but also in courthouse corridors and courtyards.

Obstacles to journalists working in parliament: Georgian Dream has sought to prevent correspondents from media outlets it considers unfavourable from entering parliament wherever possible. It uses the accreditation system as a means of imposing restrictions. Following a complaint from an MP, parliament can suspend a journalist’s accreditation for a specified period. The rules for issuing single-use accreditations have become increasingly bureaucratic, with more and more journalists being denied them.

Financial pressure: Repressive laws adopted over the past two years have reduced funding sources for independent media outlets. Georgia’s advertising market was already limited, and it has now become highly polarised, with most advertising revenue going to pro-government television companies. As a result of the financial crisis, one opposition television channel and several small regional media outlets have closed over the past two years. Some outlets have switched to remote working with reduced resources. Many journalists have been forced to change professions, while many others have emigrated.

As a result, independent media outlets in Georgia now face legal, financial and physical pressure simultaneously.

Georgia ranked 135th out of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 World Press Freedom Index, down from 114th place in 2025.

World.title: Where do you see your children’s future – in Georgia or abroad? JAMnews street poll. Video
World.content:
Where do parents see their children’s future in ten years’ time – in Georgia or abroad? What influences their choices, and how confident are they that their children can have a better life in Georgia? This time, we put these questions to passers-by on the streets of Tbilisi.

Context

Over the past few years, increasing numbers of people have been leaving Georgia. Emigration has long been one of the country’s main challenges, but its nature and scale have now changed.

In the past, those who left were mostly middle-aged people, often just one member of a family, seeking work abroad. Now, however, young people and families with children are leaving. Most have no plans to return.

According to the National Statistics Office of Georgia, 114,374 people left the country in 2025, most of them young people, official data show.

Some leave to study, others to find better jobs. Others have lost everything they had in Georgia because of the country’s ongoing political and economic crisis. People who have experienced political repression are also choosing to emigrate.

Most respondents said they would all like to live in Georgia. They enjoy life there and believe that living in one’s homeland is always better. However, they feel that opportunities to do so are becoming increasingly scarce.

Some said their children had been living abroad for a long time. They had settled there and started families of their own. “Sadly, my grandchildren do not even speak Georgian,” one respondent lamented.

Many respondents admitted that they would like their children to stay in their homeland, close to their parents. However, they do not want to deprive them of opportunities to build a better future.

Here are some of the most telling responses we received:

“My children live abroad. Not because life there is better, but because life here was bad. They want to return to Georgia. But I am a mother, and I want to make sure they do not face discrimination or disadvantage here”;

“Life in Georgia is still better. But given the current situation and the atmosphere in the country, I would not be entirely happy for my child to grow up here”;

“I will support my child whatever they want and decide. If they want to stay in Georgia, they can stay. If not, they can go abroad. Personally, I think going abroad is better because I don’t see much opportunity for development here. I cannot create the future I want for my child,” said a young woman pushing a pram with her newborn baby.

One respondent said that she had lived in Spain with her three children for several years, but the family had recently decided to return to Georgia so that the children would not forget their mother tongue.

“When they grow up, they can choose for themselves where they want to live. But I want conditions here to be good enough for them not even to think about leaving.”

Street poll in Tbilisi

World.title: Karabakh: Why have only 40,000 of planned 140,000 Azerbaijanis returned?
World.content:
Return of Azerbaijanis to Karabakh

Azerbaijan will mark Victory Day on 8 November. The first state programme, known as the “Great Return”, is due to conclude at the end of this year. According to data from the State Statistical Committee, 40,520 former internally displaced persons (IDPs) had returned to Karabakh and East Zangezur as of 1 October.

However, under the programme, 140,000 people were expected to return by the end of 2026. With just three months remaining before the programme’s conclusion, only around 29% of the target had been met.

In 2025, JAMnews reported on the social problems associated with the return of displaced people. This time, we examine a different question:

Why has less than a third of the target been achieved as the first programme nears its end, and what could the second programme change?

What do the figures show?

Indicator Target

Latest figures

Number of former internally displaced persons (IDPs) who have returned

Around 140,000 people

40,520 people (as of 1 October)

Number of settlements 100 47 (as of September)

Area cleared of landmines 280 000 hectares

Around 300,000 hectares (as of September)

Funding

More than 32bn manats (approx. $18.8bn)

More than 25bn manats (approx. $14.7bn) (2020–2026)

Sources: Official government portal, State Statistical Committee, Prime Minister Ali Asadov and Azerbaijan National Agency for Mine Action (ANAMA).

The pace of returns is increasing. At the beginning of the year, the number of returnees stood at 26,014. This means that a further 14,506 people returned to the region over nine months. If the current pace continues, it will take another five years for the remaining roughly 100,000 people to return.

The frequently cited figure of 96,068 refers to the total number of people living, working and studying in the region. In January, President Ilham Aliyev said that “120,000, 130,000 or 140,000 people” could be living and working there by the end of the year. However, he also acknowledged that implementation of the programme could take longer than expected:

“I have told everyone, and I can tell the public now, that I have never set any deadlines.”

Nevertheless, the programme itself sets the end of 2026 as the deadline for achieving its target.

Razim Amiraslanli, deputy chairman of the opposition Musavat party, told Meydan TV that around 20 of the 47 settlements had been rebuilt, while the remainder were villages that came under Azerbaijani control in 2023.

That same year, around 100,000–120,000 ethnic Armenian residents of the region were forced to flee to Armenia. Yerevan describes the events as ethnic cleansing, while Baku maintains that Armenians can return if they accept Azerbaijani citizenship.

What has the money been spent on?

In September, Prime Minister Ali Asadov said that more than 25bn manats (approximately $14.7bn) had been allocated from the state budget for the reconstruction of the region since 2020.

This year’s budget earmarked 3.5bn manats (approximately $2.06bn) for reconstruction. According to Finance Ministry figures, 1.76bn manats (approximately $1.035bn) was spent over the first nine months of the year. Of this amount, 891.8m manats (approximately $524.6m) went towards infrastructure development, while a further 692.5m manats (approximately $407.35m) was allocated to projects in education, healthcare and culture.

Ilham Aliyev explained the distribution of funds, saying: “As infrastructure projects are implemented, more funds will naturally be allocated to housing construction.”

However, critics argue that the main problem is a lack of transparency. According to Meydan TV, annual progress reports on the programme’s implementation are not publicly available, while the website of the centre responsible for monitoring the programme does not publish its findings.

How serious an obstacle do landmines remain?

According to Azerbaijan’s Mine Action Agency (ANAMA), 979 landmines and 3,070 unexploded ordnance items were discovered in October alone. The agency had previously reported that 421 people had been injured or killed by landmines and other explosive devices between November 2020 and April 2026, including 72 fatalities. In September, ANAMA chairman Vugar Suleymanov said there had also been cases of previously cleared areas becoming contaminated with landmines again as a result of flooding.

Journalist Tapdig Farhadoglu told the Caucasian Knot news outlet that much of the territory could become habitable within 10–15 years, while the full restoration of mountainous areas could take 20–30 years.

Economist Natig Jafarli, meanwhile, considers the current pace of returns justified. Speaking to the same outlet, he expressed confidence in the official statistics and noted that a phased return of displaced people made it easier to ensure their safety. He argued that too much emphasis should not be placed on deadlines and numerical targets, saying that “these are not Soviet five-year plans”.

Housing is available, but what about jobs?

Analyst Togrul Juvarli told the Caucasian Knot news outlet that the 1,200-square-metre plots of land provided with houses were insufficient for viable farming. Meanwhile, large agricultural enterprises offer local residents low-paid jobs. Economist Natig Jafarli also pointed out that internally displaced persons had not received land plots during the agricultural reforms of the late 1990s. He believes they should now be granted private ownership of land.

Razim Amiraslanli, deputy chairman of the opposition Musavat party, described the situation in an interview with Meydan TV:

“If a village has housing but no jobs, opportunities to use land are limited, starting a business is difficult, and people have to leave again to find work in other cities, it is hard to call this a genuine Great Return.”

Aytaj Amirjanli, who relocated to the village of Vangli in Aghdara district, told Radio Liberty that she had been registered with the employment service for ten months. According to her, the village has neither a pharmacy nor public transport. She claimed that “most residents are already locking up their homes and leaving for Baku”.

Meanwhile, presidential aide Hikmet Hajiyev advised residents to submit complaints directly to government officials rather than record and circulate videos expressing their grievances.

On 30 October, MP Agil Abbas told parliament that around 10,000 people originally from Aghdam were not registered in the city and did not have internally displaced person status. Parliamentary Speaker Sahiba Gafarova objected, saying: “So much work has been done. Why are you trying to discredit it?”

What could the second programme change?

In September, Prime Minister Ali Asadov said that the draft of the second programme had been submitted to the president. He also described the implementation of the first programme as successful. The targets of the new programme have yet to be made public. According to Finance Ministry projections, 13.2bn manats (approximately $7.765bn) is expected to be allocated to the region’s reconstruction between 2027 and 2030.

Under amendments approved in July, anyone who refuses housing offered by the state loses their status as an internally displaced person. Human rights defenders argue that this violates the principle of voluntary return, while pro-government media portray the changes as a restoration of property rights.

Razim Amiraslanli has called for a comprehensive audit of the first programme. He believes the new programme should focus not on the number of buildings constructed, but on the number of people who have found employment and families who have received land plots.

Новости в Азербайджане

World.title: Garibashvili case 2.0: Trial begins over second charge against Georgia’s ex-PM
World.content:
Second charge against Georgia’s ex-PM

On 2 November, Tbilisi City Court began hearing the bribery case against former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili.

This time, Garibashvili himself was present in the courtroom, marking his first appearance at a hearing in the case. He had previously described the court proceedings as a “masquerade” and maintained in letters from prison that he would not take part in them.

“It is very important that the proceedings are conducted transparently,” Irakli Garibashvili said at the start of the hearing, explaining his decision to attend.

However, the hearing was closed to the public at the prosecution’s request. Prosecutors argued that the case involved the Defence Ministry, required testimony from other senior officials and concerned personal data.

Garibashvili and his defence team strongly opposed the decision. His lawyer argued that such proceedings had never previously been held behind closed doors. He maintained that the case involved no classified information and that the decision had been made solely because Garibashvili was attending the hearing.

This is the second criminal case against Garibashvili. He was charged with accepting a bribe on 24 August 2026, an offence punishable by 11 to 15 years in prison. According to investigators, former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze handed Garibashvili, who was prime minister at the time, 750,000 lari (approximately $292,000) from a 1.5m-lari (approximately $584,590) bribe allegedly received from businessman Zurab Tukvadze, who had won a tender for the Gori Military Hospital. In effect, prosecutors allege that Burchuladze shared the bribe with Garibashvili. Burchuladze himself testified against the former prime minister. The first criminal case against Garibashvili concerned money laundering. On 12 January 2026, he pleaded guilty and reached a plea agreement with prosecutors, receiving a five-year prison sentence instead of the nine to 12 years prescribed by the Criminal Code.

“Long live the layman!”

Despite being held behind closed doors, the hearing was well attended. Those present included Irakli Garibashvili’s wife, eldest son, brother-in-law and uncle. However, only two of his allies from the ruling Georgian Dream party attended: former Justice Minister Rati Bregadze and former MP Luka Kurtanidze.

“Long live the layman!” Luka Kurtanidze cheerfully exclaimed as Garibashvili entered the courtroom, apparently seeking to emphasise that the former prime minister was now an ordinary citizen. The remark earned him a stern warning from Judge Tamar Mchedlishvili.

Garibashvili sat in a glass-enclosed dock reserved for defendants, surrounded by security guards. Dressed entirely in black, he appeared to have lost weight. He occasionally glanced towards the courtroom from behind a guard’s shoulder and smiled at his wife.

The hearing began with the standard procedure of establishing the defendant’s identity.

“First name, surname?“

“Irakli Garibashvili, son of Tariel.”

“Do you speak the state language?“

“I’m trying,” Garibashvili replied, attempting to make a joke.

“I can make jokes too, but this is a courtroom. Let’s keep things appropriate,” the judge responded sternly.

Shortly afterwards, journalists were asked to leave, and the hearing continued behind closed doors.

“Ivanishvili has been misled”

Following the hearing, Garibashvili’s family members declined to comment to the media. The former prime minister’s son, Nikoloz, tried to push reporters aside to escort his mother out of the courtroom.

Garibashvili’s lawyer and two fellow party members who had come to support him spoke to journalists.

“I came to see a friend whom I have missed very much. I want to wish him strength and hope that he will return to his family very soon,” former Justice Minister Rati Bregadze said.

Asked whether he believed his friend had committed a corruption offence, Bregadze said it was for the court to decide.

“I am truly proud to have had the opportunity to work alongside Irakli Garibashvili. The court will determine everything else. This is all very emotional for me,” he said.

The former minister declined to answer when asked whether the new charge was linked to the appointment of Mamuka Mdinaradze as head of the State Security Service.

However, Luka Kurtanidze, a former freestyle wrestler turned politician known for his fiery temperament, was more forthcoming. He called Mdinaradze a “rat” and claimed that Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili had been “misled”.

“I am happy to have seen the layman, Irakli Garibashvili. He is healthy and strong. Only fools and rats like Mdinaradze would believe this nonsense [about accepting a bribe],” he said.

“Garibashvili was subjected to psychological pressure”

Details of what Garibashvili said after journalists were ordered to leave the courtroom emerged from his lawyer, Soso Baratashvili.

According to Baratashvili, the former prime minister told the court that he had been subjected to psychological and moral pressure before the investigation began in an attempt to force him to admit to accepting a bribe.

The lawyer called on investigators to launch an inquiry, claiming that Garibashvili could provide information confirming that he had been subjected to pressure.

“He did not name anyone today. But during the investigation, he will, of course, identify who made the proposal. He will explain all the details to investigators. This allegation is not unfounded,” the lawyer said.

Baratashvili argued that the decision to hold the trial behind closed doors was unjustified and intended to conceal details of the case.

“The prosecution is using this as a tool. It wants to cover up the case and hide the details from the public, the media and human rights defenders. This is a very serious violation,” he said.

According to Baratashvili, the defence intends to appeal the judge’s decision.

Background

Irakli Garibashvili is more than just a former prime minister. For nearly two decades, he was one of the closest and most trusted associates of Bidzina Ivanishvili, who is widely regarded as Georgia’s de facto ruler.

Before entering politics, Garibashvili served as director-general of Ivanishvili’s Cartu Foundation and represented his business group. When Ivanishvili stepped down as prime minister in 2013, he effectively handed the position to Garibashvili, who was just 31 at the time.

Garibashvili served as prime minister from 2013 to 2015. He later became defence minister before Ivanishvili backed his return to the premiership in 2021.

In April 2025, Garibashvili announced his retirement from politics. Later that year, he was imprisoned on money-laundering charges.

World.title: ‘Certain circles in Russia and Eurasian Economic Union back secret plan by Armenian opposition’ – Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on secret plan by Russia and Armenian opposition

Armenia has reached a very important historic turning point, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said during a discussion of the 2027 state budget. He described it as a moment that would have a decisive impact on the country’s political, economic and social development.

However, he said that forces both inside Armenia and abroad were seeking to prevent this historic moment from arriving. According to Pashinyan, similar forces had opposed Armenian statehood in the past, dating back to 2018. That was the year of Armenia’s “Velvet Revolution”, which brought him and his team to power. “But this year, their cards have been laid bare,” Pashinyan stressed.

He singled out the so-called “secret plan”, which opposition circles have been discussing recently.

“The aim of this plan is to prevent Armenia from continuing on its path of economic development. There are not enough resources inside Armenia to implement this secret plan, so its authors must do everything possible to secure resources from abroad,” he said.

The prime minister spoke about this “secret plan” a couple of weeks ago, but did not specify which countries he meant. This time, however, he openly named them:

“I do not want to hide the fact that certain circles within the Eurasian Economic Union, led by Russia, and in the Russian Federation itself support this plan. And there are reasons for this, because people have been sent to Armenia with specific promises and guarantees.”

Samvel Karapetyan, leader of the pro-Russian opposition Strong Armenia party, has repeatedly spoken about a “secret plan” to change the government in Armenia. He made these remarks in response to a question about the steps the opposition intended to take to oust the current authorities. At his weekly briefing on 22 October, Nikol Pashinyan said that forces both inside Armenia and abroad were taking steps to effectively eliminate the country: “The aim is to provoke political instability inside Armenia. As a result, they intend to take control of the Armenian state. In other words, they want to strip Armenia of its independence – first de facto, and then de jure.” The prime minister also said that several similar attempts had taken place over the past three years. He cited, in particular, the events in Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023 and hybrid attacks on Armenia during the parliamentary elections, which took place in June this year. He believes a third attempt is now under way. In particular, he was referring to an expert forecast by the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council, which warned of an allegedly catastrophic economic downturn in Armenia if the country left the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU. “This is part of the ‘secret plan’ that people are actively discussing now,” Pashinyan said.

“Armenia’s political forces must understand that the people are their only guarantee”

The prime minister said that certain opposition figures had “received specific guarantees and been sent to Armenia”. He then asked: “So why are these guarantees not being honoured?” He went on to answer his own question, urging the opposition to look back at the history of the Armenian people. He said that whenever such “guarantors” had emerged, the outcome had invariably been another catastrophe.

“I am essentially doing our opposition colleagues a favour by pointing out that they still have time to avoid a similar catastrophe. I am talking about the political catastrophe facing opposition parties, which you all know about. I hope they will seize this opportunity to avoid it.”

He recalled that he had previously urged the opposition to stop relying on these “guarantors” and instead focus its efforts on strengthening Armenia’s independence and sovereignty. However, his proposal went unanswered.

“In effect, it was rejected through silence. I believe the window of opportunity has not yet closed. Ultimately, our political forces must understand that there is only one guarantee – the people of Armenia,” he stressed.
