World.title: Decisive choice in Iran-US confrontation: Deal or war?
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 4. Over the past 50 years, November 4 has acquired particular significance in relations between Iran and the United States. Numerous events and developments involving the Islamic Republic of Iran and the United States have been associated with this date. In Iran, November 4 is marked on the calendar as the National Day of Fighting Global Arrogance. Historical events involving Iran and the United States are particularly prominent on this day. Interestingly, the defeat of Republicans by their Democratic rivals in elections to both chambers of the US Congress on November 4 has created a particular atmosphere in Iran.

The first high-level reaction in Iran to the US elections came from Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who led the Iranian negotiating delegation at the Islamabad talks. In a post on X, he said that Americans had said "no" to war and that Iran supported this position. He also noted that Iran would respond if the US government betrayed the will of its own people.

A number of other Iranian officials subsequently issued statements. Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Eje'i, Chief Justice of Iran, one of the country's three main branches of government, also wrote on X that the US president had lost both the war and the political battle. Iran, he said, would demonstrate further defeats for the United States. This is only the beginning.

Iran's new Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, took a somewhat different approach to the US elections. He said that those who hoped a change of party or conduct, or the granting of any concessions to the United States, would lead Washington to abandon its hostility toward Iran were mistaken.

"Iran's imposition of control over the Strait of Hormuz and its attacks on US military bases in countries across the region were intended as a response to US attacks. At the same time, this is considered the first war against the United States at the regional level. If attacks against Iran are repeated, their scale will be much broader and greater," he said.

Now, let us turn to the main question: how likely are further attacks against Iran following the US elections? More broadly, what direction will relations between Iran and the United States take?

Both sides - the United States and Iran - have serious reservations about negotiations, reaching an agreement and ensuring that it is implemented and not abandoned. Each side seeks to blame the other for the lack of progress.

In recent months, alongside Pakistan and Qatar, Russia and China have also become increasingly active in matters related to Iran's nuclear program, the Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and broader regional developments. Visits by Iranian officials to both Russia and China, the Russian foreign minister's trip to Tehran and other exchanges indicate that regional actors are in favour of ending the war. Both Iran and the United States have put forward demands, but they have been unable to find common ground on these issues for at least the past year and a half. As a result, attacks against Iran began, prompting Tehran to launch strikes against the other side's positions.

It can be assumed that major international players will seek to reduce tensions in the region by promoting an agreement similar to the 2015 nuclear deal, or one that incorporates the demands and concessions of both sides. The fate of more than 400 kilograms of uranium enriched by Iran to 60% is among the issues most frequently raised by the United States and the International Atomic Energy Agency.

At present, diplomatic exchanges between Iran and the United States are continuing through Qatar's mediation. As far as is known, neither side intends to back down from the conditions it has put forward. While it may seem unreasonable to expect Iran to have confidence in diplomatic efforts when the United States has taken no practical steps, serious proposals from China and Russia could help Tehran place greater trust in the diplomatic process.

The meeting in Tehran of the parties to the Mecca Pact should also be taken into account. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye are seeking to reduce regional tensions, depending on Iran's approach to this regional agreement.

From an economic perspective, the situation appears highly tense. The Strait of Hormuz, which once served as a route for the transportation of 15% of the world's energy supplies, along with other essential commodities, is now under threat. This is clearly unacceptable to any of the parties involved.

A large share of Iran's trade is conducted through its southern ports. The naval and air blockade is having a negative impact on the country's trade. Despite the economic and trade restrictions it faces, Iran remains unwilling to back down from its position in the face of the United States. The United States, meanwhile, is also facing certain difficulties as energy prices rise.

Taking all these developments and circumstances into account, the current picture suggests that the likelihood of a further escalation and a new outbreak of war in the near future is quite low.

However, it should not be forgotten that UN Security Council Resolution 2231, adopted in 2015, is no longer in force. The six resolutions that preceded it, along with the extensive sanctions imposed on Iran over its nuclear program, have been reinstated. This signals that unless the parties reach an agreement in the near future, war and tensions could flare up again.

World.title: Algeria, Azerbaijan plan to hold first joint commission meeting in 2027
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 4. Algeria and Azerbaijan plan to hold the first meeting of their joint commission in 2027, Algerian Ambassador to Azerbaijan Zakia Ighil said, Trend's correspondent reports.

She made the announcement at an event in Baku marking the 72nd anniversary of the start of the Algerian Revolution.

“The establishment of a joint commission this year marked an important milestone in the development of bilateral cooperation. We expect its first meeting to be held in Baku in the first half of 2027,” the ambassador said.

She also noted that cooperation between the two countries is gaining new momentum thanks to political dialogue, interparliamentary exchanges, the development of cultural ties, and collaboration within international and regional organizations.

In addition, the ambassador noted significant potential for deepening the partnership in the fields of hydrocarbons, natural gas, petrochemicals, and renewable energy: “In this regard, we welcome this year’s ratification of the memorandum of understanding on cooperation in the oil and gas sector.”

World.title: Azerbaijan forecasts 4.4% annual non-oil GDP growth through 2030
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 4. Azerbaijan projects average annual real GDP growth of 3.3% in 2027–2030, while non-oil and gas GDP is expected to grow by an average of 4.4% annually. The non-oil and gas sector is expected to become the main driver of economic growth during this period.

According to the draft package of budget documents for 2027, the macroeconomic forecasts take into account the country's economic growth trends, the potential impact of global economic developments on Azerbaijan, existing sectoral strategic documents, medium-term development targets, ongoing reforms and budget policy parameters.

The main framework for the next strategic period will be defined by the Strategy for Socio-Economic Development in 2027–2030 and the Second State Program on the Great Return.

GDP growth to be driven mainly by the non-oil sector

According to the forecasts in the draft, Azerbaijan's nominal GDP will amount to 141 billion manat ($82.9 billion) in 2027. For comparison, this figure stood at 126.5 billion manat ($74.4 billion) in 2024, is expected to reach 129.1 billion manat ($75.9 billion) in 2025 and 138 billion manat ($81.2 billion) in 2026.

Real GDP growth is projected at 2.7% in 2027. Average annual real growth is expected to reach 3.3% in 2027–2030.

The role of the non-oil and gas sector in the economy is expected to strengthen further during this period. Non-oil and gas GDP is projected to reach 109.1 billion manat ($64.2 billion) in 2027, with real growth of 4.4%. The sector's average annual real growth rate is also forecast to reach 4.4% in 2027–2030.

For comparison, non-oil and gas GDP amounted to 86.2 billion manat ($50.7 billion) in 2024 and 92.3 billion manat ($54.3 billion) in 2025, and is expected to reach 100 billion manat ($58.8 billion) in 2026.

Oil and gas sector expected to continue contracting

Meanwhile, the oil and gas sector is expected to maintain a downward trend in the coming years, reflecting production dynamics.

The sector's GDP contribution is projected at 31.9 billion manat ($18.8 billion) in 2027, down from an expected 38 billion manat ($22.4 billion) in 2026. Real output in the oil and gas sector is forecast to decline by 1.8% in 2027, with an average annual contraction of 0.4% in 2027–2030.

The document notes that declining oil production in recent years has had a negative effect on the sector's growth. Oil and gas production forecasts were prepared based on data provided by the relevant organizations.

Based on production projections, the oil and gas sector is expected to contract by 1.8% in 2027, followed by average growth of 0.1% in 2028–2030 as oil production stabilizes.

Oil and gas production forecasts

According to the figures included in the draft budget package, oil production in Azerbaijan is projected to decline from 29.1 million tons in 2024 to 26.6 million tons in 2027. Production is expected to reach 26.1 million tons in 2028, 26.6 million tons in 2029 and 26.3 million tons in 2030.

Natural gas production increased from 38.6 billion cubic meters in 2024 to 38.9 billion cubic meters in 2025. It is projected at 37.8 billion cubic meters in 2026 and 35.6 billion cubic meters in 2027.

Gas production is expected to decline further to 33.2 billion cubic meters in 2028 before recovering to 35.3 billion cubic meters in 2029 and 36.6 billion cubic meters in 2030.

What will drive growth in the non-oil and gas sector?

The draft document states that despite ongoing geopolitical and geoeconomic tensions, as well as persistent uncertainty and risks in the global economy, Azerbaijan's economy, including its non-oil and gas sector, maintained positive growth in 2025 and during the period elapsed in 2026.

It notes that improvements to credit guarantee and interest rate subsidy mechanisms for businesses, support for transportation costs associated with non-oil and gas exports, compensation for export clearance costs, and subsidies for electricity grid connection fees for industrial and agricultural facilities will contribute to the sector's development over the medium term.

At the same time, several priorities have been identified to ensure sustainable economic growth in the non-oil and gas sector.

These include accelerating economic and export diversification, improving the effectiveness of government support mechanisms for businesses, strengthening the role of the financial sector in economic activity, promoting private investment and attracting foreign direct investment into the non-oil and gas sector.

Other key priorities include expanding public-private partnership mechanisms, improving the economic efficiency of state-owned legal entities, managing public assets more effectively, and gradually transferring them to private-sector management and ownership.

Further priorities include expanding the use of artificial intelligence and innovation, accelerating digital transformation, increasing productivity in industry, agriculture and services through modern technologies, boosting renewable energy generation and deepening the energy transition.

The document also identifies the reintegration of liberated territories into the national economy, reconstruction and development in the Karabakh and East Zangezur economic regions, faster regional socioeconomic development and effective use of opportunities offered by the Middle Corridor as factors supporting economic growth.

According to the draft, medium-term growth in the non-oil and gas sector will be driven mainly by the continued development of non-oil and gas industry, construction, tourism, trade and transport.

World.title: How will Azerbaijan's budget balance change if inflation rises? - Prognoses until 2030
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 4. Deviations in Azerbaijan’s inflation from the forecast level are expected to have a limited impact on fiscal indicators in the medium term. At the same time, rising inflation could lead to a deterioration in the consolidated budget-to-GDP ratio, while lower-than-projected price increases could lead to an improvement in this indicator.

This was reported in the fiscal risk analysis included in the draft state and consolidated budgets for 2027.

The document notes that persistent high uncertainty in the global economic environment, price trends among major trading partners, and volatility in international commodity markets are the main external risk factors for inflation.

“In particular, continued geopolitical tensions in the Middle East could create additional volatility in energy and other commodity prices. At the same time, a weakening of the nominal effective exchange rate could accelerate the pass-through of imported inflation to domestic prices.

As for domestic factors, under current fiscal and monetary policies, the likelihood of aggregate demand rising to a level that would significantly increase inflationary pressure is assessed as low,” the report notes.

In assessing the potential impact of inflation on fiscal indicators, the effects of price-level changes on nominal GDP, government budget revenues, and the ratio of fiscal indicators to GDP were taken into account.

To this end, various scenarios were developed for 2027–2030 based on inflation deviating from the baseline forecast by 0.5, 1, and 1.5 percentage points above and below.

According to the calculations, changes in inflation will have a limited impact on the ratio of the non-oil primary deficit to non-oil GDP under the existing scenarios. However, according to projections, this ratio, which stands at approximately 18% in 2026, is expected to approach 12% by 2030 under the baseline scenario.

The document emphasizes that, under the most pessimistic scenario, the 12% interim target for the ratio of the non-oil primary deficit to non-oil GDP could be exceeded by 0.5 percentage points in 2030. Thus, under this scenario, the ratio is projected to reach 12.5%.

As for the consolidated budget balance-to-GDP ratio, the data show a surplus of 6.6% in 2022, 8.7% in 2023, 4.7% in 2024, and 3.4% in 2025. In 2026, this figure is projected to approach zero and amount to approximately 0.2%.

According to forecasts, the consolidated budget balance-to-GDP ratio is expected to shift to a deficit of approximately 2.2% in 2027, followed by a gradual improvement in subsequent years, reaching a deficit of 1.1% in 2030.

Inflation exceeding the baseline scenario is assessed as a factor that worsens the consolidated budget balance-to-GDP ratio, while inflation below the baseline scenario is assessed as a factor that improves it. The scenario ranges also show that, by 2030, this indicator could settle at different levels depending on changes in inflation.

Measures to Mitigate Inflationary Risks

The document notes the importance of implementing flexible fiscal policy and targeted social protection programs to manage fiscal risks in an inflationary environment.

It is reported that the use of preventive financial mechanisms to minimize the negative consequences of unexpected price increases can both protect government revenue and ensure sustainable economic growth.

World.title: Director-General of ICESCO congratulates President Ilham Aliyev
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 4. Salim bin Mohammed AlMalik, Director-General of ICESCO has sent a congratulatory letter to President Ilham Aliyev.

The text of the letter was published on the official website of the President of Azerbaijan.

"Excellency,

On the occasion of Victory Day, celebrated on 8 November, I have the honor to extend my warmest congratulations to Your Excellency and to the people of the Republic of Azerbaijan, together with my sincere wishes for the continued peace, prosperity and well-being.

This important national occasion reflects the resilience, unity and determination of the Azerbaijani people, while embodying the profound value of peace and the aspirations of future generations for stability, security and a prosperous future. May the spirit of this day continue to inspire further achievements for Azerbaijan and its people.

It was a great pleasure to participate in the 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue in Baku, a distinguished international platform that continues to foster mutual understanding and build bridges among cultures and civilizations. The opportunity to be received by Your Excellency was a particular honor, allowing for a valuable exchange of views on our shared priorities and the further strengthening of cooperation between ICESCO and the Republic of Azerbaijan.

The warm and constructive relationship between ICESCO and the Republic of Azerbaijan remains highly valued, as reflected in our ongoing cooperation in promoting educational opportunities, safeguarding cultural heritage and fostering dialogue among peoples and civilizations. I am confident that this partnership will continue to grow in depth and impact, opening new avenues for joint initiatives that serve our Member States and contribute to a more peaceful and harmonious world.

Please accept, Excellency, the assurances of my highest consideration and my sincere wishes for the continued peace, prosperity and well-being of the friendly people of the Republic of Azerbaijan," the letter reads.

World.title: Pensioner fears delays for urgent medical scope as waitlist grows
World.content:
Greg Twigger has been waiting three months for a colonoscopy, despite being considered an urgent case.

The 69-year-old has been happily living in Hobart for eight years, but recently he's considered leaving the state to get a timely medical procedure.

He returned a positive test from a routine bowel screening kit in August, and the wait for results has left him worried and out of options.

"I'm sick and tired," Mr Twigger said.

" I'm on the pension, but I can't wait. "

Greg Twigger, 69, has been waiting three months for a colonoscopy, despite being considered an urgent case. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

A positive screening test means blood was detected, but it does not determine that a person has bowel cancer, or other health conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease.

For Mr Twigger, the result places him as a category 1 patient for a type of endoscopy called a colonoscopy — a day procedure using an internal scope to diagnose the cause of the bleeding — which is clinically recommended to be performed within 30 days.

After consulting with his doctor, Mr Twigger is considering paying out-of-pocket for private medical care.

"I've been told 120 days is a very, very common wait time," he said.

" This problem isn't going away until I cough up the thousands of dollars to get a private assessment. "

Increased demand outstrips health response

While waitlists and the percentage of patients seen within clinically recommended wait times for elective surgeries in Tasmania are made publicly available, statistics for endoscopies are not.

'A bunch of platitudes': Colonoscopy waitlist leaves man in limbo Tony returned a positive result from a bowel cancer screening kit in June. Almost three months later, he is still waiting for an endoscopy to find out if he has cancer.

The ABC requested the most recent data from the Tasmanian Health Department in mid-September.

The new data, which was provided to the ABC on Tuesday, shows the number of patients on the category 1 endoscopy list has grown from 2,878 in July 2024 to 3,864 in June this year.

The number of category 1 procedures being performed within that 30-day window has not kept up with the demand.

In July 2024, 27 per cent of the most urgent category of endoscopy procedures were completed within 30 days.

In June this year, just over 15 per cent of category 1 endoscopies were performed within the clinically recommended timeframe.

On Wednesday, state Health Minister Bridget Archer announced a $40 million investment over three years to improve endoscopy services across the state.

Bridget Archer says the three-year investment would deliver 9,000 endoscopies. (ABC News: Jonny McNee)

Ms Archer said the investment would deliver 9,000 endoscopies, with an immediate focus on the most urgent presentations and a goal of clearing the category 1 waitlist by the end of June 2028.

"That will be achieved by a range of things, possibly some additional Saturday lists as well as some opportunities for outsourcing as well," Ms Archer said.

Funding labelled as 'bandaid' fix

The health minister said the increase in demand for endoscopy services could be partially attributed to the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program, a federal initiative that sends free bowel cancer screening kits to Australians aged between 50 and 74.

"It hasn't come with any additional resources to states to respond to the outcomes of that," Ms Archer said of the program.

Tasmanian Labor MP Sarah Lovell said while the funding announcement would be welcomed by those waiting for a procedure, it amounted to a "bandaid fix" that she did not believe would clear category 1 wait lists.

Sarah Lovell is sceptical that the funding would deliver the intended outcomes. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

She also questioned how the funding would address waiting times.

"This is an announcement that they have made because we had somebody speak out really bravely about their situation just a couple of months ago," Ms Lovell said.

Mr Twigger said the government's investment had not reduced the significant emotional distress he has experienced as he continues to try to secure a procedure.

"I saw my GP this morning, and they said, 'we're going to send that request through again. This happens all the time'," he said.

"It's category 1. Well, if that's the rating that I got, then God help the people in category 2 and 3."

World.title: Survey reveals Australia's multicultural society 'more divided'
World.content:
Australia's multicultural society is becoming more divided, less trusting and "more pessimistic" as households report more cost-of-living concerns, according to the latest Scanlon Foundation social cohesion survey.

The Mapping Social Cohesion study, now in its 20th year, surveyed 10,000 adults about issues including immigration, multiculturalism, life satisfaction, and household finances.

The report's introduction says it has been a "shocking year for Australia", noting the Bondi terrorist attack, instances of intolerance and racism, and persistent worry about financial stress stemming from the Iran conflict and rising interest rates.

"People are feeling there isn't a lot of opportunity for them to be able to achieve the things they want to," Scanlon Foundation chief executive Anthea Hancocks said.

"There tends to be people who are quite despondent about the state of affairs."

Anthea Hancocks says survey respondents are more pessimistic now than in previous years. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

This year, one in three respondents expressed anxiety about their future, agreeing with the statement that their life "will be a little or much worse" in the next three to four years.

That is a three-fold increase since the survey began in 2006.

Likewise, respondents who state they were "happy or very happy" have been slowly declining over the past 20 years.

Mounting financial stresses left many households unable to pay for the essentials, including meals (13 per cent), rent or mortgage (13 per cent), medicine or healthcare (21 per cent), and household heating and cooling (19 per cent).

Those most likely to experience financial hardship were young and middle-aged adults, especially women and single-income households.

Ms Hancocks said people's "sense of belonging" shrinks when they feel "financially compromised".

"They tend to become more insular," she said.

When it comes to fixing the problem, trust in the federal government has been reversing from its early COVID-19 pandemic high, with more than one in five people now believing it will "almost never" do the right thing.

Almost half of the respondents (48 per cent) felt Australia's "system of government" needed "major change" or "should be replaced" — the highest number since the question was first asked in 2014.

"The level of trust in government has for the vast majority of the population been fairly stable," Ms Hancocks said.

"But the impact of One Nation voters who have very strong views about not being able to trust government has dragged the numbers down."

Disillusionment over immigration, report finds

A key trend identified in the report is growing disillusionment towards immigration.

The number of people believing immigration levels were "too high" has surged since the COVID-19 pandemic, reaching 59 per cent in 2026, the highest result on record.

A majority of respondents still believed that accepting immigrants made Australia stronger, but the proportion has fallen recently (from 78 per cent in 2022 down to 64 per cent this year).

Nearly two in five respondents (38 per cent), the highest rate on record, agreed immigrants "take jobs".

Those who supported One Nation were, by far, the least likely to support immigration and overwhelmingly felt immigrants were not adopting "Australian values" — a term the survey noted had varying meanings to different people.

The party's voters were also found to be the most pessimistic about Australia's future, while also being a significant outlier when it came to distrusting others.

The Scanlon Foundation survey found One Nation supporters were particularly pessimistic about Australia's future. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica )

"The feelings towards immigration are very much influenced by people's political leanings," Ms Hancocks said.

"It's a perspective, not necessarily the actual situation. People are still listening to narratives that are telling them that there are these waves and waves of people coming into Australia, which is not really accurate."

While the report noted that debate about immigration was fair game, it expressed concern that "racial hatred" and "violence" had become "common", placing a strain on Australia's "multicultural fabric".

Ms Hancocks said many respondents felt social cohesion was getting worse (62 per cent) but stressed the report's actual social cohesion index has been flat in recent years.

"Australia's social cohesion is very resilient," she said.

"Primarily the reason for that is because of the strength that exists within people's neighbourhoods."

Financial strain no excuse for intolerance

Former Australian of the Year Amar Singh said the report's findings were unsurprising, as he had noted an increase of racist slurs and attacks towards Indian Australians.

Flashback: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese presented Australia's Local Hero award to equality campaigner Amar Singh back in 2023. (ABC News: Georgia Roberts )

This included online abuse against him, with one recent email stating Mr Singh needed "to die".

"Last week we had a senior citizen in Perth who got assaulted," he said.

"Somebody assaulted him and took his turban off in a shopping centre.

"It is really scary," he said.

Mr Singh, who runs the food relief charity Turbans 4 Australia, said demand for the service had gone up "tenfold", while donations were going backwards.

"We're finding it very hard to keep up with the demand," he said.

One in four young men now say violence for a cause can be justified Trust in politicians is down but Australians remain confident in key institutions, according to a new survey examining the country's democracy.

"I could get a text or an email to say, 'hey, I'll move into a shelter, or I've only got the couple of pairs of clothing that I'm wearing.'"

" That is the dire situation people are in. "

But he added that financial strain was no excuse for intolerance.

"This financial crunch is being felt by everybody," he said.

World.title: Australians not scared enough of manosphere threat, DV commissioner says
World.content:
Domestic, family and sexual violence (DFSV) commissioner Micaela Cronin says Australians are not scared enough of "manosphere" content drawing young Australian men into radical, violent and misogynistic views.

The commissioner is urging state and federal governments to take more action to prevent misogynistic influencers online from undermining decades of work to end violence against women and children.

"I don't think we are scared enough about what is coming down the pipeline," she told the ABC.

"Governments, both the Commonwealth and states and territories, have to collectively grapple with the scale of the problem we're facing."

Ms Cronin said the upcoming second action plan, which provides specific details on what governments have agreed to do to end violence against women and children, should be accompanied by substantial funding increases to frontline services and prevention programs.

As Ms Cronin enters the final 12 months of her five-year term as the first DFSV commissioner, she is particularly concerned by the rate of young people perpetrating sexual violence against one another.

She said that while there were a number of factors contributing to the problem, including an increase in violence against children who then go on to replicate the behaviour, the internet is partly to blame.

"[Part of the problem is] the increase of the impact of the online environment on children and young people's understanding of the world and themselves and relationships and sexual relationships," she said.

"[Along with] the rise of the influence of harmful pornography on how children are being educated about what sex is."

Authorities still playing catch-up

Young men are routinely being fed male-supremacist content on social media, and it appears to be affecting their behaviour in the real world.

Studies from Monash University and the University of Adelaide have described a rise in sustained, sexist behaviour of boys in school, which teachers link to an increased exposure to extreme, anti-women content.

Men's behaviour change groups could soon face new rules Programs range from one day sessions in schools educating boys on respectful relationships to months-long programs working with men who have abused their partners and children.

In another Monash survey of 2,600 teachers, educators said they had been subjected to sexual harassment, degrading behaviour and violent threats.

The academics who led the study describe it as "misogynistic radicalisation".

Ms Cronin said the impact the online world was having on young people kept her up at night.

"I'm very worried about that … the difference in what we are seeing about young men's attitudes than their grandfather's attitudes, the increase in misogyny online, the impact that is having both on young women and young men, gender-diverse people, about their views about relationships."

Do you know more about this story? Get in touch via Signal (claudialong.01) or email claudialong@proton.me

Earlier this year, a Melbourne University study found younger men are more likely than older men to hold misogynistic views about a woman's place in society and violence against women.

Almost a quarter of gen Z men believed the movement for women's equality should be violently resisted, with researchers finding that content that is misogynistic and endorses violence against women is the most likely influence on extremist attitudes in Australia.

Asked whether growing male-supremacist beliefs and violence against women are being taken seriously enough as a national security issue, Ms Cronin said progress was being made, but authorities were still catching up to the scale of the problem.

Micaela Cronin is frustrated governments have not adopted her recommendations. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

"I think we're getting there … there's a catch-up process still around information sharing.

"If you're going to be thinking about how do you use what we're learning about online misogyny to keep women safe in their homes, [it] is different than when you are talking about terrorism and community acts.

"[But] there are similar processes about developing those attitudes absolutely, and we need to be thinking about that in our prevention and early intervention approaches."

What action is being taken?

One prevention measure the commissioner endorses is the federal government's digital duty of care, which she said could help subdue some radical anti-women content online.

Loading...

"We need to be thinking about safety and principles of safety from the very outset, not as an afterthought, not putting up guardrails after the horse is already bolted," she said.

But Ms Cronin said there were still more federal and state governments needed to do, such as implement the hundreds of recommendations from previous reviews, royal commissions and inquests into violence against women and children.

These recommendations include cutting off late-night alcohol deliveries earlier in the evening, funding justice-system navigators to support those going through the courts for sexual-violence matters and investing more in frontline services.

"What I'm really looking forward to is the launch of the second action plan and seeing the investment that is required to implement what we already know needs to be done," she said.

That plan is expected to be released in the first half of 2027.

World.title: Meta is still training its AI on Australians, but now you can stop it
World.content:
Meta has quietly introduced a way for Australians to stop the tech giant from training its AI on their user data, but the company never announced it, leaving the choice effectively hidden for more than a year.

There was furious public backlash in mid-2024 when it was revealed Meta was using photos, posts and comments stretching back to 2007 to train its AI.

At the time, Australians were told that unlike EU citizens, they could not opt out because of weaker privacy protections in Australia.

But ABC News has learned an "objection" form has been available locally since July 2025, buried within privacy settings.

Social media already trains Meta's AI If you're among the majority of Australians with Facebook or Instagram accounts, your social activity on those platforms might be training Meta's artificial intelligence (AI) tools.

"You have to go digging through their privacy policies and their support pages … certainly they haven't been doing outreach to users," said Tom Sulston from Digital Rights Watch.

"A lot of people who would like to use that option are not going to find out about it.

"And you can understand why — there's a commercial imperative for [Meta] to get their hands on as much of our data as they can."

The objection form has been available in the EU since 2024, but the ABC has confirmed that no separate announcement was made when it was added in Australia a year later.

Nor have there been any reports of users being notified directly by Meta.

Instead, the information has only recently been filtering out via user-generated posts.

"While it's good that we can opt out … we haven't really been given a choice if we're not made aware of that choice in the first place," Mr Sulston said.

How to opt out of Meta's AI training

A step by step guide:

Loading

Alternatively, if you're logged in to your Facebook account, the form can be found here.

According to Meta, users who submit a form will get an email confirming the company will not use their public data to train its AI in the future.

It also explains that accounts set to "private", are already exempt, as are all private messages, and accounts listed as belonging to under 18s.

Why did Meta start offering Australians an opt out?

Meta has not shared why it made the decision and the relevant sections of the Australian Privacy Act have not changed in recent years.

One possible explanation is that the question of how the law applies is not entirely settled.

The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) previously issued public guidance that "just because data is publicly available … does not mean it can legally be used to train … AI models".

Since Meta's AI training practices were first revealed, the OAIC has been assessing the company's behaviour.

"The issue of whether social media platforms are permitted under Australian privacy law to train AI models on user data is a matter the OAIC has had under consideration for some time," a spokesperson said.

According to Meta, users who submit a form will get an email confirming the company will not use their public data to train its AI. (REUTERS/Yves Herman)

"We have engaged extensively with Meta and other platforms, and intend to publish the results of our investigations in the coming months."

Some privacy advocates believe Meta's decision might be a response to that legal ambiguity, or even a pre-emptive move, as the government mulls further changes to privacy rules.

"By doing something, [Meta] can claim that they've done something, and then it's easier for them to use our data everywhere else to train AI," Mr Sulston said.

"The problem is, of course … we're not informed about how we might make that decision.

"So it lets them meet some obligations … but at the same time it doesn't really fundamentally change anything".

Meta was approached for comment.

World.title: Will Trump's midterms wipeout hit Australia's already shaky economy?
World.content:
"It's a brilliant situation."

That was Donald Trump's bizarrely upbeat summation yesterday of the politically devastating war in Iran, just before the brutal verdict of US mid-term voters began rolling in.

"We seem to be getting everything we want," the president told the Financial Times, talking up the amount of oil now flowing through the Strait of Hormuz.

American voters clearly see things differently. Fed up with what they're paying for that oil, and with another drawn out foreign entanglement, they've taken their anger out at the ballot box with a stinging rebuke across once reliably Republican states including Texas, Iowa and Kansas.

The question now is what a weakened and famously unpredictable president does next.

Trump's immediate pledge to work with Democrats in Congress was a positive sign. How long that may last is anyone's guess.

If this election was a repudiation of the war, how will Trump respond?

The arguments inside his administration now matter even more. Vice President JD Vance is seen to be in the de-escalation camp, preferring a negotiated settlement. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is said to favour escalation and a more intense bombing campaign.

Trump's own description of the status quo as "brilliant" suggests there are no easy answers, and he may prefer to muddle along with things as they are.

The voters have just made that considerably harder.

Cost-of-living casualties

What Trump does next won't matter just in Washington.

US allies, including Australia, are becoming increasingly outspoken about this war and its shock wave of inflation.

The Albanese government initially supported the US strikes aimed at denying Iran a nuclear capability. It didn't anticipate the economic damage this would ultimately create. Nor did it expect the conflict to drag on for 9 months and counting.

American democracy has spoken but will Donald Trump listen? These midterm election results are an emphatic defeat for the US president, but anyone who thinks he is a lame duck does so at their own peril.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers, with the authorisation of colleagues, has led the escalating rhetorical charge.

"If it was up to me, from an economic point of view, the war in the Middle East would end today," the treasurer told Radio National, "because Australians are the cost-of-living casualties of decisions taken in DC and Tehran."

After this mid-term result, expect even bolder calls to end this war.

The risk for the treasurer is the louder he blames the US and Iran, the more he is seen to be passing the buck on his own responsibilities for inflation.

Jim Chalmers is expected to increase his criticism of the war in Iran, particularly how it's impacting the hip pockets of Australians. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

As the Reserve Bank governor made clear, this week's interest rate hike, the fifth this year, was not due to the "direct impact of oil prices on inflation". Michele Bullock said this was about dealing with "domestic capacity pressures".

But the Reserve Bank is hardly pretending global oil price is playing no role here. It clearly is.

Either way, the government knows it must do more to tackle inflation. It's promising spending cuts in what is now looming as a crucial mid-year budget update next month.

If Labor is judged to be unserious about this challenge, when Bullock is warning the next 12 months will "feel like a recession", the government will be in even more political strife.

Loading

The uncertainty of the moment

But this is not as straightforward as it might seem. The economy is at a delicate point, particularly after this latest rate rise. There are real and widespread concerns within the government about cutting too hard.

The downturn in the housing market is proving sharper than was expected when the negative gearing and capital gains tax changes were announced in May. While lower house prices alone aren't seen as a problem, the impact on already soft consumer sentiment and spending is.

There's also a growing concern within the government about the jobs market deteriorating faster than was expected.

The story behind the RBA's inflation target How did the Reserve Bank choose its 2 to 3 per cent inflation target?

This nervousness about tipping an economy that already "feels like a recession" into an actual downturn explains the reluctance to commit to "net savings" in the budget update.

The prime minister remains confident inflation and interest rates will come down in time for the 2028 election. A recession along the way is most definitely not part of his plan.

A mid-year slash and burn to tame the inflation dragon is not on the cards.

The government is left in an awkward situation. Cut too little and look weak on inflation. Cut too hard and risk making a bad economic situation worse.

Even the Reserve Bank governor acknowledges the uncertainty of the moment.

"We do our best with our forecasts," Bullock said after delivering this week's rate hike, "but they're uncertain, and things change, and who knows?"

To all that economic uncertainty, Australia can now add another variable: a wounded Donald Trump.

"Brilliant" is hardly a word the Albanese government would use to describe this outlook.

David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or on iview.

World.title: Women vulnerable to eating disorders and body image issues in midlife
World.content:
Alone and frustrated.

That's how Sue Cody felt when seeking help for an eating disorder in her 50s.

Even after losing a significant amount of weight, Ms Cody said it was a constant struggle to have her symptoms taken seriously and get the help she needed.

A new analysis from Women’s Mental Health Australia and national eating disorder charity Butterfly Foundation suggests key life transitions, including perimenopause and menopause, can intensify body image concerns.

This is what happened to Ms Cody, who lived with bulimia until her late 20s when her daughter was born.

"My focus become more on becoming a mother, so the eating disorder was still there, it just sort of reared its head when life got stressful," she said.

Sue Cody developed bulimia in her early 20s, which largely receded during early motherhood. (Supplied: Sue Cody)

But during perimenopause, Ms Cody's body changed, her self-esteem plummeted and her only child moved out of home.

This had a cumulative impact on her mental health and led to her developing anorexia.

Experts say there is a need for more awareness and support for older women experiencing body image concerns or living with an eating disorder.

Body confidence drops with age

The Butterfly Foundation estimates 1.1 million Australians live with an eating disorder, with recent research showing we have the highest rate of anorexia and bulimia in the world.

While the most common age group is 15–19 years, older women are also vulnerable: 42 per cent of women living with an eating disorder are aged 35 and older, and 16 per cent are aged 50 and older.

Global rise of anorexia Researchers have analysed the global numbers of people with anorexia and bulimia nervosa, finding an increase of 71 per cent worldwide since 1990.

Mel Wilton, head of communications and engagement at Butterfly Foundation, said middle-aged women typically faced a number of challenges, including menopause-related biological changes, relationship shifts and added caring responsibilities.

"As we get older, we go through different life stages: perimenopause, menopause, caring for aging parents, kids leaving home and older kids," she said.

"And all of the pressures are combined with society telling us that aging is an illness, that you need to avoid it at all costs."

A small survey from the Butterfly Foundation found that body confidence in women declined with age, with fewer than one in 10 baby boomers (61 to 80 years) reporting feeling confident about their own bodies, compared to one in five women under 45 years.

"The expectation is that as we get older, we become less concerned [about body image] but it's apparent that that's actually not true," she said.

42 per cent of women living with an eating disorder are aged 35 and older, and 16 per cent are aged 50 and older. (Unsplash: Vonecia Carswell)

Katrina Locandro, chief operating officer of Women's Mental Health Australia, said the figures on eating disorders in older women were likely an underestimation.

"One in four women experiencing menopause are also experiencing body image issues," she said.

" Body image doesn't have an expiry date, we need to stop treating it as a young woman's issue and start recognising it as a women's health issue across the life span. "

Social media content contributing to problem

Social media can have a negative impact on how a person views their own body.

Karen Spielman, a Sydney-based GP and research associate at InsideOut Institute for Eating Disorders who did not contribute to the new analysis, said content in recent years had pivoted from body positivity to idolising skinny bodies.

"It's so upsetting," she said.

"It makes it harder to promote overall body positivity, to look at the whole person rather than just the number on the scale."

Dr Spielman said this change was, in part, driven by the rise in popularity of GLP-1 receptor agonists, sold under brands such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro.

Trevor Steward is running a trial looking at the impact of GLP-1s on people living with binge eating disorders. (Getty Image: Tatsiana Volkava)

Trevor Steward, an associate professor at the University of Melbourne and director of the Brain and Mental Health Hub who did not contribute to the new analysis, was also concerned about content he saw online.

"You're creating this perfect storm, where a person is receiving these images on the one hand to say: 'I should look a certain way', and then receiving ads for an online pharmacy which say: 'GLP-1s delivered to my doorstep tomorrow,'" he said.

" This just really, in my opinion, is taking advantage of people who are in a very vulnerable position. "

Experts have previously voiced concerns that injectable weight-loss drugs may put people living with or at risk of an eating disorder at further risk.

Screening tools for warning signs

Dr Spielman said a GP was typically the "first port of call" for many people living with an eating disorder seeking help.

But not all health professionals know the warning signs to look out for, or the best advice to give patients, she said.

To address this gap, Dr Spielman and her colleagues developed resources and screening tools for GPs to use.

"It's super important to take this seriously, it's not easy for patients to present for help," she said.

Ms Locandro wants all healthcare clinicians, not just GPs, to proactively ask patients questions about their mental health, instead of relying on patients' self-reporting.

Katrina Locandro says stigma surrounding eating disorders can make it hard to seek help. (Supplied: Katrina Locandro)

"There is a level of shame that some women really place on having an eating disorder later in life or body image issues later in life," she said.

"A lot more [research] needs to be done to find out the real scope."

Ms Cody, still in recovery, wanted older women to know they were not alone.

After struggling to find help locally, Ms Cody found support online and said it had also been useful to connect with others of a similar age living with an eating disorder.

"At the end of the day, I don't want to look back on my life and remember what I weighed, I want to remember how much I lived," she said.

World.title: Live: Trump says Iran war worth it despite Republican midterm losses
World.content:
The bottom-line is we don’t know yet.

America still has an unpredictable president in office who tends to control the foreign policy strings largely outside of Congress.

But we can make some informed judgements.

The Democratic blue wave is unlikely to offer Europe immediate relief.

With President Donald Trump now constrained at home - that leaves him free to meddle further on foreign policy and trade from the US executive branch, where there are fewer congressional checks.

The key things Europeans are watching for is how he’ll handle trade, the NATO alliance and the war in Ukraine going forward.

Javier Carbonell from the European Policy Centre. (ABC News)

Javier Carbonell from the European Policy Centre said he doesn’t see Trump changing his approach to Europe.

"Trump sees Europe as basically some kind of vassal state and foreign policy is really governed by the executive branch. So, I don't think that's gonna be much difference there," he told the ABC. "If Europe does something that he doesn't like or there's a strategic reason that he wants to do something to Europe, he will still do it."

While we won’t know for some time if a defeated Trump will lash out abroad, what is certain is the far-right wave has been rebuked.

Carbonell said that will have a positive impact across Europe as it gears up for an election super cycle next year.

World.title: Essential workers being priced out of rental market, report shows
World.content:
Essential workers are being priced out of Australia's private rental market as affordability plummets, new research shows.

Anglicare's annual Rental Affordability Snapshot has revealed key occupations, including retail workers, social workers and cleaners, can afford fewer than 1 per cent of rental listings.

Other essential jobs, such as nursing and teaching, are not faring much better, with just 1.1 and 3.3 per cent of listings deemed affordable, respectively.

Social worker Allie Thompson is about to move into a new rental in inner north Brisbane for $740 per week, which will take up about half of her income.

The single mother has chosen to stop taking some of her medications to be able to afford the shift.

"I just avoid going to the doctor's as much as I can unless it's absolutely urgent, and I haven't been to the dentist in probably 10 years," she said.

"My son is the priority, so he gets the dentist, he gets the medical appointments and the mental health appointments.

"I'll choose that any day, but that means I've had to cut back on those other things that are still important."

Nurse Silvia Laing says she has cut back on luxuries to afford rent. (Supplied.)

Silvia Laing has worked as a nurse for more than 40 years, and now supports cancer patients living at home.

The 64-year-old pays $550 a week for rent in Albany, WA, which she splits with her partner.

Ms Laing said that constitutes about a third of her income.

"Holidays are one thing that I've had pretty much cut, and going out for meals has reduced considerably," she said.

"Accommodation and health are on the top priority list, and everything that's somewhat luxury is just not going to be afforded."

Anglicare's own staff are not immune to the impact of rental prices in the north west of WA.

Meenaaz Adams is the organisation's new Pilbara Service Manager and has only just found a rental, eight weeks after moving to the town of Karratha.

Ms Adams was provided with a month of accommodation but did not realise how difficult securing a long-term home would be.

Meenaaz Adams works for Anglicare and has also found difficulty securing a rental. (ABC News: Amy Rossbach)

"We thought that 'oh we'll secure something in four weeks'," she said.

"No, we were declined three times, something I've never experienced."

Increased demand from resource companies had put pressure on the local market, with the average weekly rent sitting at around $1,700.

Wages not keeping up with rent

The Anglicare report surveyed 48,776 rental listings across Australia, measuring each property against the full-time minimum wage for workers in 16 essential occupations.

There are no affordable rental properties for a hospitality worker in the Northern Territory, the report shows. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

Of the jobs included in the research, only three saw an increase in affordability compared to 2025, while the other 13 either decreased or remained stagnant.

For a hospitality worker in the Northern Territory, there are no affordable rentals available in the state.

Elsewhere, only 338 listings remained.

Anglicare Australia executive director Kasy Chambers said wage growth had not kept up with rent increases in recent years.

Kasy Chambers says wages have not increased at the same rate as rents. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"We would have had a social contract or an understanding some years ago that if you worked full-time, if you trained for these kinds of jobs, you would be able to find affordable housing," she said.

" You would be able to live a decent, if not opulent, lifestyle. That's no longer the case. "

Data from real estate analyst Cotality showed unit rents have increased by 44.3 per cent in the last five years, while house rents have gone up by 36.6 per cent.

Ms Chambers said wages have increased by less than half that rate in the same period.

"For those who are paying in the private rental market, sadly, most of that increase has just been swallowed up by rents."

Calls for more social housing

Ms Chambers said the growing disparity between wages and rental affordability was due to an over-reliance on the private market to deliver housing.

"Over the last 40 years in Australia, consecutive governments have stopped building and funding housing," she said.

Anglicare says more social housing is needed to improve affordability. (ABC News: Mitch Edgar)

"We don't necessarily need to build more houses, but what we need to do is build more social housing or shift some pre-existing housing into social housing.

"That's what we need in order to enable these people on these wages to rent affordably."

The federal housing minister was contacted for comment.

Ms Thompson said it was sometimes difficult to justify staying in her profession when money is tight.

"There have been times where I've felt like I'm giving to the community and I'm trying to support our community and the government doesn't care.

"I want to show up and do this job, but why am I in this job if it's not paying as well as it needs to be paying for me to actually have access to those other things I require as well?"

World.title: ASX set to jump as Wall Street soars; Trump Media, Tesla, SpaceX tumble; Oil prices slump
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to jump as Wall Street soars; Trump Media, Tesla, SpaceX tumble; Oil prices slump Stan Choe and David McHugh November 5, 2026 — 5:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

US stocks are soaring after President Donald Trump’s party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections. Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm US election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 jumped 1.8 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 1,524 points, or 2.9 per cent, as of noon Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 2.1 per cent higher. Wall Street soared higher. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to surge higher, with futures pointing to a rise of 172 points, or 1.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.6 per cent on Wednesday. Stocks of solar-power companies, dollar stores and hospital owners helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners from losers following the widespread losses for Republicans. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump’s social-media company, the artificial-intelligence industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans.



The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell below $US100 for the first time in nearly a month. Vice President JD Vance blamed the war with Iran, which caused a spike in oil prices, for Republicans’ midterm losses. Related Article Opinion

US midterms We’ve seen peak Trump, but the next two years will be a rocky ride Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Strategists along Wall Street had been urging investors not to get swept up in the election because it may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington. “Earnings trump elections,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. Still, Wall Street may have gotten a preferred political scenario as Democrats are set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the economy.



Much remains impossible to predict, of course, and Trump retains executive authority over key areas such as defence, foreign policy and in some instances trade. A downbeat forecast could be that “Trump is not now a lame duck, but an angry duck” who might restart tensions over tariffs and NATO allies’ levels of military spending, said Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING Bank. An optimistic view, Brzeski said, is that Trump becomes “a tame duck ... that he will slow down any disruptive efforts and that he will put more focus on trying to win the Nobel Peace Prize by ending the two big wars without big disruption, and on trade, nothing happens but a few words.” Trump’s social-media company, Trump Media & Technology Group, was one of the market’s bigger losers, down 12.2 per cent. Since briefly touching a peak of $US175 five years ago, it’s dropped toward $US5. Its main business is Truth Social, which is most well known for Trump’s postings on the platform.



Elon Musk’s businesses also struggled. Tesla fell 3.4 per cent, and SpaceX sank 3 per cent. Musk, a former top Trump adviser, is among the possible targets for investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress. Trump has been a big backer of the AI industry, and Democratic victories across the country could mean more regulation or restrictions. Concerns have grown across political parties about AI in general. Elon Musk’s companies are suffering heavy losses after the midterms. AP Investors see Democratic wins in Texas in particular as possibly slowing the build out of further AI data centers. AI-related stocks came into Election Day already under pressure because of worries their prices had shot too high. Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the poster child of the frenzy around AI-related stocks, sank 1.3 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, dropped 9.2 per cent



Advanced Micro Devices, another chip giant, held up better. It added 1 per cent after reporting much stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Companies that have been spending heavily on AI chips also did better. Alphabet rose 4.2 per cent, for example, after it tumbled more than 12 per cent Thursday to its worst loss ever on worries that it was spending too much on AI investments. A Democratic-led Congress could push Trump to pull back on the war with Iran. That helped send down stocks of companies that make weapons and other equipment for the US military, including drops of 6.6 per cent for Lockheed Martin, 4.6 per cent for Northrop Grumman and 2.5 per cent for General Dynamics. Democratic control of Congress could light the way for companies in the solar and wind industries. First Solar jumped 9.4 per cent, and Enphase Energy climbed 9.8 per cent.



Stocks of big oil companies, meanwhile, sank. ExxonMobil fell 4.8 per cent, and ConocoPhillips dropped 5.9 per cent. They had been rallying for much of the year after Trump and Israel began the war with Iran, which sent crude prices much higher. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, plunged 9.2 per cent Wednesday to $US94.11. The price for the most actively traded contract in the Brent market has been veering between roughly $US70 and $US120 per barrel since just before the war with Iran began. A Democratic-led Congress could try to reverse some of the cuts to federal healthcare and food assistance that Republicans approved during the summer in their “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” That helped stocks climb across the healthcare industry, including a rise of 9.8 per cent for HCA Healthcare, which runs hospitals and ambulatory sites.



Retailers also benefited on hopes that Democrats may push policies to help Americans struggling to keep up with the fast-rising cost of living. DollarTree, which focuses in particular on lower-income Americans, had one of the market’s bigger leaps and rose 10 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Scorched earth: Iran’s revenge against Trump will be devastating In the bond market, Treasury yields eased. That could be a signal investors see less risk of Washington piling even more debt onto its already big mountain with the coming end to one-party control. Treasury yields had surged through the summer and reached their highest levels in decades because of worries about the US government’s big debt, along with higher inflation and other concerns. A Congress controlled by Democrats could provide a check against more spending and cuts to taxes that would widen Washington’s deficit. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.90 per cent from 4.95 per cent late Tuesday.



Stocks jump in much of the world Indexes climbed across most of the world. Stocks leaped 2 per cent in Paris, 2.2 per cent in Shanghai and 1.8 per cent in London. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was an outlier and fell 1.4 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: After 41 Aussie tours, Suzi Quatro rocks her favourite spots for pasta, duck and daiquiris
World.content:
FoodThe dish After 41 Aussie tours, Suzi Quatro rocks her favourite spots for pasta, duck and daiquiris The American rock legend is about to return for tour number 42. We think we might know where to find her in Sydney and Melbourne. Jane Rocca November 5, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

American rock royalty Suzi Quatro likes to call Australia her second home — unsurprising really considering she’s already toured here 41 times, and will soon return for tour number 42 in November. There’s been lots of change since she first toured in 1974, the era of breakout hits like Can the Can and 48 Trash, but some rituals live on: a booking at her favourite Italian and Chinese restaurants are a non-negotiable. Suzi Quatro will rock Australia in November. “I love coming to Australia and have many friends there. It really feels like a second home,” says Quatro. The 76-year-old took some time out from rocking on to share her favourite places to dine while on the road and when relaxing at home. Eating out



Favourite hometown restaurant Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Lelli’s in Detroit is a classic Italian spot. It’s the only place my grandfather would go to eat good quality food – it’s an Italian steakhouse that originally opened in 1939. Lafayette Coney Island in downtown Detroit is another classic spot for a Coney Dog. Suzi is a fan of Melbourne icon Pellegrini’s. Justin McManus In Melbourne I always go to my favourite restaurant Tipo 00. I do love the pasta dishes here, you can’t go wrong with anything on the specials. I always used to go to Rosetta at Crown Melbourne and eat their tagliatelle Bolognese, but they’re no longer around. It was a blow when that closed down.



Pellegrini’s is where I go for a single espresso and enjoy a serve of their ravioli. I also like Attica – excellent food and service. We go for the degustation menu for two. “When I said, ‘Hi, I’m Suzi Quatro’, they said ‘come in’ and gave us the best table.” The Flower Drum is also another favourite spot. I couldn’t get a booking on the phone when I was last in town, so I took a chance and went down to the restaurant anyway. When I said, “Hi, I’m Suzi Quatro”, they said “come in” and gave us the best table. I ate the most fantastic Peking duck. The tip to dine here came from a Qantas air steward who said the food is fantastic and they were right. Flower Drum’s “fantastic” Peking duck. Simon Schluter Shark Fin Houseis also a great spot for a quick meal.



I like The Tea Rooms 1892 in Block Arcade for a cup of tea and cake on my walk through the city. As I always stay at Crown, I usually grab a bite at Mr Hive and have a breakfast omelette with toast. They also make a great fish and chips here. I’ll often go to Atrium Bar at Crown for a glass of chardonnay. I also really like Cecconi’s in Flinders Lane in Melbourne. It has great quality food and a great vibe. The pasta and rib-eye steak are fantastic. You might bump into Susie at the Shell House bar. In Sydney



I enjoy Shell House for a glass of chardonnay, it has a great atmosphere here. I’m also a fan of Alfredo Authentic Italian Restaurant near Circular Quay for their sirloin steaks. I also love a margarita cocktail from their underground cocktail bar. The dirty daiquiri at Razz Room. Dion Georgopoulos I go to Razz Room in York street, for the dirty daquiris and music – it’s a great underground 1970s NYC style bar. And you’ll also find me at The Duke of Enmore pub and rock and roll venue. It’s a live music spot and where I get a margarita cocktail. Favourite Food City I love going back to Hamburg, Germany. It’s where my husband Rainer Haas [concert promoter] is originally from. I highly recommend Theo’s Steakhouse Grand Elysee. The rib-eye and Theo’s Caesar Salad prepared at the table is the best I have ever tasted anywhere in the world. Hold the anchovies – they’re not for me.



Suzie likes a vegie pasta, like Adam Liaw’s pesto pappardelle with cherry tomatoes. William Meppem Eating in Signature dish at home I love making a vegetable pasta that will last me three days in the fridge. I also make mushroom pesto, eggs over easy and BLTs are my speciality. Guilty pleasure: Popcorn in the microwave.

World.title: ‘Raising my children was tough’: Shaynna Blaze’s journey from single mum to grandmother
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life ‘Raising my children was tough’: Shaynna Blaze’s journey from single mum to grandmother Jane Rocca November 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

TV presenter and interior designer Shaynna Blaze is best known as a judge on Nine’s The Block*. Ahead, the 63-year-old discusses the important men in her life, including her son, Jess, and her co-star Darren Palmer. Shaynna Blaze says she got her enterprising spirit from her late father, Basil. My paternal grandfather, who went by the nickname of Snowy, died when I was very young. His white-blond hair has made its way down the family tree from my dad Basil, to my older brother and now my granddaughter. My maternal grandfather, Roy, moved from Melbourne to Queensland for warmer weather and wasn’t in our lives much growing up. He was a builder who helped build the house I grew up in with my dad. He lived into his 70s. Dad was a fitter and turner and handyman who loved to build everything from scratch. He built garages, laid bricks, did the home extension – there wasn’t anything he didn’t attempt. I really got that spirit from him. We are both Aries and used to butt heads a lot because of our strong personalities. Dad got to be a grandfather and met my two kids. He was kind and gentle.



Dad and I were very close until he died of a heart attack suddenly in 1998. He’d had a heart attack in his 40s that led to a quadruple bypass and went to see his heart surgeon two weeks before he died – there was nothing to indicate anything was wrong. Mum [Annette] packed his lunch for work and never saw him alive again. Twenty-four hours later we turned off the life support and were in shock for a long time. Mum was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s a year later; we felt it was due to the grief of losing dad. She lived with it for 16 years and died 10 years ago. My first boss, Alan Wilson, was a big inspiration. He allowed me to make mistakes and gave me the confidence at 19 to make big decisions. Dad met Mum at a local dance – she was standing on a balcony with her sister, Dad was with his best friend. He pointed to Mum and said, “I’m going to marry that girl.” He hadn’t even danced with her yet! They eventually did dance and he drove her and her sister home. Theirs was a beautiful romance. I have two brothers – one older and one younger. As kids, we’d play outside until it was dark. It was me and the boys going to creeks and rivers, riding bikes and knocking on people’s doors and running away. As teenagers, my brothers and I fought like hell, but as adults my older brother and I are very close. He is my biggest supporter and always says he’s there for me. My first kiss happened at high school in Mitcham [in Melbourne’s east] behind the shelter shed. It was awful – I can’t say I enjoyed it.



Having an older brother and being around his friends didn’t mean my teenage years were full of romance. When I was 15, I looked about 12. Related Article Sunday Life ‘I chose the bigger world’: Musician Emma Louise reflects on men, music and heartbreak My first boss, Alan Wilson, was a big inspiration. He challenged me – gave me a long piece of string, as it were – to design things and come up with ideas. He allowed me to make mistakes and gave me the confidence at 19 to make big decisions with huge budgets. As I got older, I got into relationships that weren’t quite suited to me. It took me a long while to get it right. It came with a lot of learning, but I wouldn’t be where I am now if I didn’t make those mistakes. My first relationship wasn’t a good one, and I’d prefer not to speak about it. I was 24 when I had my daughter Carly and then got married [for the first time]. At 26, I had my son, Jess. By 31, I was divorced. I did marry again [to personal trainer Steve Vaughan] and we had a great relationship, but are now divorced. Nowadays, I don’t like talking about my relationships.



The Block’s Darren Palmer and I first met on set and were quite wary of each other. We did a photo shoot together and it was all about the angles. He was trying to get his best angle, and I said, “Luckily, I have two good sides.” We started joking about each other. Then we got drunk at the Logies and hit it off. We talked out any fears we had about each other and we’ve been great mates ever since. Blaze with Darren Palmer on their new show, 1 Euro House. Raising my children as a single mum was tough, but seeing my son become a kind, thoughtful and generous man who is now a father is a joy. Shaynna Blaze stars in 1 Euro House on Nine and 9Now. * Nine is the owner of this masthead. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.
