World.title: ‘Priced out of parenthood’: Why Dan and Tamaiya had to leave Sydney
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWFertility ‘Priced out of parenthood’: Why Dan and Tamaiya had to leave Sydney Matt Wade and Bronte Gossling November 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

High property prices and cost of living pressures have combined to drive down the number of babies born in parts of Sydney that previously had relatively high birth rates. New analysis shows that as house prices rose in more affordable Sydney suburbs between 2019 and 2024, the numbers of births in many of those areas fell. Tamaiya and Dan Weeitch left the apartment they loved and moved to Newcastle. Janie Barrett Tamaiya and Dan Weeitch loved living in their rented two-bedroom warehouse-like apartment at Camperdown in Sydney’s inner west with their two daughters. But three years ago, wanting to buy, they fled to Newcastle for a larger home. “Teenage girls cannot share a tiny bedroom,” said Tamaiya, 50.



Related Article Fertility Sydney, where have all the babies gone? See how your suburb has changed over time Dan, 48, never wanted to leave Sydney, but the couple agreed it was “now or never” when their eldest daughter was about to start high school. “We would have stayed in Camperdown if we could afford it,” he said. In 2019, there were 199 Sydney neighbourhoods where the median house price was between $400,000 and $900,000. In those areas, 41,872 births were registered that year – or nearly two thirds of all the babies born in the city. By 2024, about half those neighbourhoods had moved into higher house-price brackets – many to the $900,000 and $1.2 million range – but the overall number of births across all price brackets was much lower.



There were only 86 Greater Sydney neighbourhoods left in the $400,000 to $900,000 price range by 2024 and a total of 17,262 births were registered in those locations that year. These trends coincided with a citywide slump in babies: in 2024, the number of births in Greater Sydney fell to a 20-year low of 58,122 – that’s 8535 lower than in 2019. KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley, who did the analysis, says housing affordability has become an increasingly important factor influencing household formation and family size in Sydney. “If you give people affordable housing, which is the biggest expenditure item in anyone’s household spending basket, they will have more kids,” he says. “But if you make housing progressively more expensive, people will be priced out of parenthood.”



The KPMG analysis showed in the western suburbs neighbourhood of Doonside-Woodcroft, the median house price rose by $294,000 (up 46 per cent) between 2019 and 2024, but that coincided with a 25 per cent fall in births. Related Article Fertility Cash, WFH, childcare overhaul? If we want Australians to have more babies, everything needs to change In the Guildford-South Granville area, the median house price rose by $242,000 (a rise of 36 per cent) between 2019 and 2024, and the number of births fell by 21 per cent. “Young families having to find an additional $250,000 or 300,000 for a mortgage can make it much more difficult to have additional children,” says Rawnsley. “Renters would be facing steep increases in these areas as well. The challenge is how does Sydney produce more affordable homes which are suitable for children with families.”



Many couples opt for a relatively small, affordable home which, in turn, limits the number of children they can consider. And each year a steady flow of young families leaves Sydney for more affordable locations. “We have a beautiful house and a view, we have a pool, we’re close to the beach,” said Tamaiya. Janie Barrett At the time the Weeitches moved, a four-bedroom house was pushing $3 million to $4 million. They paid $1.53 million for their four-bedroom Newcastle home – similar to the price the two-bedroom apartment in Camperdown they had been renting ended up selling for. “We just couldn’t live where we wanted to live. We could have bought in Sydney and moved out further away from the CBD, but neither of us wanted to do that,” Dan said.



Related Article Exclusive

Fertility There’s never been a better time to not have a baby Dan had to resign from his warehouse manager job at a Marrickville brewery, but got a new a job as a sales rep for the same company. He travels to Sydney for work every four to five weeks and stays with his mother in Stanmore. The family lives in Highfields, about a 10-minute drive from Newcastle’s CBD. “We have a beautiful house and a view, we have a pool, we’re close to the beach,” said Tamaiya who, with Dan, told the family’s housing story to the Home of the Century podcast. Sydney’s fertility rate – which measures the expected number of births per woman – has fallen by nearly 20 per cent during the past decade to a historic low of 1.4, Australian Bureau of Statistics figures show. That’s below the benchmark “replacement” level of 2.1 needed to replace the population from one generation to the next without immigration.



The KPMG analysis revealed a growing fertility gap between Sydney and regional areas, where housing is more affordable. The fertility rate for NSW outside of Sydney was a relatively healthy 1.98 in 2024. “Greater housing availability and affordability in regional Australia have provided younger households with a more achievable pathway into home ownership,” Rawnsley said. Sydney’s citywide median house price peaked in late 2025 at about $1.8 million but has since fallen by almost 8 per cent, Domain data shows. Despite the downturn, the median home value of $1.66 million is still $509,000 – or 44 per cent – higher than Australia’s second most expensive city, Brisbane (with a median of $1.15 million).



The hit to fertility rates caused by expensive housing has been compounded by persistent cost of living pressures since 2022. Professor Amanda Davies, a social scientist and demographer at the University of Western Australia, says rising costs – interest rates, electricity prices, grocery bills – are delaying the process of setting up a home. “This somewhat links into our decline of fertility,” says Davies. “So that process of setting up home is taking longer because of the costs, and then fertility is being delayed, which then results in people having fewer children.” Davies says there is an urgent need for more detailed evidence about how the price, size and location of housing is affecting family sizes nationwide. In 2024, the fertility rate of Camperdown – the suburb Tamaiya and Dan Weeitch left behind in 2023 – was 0.92. Janie Barrett



“We are heading for hyper-low fertility rates. This means it’s harder for there to be policy interventions to return to a more stable position,” says Davies. Related Article Parenting What it’s really like to have a big family today A decade ago, much of the western Sydney region had a fertility rate at or above the replacement level of 2.1 births per woman. But fertility rates in many neighbourhoods have declined in that period: Blacktown West has gone from 2.21 to 1.68, Granville-Clyde from 2.26 to 1.62, and Bankstown North from 2.6 to 1.75. By 2024, only 6 per cent of Greater Sydney neighbourhoods had a fertility rate above the replacement level of 2.1 expected births per woman. That compares with about 17 per cent of suburbs a decade earlier, most of them in western Sydney. In the major statistical district covering “Sydney City and Inner South”, which includes Redfern, Glebe, Newtown, Marrickville and Alexandria, the fertility rate was only 0.8 in 2024.

World.title: ‘They believed I needed fixing’: Love on the Spectrum star on what workplaces get wrong
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend ‘They believed I needed fixing’: Love on the Spectrum star on what workplaces get wrong The actor and neurodiversity advocate insists he’s a hopeless romantic, especially when it comes to leg-pulling in a foreign accent. Benjamin Law November 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Each week, Benjamin Law asks public figures to discuss the subjects we’re told to keep private by getting them to roll a die. The numbers they land on are the topics they’re given. This week, he talks to Michael Theo, the actor, voice-over artist and neurodiversity advocate who rose to global fame in the reality TV series Love on the Spectrum. Theo now stars in the ABC TV comedy-drama Austin. Michael Theo, who rose to global fame in the reality TV series Love on the Spectrum, stars in comedy Austin. MONEY Are you good with money? Yeah, I would say I am because I don’t gamble, I don’t smoke and I don’t take drugs. I’m only a social drinker and there are certain things I would never spend any money on, like sports cars or a mansion. But I do like to collect things. What do you like to collect? Lego mini figures, Funko Sodas of Hanna Barbera characters, Squishmallows and Yowies.



Growing up, how did you want to make money? My idea of making money was to become an actor. It’s what I always wanted to be. Related Article Good Weekend He’s known as TV’s obnoxious loser. Now he’s taking on a classic Aussie romantic lead role Which you’ve now achieved, albeit through an unconventional path, right? [Nods] It has been a very interesting journey. Prior to Love on the Spectrum, what kind of work did you do? Was it easy to get work? Straight after I finished school, I went into a training programme called Transition to Work. I also used to be a client of at Work Australia, an agency that helps people with disabilities look for employment. Working as a kitchen manufacturer was my first full-time job, but 10 years ago, in 2016, I was called a lot of names by one of my colleagues in one of his attempts to toughen me up. The company believed I needed “fixing” because I’m on the spectrum. Gee, that sounds like a horrible experience. Yeah, it was.



What do you want employers to know about making workplaces more accessible and friendly to autistic people? Be patient with your colleagues who are autistic because they need to be given the space and time to grow as employees. The best thing you can do is not micromanage them. I prefer to be left alone so I can get my work done in peace without fuss. And every company and boss should do seminars on how to interact with employees who are autistic or have other kinds of disabilities. They’re not the same as everybody else: they’re wired differently. SEX On Love on the Spectrum, you declared that becoming a husband was your number-one dream. Is that still the case? Yeah, it still is. Being an actor and a husband are both dreams of mine. Why is being a husband still so important to you? Because I love the idea of sharing my life with a person – with a woman – because I see romantic love as a sacred treasure. And because when you are married to someone, that means you can grow with someone in spirit and as a person. You get to come home to them every night, and you get to kiss them and hug them every day, and always have the opportunity to show them how much they mean to you. Do you have a sense of what kind of husband you’ll make? Oh, definitely. The kind of husband I see myself being is someone who’d be loving, encouraging and supportive of her choices, whether it be friendships or career. Even if she chose to do something that I may not personally agree with, if it made her happy, then I’d be happy for her. I also want to be the kind of husband that’s different from a lot of men and not say things like “We’ll talk about it later” because that’s a man’s way of saying, “I don’t want to talk about it and expect this never to be brought up again”. I’m willing to spare five or 10 minutes to listen to what she has to say because it could be important.



When you signed up to do Love on the Spectrum, did you have something to prove about autistic people and romance? Maybe a small part of me wanted to show something to the world. But the main reason that I went on the show was because I wanted a girlfriend – and I still do! What turns you off in a potential partner? Smoking, taking drugs, tongue piercings, belly piercings, face piercings. What about turn-ons? Certain accents, like British or Colombian or Italian or Spanish. Also, the ability to insult me in forms of banter because that would give me the opportunity to give it back. Because if a woman ever called me a lizard, do you know what I’d say to her? Tell me. I would say, “Well, joke’s on you. You didn’t specify the subspecies of lizard.” [Laughs] Wait, what?! I didn’t come up with that myself. I got it from Brooklyn Nine-Nine. They’ve got some of the most original, well-written insults I’ve ever heard.



DEATH If you were to die today, what would you regret not having done yet? Finding a wife. What would you be happy that you have done? Accomplishing the dream of being an actor because it’s the one thing I was destined to do since birth. What’s the last thing you want to eat before you die? Three rounds of assorted meats – ribs, T-bone and steak – then green vegetables. Love that balance. Then various fruits like green apples, strawberries, blueberries, star fruit, white peaches, watermelon, along with British and European cheeses.



Are you scared of death? Nope. Lots of people are. Why aren’t you? It’s because my father told me the truth about death a long time ago. Which is? When a person dies, their spirit leaves their body. Bodies are just the temples of our souls. When the spirit leaves that body, it ascends to the afterlife or spirit realm and stays there for some time until God decides it’s time for it to be put into a different body. What – or who – would you like come back as? That would be up to God or the universe to decide. How would you like to die – ideally? Be shot by a woman in my sleep on the 28th of May.



That’s so specific, Michael. Why that date? Why that method? Because it’s the exact same way my hero [Canadian-American comic actor] Phil Hartman went out [in 1998]. Wow, you’ve really thought about this. How would you not like to die? In an explosion. Austin Season 3 is on ABC and iview from November 11. diceytopics@goodweekend.com.au Read more Dicey Topics from Good Weekend magazine:

World.content:
Reviews & adviceThe Traveller Guide To This daunting ancient ritual may be the best thing you do on holiday Lee Tulloch November 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Unless you’re attending a private hammam, the first thing you need to know is that you will get very naked in front of other people but rest assured, men and women are segregated. When you do get naked no one will care, but if you’re shy or it’s your first time, it’s going to be disconcerting. Don’t stare and if you’re with friends, don’t chatter, and if you have to speak, do it in hushed tones. The second thing you need to know is that you’ll get very intimate with your bath attendant who will scrub crevices you didn’t know you had, or cradle you like a baby when they’re soaping your hair. Don’t resist any of it. The more jelly-like you are, the more wonderful the result. Sultan Amir Ahmad Bathhouse in Kashan, Iran, was constructed in the 16th century. iStock In Islamic cultures, a hammam is a steam bath and a place of public bathing. In earlier times, the baths were a way of cleaning the body, an essential ritual in Islam, when there was no private plumbing, but they are also a social gathering place.



Most hammams, whether neighbourhood baths or the glammed-up versions for tourists, consist of a series of rooms: a changing room, a cold room, a warmer room and a hot room, filled with steam that is produced in furnaces and cisterns under the floors in traditional bathhouses. 



In both styles of treatments, you’ll enter a steamy room and be asked to lie on the hard, warm slab, where you’ll be sluiced with water, left to steam for 15 or 20 minutes, then scrubbed vigorously with an exfoliating glove. Related Article Opinion

Travel tips ‘Get undressed, or get out’: Here, it’s normal to get naked with colleagues Keith Austin Travel writer In Moroccan hammams, black soap, a buttery soap made from olives, is used for the massage and to get your skin prepped for the vigorous scrub. This always feels dangerous – you’ll slip and slide all over the marble slab until it’s washed off. In Turkey, the massage might involve foaming bubbles that envelop you in pink froth. You might be sitting on a stool rather than lying down. After the vigorous scrub, which may feel like you’ve lost several layers of skin, there’s the moment we all live for: when the hair is gently washed (in Morocco the shampoo is orange-blossom scented), you’re dried carefully, wrapped in towels, and sent back out to the warm “cold” room for mint tea and recovery, like a very clean and happy baby.

World.title: House-made charcuterie, premium wines: Bar Copains team to open dine-in butcher shop
World.content:
Eating outComing soon House-made charcuterie, premium wines: Bar Copains team to open dine-in butcher shop Everything you need to know about Sasi & Sons, the latest Potts Point venture from one of Sydney’s fastest-growing hospitality groups. Bianca Hrovat November 5, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Nathan and Sali Sasi and Morgan McGlone from Goodies Hospitality, outside their latest venture, Sasi & Sons. The Sydney hospitality group behind hatted venues Bar Copains, Bessie’s, Vin-Cenzo’s and La Buvette has today announced a new direction for its next venture: a dine-in butcher shop in Potts Point. Sasi & Sons is set to open next autumn on Macleay Street, offering Potts Point residents an independent nose-to-tail butchery for the first time since Whole Beast Butchery moved to Marrickville in 2020. The venue plans to work directly with top Australian producers, including Westholme, and create its own line of smallgoods and ready-made meals to sell alongside premium wines, kitchenware and fresh cuts of meat. “People will be able to come in, buy some meat, grab a bottle of wine and choose from some incredible house-made products,” says chef Nathan Sasi, who co-owns The Goodies Hospitality group with Sali Sasi and Morgan McGlone.



“It’s almost like a one-stop shop for everything, curating a selection of great domestic and international products.” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up (From left) Restaurateurs Sali and Nathan Sasi and Morgan McGlone in the doorway of wine bar La Buvette. Andrea Veltom The concept was inspired by Nathan’s late father Les Sasi, a Hungarian migrant who worked at a Rushcutters Bay butcher shop during his childhood. “I got into hospitality because of my dad’s work, it kind of inspired me to get into cooking at a young age,” he says. “I always wanted to do something that paid homage to my dad – he’s not around any more, but it’s a really great opportunity to follow in his footsteps.” Though details are yet to be finalised, there are plans to reference that inspiration throughout the venue. Expect a nostalgic fit-out (designed by long-time collaborators Studio Gram), house-made cevapi and the possibility of ready-made braised cabbage rolls come wintertime.



The team will also use the site to train staff and supply specialty products to Goodies venues across the inner east. La Buvette in Potts Point has become a place to be seen. Jennifer Soo “We’re going to have a massive in-house salami program,” says Sasi. The chef previously ran an ambitious charcuterie program when he opened Nomad in Surry Hills in 2013, before expanding operations at Mercado in the CBD, where he sourced whole beasts and used them to make everything from fresh chorizo to wagyu cecina in the basement. “That’s the thing I’m really most excited about, to go back to making charcuterie in-house – finding the time and resources to do that over the past few years has been kind of tough.” The butcher will also serve a tight, seasonal menu from Thursday to Saturday nights, with limited seating around the butcher’s counter. Dishes are still in development, but if the setups at Carne & Cucina in Erina Heights (butcher by day, restaurant by night) or Victor Churchill in Melbourne (where you can shop for full-blood wagyu steaks, or eat one for dinner) are anything to go by, it’s a fair bet we’ll see a range of butcher’s cuts hitting the grill.



“Like with a lot of things we do, there’ll be a heavy European influence, but … it’ll just be about really trying to elevate the produce rather than overly complicating it,” Sasi said. The dining room at Bar Copains, Surry Hills. Dion Georgopoulos Sasi & Sons will become the sixth venue in the Goodies Hospitality portfolio, which has expanded rapidly since launching Bar Copains in Surry Hills in December 2022. They’ve gone big on a couple of occasions, but they’ve also become experts at squeezing the most out of small spaces: the seating at Bar Copains is famously tight, while La Buvette, a neighbourhood wine bar that’s fast-become a see-and-be-seen destination for chilled Beaujolais-Villages and French-inspired snacks, only has nine bookable seats. “As the years have gone on, these small mum-and-dad operators have been out-competed by the big guys and we’ve started to lose that identity here in Australia,” says Sasi, reflecting on Potts Point’s lack of butcher shops. “I think that’s why we’ve always chosen to open restaurants in the suburbs, because we want to become an integral part of the community … somewhere all the locals can come to, and think, ‘Oh man, I’m lucky to have something like this in my suburb.’”

World.title: ‘A passion for bark and leaves’: The billionaire couple donating $120m to boost nature
World.content:
Exclusive EnvironmentConservationPhilanthropy ‘A passion for bark and leaves’: The billionaire couple donating $120m to boost nature Caitlin Fitzsimmons November 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Perth billionaire couple Alexandra and Julian Burt are making one of the biggest gifts to environmental causes in Australian history, announcing a donation of more than $120 million to be shared between 10 organisations by the end of the year. Alexandra Burt – the granddaughter of Peter Wright of Hancock and Wright prospecting fame and a businesswoman in her own right with interests in agriculture, winemaking and tourism – was worth an estimated $7.86 billion jointly with her sister, Leonie Baldock, on the AFR Rich List this year. Perth couple Julian and Alexandra Burt have made a $120 million donation to environmental causes through their charitable foundation. Julian Burt, a descendant of Sir Archibald Burt, Western Australia’s first chief justice, was last year made a Member of the Order of Australia for his service to the arts, the church and the environment. The donations are through the couple’s charitable fund, the Wright Burt Foundation, which also supports the arts and heritage, education and community causes.



In an exclusive interview with this masthead, Julian Burt said it was unusual for the couple to talk about their philanthropy. “We both prefer not to draw too much attention to ourselves,” he said. “We just like to probably be a little bit more quiet about it all. Only because my wife and I don’t like a lot of publicity. I suppose it’s just a natural thing for us not to sort of want to let everyone know what we’re doing.” Aerial view of a river on Bullo River Station, land in the Northern Territory owned by the Burts and managed in partnership with the Australian Wildlife Conservancy. Brad Leue / Australian Wildlife Conservancy Julian Burt with ecologist Dr Eridani Mulder, formerly of Australian Wildlife Conservancy. Brad Leue / Australian Wildlife Conservancy Alexandra Burt said in a recorded video statement that she hoped speaking about the gift would encourage others in philanthropy, as well as in the corporate sector and government, to identify where they could do more to help the environment.



Australian Wildlife Conservancy, Bush Heritage Australia and Greenpeace will each receive $25 million. Great Southern Land Conservancy, a new charitable organisation founded by former NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service head Atticus Fleming, and BirdLife Australia will each receive $10 million. Aussie Ark, Conservation Partners, the Great Barrier Reef Foundation, Rainforest Rescue and South Endeavour Trust will each receive $5.33 million. Julian Burt said the couple wanted to share the donation because “it’s a big number” and the environment was a cause close to their hearts. “We thought the environment was pretty critical right now, and it’s turned out to be really good timing.” Julian Burt



“We just have a lot of passion for bark and leaves,” he said. “My parents would attest that’s been a passion for me since I was six years old. I kept ant farms, and raised pigeons when I was eight, and kept redback spiders in jars.” His wife did not keep pet ants or spiders, Julian Burt said, but she always had an environmental consciousness. He pointed to the big sustainability improvements she made at the family winery in the Margaret River after inheriting from her father, Michael Wright, in 2012. Aussie Ark operations manager Dean Reid transfers Tasmanian devils between sanctuaries. Aussie Ark Aussie Ark chief conservation officer Hayley Shute releases a Manning River turtle into the Barrington River in February 2026. Janie Barrett Alexandra Burt’s grandfather, Peter Wright, was Lang Hancock’s business partner, and part of the 1963 deal with Rio Tinto to transfer their Pilbara iron-ore mining leases in exchange for 2.5 per cent royalties, a deal that has made billions for both families.



Julian Burt said he supported the role of the mining industry, which was critical to Western Australia’s wealth. “And let’s be frank, it’s done well for Alex’s family,” he added. “As a metaphor, [the wealth] has come out of the ground, and we’re putting it back into the ground, and that’s what we want to do,” Julian Burt said. Julian Burt said he supported Australia’s transition to renewable energy, though he thought fossil fuels would remain in the mix for the short to medium term. The couple did not derive any wealth from fossil fuels, he said. A seagrass flower-picking event at Curtis Island near Gladstone, Queensland, was part of a habitat restoration project. Fiona Ayers / Great Barrier Reef Foundation A green sea turtle rests on a sandy patch in a seagrass meadow near Magnetic Island. Kobie Rhodes / Great Barrier Reef Foundation



Australia’s Environment Report 2025, published by the Australian National University and the Terrestrial Ecosystem Research Network, recorded 39 new additions to the threatened species list in 2025, taking the total to 2175, with climate change the main threat to nine out of 10 newly listed species. “We thought the environment was pretty critical right now, and it’s turned out to be really good timing, with everything that’s happening,” Julian Burt said. “There’s a lot of negative publicity out there about wildfires, temperature rises in Europe, and biodiversity loss. It’s just nice if something like this comes out and, hopefully, it makes people feel a little better.” The critically endangered kyloring or western ground parrot (Pezoporus flaviventris) from Western Australia. Alan Danks / BirdLife Australia Julian Burt said the foundation had done due diligence on all the organisations and their leaders long ago. The size of each gift was proportional to the size of the organisation and whether it would be able to immediately put the money to good use, he said.



Related Article Exclusive

Environmental protection The $25m bid to protect a vast swath of Australia’s tropical wilderness The recipients are mostly focused on conservation, ecosystem restoration and saving threatened species. The exception is Greenpeace, which has a campaigning focus. “It was a different choice,” he said. “There is a relationship there as well. They’re a good organisation, and under the leadership [of David Ritter], there’ll be some real sensible and practical and good outcomes.” Great Southern Land Conservancy chief executive Atticus Fleming said he thought the $120 million donation could be the biggest conservation gift in Australian history, or at least in his 30 years working in the sector. Australian Environmental Grantmakers Network chief executive Claire O’Rourke, whose organisation was not involved in the Wright Burt Foundation donation, said it was a really significant gift for the environment.



“It’s exciting to see,” O’Rourke said. “It’s also not outrageously surprising because we do see those growing trends of interest amongst philanthropy in committing to environmental causes, and I think that’s because philanthropy is recognising that a healthy environment is essential to safeguarding our communities, protecting our health, ensuring our food security, and delivering economic growth for the country, too.” While O’Rourke said philanthropic giving was lower in Australia than some other countries such as the United States, the proportion going to environmental causes was higher. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: ASX set to jump as Wall Street soars; Trump Media, Tesla, SpaceX tumble; Oil prices slump
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to jump as Wall Street soars; Trump Media, Tesla, SpaceX tumble; Oil prices slump Stan Choe and David McHugh November 5, 2026 — 5:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. US stocks are soaring after President Donald Trump’s party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections. Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm US election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 jumped 1.8 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 1,524 points, or 2.9 per cent, as of noon Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 2.1 per cent higher. Wall Street soared higher. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to surge higher, with futures pointing to a rise of 172 points, or 1.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.6 per cent on Wednesday. Stocks of solar-power companies, dollar stores and hospital owners helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners from losers following the widespread losses for Republicans. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump’s social-media company, the artificial-intelligence industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans.



The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell below $US100 for the first time in nearly a month. Vice President JD Vance blamed the war with Iran, which caused a spike in oil prices, for Republicans’ midterm losses. Related Article Opinion

US midterms We’ve seen peak Trump, but the next two years will be a rocky ride Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Strategists along Wall Street had been urging investors not to get swept up in the election because it may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington. “Earnings trump elections,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. Still, Wall Street may have gotten a preferred political scenario as Democrats are set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the economy.



Much remains impossible to predict, of course, and Trump retains executive authority over key areas such as defence, foreign policy and in some instances trade. A downbeat forecast could be that “Trump is not now a lame duck, but an angry duck” who might restart tensions over tariffs and NATO allies’ levels of military spending, said Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING Bank. An optimistic view, Brzeski said, is that Trump becomes “a tame duck ... that he will slow down any disruptive efforts and that he will put more focus on trying to win the Nobel Peace Prize by ending the two big wars without big disruption, and on trade, nothing happens but a few words.” Trump’s social-media company, Trump Media & Technology Group, was one of the market’s bigger losers, down 12.2 per cent. Since briefly touching a peak of $US175 five years ago, it’s dropped toward $US5. Its main business is Truth Social, which is most well known for Trump’s postings on the platform.



Elon Musk’s businesses also struggled. Tesla fell 3.4 per cent, and SpaceX sank 3 per cent. Musk, a former top Trump adviser, is among the possible targets for investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress. Trump has been a big backer of the AI industry, and Democratic victories across the country could mean more regulation or restrictions. Concerns have grown across political parties about AI in general. Elon Musk’s companies are suffering heavy losses after the midterms. AP Investors see Democratic wins in Texas in particular as possibly slowing the build out of further AI data centers. AI-related stocks came into Election Day already under pressure because of worries their prices had shot too high. Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the poster child of the frenzy around AI-related stocks, sank 1.3 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, dropped 9.2 per cent



Advanced Micro Devices, another chip giant, held up better. It added 1 per cent after reporting much stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Companies that have been spending heavily on AI chips also did better. Alphabet rose 4.2 per cent, for example, after it tumbled more than 12 per cent Thursday to its worst loss ever on worries that it was spending too much on AI investments. A Democratic-led Congress could push Trump to pull back on the war with Iran. That helped send down stocks of companies that make weapons and other equipment for the US military, including drops of 6.6 per cent for Lockheed Martin, 4.6 per cent for Northrop Grumman and 2.5 per cent for General Dynamics. Democratic control of Congress could light the way for companies in the solar and wind industries. First Solar jumped 9.4 per cent, and Enphase Energy climbed 9.8 per cent.



Stocks of big oil companies, meanwhile, sank. ExxonMobil fell 4.8 per cent, and ConocoPhillips dropped 5.9 per cent. They had been rallying for much of the year after Trump and Israel began the war with Iran, which sent crude prices much higher. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, plunged 9.2 per cent Wednesday to $US94.11. The price for the most actively traded contract in the Brent market has been veering between roughly $US70 and $US120 per barrel since just before the war with Iran began. A Democratic-led Congress could try to reverse some of the cuts to federal healthcare and food assistance that Republicans approved during the summer in their “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” That helped stocks climb across the healthcare industry, including a rise of 9.8 per cent for HCA Healthcare, which runs hospitals and ambulatory sites.



Retailers also benefited on hopes that Democrats may push policies to help Americans struggling to keep up with the fast-rising cost of living. DollarTree, which focuses in particular on lower-income Americans, had one of the market’s bigger leaps and rose 10 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Scorched earth: Iran’s revenge against Trump will be devastating In the bond market, Treasury yields eased. That could be a signal investors see less risk of Washington piling even more debt onto its already big mountain with the coming end to one-party control. Treasury yields had surged through the summer and reached their highest levels in decades because of worries about the US government’s big debt, along with higher inflation and other concerns. A Congress controlled by Democrats could provide a check against more spending and cuts to taxes that would widen Washington’s deficit. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.90 per cent from 4.95 per cent late Tuesday.



Stocks jump in much of the world Indexes climbed across most of the world. Stocks leaped 2 per cent in Paris, 2.2 per cent in Shanghai and 1.8 per cent in London. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was an outlier and fell 1.4 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: After 41 Aussie tours, Suzi Quatro rocks her favourite spots for pasta, duck and daiquiris
World.content:
FoodThe dish After 41 Aussie tours, Suzi Quatro rocks her favourite spots for pasta, duck and daiquiris The American rock legend is about to return for tour number 42. We think we might know where to find her in Sydney and Melbourne. Jane Rocca November 5, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

American rock royalty Suzi Quatro likes to call Australia her second home — unsurprising really considering she’s already toured here 41 times, and will soon return for tour number 42 in November. There’s been lots of change since she first toured in 1974, the era of breakout hits like Can the Can and 48 Trash, but some rituals live on: a booking at her favourite Italian and Chinese restaurants are a non-negotiable. Suzi Quatro will rock Australia in November. “I love coming to Australia and have many friends there. It really feels like a second home,” says Quatro. The 76-year-old took some time out from rocking on to share her favourite places to dine while on the road and when relaxing at home. Eating out



Favourite hometown restaurant Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Lelli’s in Detroit is a classic Italian spot. It’s the only place my grandfather would go to eat good quality food – it’s an Italian steakhouse that originally opened in 1939. Lafayette Coney Island in downtown Detroit is another classic spot for a Coney Dog. Suzi is a fan of Melbourne icon Pellegrini’s. Justin McManus In Melbourne I always go to my favourite restaurant Tipo 00. I do love the pasta dishes here, you can’t go wrong with anything on the specials. I always used to go to Rosetta at Crown Melbourne and eat their tagliatelle Bolognese, but they’re no longer around. It was a blow when that closed down.



Pellegrini’s is where I go for a single espresso and enjoy a serve of their ravioli. I also like Attica – excellent food and service. We go for the degustation menu for two. “When I said, ‘Hi, I’m Suzi Quatro’, they said ‘come in’ and gave us the best table.” The Flower Drum is also another favourite spot. I couldn’t get a booking on the phone when I was last in town, so I took a chance and went down to the restaurant anyway. When I said, “Hi, I’m Suzi Quatro”, they said “come in” and gave us the best table. I ate the most fantastic Peking duck. The tip to dine here came from a Qantas air steward who said the food is fantastic and they were right. Flower Drum’s “fantastic” Peking duck. Simon Schluter Shark Fin Houseis also a great spot for a quick meal.



I like The Tea Rooms 1892 in Block Arcade for a cup of tea and cake on my walk through the city. As I always stay at Crown, I usually grab a bite at Mr Hive and have a breakfast omelette with toast. They also make a great fish and chips here. I’ll often go to Atrium Bar at Crown for a glass of chardonnay. I also really like Cecconi’s in Flinders Lane in Melbourne. It has great quality food and a great vibe. The pasta and rib-eye steak are fantastic. You might bump into Susie at the Shell House bar. In Sydney



I enjoy Shell House for a glass of chardonnay, it has a great atmosphere here. I’m also a fan of Alfredo Authentic Italian Restaurant near Circular Quay for their sirloin steaks. I also love a margarita cocktail from their underground cocktail bar. The dirty daiquiri at Razz Room. Dion Georgopoulos I go to Razz Room in York street, for the dirty daquiris and music – it’s a great underground 1970s NYC style bar. And you’ll also find me at The Duke of Enmore pub and rock and roll venue. It’s a live music spot and where I get a margarita cocktail. Favourite Food City I love going back to Hamburg, Germany. It’s where my husband Rainer Haas [concert promoter] is originally from. I highly recommend Theo’s Steakhouse Grand Elysee. The rib-eye and Theo’s Caesar Salad prepared at the table is the best I have ever tasted anywhere in the world. Hold the anchovies – they’re not for me.



Suzie likes a vegie pasta, like Adam Liaw’s pesto pappardelle with cherry tomatoes. William Meppem Eating in Signature dish at home I love making a vegetable pasta that will last me three days in the fridge. I also make mushroom pesto, eggs over easy and BLTs are my speciality. Guilty pleasure: Popcorn in the microwave.

World.title: ‘Raising my children was tough’: Shaynna Blaze’s journey from single mum to grandmother
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life ‘Raising my children was tough’: Shaynna Blaze’s journey from single mum to grandmother Jane Rocca November 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. TV presenter and interior designer Shaynna Blaze is best known as a judge on Nine’s The Block*. Ahead, the 63-year-old discusses the important men in her life, including her son, Jess, and her co-star Darren Palmer. Shaynna Blaze says she got her enterprising spirit from her late father, Basil. My paternal grandfather, who went by the nickname of Snowy, died when I was very young. His white-blond hair has made its way down the family tree from my dad Basil, to my older brother and now my granddaughter. My maternal grandfather, Roy, moved from Melbourne to Queensland for warmer weather and wasn’t in our lives much growing up. He was a builder who helped build the house I grew up in with my dad. He lived into his 70s. Dad was a fitter and turner and handyman who loved to build everything from scratch. He built garages, laid bricks, did the home extension – there wasn’t anything he didn’t attempt. I really got that spirit from him. We are both Aries and used to butt heads a lot because of our strong personalities. Dad got to be a grandfather and met my two kids. He was kind and gentle.



Dad and I were very close until he died of a heart attack suddenly in 1998. He’d had a heart attack in his 40s that led to a quadruple bypass and went to see his heart surgeon two weeks before he died – there was nothing to indicate anything was wrong. Mum [Annette] packed his lunch for work and never saw him alive again. Twenty-four hours later we turned off the life support and were in shock for a long time. Mum was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s a year later; we felt it was due to the grief of losing dad. She lived with it for 16 years and died 10 years ago. My first boss, Alan Wilson, was a big inspiration. He allowed me to make mistakes and gave me the confidence at 19 to make big decisions. Dad met Mum at a local dance – she was standing on a balcony with her sister, Dad was with his best friend. He pointed to Mum and said, “I’m going to marry that girl.” He hadn’t even danced with her yet! They eventually did dance and he drove her and her sister home. Theirs was a beautiful romance. I have two brothers – one older and one younger. As kids, we’d play outside until it was dark. It was me and the boys going to creeks and rivers, riding bikes and knocking on people’s doors and running away. As teenagers, my brothers and I fought like hell, but as adults my older brother and I are very close. He is my biggest supporter and always says he’s there for me. My first kiss happened at high school in Mitcham [in Melbourne’s east] behind the shelter shed. It was awful – I can’t say I enjoyed it.



Having an older brother and being around his friends didn’t mean my teenage years were full of romance. When I was 15, I looked about 12. Related Article Sunday Life ‘I chose the bigger world’: Musician Emma Louise reflects on men, music and heartbreak My first boss, Alan Wilson, was a big inspiration. He challenged me – gave me a long piece of string, as it were – to design things and come up with ideas. He allowed me to make mistakes and gave me the confidence at 19 to make big decisions with huge budgets. As I got older, I got into relationships that weren’t quite suited to me. It took me a long while to get it right. It came with a lot of learning, but I wouldn’t be where I am now if I didn’t make those mistakes. My first relationship wasn’t a good one, and I’d prefer not to speak about it. I was 24 when I had my daughter Carly and then got married [for the first time]. At 26, I had my son, Jess. By 31, I was divorced. I did marry again [to personal trainer Steve Vaughan] and we had a great relationship, but are now divorced. Nowadays, I don’t like talking about my relationships.



The Block’s Darren Palmer and I first met on set and were quite wary of each other. We did a photo shoot together and it was all about the angles. He was trying to get his best angle, and I said, “Luckily, I have two good sides.” We started joking about each other. Then we got drunk at the Logies and hit it off. We talked out any fears we had about each other and we’ve been great mates ever since. Blaze with Darren Palmer on their new show, 1 Euro House. Raising my children as a single mum was tough, but seeing my son become a kind, thoughtful and generous man who is now a father is a joy. Shaynna Blaze stars in 1 Euro House on Nine and 9Now. * Nine is the owner of this masthead. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: ‘Priced out of parenthood’: Why Dan and Tamaiya had to leave Sydney
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWFertility ‘Priced out of parenthood’: Why Dan and Tamaiya had to leave Sydney Matt Wade and Bronte Gossling November 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

High property prices and cost of living pressures have combined to drive down the number of babies born in parts of Sydney that previously had relatively high birth rates. New analysis shows that as house prices rose in more affordable Sydney suburbs between 2019 and 2024, the numbers of births in many of those areas fell. Tamaiya and Dan Weeitch left the apartment they loved and moved to Newcastle. Janie Barrett Tamaiya and Dan Weeitch loved living in their rented two-bedroom warehouse-like apartment at Camperdown in Sydney’s inner west with their two daughters. But three years ago, wanting to buy, they fled to Newcastle for a larger home. “Teenage girls cannot share a tiny bedroom,” said Tamaiya, 50.



Related Article Fertility Sydney, where have all the babies gone? See how your suburb has changed over time Dan, 48, never wanted to leave Sydney, but the couple agreed it was “now or never” when their eldest daughter was about to start high school. “We would have stayed in Camperdown if we could afford it,” he said. In 2019, there were 199 Sydney neighbourhoods where the median house price was between $400,000 and $900,000. In those areas, 41,872 births were registered that year – or nearly two thirds of all the babies born in the city. By 2024, about half those neighbourhoods had moved into higher house-price brackets – many to the $900,000 and $1.2 million range – but the overall number of births across all price brackets was much lower.



There were only 86 Greater Sydney neighbourhoods left in the $400,000 to $900,000 price range by 2024 and a total of 17,262 births were registered in those locations that year. These trends coincided with a citywide slump in babies: in 2024, the number of births in Greater Sydney fell to a 20-year low of 58,122 – that’s 8535 lower than in 2019. KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley, who did the analysis, says housing affordability has become an increasingly important factor influencing household formation and family size in Sydney. “If you give people affordable housing, which is the biggest expenditure item in anyone’s household spending basket, they will have more kids,” he says. “But if you make housing progressively more expensive, people will be priced out of parenthood.”



The KPMG analysis showed in the western suburbs neighbourhood of Doonside-Woodcroft, the median house price rose by $294,000 (up 46 per cent) between 2019 and 2024, but that coincided with a 25 per cent fall in births. Related Article Fertility Cash, WFH, childcare overhaul? If we want Australians to have more babies, everything needs to change In the Guildford-South Granville area, the median house price rose by $242,000 (a rise of 36 per cent) between 2019 and 2024, and the number of births fell by 21 per cent. “Young families having to find an additional $250,000 or 300,000 for a mortgage can make it much more difficult to have additional children,” says Rawnsley. “Renters would be facing steep increases in these areas as well. The challenge is how does Sydney produce more affordable homes which are suitable for children with families.”



Many couples opt for a relatively small, affordable home which, in turn, limits the number of children they can consider. And each year a steady flow of young families leaves Sydney for more affordable locations. “We have a beautiful house and a view, we have a pool, we’re close to the beach,” said Tamaiya. Janie Barrett At the time the Weeitches moved, a four-bedroom house was pushing $3 million to $4 million. They paid $1.53 million for their four-bedroom Newcastle home – similar to the price the two-bedroom apartment in Camperdown they had been renting ended up selling for. “We just couldn’t live where we wanted to live. We could have bought in Sydney and moved out further away from the CBD, but neither of us wanted to do that,” Dan said.



Related Article Exclusive

Fertility There’s never been a better time to not have a baby Dan had to resign from his warehouse manager job at a Marrickville brewery, but got a new a job as a sales rep for the same company. He travels to Sydney for work every four to five weeks and stays with his mother in Stanmore. The family lives in Highfields, about a 10-minute drive from Newcastle’s CBD. “We have a beautiful house and a view, we have a pool, we’re close to the beach,” said Tamaiya who, with Dan, told the family’s housing story to the Home of the Century podcast. Sydney’s fertility rate – which measures the expected number of births per woman – has fallen by nearly 20 per cent during the past decade to a historic low of 1.4, Australian Bureau of Statistics figures show. That’s below the benchmark “replacement” level of 2.1 needed to replace the population from one generation to the next without immigration.



The KPMG analysis revealed a growing fertility gap between Sydney and regional areas, where housing is more affordable. The fertility rate for NSW outside of Sydney was a relatively healthy 1.98 in 2024. “Greater housing availability and affordability in regional Australia have provided younger households with a more achievable pathway into home ownership,” Rawnsley said. Sydney’s citywide median house price peaked in late 2025 at about $1.8 million but has since fallen by almost 8 per cent, Domain data shows. Despite the downturn, the median home value of $1.66 million is still $509,000 – or 44 per cent – higher than Australia’s second most expensive city, Brisbane (with a median of $1.15 million).



The hit to fertility rates caused by expensive housing has been compounded by persistent cost of living pressures since 2022. Professor Amanda Davies, a social scientist and demographer at the University of Western Australia, says rising costs – interest rates, electricity prices, grocery bills – are delaying the process of setting up a home. “This somewhat links into our decline of fertility,” says Davies. “So that process of setting up home is taking longer because of the costs, and then fertility is being delayed, which then results in people having fewer children.” Davies says there is an urgent need for more detailed evidence about how the price, size and location of housing is affecting family sizes nationwide. In 2024, the fertility rate of Camperdown – the suburb Tamaiya and Dan Weeitch left behind in 2023 – was 0.92. Janie Barrett



“We are heading for hyper-low fertility rates. This means it’s harder for there to be policy interventions to return to a more stable position,” says Davies. Related Article Parenting What it’s really like to have a big family today A decade ago, much of the western Sydney region had a fertility rate at or above the replacement level of 2.1 births per woman. But fertility rates in many neighbourhoods have declined in that period: Blacktown West has gone from 2.21 to 1.68, Granville-Clyde from 2.26 to 1.62, and Bankstown North from 2.6 to 1.75. By 2024, only 6 per cent of Greater Sydney neighbourhoods had a fertility rate above the replacement level of 2.1 expected births per woman. That compares with about 17 per cent of suburbs a decade earlier, most of them in western Sydney. In the major statistical district covering “Sydney City and Inner South”, which includes Redfern, Glebe, Newtown, Marrickville and Alexandria, the fertility rate was only 0.8 in 2024.
