World.title: ‘They believed I needed fixing’: Love on the Spectrum star on what workplaces get wrong
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend ‘They believed I needed fixing’: Love on the Spectrum star on what workplaces get wrong The actor and neurodiversity advocate insists he’s a hopeless romantic, especially when it comes to leg-pulling in a foreign accent. Benjamin Law November 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Each week, Benjamin Law asks public figures to discuss the subjects we’re told to keep private by getting them to roll a die. The numbers they land on are the topics they’re given. This week, he talks to Michael Theo, the actor, voice-over artist and neurodiversity advocate who rose to global fame in the reality TV series Love on the Spectrum. Theo now stars in the ABC TV comedy-drama Austin. Michael Theo, who rose to global fame in the reality TV series Love on the Spectrum, stars in comedy Austin. MONEY Are you good with money? Yeah, I would say I am because I don’t gamble, I don’t smoke and I don’t take drugs. I’m only a social drinker and there are certain things I would never spend any money on, like sports cars or a mansion. But I do like to collect things. What do you like to collect? Lego mini figures, Funko Sodas of Hanna Barbera characters, Squishmallows and Yowies.



Growing up, how did you want to make money? My idea of making money was to become an actor. It’s what I always wanted to be. Related Article Good Weekend He’s known as TV’s obnoxious loser. Now he’s taking on a classic Aussie romantic lead role Which you’ve now achieved, albeit through an unconventional path, right? [Nods] It has been a very interesting journey. Prior to Love on the Spectrum, what kind of work did you do? Was it easy to get work? Straight after I finished school, I went into a training programme called Transition to Work. I also used to be a client of at Work Australia, an agency that helps people with disabilities look for employment. Working as a kitchen manufacturer was my first full-time job, but 10 years ago, in 2016, I was called a lot of names by one of my colleagues in one of his attempts to toughen me up. The company believed I needed “fixing” because I’m on the spectrum. Gee, that sounds like a horrible experience. Yeah, it was.



What do you want employers to know about making workplaces more accessible and friendly to autistic people? Be patient with your colleagues who are autistic because they need to be given the space and time to grow as employees. The best thing you can do is not micromanage them. I prefer to be left alone so I can get my work done in peace without fuss. And every company and boss should do seminars on how to interact with employees who are autistic or have other kinds of disabilities. They’re not the same as everybody else: they’re wired differently. SEX On Love on the Spectrum, you declared that becoming a husband was your number-one dream. Is that still the case? Yeah, it still is. Being an actor and a husband are both dreams of mine. Why is being a husband still so important to you? Because I love the idea of sharing my life with a person – with a woman – because I see romantic love as a sacred treasure. And because when you are married to someone, that means you can grow with someone in spirit and as a person. You get to come home to them every night, and you get to kiss them and hug them every day, and always have the opportunity to show them how much they mean to you. Do you have a sense of what kind of husband you’ll make? Oh, definitely. The kind of husband I see myself being is someone who’d be loving, encouraging and supportive of her choices, whether it be friendships or career. Even if she chose to do something that I may not personally agree with, if it made her happy, then I’d be happy for her. I also want to be the kind of husband that’s different from a lot of men and not say things like “We’ll talk about it later” because that’s a man’s way of saying, “I don’t want to talk about it and expect this never to be brought up again”. I’m willing to spare five or 10 minutes to listen to what she has to say because it could be important.



When you signed up to do Love on the Spectrum, did you have something to prove about autistic people and romance? Maybe a small part of me wanted to show something to the world. But the main reason that I went on the show was because I wanted a girlfriend – and I still do! What turns you off in a potential partner? Smoking, taking drugs, tongue piercings, belly piercings, face piercings. What about turn-ons? Certain accents, like British or Colombian or Italian or Spanish. Also, the ability to insult me in forms of banter because that would give me the opportunity to give it back. Because if a woman ever called me a lizard, do you know what I’d say to her? Tell me. I would say, “Well, joke’s on you. You didn’t specify the subspecies of lizard.” [Laughs] Wait, what?! I didn’t come up with that myself. I got it from Brooklyn Nine-Nine. They’ve got some of the most original, well-written insults I’ve ever heard.



DEATH If you were to die today, what would you regret not having done yet? Finding a wife. What would you be happy that you have done? Accomplishing the dream of being an actor because it’s the one thing I was destined to do since birth. What’s the last thing you want to eat before you die? Three rounds of assorted meats – ribs, T-bone and steak – then green vegetables. Love that balance. Then various fruits like green apples, strawberries, blueberries, star fruit, white peaches, watermelon, along with British and European cheeses.



Are you scared of death? Nope. Lots of people are. Why aren’t you? It’s because my father told me the truth about death a long time ago. Which is? When a person dies, their spirit leaves their body. Bodies are just the temples of our souls. When the spirit leaves that body, it ascends to the afterlife or spirit realm and stays there for some time until God decides it’s time for it to be put into a different body. What – or who – would you like come back as? That would be up to God or the universe to decide. How would you like to die – ideally? Be shot by a woman in my sleep on the 28th of May.



That’s so specific, Michael. Why that date? Why that method? Because it’s the exact same way my hero [Canadian-American comic actor] Phil Hartman went out [in 1998]. Wow, you’ve really thought about this. How would you not like to die? In an explosion. Austin Season 3 is on ABC and iview from November 11. diceytopics@goodweekend.com.au Read more Dicey Topics from Good Weekend magazine:

World.title: This daunting ancient ritual may be the best thing you do on holiday
World.content:
Reviews & adviceThe Traveller Guide To This daunting ancient ritual may be the best thing you do on holiday Lee Tulloch November 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Unless you’re attending a private hammam, the first thing you need to know is that you will get very naked in front of other people but rest assured, men and women are segregated. When you do get naked no one will care, but if you’re shy or it’s your first time, it’s going to be disconcerting. Don’t stare and if you’re with friends, don’t chatter, and if you have to speak, do it in hushed tones. The second thing you need to know is that you’ll get very intimate with your bath attendant who will scrub crevices you didn’t know you had, or cradle you like a baby when they’re soaping your hair. Don’t resist any of it. The more jelly-like you are, the more wonderful the result. Sultan Amir Ahmad Bathhouse in Kashan, Iran, was constructed in the 16th century. iStock In Islamic cultures, a hammam is a steam bath and a place of public bathing. In earlier times, the baths were a way of cleaning the body, an essential ritual in Islam, when there was no private plumbing, but they are also a social gathering place.



Most hammams, whether neighbourhood baths or the glammed-up versions for tourists, consist of a series of rooms: a changing room, a cold room, a warmer room and a hot room, filled with steam that is produced in furnaces and cisterns under the floors in traditional bathhouses. 



In both styles of treatments, you’ll enter a steamy room and be asked to lie on the hard, warm slab, where you’ll be sluiced with water, left to steam for 15 or 20 minutes, then scrubbed vigorously with an exfoliating glove. Related Article Opinion

Travel tips ‘Get undressed, or get out’: Here, it’s normal to get naked with colleagues Keith Austin Travel writer In Moroccan hammams, black soap, a buttery soap made from olives, is used for the massage and to get your skin prepped for the vigorous scrub. This always feels dangerous – you’ll slip and slide all over the marble slab until it’s washed off. In Turkey, the massage might involve foaming bubbles that envelop you in pink froth. You might be sitting on a stool rather than lying down. After the vigorous scrub, which may feel like you’ve lost several layers of skin, there’s the moment we all live for: when the hair is gently washed (in Morocco the shampoo is orange-blossom scented), you’re dried carefully, wrapped in towels, and sent back out to the warm “cold” room for mint tea and recovery, like a very clean and happy baby.

World.title: House-made charcuterie, premium wines: Bar Copains team to open dine-in butcher shop
World.content:
Eating outComing soon House-made charcuterie, premium wines: Bar Copains team to open dine-in butcher shop Everything you need to know about Sasi & Sons, the latest Potts Point venture from one of Sydney’s fastest-growing hospitality groups. Bianca Hrovat November 5, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Nathan and Sali Sasi and Morgan McGlone from Goodies Hospitality, outside their latest venture, Sasi & Sons. The Sydney hospitality group behind hatted venues Bar Copains, Bessie’s, Vin-Cenzo’s and La Buvette has today announced a new direction for its next venture: a dine-in butcher shop in Potts Point. Sasi & Sons is set to open next autumn on Macleay Street, offering Potts Point residents an independent nose-to-tail butchery for the first time since Whole Beast Butchery moved to Marrickville in 2020. The venue plans to work directly with top Australian producers, including Westholme, and create its own line of smallgoods and ready-made meals to sell alongside premium wines, kitchenware and fresh cuts of meat. “People will be able to come in, buy some meat, grab a bottle of wine and choose from some incredible house-made products,” says chef Nathan Sasi, who co-owns The Goodies Hospitality group with Sali Sasi and Morgan McGlone.



“It’s almost like a one-stop shop for everything, curating a selection of great domestic and international products.” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up (From left) Restaurateurs Sali and Nathan Sasi and Morgan McGlone in the doorway of wine bar La Buvette. Andrea Veltom The concept was inspired by Nathan’s late father Les Sasi, a Hungarian migrant who worked at a Rushcutters Bay butcher shop during his childhood. “I got into hospitality because of my dad’s work, it kind of inspired me to get into cooking at a young age,” he says. “I always wanted to do something that paid homage to my dad – he’s not around any more, but it’s a really great opportunity to follow in his footsteps.” Though details are yet to be finalised, there are plans to reference that inspiration throughout the venue. Expect a nostalgic fit-out (designed by long-time collaborators Studio Gram), house-made cevapi and the possibility of ready-made braised cabbage rolls come wintertime.



The team will also use the site to train staff and supply specialty products to Goodies venues across the inner east. La Buvette in Potts Point has become a place to be seen. Jennifer Soo “We’re going to have a massive in-house salami program,” says Sasi. The chef previously ran an ambitious charcuterie program when he opened Nomad in Surry Hills in 2013, before expanding operations at Mercado in the CBD, where he sourced whole beasts and used them to make everything from fresh chorizo to wagyu cecina in the basement. “That’s the thing I’m really most excited about, to go back to making charcuterie in-house – finding the time and resources to do that over the past few years has been kind of tough.” The butcher will also serve a tight, seasonal menu from Thursday to Saturday nights, with limited seating around the butcher’s counter. Dishes are still in development, but if the setups at Carne & Cucina in Erina Heights (butcher by day, restaurant by night) or Victor Churchill in Melbourne (where you can shop for full-blood wagyu steaks, or eat one for dinner) are anything to go by, it’s a fair bet we’ll see a range of butcher’s cuts hitting the grill.



“Like with a lot of things we do, there’ll be a heavy European influence, but … it’ll just be about really trying to elevate the produce rather than overly complicating it,” Sasi said. The dining room at Bar Copains, Surry Hills. Dion Georgopoulos Sasi & Sons will become the sixth venue in the Goodies Hospitality portfolio, which has expanded rapidly since launching Bar Copains in Surry Hills in December 2022. They’ve gone big on a couple of occasions, but they’ve also become experts at squeezing the most out of small spaces: the seating at Bar Copains is famously tight, while La Buvette, a neighbourhood wine bar that’s fast-become a see-and-be-seen destination for chilled Beaujolais-Villages and French-inspired snacks, only has nine bookable seats. “As the years have gone on, these small mum-and-dad operators have been out-competed by the big guys and we’ve started to lose that identity here in Australia,” says Sasi, reflecting on Potts Point’s lack of butcher shops. “I think that’s why we’ve always chosen to open restaurants in the suburbs, because we want to become an integral part of the community … somewhere all the locals can come to, and think, ‘Oh man, I’m lucky to have something like this in my suburb.’”

World.title: ‘A passion for bark and leaves’: The billionaire couple donating $120m to boost nature
World.content:
Exclusive EnvironmentConservationPhilanthropy ‘A passion for bark and leaves’: The billionaire couple donating $120m to boost nature Caitlin Fitzsimmons November 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Perth billionaire couple Alexandra and Julian Burt are making one of the biggest gifts to environmental causes in Australian history, announcing a donation of more than $120 million to be shared between 10 organisations by the end of the year. Alexandra Burt – the granddaughter of Peter Wright of Hancock and Wright prospecting fame and a businesswoman in her own right with interests in agriculture, winemaking and tourism – was worth an estimated $7.86 billion jointly with her sister, Leonie Baldock, on the AFR Rich List this year. Perth couple Julian and Alexandra Burt have made a $120 million donation to environmental causes through their charitable foundation. Julian Burt, a descendant of Sir Archibald Burt, Western Australia’s first chief justice, was last year made a Member of the Order of Australia for his service to the arts, the church and the environment. The donations are through the couple’s charitable fund, the Wright Burt Foundation, which also supports the arts and heritage, education and community causes.



In an exclusive interview with this masthead, Julian Burt said it was unusual for the couple to talk about their philanthropy. “We both prefer not to draw too much attention to ourselves,” he said. “We just like to probably be a little bit more quiet about it all. Only because my wife and I don’t like a lot of publicity. I suppose it’s just a natural thing for us not to sort of want to let everyone know what we’re doing.” Aerial view of a river on Bullo River Station, land in the Northern Territory owned by the Burts and managed in partnership with the Australian Wildlife Conservancy. Brad Leue / Australian Wildlife Conservancy Julian Burt with ecologist Dr Eridani Mulder, formerly of Australian Wildlife Conservancy. Brad Leue / Australian Wildlife Conservancy Alexandra Burt said in a recorded video statement that she hoped speaking about the gift would encourage others in philanthropy, as well as in the corporate sector and government, to identify where they could do more to help the environment.



Australian Wildlife Conservancy, Bush Heritage Australia and Greenpeace will each receive $25 million. Great Southern Land Conservancy, a new charitable organisation founded by former NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service head Atticus Fleming, and BirdLife Australia will each receive $10 million. Aussie Ark, Conservation Partners, the Great Barrier Reef Foundation, Rainforest Rescue and South Endeavour Trust will each receive $5.33 million. Julian Burt said the couple wanted to share the donation because “it’s a big number” and the environment was a cause close to their hearts. “We thought the environment was pretty critical right now, and it’s turned out to be really good timing.” Julian Burt



“We just have a lot of passion for bark and leaves,” he said. “My parents would attest that’s been a passion for me since I was six years old. I kept ant farms, and raised pigeons when I was eight, and kept redback spiders in jars.” His wife did not keep pet ants or spiders, Julian Burt said, but she always had an environmental consciousness. He pointed to the big sustainability improvements she made at the family winery in the Margaret River after inheriting from her father, Michael Wright, in 2012. Aussie Ark operations manager Dean Reid transfers Tasmanian devils between sanctuaries. Aussie Ark Aussie Ark chief conservation officer Hayley Shute releases a Manning River turtle into the Barrington River in February 2026. Janie Barrett Alexandra Burt’s grandfather, Peter Wright, was Lang Hancock’s business partner, and part of the 1963 deal with Rio Tinto to transfer their Pilbara iron-ore mining leases in exchange for 2.5 per cent royalties, a deal that has made billions for both families.



Julian Burt said he supported the role of the mining industry, which was critical to Western Australia’s wealth. “And let’s be frank, it’s done well for Alex’s family,” he added. “As a metaphor, [the wealth] has come out of the ground, and we’re putting it back into the ground, and that’s what we want to do,” Julian Burt said. Julian Burt said he supported Australia’s transition to renewable energy, though he thought fossil fuels would remain in the mix for the short to medium term. The couple did not derive any wealth from fossil fuels, he said. A seagrass flower-picking event at Curtis Island near Gladstone, Queensland, was part of a habitat restoration project. Fiona Ayers / Great Barrier Reef Foundation A green sea turtle rests on a sandy patch in a seagrass meadow near Magnetic Island. Kobie Rhodes / Great Barrier Reef Foundation



Australia’s Environment Report 2025, published by the Australian National University and the Terrestrial Ecosystem Research Network, recorded 39 new additions to the threatened species list in 2025, taking the total to 2175, with climate change the main threat to nine out of 10 newly listed species. “We thought the environment was pretty critical right now, and it’s turned out to be really good timing, with everything that’s happening,” Julian Burt said. “There’s a lot of negative publicity out there about wildfires, temperature rises in Europe, and biodiversity loss. It’s just nice if something like this comes out and, hopefully, it makes people feel a little better.” The critically endangered kyloring or western ground parrot (Pezoporus flaviventris) from Western Australia. Alan Danks / BirdLife Australia Julian Burt said the foundation had done due diligence on all the organisations and their leaders long ago. The size of each gift was proportional to the size of the organisation and whether it would be able to immediately put the money to good use, he said.



Related Article Exclusive

Environmental protection The $25m bid to protect a vast swath of Australia’s tropical wilderness The recipients are mostly focused on conservation, ecosystem restoration and saving threatened species. The exception is Greenpeace, which has a campaigning focus. “It was a different choice,” he said. “There is a relationship there as well. They’re a good organisation, and under the leadership [of David Ritter], there’ll be some real sensible and practical and good outcomes.” Great Southern Land Conservancy chief executive Atticus Fleming said he thought the $120 million donation could be the biggest conservation gift in Australian history, or at least in his 30 years working in the sector. Australian Environmental Grantmakers Network chief executive Claire O’Rourke, whose organisation was not involved in the Wright Burt Foundation donation, said it was a really significant gift for the environment.



“It’s exciting to see,” O’Rourke said. “It’s also not outrageously surprising because we do see those growing trends of interest amongst philanthropy in committing to environmental causes, and I think that’s because philanthropy is recognising that a healthy environment is essential to safeguarding our communities, protecting our health, ensuring our food security, and delivering economic growth for the country, too.” While O’Rourke said philanthropic giving was lower in Australia than some other countries such as the United States, the proportion going to environmental causes was higher. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: What should I do if my partner and I don't agree on politics?
World.content: Hartfield says because our political beliefs are usually attached to the values we hold, it can be really difficult to speak about them without passion, especially if we are wanting the person who we are talking to, to understand you, or be influenced by you. But she agrees finding points of agreement can be key.

World.title: Graduate takes fight to be lawyer all the way to Supreme Court
World.content:
A law graduate who failed the Law Society's good character test has appealed the decision all the way to the Supreme Court where a judge has now decided his case is "weak but not wholly devoid of merit".

The man, referred to by the court as Mr Gold, was refused a certificate of good character on grounds the Law Society said included a Family Court case where a judge made previously reported findings of physical and psychological abuse of his wife.

While he denied the allegations, he completed a stopping violence programme required by the court. The Law Society said there were other aspects of his character indicating he was unfit, and his character references were "insubstantial".

The beneficiary's bid to practise the law then became a matter for the courts as he challenged the decision.

Years on, it has now arrived at the country's highest court where Justice Campbell overturned a decision allowing Gold to file an application for leave to appeal without paying the fee of about $1500.

It meant Gold could now apply for permission to challenge an earlier lower court ruling that he was out of time for further appeals.

The Law Society was approached by RNZ, and declined to comment on the judgment made publicly available last week.

An appeals journey begins

The Law Society's refusal to grant Gold a certificate of character - necessary for admission to the bar - prompted his application to the High Court, challenging the decision.

But in a February 2025 High Court ruling, Justice O'Gorman upheld the society's decision.

She said she was not satisfied that Gold was "a fit and proper person", claiming "a defect in character reflected in disproportionate and misguided aggravation against persons he perceives to have wrongly challenged him, coupled with the tendency to blame others".

She declined to admit him as a barrister and solicitor. Gold was also ordered to pay court costs.

Gold then tried to appeal the judgments but didn't do so within the required timeframe, and the Court of Appeal declined to extend the timeframe.

Gold sought leave to appeal that decision not to give an extension in the Supreme Court, where he also asked for the $1500 filing fee to be waived on the basis that he was on the benefit and couldn't afford it.

In his judgment published last week, Campbell said the deputy registrar had to weigh whether waiving the fee would promote access to justice.

He said the deputy registrar accepted that Gold was unable to pay, but declined the waiver, considering the proposed appeal was "wholly devoid of merit, was vexatious and would not be pursued by a reasonable and solvent litigant".

It appeared to be a further manifestation of what the High Court characterised as a "tendency to make personalised attacks and retaliate by inappropriate use of legal processes", Campbell said.

"The vast majority of the submissions were not relevant to an appeal against the Court of Appeal decision and instead were devoted to alleging misconduct by the NZLS [Law Society], officers of the court and the judiciary."

Gold asked for the deputy registrar's decision to be reviewed alongside his revised submissions supporting his application for leave to appeal.

In assessing both, Campbell said the merits of Gold's application were "weak, but not wholly devoid of merit".

"His underlying claim is not frivolous. While he has pursued the proceeding with much vigour, he has not crossed the border into vexatiousness.

"I therefore do not consider that the high threshold for declining to waive the filing fee has been met," Campbell said.

"The filing fee payable for the application for leave to appeal is waived."

World.title: 'I've put the hard yards in': Older jobseekers say ageism stopping them from getting work
World.content:
Older jobseekers say they face discrimination in securing work but an expert says businesses will have to embrace them if the age of superannuation is raised.

The unemployment rate rose to 5.7 percent nationally in September, with the underutilisation rate for over-55s averaging 8.5 percent.

Lisa Dudley, 57, said she'd been looking for part-time work for the past eight years and blamed ageism in part.

"[Employers] see an older person and they think: 'Oh, well, we are not going to get much use out of them because they're not going to be in work much longer'."

She said she had 40 years' worth of experience in customer service and was qualified for the jobs she was applying to.

She had a couple of stipulations: no shift work and no weekends, so she could spend time with her husband and grandson.

"I've put the hard yards in, so now I want something for me."

She said she was lucky in that she wanted to work rather than needed to, but time was ticking for her to save for retirement.

"It's frustrating because I know my KiwiSaver is really, really low compared to what I'm going to need when I do get eight years down the line."

Dudley said she and her husband, 77, wanted to move out of Canterbury to the North Island to be closer to family but he had struggled to find work elsewhere.

"It really is getting frustrating and it's annoying that people aren't willing to take that chance."

She said she suspected some employers might not want to hire older workers, whose experience often came with a higher salary.

"For what they'd have to pay me, they can probably get two people for lesser value."

She said she had also been advised to "dumb down" her CV to not appear overqualified.

Fellow jobseeker Melinda Netto, 55, said employers were reluctant to hire someone they viewed as a flight risk for being older and overqualified.

"People look at [my CV] and think, oh, she's experienced, you might get another job."

She said she had applied for 100 jobs since February after she chose not to renew a contract with her previous employer - only 42 had even replied.

She said she'd been looking for local jobs with lower pay and perks, despite her two decades of experience in financial services.

"In all honesty, I would rather work in a warehouse than the financial services because you're sitting on your bum. Ten years down the line, you're going to pay for it."

She said she was lucky because she was coping well but she said the constant rejection could affect other people's mental health.

"For me, I don't care because it's their loss."

Seniors@work founder Ian Fraser. Supplied / Seniors@work

Director and founder of Seniors@work Ian Fraser, 77, said he decided to set up the job platform dedicated to over-50s seven years ago because of his own difficulty finding work in his late 50s and early 60s.

"I applied for over 100 roles and I just had three interviews."

He said there was a lot of attention on younger jobseekers - but he argued they had time on their side and often could lean on parents financially.

"I constantly hear about [seniors] who are really struggling to find work, who desperately need to work so they can put food on the table.

"In many cases, they've got rent and mortgages to pay. They don't have enough retirement funds. And they've got ongoing growing medical costs."

In the past 12 months, registrations on his websites more than doubled - reaching 9500 users.

According to Stats NZ's Household Labour Force Survey, more than a quarter of over-65s were employed, rising by a percentage point on the year.

Business NZ analysis found employment rates for 65- to 69-year-olds and over-70s had tripled and quadrupled respectively since 2000.

Fraser added that seniors might be expected to work longer if the superannuation age was raised.

"So my questions are, if we are asking people to work longer, are we actually prepared to employ longer?"

He said that if someone was suitable for a job at 55, they should still be suitable by 67.

Age Concern chief executive Karen Billings-Jensen. Mike Clare / supplied

Age Concern chief executive Karen Billings-Jensen said getting employers to embrace older generations was an education issue.

"There's a myth that older people might be less reliable and need time off for health appointments.

"But that's been disproved. They're more likely to be committed. They're less likely to decide to move to Australia."

World.title: Hope for Westport families as aged care home expands
World.content:
Work is set to begin on a desperately needed extension to Westport's only aged care home, with hope it will reunite families.

The O'Conor Home is not big enough for the number of people who need care, meaning many have to go to Canterbury at great stress to them and their families.

This week, the Government announced it would give the home a $2.1 million loan from the Regional Infrastructure Fund.

The chair of O'Conor Home's management trust, Garry Howard, said it now had enough money to start work - likely by 16 November.

"It's really exciting for all the West Coast area, it's something that's been a long time coming," he said.

The home had 68 beds, and the build would add 24, including a dementia wing, he said.

Howard hoped it would mean more people could stay close to home if they needed high-level care.

"It's a big enough change going into daycare let alone moving away from home and family and loved ones. So it's quite critical, this service," he said.

There were currently 18 people on the waitlist for O'Conor Home, with some of them already in care in other places.

He hoped some would be able to come home.

"It just adds so much stress - not only to the person who may have dementia or who may need hospital-level care but to their families having to do a three-day trip to go and visit their loved ones for a few hours in Christchurch or even further south. It's not really humane," Howard said.

The expansion would cost $13.9m.

Not all of the money had been raised, but the loan, alongside a grant of $500,000 from Development West Coast, meant the build could now begin, Howard said.

The project would be a boost beyond the aged care sector, he said.

"We're using as many local contractors as we can so it's good for the building and economics of the Westport area," he said.

More than 50 aged care beds had been lost in the Buller District in the past decade as various services shut down or moved on.

The Aged Care Association's Tracey Martin said the district was not the only community struggling.

World.title: Nursing teachers blame short-staffing on better frontline pay gap
World.content:
Audio player for " Nursing schools face growing pressure from staff shortages " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2347918%2Fnursing-teachers-blame-short-staffing-on-better-frontline-pay-gap

Nursing schools face growing pressure from staff shortages Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Nursing teachers say their jobs are becoming increasingly difficult as they cope with bigger class sizes and a shortage of staff.

Their union says nurses are not taking up jobs as academics as often as they used to, because the pay isn't as good as frontline nursing roles.

Tui Smith, a Tertiary Education Union delegate and nursing lecturer, explained wages for nurse educators had not kept pace with that of frontline nurses.

"They're not moving from the profession to teaching in the way that they might have in the past."

Teachers developed and delivered lectures and tutorials, ran labs and simulations, marked assessments and provided clinical supervision and pastoral care, alongside research.

"These jobs used to be billed as family friendly," Smith said. Now, they faced increasing workloads due to rising enrolments and inadequate staff numbers.

Plus, a large number of nurses approaching retirement age would soon coincide with the increasing demands of an ageing population.

There was no shortage of prospective students. "We have applications coming out our ears," Smith said.

One of the country's bigger nursing schools, Otago Polytechnic, told RNZ it was short three fulltime staff out of 24. Another, Ara Institute of Canterbury, was short one teacher, having filled another position in recent weeks.

Last month, the Tertiary Education Commission wrote to nursing schools asking them to limit enrolments next year to 2025 levels, as there weren't enough student placements available in hospitals to accommodate more.

Smith said in some places every nurse had a nursing student with them, learning on the job.

"If we had more academic nursing staff, we could facilitate a wider range of clinical placement opportunities and stagger our intakes more to avoid such bottlenecks."

Otago Polytechnic is one of the country's bigger nursing schools. Google Street View

Greer Smit, a nursing lecturer at Ara Institute of Canterbury and a senior professional fellow in the University of Otago's nursing department, had recently published a masters thesis on the subject, drawing on the experiences of 15 other nurse lecturers.

In her own experience, classes 10 years ago were generally a manageable size, and there weren't too many lecturer vacancies.

But that had been changing in recent years. "Instead of teaching one to 20, we would have one to 30. Sometimes if a lecturer is called in sick, you would have one to 60," she said.

Her research found teachers were no longer getting to know the students as well as they used to. "We don't know their learning needs. We don't know what they don't know."

And large classes could make it difficult for students to ask for help. "They don't feel confident to speak up."

Dawn Blyth, co-chair of the Nurses Organisation's national student unit, said teachers off sick or unavailable occasionally meant their class of 20 to 30 was joined by another, meaning 60 to 100 students in the same session.

"Sometimes you don't have a chance to ask the questions that you might do in a smaller classroom ... you've got other noises going on ... if you're sitting at the back of the classroom, you don't always hear as clearly."

One-on-one time was not often possible. "[For] our practical skills, we often get broken down into smaller groups, but that is still anywhere between 12 to 15."

On placements, it was often challenging to find enough experienced nurses to teach students, she said.

In response to questions about how schools were maintaining standards, the Nursing Council said it took any concerns about the quality of nurse education seriously.

"Our role is to protect the health and safety of the public by setting and monitoring standards for nursing education and practice," it said in a statement.

Health NZ told RNZ it had support systems in place for graduate nurses to enable a smooth transition into the workforce and ongoing professional development.

There are more than 20 institutions providing nursing training around the country.

One of the key providers, Otago Polytechnic, told RNZ when fully staffed, it employed 24 full-time academics in the School of Nursing at its Dunedin campus.

It was currently advertising for three full-time nursing educator roles.

Associate Professor Hayden Croft, head of the health college, said despite recent vacancies, in 2025 it'd had a 99.5 percent retention rate for students in the Bachelor of Nursing programme, and a 98.4 percent completion rate.

Dr Claire Minton, head of nursing at Ara Institute of Canterbury. Supplied / Ara Institute of Canterbury

Dr Claire Minton, head of nursing at Ara Institute of Canterbury, said the school was thinking carefully about recruiting and retaining teachers.

Recent hires meant its nursing leadership team was fully staffed, and it was seeing "strong interest" in current educator vacancies - it was currently interviewing for one role and another was filled in recent weeks.

Minton explained it could take several years for a nurse to become a teacher.

World.title: Swimming against the tide - the Kiwis crossing the ditch to move home
World.content:
It is not yet midday on a Friday but Wellington office workers are already lining up for a sandwich from Humphrey's Counter. Behind that counter, owner James Meek is serving up his most popular baguette, the Original Beef Drip, filled with slow cooked beef brisket, and warmly greeting regulars and new customers alike.

The born-and-bred Wellingtonian spent nearly 20 years in Sydney building a successful career in hospitality, including co-owning two popular cafes in Bondi. He also sold a cookie-dough product that went viral and was eventually stocked in 600 supermarkets across Australia.

But last year Meek sold up his businesses, moving back to Wellington with his English partner Anna Lancaster, their two sons and pet dog in tow. Humprey's Counter opened in July.

Setting up shop in a cost-of-living crisis, and amidst thousands of public sector job cuts, might seem crazy - but, so far, city workers can't get enough of Humphrey's loaded baguettes and homemade cookies, with queues frequently out the door of the Brandon Street premises. Meek said he sells around 150 sandwiches daily.

The move to Australia two decades ago happened naturally. "After university, like most New Zealanders, we go and we travel. Bright lights, big city, travel with all my friends. I didn't see myself as migrating. It's just, 'this is what we're doing, we're finishing university, so let's go over here.

"It's sunny. You earn better money, and there's lots more people and things to see and do. Then, after a while, it does become your home."

For most of that time, Meek never thought about moving back to Aotearoa. "I'd come back to visit family in Wellington and it was always nice enough, but I was fully focused on living in Sydney, loving the beach culture, the big city life, all that sort of stuff."

But the pandemic and having a young family, changed his thoughts on living abroad. Life was hectic, as a new father while managing 20 staff across two venues.

"When Covid happened, as much as I was concerned for the businesses, I found myself a little bit relieved. I was pretty exhausted and stressed."

Not owning a house was also playing on his mind. "It felt like the walls were closing in, thinking 'can we afford to live here?'. We lived in a lovely area but even if you moved an hour away, you're still talking $1.5 million to get a house that would be suitable [and] that we would want to live in."

Meek missed his large family - "I'm number five of six children" - and he wanted his sons to grow up as Kiwis kids. There are "great people in Australia ... But there is something that I personally enjoy about New Zealand. There's a humbleness, and an accessibility to a lot of things ... it comes from having a smaller population or something."

The family has settled in Island Bay. "My kids have loved being back here because they've got their grandparents and aunties and uncles and cousins around, and they ride their bikes to school. It's a lovely community school, and there's great people around us. It feels like we've quickly folded in."

James Meek and his family have settled in Island Bay. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Firefighter Dee Berghan-Carrick grew up in Melbourne, but his mum is from New Zealand - where he spent many childhood summers. Those holidays spurred him on to one day move to Aotearoa, to connect with his whakapapa Māori.

"Every time I was on this whenua, in this country, I felt like I was home in a way that I just didn't feel back home always. That always stuck with me."

His mum "grew up in an era where it wasn't really okay to talk about her history, [and] where she was made to feel a lot of shame about her Māori side.

"Over the last few years we have been on a process of healing, starting to learn a little bit of te reo, starting to understand our roots a little bit more. It's a big journey, and we're only at the start of that. But we're on that waka now and it's pretty cool."

Berghan-Carrick moved here a year ago, and, after a stint in Rotorua where he met his now-partner, he landed in the capital in December. The couple recently set up home in Evans Bay.

Dee Berghan-Carrick in Evans Bay. RNZ / Rachel Helyer-Donaldson

So far he's loving Wellington and its proximity to the outdoors. "It feels creative and friendly but more personable. It's got a great little arts scene, and great cafes. I also get to explore the beautiful taio around here, the nature is unbelievable ... I'd be hard pressed to find a better place."

As a former barista in Melbourne - arguably the world's coffee capital - Berghan-Carrick's "one gripe with Welly" is the coffee. "The good coffee is up there with the best in Melbourne, without a doubt, and the service is even better. But I do wish more places did good filter coffee - it's my drink of choice."

He was warned about the city's notorious winds, and heard the city was going through tough times. "There's definitely some closed-up shops in town, but it still feels like there's some heart here. I hope more people come and realise how awesome this place is, and keep making it home."

The number of New Zealanders returning from Australia has increased 14 percent in the past year, according to Stats NZ, but the number of people moving to Aussie is still more than double.

Stats NZ figures released last week showed that of the six New Zealand cities to see their populations drop in the past year, Wellington's fell furthest.

Infometrics economist Nick Brunsdon. Supplied / Infometrics

Infometrics economist Nick Brunsdon said there was a clear link between the public sector job cuts and the falling population. "If we look at employment in Wellington city, from 2024, which is sort of the peak, to 2026, it's fallen by around 6000 jobs. That's highly likely to be the main driver behind people choosing to migrate away from Wellington."

While Australia currently offered better job prospects, that was likely to change in the next couple of years as the job market softened, he said.

It could result in more New Zealanders coming home, he added. "Definitely at the national level. Whether that plays out in the same way for Wellington remains to be seen. That's going to rely on job opportunities being made available in the city."

Back at Humphrey's Counter, Meek said he knew Wellington had been doing it tough and hoped it would pick up soon. Until then, he'd focus on selling delicious sandwiches to the masses.

World.title: Is buying overseas carbon credits the only way to meet Paris Agreement? Parties disagree
World.content:
A future government will have to purchase overseas carbon credits if it wants to honour its Paris Agreement promises, the Opportunity and Green parties say.

Most of their political rivals say they also remain committed to both the global climate agreement and New Zealand's obligations - but diverge about how the country should meet them.

This year's election takes place just days before the annual UN climate change conference - COP31 - kicks off in Antalya, Türkiye.

The Paris Agreement was adopted at a previous COP, in 2015, and - among other things - the annual gathering is a chance to take stock of progress towards the agreement's overall goal of limiting global warming to 1.5°C.

New Zealand's current commitment to that goal, known as a 'nationally determined contribution' or NDC, is to halve emissions from 2005 levels, by 2030.

Current projections show the country falling short of that target by 86 million tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions - approximately a year's worth of emissions.

At the time the target was set, then-climate minister James Shaw said New Zealand could not meet it just by cutting emissions at home, and would have to purchase offshore carbon credits to make up the shortfall - in other words, paying other countries to cut their emissions instead.

Earlier this year, Treasury released analysis showing that cost could be up to $5 billion, after giving Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick an undertaking to provide an estimate.

Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick. Nick Monro

Incumbent Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said at the time that was a bill his government would not pay.

"We certainly aren't sending billions of dollars offshore."

The government would "do everything we can" to meet the goal without offshore credits, he said.

National Party climate spokesperson Simon Watts - who would head to COP31 as caretaker climate minister - told RNZ that remained the National Party's position.

"Our current policy is that National remains committed to the Paris Agreement, meeting our climate targets and building community resilience," he said in a written statement.

National Party climate spokesperson Simon Watts. RNZ/Baz Macdonald

The party was prioritising domestic climate action and had "no current plans to buy offshore credits".

In a statement, Labour Party climate spokesperson Deborah Russell, who would also attend COP, said National had made meeting the target harder "by going backwards on climate".

Labour stood by New Zealand's Paris Agreement commitments but planned to prioritise cutting emissions at home, she said.

"Every tonne we reduce here is a tonne we don't pay for overseas."

However, she did not directly respond to a question about whether the party would pay for offshore credits if they were still needed to close the gap.

Labour Party climate spokesperson Deborah Russell. VNP/Phil Smith

Opportunity Party climate spokesperson Kayla Kingdon-Bebb said it was "just not possible" to honour New Zealand's pledge without using offshore credits.

"With four years to go to 2030, no credible political party is going to be able to close that gap with domestic action alone."

Opportunity's plan was to cut New Zealand's own emissions as much as possible, including through new policies to help decarbonise industry and electrify the transport system.

"Then we will, as a nation, need to look to cover the remainder of the gap with high integrity international mitigations," Kingdon-Bebb said.

The party favoured putting that liability onto the Crown balance sheet "as soon as possible" - something that subsequent governments had not done.

"It's not just about accounting and transparency," she said.

"Our strong view is that once the cost of [overseas] emissions reduction is visible, every tonne of emissions cut at home becomes a savings to taxpayers and that changes incentives for the way that government invests in different policy initiatives."

Opportunity Party climate spokesperson Kayla Kingdon-Bebb. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick, who had previously pushed for the liability to be included on Crown accounts, said that needed to happen "preferably yesterday, but the next best-case scenario is as soon as we kick this government out of office".

The Greens would "much prefer" to meet the target with domestic emissions cuts alone but that had been unrealistic for years, she said.

It had been made even more difficult by the current government's "shredding of climate action", she said.

"For every political party right now who is saying that we are committed to meeting the Paris Agreement, it is unfortunately going to require us to pay for offshore mitigation."

Reinstating and introducing policies to cut emissions could still help to minimise the number of overseas credits needed, and ease the cost of living at the same time by reducing the country's reliance on fossil fuels, Swarbrick said.

The Greens' fiscal plan included paying for the remaining offshore credits using part of its unallocated operating allowance.

ACT agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

ACT was campaigning on leaving the Paris Agreement unless New Zealand replaced its current pledge with a 'split gas target', which would set separate goals for carbon dioxide - a long-lived gas - and methane, which is short-lived but has much a much stronger warming effect for the time it persists in the atmosphere.

ACT agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard said that would align New Zealand's pledge with its domestic targets, which were already split into short- and long-lived gases.

Uruguay had already done that and faced "absolutely no challenge" from other Paris members.

The party has also proposed scrapping the domestic net zero 2050 target.

David Seymour, as ACT's sole MP in 2019, was the only politician to vote against the Zero Carbon Act that introduced the target that year.

World.title: Swans star returns positive drug test during roadside stop
World.content:
Sydney Swans star Tom Papley has returned a positive preliminary drug test after being pulled over by NSW Police, who allege he was driving with a suspended licence.

NSW Police confirmed a 30-year-old-man was stopped around 10.30am on Monday, November 2, for random testing.

Police said the man allegedly returned a positive result for methylamphetamine.

In their own statement, the Sydney Swans said Papley was pulled over by police on Monday for a roadside licence check.

Papley was issued with a court attendance notice for driving with a suspended licence, due to an unpaid parking fine.

Papley then completed a random drug test that returned a positive preliminary indication. A second sample was taken for analysis.

The results of that second sample will not be received for at least four weeks.

The Swans said Papley informed the club of the matter "immediately". The AFL has also been informed.

Papley has played 216 games for Sydney and is one of the Swans' best players. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Papley, who has played 216 games for the Swans, is one of the club's best players and widely regarded as one of the AFL's best small forwards.

It has been a controversial few months for the Sydney Swans, headlined by the scandal at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne in August.

Vice-captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice were stood down from round 24 and the club's two finals for what the Swans termed a "serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

Those AFL-endorsed club bans were separate from the ongoing police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel. No charges have been laid, and there is no suggestion of wrongdoing on the part of the suspended players.

World.title: Staggs says he means no harm by refusing to sing Australian anthem
World.content:
Kotoni Staggs says his decision not to sing the national anthem comes from a place of respect, as he and his Kangaroos teammates find themselves at the centre of a culture war.

Staggs and several fellow Australia team members, who will face Samoa in Sunday's World Cup semifinal at the Sydney Football Stadium, have been criticised throughout the tournament because of their refusal to sing the pre-game anthem.

The Brisbane centre received the backing of Broncos teammate Pat Carrigan for his stance, hoping the decision would open up a wider discussion about Australia's history.

Kangaroos pile on the points in World Cup thrashing of Cook Islands The Kangaroos go undefeated through the group stage of the Rugby League World Cup as they close out the Pool A action with a 66-6 win over Cook Islands in Townsville.

Staggs, who has won nine caps for the Kangaroos since his debut in 2023, said: "I'm a proud Wirajudri boy and I'm proud of who I am and where I come from, and me not singing an anthem doesn't mean that I'm not grateful.

"I still love wearing that jersey. When the anthem is getting played you look around and get emotional.

"But me not singing, it's a whole different meaning to that and that's just me."

Staggs said his position on singing Advance Australia Fair came from wanting to honour his ancestors.

"Obviously in the past and what happened back in the day I've just learned from that," Staggs said.

"You also talk to your elders from back home and grandparents and stuff and [understand] what they had to go through. It's more of a respect for my elders and my family.

Kotoni Staggs says his refusal to sing the national anthem does not take away from his love of representing Australia. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

"I'm a proud Australian as well but at the end of the day it's just something that I've lived by, and I've got no harm in it. It doesn't take anything away from the jersey I wear."

Criticism of Staggs and other Indigenous Kangaroos stars, including Latrell Mitchell, is nothing new.

Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner, a proud Barkindji and Māori woman, has also stressed the importance of walking out alongside the Australian, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island flags during the World Cup.

"All three flags have separate meanings for our country, and it represents that we're a diverse country with many different cultures," she said.

Jillaroos players hold the Torres Strait Island flag over their shoulders during a national anthem at the World Cup. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"Our team, in particular, this 23, and our staff come from all different walks of life and cultural backgrounds, and we celebrate that diversity. That's a reflection of our country.

"You know, the blue flag is really important to everybody, just as equally as our Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flag.

"So when you look at the values of that and you educate yourself about those flags, then you can't help but be passionate to be a proud Australian."

Former Australian Test coach Mal Meninga previously defended players for their firm stance on the matter of the anthem.

Carrigan is of the opinion athletes should have the right to stand up for what they believe in.

Pat Carrigan says players should have the freedom to stand up for their beliefs. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"As sports people there's a focus on us as role models, but it probably points to a greater conversation for us to have as a society outside of football," Carrigan said.

"And about the reason why the boys feel the way about the anthem and perhaps our history as a country too.

"I know that each and every boy here is proud to pull on the green and gold.

"People may say it's represented in singing an anthem. I love Australia and I'm proud to pull on this jersey and I love running out with these guys too.

"I think it's a unique opportunity in sport that we get to be role models and voice opinions on different things, and maybe that's a way for us to look at ourselves as a country and how we can continue to come together."

AAP/ABC

World.title: Gold Coast triple header as Tszyu goes for two-weight glory
World.content:
Tim Tszyu will headline a stacked triple-header boxing card at Robina Stadium on the Gold Coast.

The 32-year-old will look to become a two-weight world champion when he takes on Cuban-American fighter Erislandy Lara for the WBA middleweight world title on December 13.

That is one of three all-star fights to take place on the night though, with former undisputed super welterweight world champion Jermell Charlo (35-2-1) stepping into the ring for the first time in three years when he takes on Australian power puncher Brock Jarvis (23-1).

Liam Wilson (18-3) will also meet Elnur Samedov (22-1) for the WBA super featherweight world title.

"This is the biggest and best fight card in Australia, full stop," No Limit Boxing chief executive George Rose said.

"A reigning world champion, a former undisputed world champion and two world titles, in a stadium on the Gold Coast. Nothing else comes close."

Tszyu (28-3) has enjoyed a career resurgence since stepping up to middleweight, winning his last three fights at the weight following a run of three defeats in four at light middleweight.

The Australian was crowned WBO light middleweight champion on the Gold Coast in 2023, defeating Brian Mendoza after being elevated from interim champion in the lead up.

His last stadium fight took place in Townsville against Jeff Horn in 2020.

Tim Tszyu is the WBO International Super Middleweight Title holder. (Getty Images: Jeremy Ng)

"This is what I live for," Tszyu said in a statement.

"Lara is a great champion and one of the most avoided fighters in the world. That is exactly why I wanted him. Spence was the first step. This is the one that matters.

"Queensland and the Gold Coast have always backed me.

"I'm ready to take that belt off Lara on the Gold Coast."

Lara (32-3-3), the 43-year-old veteran southpaw, is a two-division world champion and has been the WBA middleweight world champion since 2021.

The former amateur world champion has made four successful defences of the belt, including knocking out Michael Zerafa in two rounds in Las Vegas in 2024.

"Tim Tszyu wanted the best middleweight in the world," Rose said.

"And we got him."

Lara, like Tszyu, has three career defeats, all via the scorecards, losing by majority decision to Paul Williams and split decision defeats to Canelo Álvarez and Jarrett Hurd.

"I'm going to Australia with one goal … to defend my title, put on a great performance and give the fans a fight they'll remember for a long time," Lara said.

Charlo was supposed to fight Tszyu in 2023 before a broken hand scuppered those plans.

Jermell Charlo (right) has not fought in three years. (Getty Images: Sarah Stier)

The then WBA, WBC, IBF and WBO light middleweight champion had been set to fight Tszyu despite the hand injury, only for him to repeatedly delay and ultimately pull out to face Álvarez at super middleweight instead.

Charlo famously said fighting Tszyu "does nothing for my career" by way of explanation, however fighting and losing to Álvarez ultimately cost the American all four of his belts, with the 36-year-old looking to restart his career in Australia.

"I've heard all the talk, and now it's time to remind everybody why Jermell Charlo is still him," Charlo said.

"I'm willing to fight on a co-main event all the way in Australia because that's how hungry I am. I've got so much in me and I wasn't going to let this year end without giving my fans what they've been waiting for."

Jarvis, who has 21 knock out wins in his 24 fights, said his aim was to "ruin" Charlo's comeback.

In the other world title fight, Liam Wilson (18-3), who fought at the Commonwealth Games on the Gold Coast in 2018, will meet Azerbaijani fighter Samedov.

Liam Wilson has twice challenged for the world title. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Wilson is a two-time world title challenger who came agonisingly close to winning the world title in 2023 and 2024 against Emanuel Navarrete and Oscar Valdez respectively.

"I have chased this shot around the world," Wilson said.

"My career hasn't been easy but I've felt the love from fans every step of the way. I have never backed down from anyone and I am not starting now.

"Samedov is the champion. Good. Taking it off the champion means more.

"I boxed for Australia on the Gold Coast at the Commonwealth Games almost a decade ago. Now, I get the chance to win a world title in the same city. You can't not love that."

World.title: NZ teammates stunned as Ponga eyes return 22 days after breaking arm
World.content:
Teammates are marvelling at Kalyn Ponga's resilience as the New Zealand game changer eyes a miracle World Cup return 22 days after breaking an arm.

After being named on an extended bench, Ponga and fellow Newcastle fan favourite Phoenix Crossland could spell double trouble for Tonga in Saturday night's semifinal at Newcastle's McDonald Jones Stadium.

Ponga played with his injury for more than 20 minutes during New Zealand's epic tournament-opening 24-22 loss to Australia before undergoing surgery in the hope of returning for the finals.

A month after playing together in Newcastle's 19-18 NRL grand final loss to the Sydney Roosters, centre Dane Gagai is backing the former Dally M Medallist to terrorise Tonga in what would be a huge boost for the Kiwis.

Ponga (left) played over 20 minutes with a broken arm against Australia earlier in the World Cup. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"That'll just come down to the boxes he'll have to tick with the physios and stuff, but one thing that's never in question is Kalyn's toughness, and I don't think he gets enough credit or praise for it," Gagai said.

"Some of the games, he's played with injury. It was only maybe a year or two ago with his AC and getting that injected, but he'll put his head in most places that people won't put their hands.

"So I've got no doubt he'll do everything he can to make sure he can take that field. It's just a case of whether he can tick those boxes, and he'll know whether he's capable of playing or not.

"He won't put himself before the team, but we'd obviously love to have him out there."

Phoenix Crossland could potentially return for his first game since being suspended after the preliminary final. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Crossland could also be a late inclusion after completing a four-game suspension for a hip-drop tackle that broke Nathan Cleary's ankle in Newcastle's preliminary final victory over Penrith.

Knowing New Zealand will need their strongest possible line-up to keep Tonga at bay, Gagai has also welcomed the prospect of the classy hooker featuring in the do-or-die showdown.

"He's come in a bit later into camp, but even though he wasn't playing, he's he's always himself and brings a lot of energy," Gagai said.

"He's awesome to have around the place. It's going to be good to be able to chuck this jersey on with him and nice to know that the game against Penrith wasn't our last together.

"So I'm definitely looking forward to that and I'm super happy for him."

AAP

World.title: Man United claims comeback win after fans launch tennis balls in protest
World.content:
Manchester United has staged a stunning comeback to recover from its worst start to a European home game by beating Roma 3-2 in the UEFA Champions League.

Elsewhere, Paris Saint-Germain set a new record as the fastest team to score four goals in European soccer's top competition by powering into a 4-0 lead after 17 minutes against Villarreal on its way to a 6-0 win.

In other major results, Barcelona beat Aston Villa 3-0 and Bayern Munich won 2-0 at Atletico Madrid.

But the biggest drama of the night came at Old Trafford, where United's troubled season looked set to plunge deeper into crisis after going 2-0 down after 17 minutes against Roma.

It was the fastest United had conceded twice in any European game at its iconic stadium.

But a rousing second-half performance saw Bruno Fernandes convert a retaken penalty and Matheus Cunha score twice before being sent off to seal a much-needed win for under-fire coach Michael Carrick.

The joyous scenes at the end were in stark contrast to earlier, when furious United fans attempted to disrupt the match by throwing tennis balls on to the field.

The pre-planned protest was the latest show of dissent from supporters who have long called for the club's American owners, the Glazer family, to sell their controlling stake.

A small number of balls were thrown in the 21st minute to mark 21 years since the Glazers staged a leveraged buyout of the storied club.

By then, Roma had already raced to a 2-0 lead through Matias Soule's 11th-minute strike and Donyell Malen's penalty.

It could have been worse by the break, with Roma having more chances to extend the lead.

But the game was turned on its head after half-time, with Fernandes's twice-taken penalty giving the home fans hope and then Cunha sealing the comeback with goals in the 83rd and 86th.

AP

World.title: Woman, 24, dies in NY Marathon as father reveals she had rare condition
World.content:
A young Pennsylvania woman running the New York City Marathon for the first time to raise money for charity collapsed in Central Park, just over 3 kilometres from the finish line, and later died.

Rachel Apa, 24, of Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, was approaching the finish line in last weekend's event when she collapsed, according to the New York Police Department. The city medical examiner's office said it was investigating the cause of Apa's death.

Her father told The New York Times that she had rhabdomyolysis, a rare condition in which muscles can break down during exertion, releasing substances that can poison the body. It was her first marathon, Steve Apa said.

Rachel Apa during the New York Marathon. (Supplied)

New York Road Runners, the nonprofit club that stages the race, said in a news release that a bystander administered CPR to Apa, and event medical staffers also performed CPR and used a defibrillator. Paramedics arrived and took her to a hospital but were unable to save her.

Apa, an industrial-technology product manager and former college field hockey player, had run to raise money for Parkinson's disease in honour of her grandfather.

"It's unfathomable," her father told The Times. He said his daughter had been in "perfect health".

Michaela Nicholas was watching the race, cheering on any runners whose names she could discern from their bibs, when Apa passed. Nicholas recalled on Tuesday, local time, that she called out a message of encouragement, then saw Apa collapse about 15 metres further along the route.

Nicholas, a hospital social worker, said she tried to comfort Apa while two other race spectators administered CPR.

"I just held Rachel's hand and talked to her and told her that she wasn't alone and that she's loved, and I prayed for her," Nicholas, a clinical social worker, said by phone.

The death occurred as the marathon marked 50 years in its five-borough format. Early editions of the race had been run only in Central Park. A record 61,000 runners reached the finish line.

Strintzos fifth in NY Marathon, Olympics in sight Australia's Haftu Strintzos takes a giant step towards the LA28 Olympics with a top-five finish at the New York Marathon.

"We are deeply saddened by Rachel's passing following running in Sunday's race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with her family, friends and the entire running community," New York Road Runners said in its statement.

As word of Apa's death spread on Tuesday, money poured into her "Parkinson's Champions" fundraising page, quickly exceeding her $4,000 goal. The fundraiser was sponsored by the Parkinson's Foundation.

On the page, Apa said her grandfather, who had Parkinson's disease and died in 2022, "taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement".

Apa worked for TE Connectivity, which makes various electrical components and electronics. The company was grappling with the news on Tuesday and expressed condolences. So did Bucknell University, where Apa graduated in 2024 with a degree in markets, innovation and design, and where she scored a total of 17 goals for the school's field hockey team.

USA Field Hockey, the sport's governing body, said on social media that "Rachel's impact on the sport and those around her will not be forgotten".

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: Spanish footballer dies after on-field collision
World.content:
Warning: the video in this article may cause distress for some readers

Spanish police have opened an investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter after a football player died following an on-field collision with the opposing team's goalkeeper in a second-division match.

Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel died after he suffered cardiac arrest following the on-field collision, his club said late on Tuesday night (AEDT). He was 30.

De Miguel was challenging for the ball near midfield on Monday when he was struck in the chest by FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono, who came running from the opposite direction in an apparent attempt to make a clearance. Owono was shown a straight red card for the incident, which happened in added time.

Spain's national police said on Tuesday, local time, that they had opened an investigation. Under Spanish law, deaths from non-natural causes, including accidents, are subject to judicial investigation.

Santa Cruz de Tenerife chief prosecutor José Luis Sánchez-Jáuregui told Spanish news agency EFE that criminal proceedings were unlikely, noting that the collision occurred during play.

De Miguel was taken to a hospital and the match, tied 2-2, was abandoned after the incident.

The club, based in Spain's Canary Islands, said it was "heartbroken."

Fans laid flowers in memory of Jesus de Miguel at the Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez Stadium upon hearing the news of his death. (Europa Press Canarias via Getty Images)

Tenerife's largest shareholder Rayco García told reporters that De Miguel's body would be transported to Navahermosa, in the Toledo province, at the request of his family. He said De Miguel's teammates and club officials would be present for a "final farewell."

On Saturday, fans will gather at the team's stadium to honour the player, García said.

"We will all join forces and get through this together," García said.

Club president Felipe Miñambres said players and their families would likely need help to cope with De Miguel's death.

Teams playing in the Champions League on Wednesday morning observed a minute's silence in memory of de Miguel. (John Walton/PA Images via Getty Images)

"We will need professional help and the help of all of our fans," he said. "They will be feeling the same way that we are feeling today."

The club has asked to postpone its league game at Granada this weekend.

The heavy collision happened when Owono rushed out of his area all the way to midfield to challenge for a long ball that De Miguel was trying to reach.

De Miguel initially curled on his knees, clutching his torso for a few seconds, before he fell over onto his back, with his arms falling to his sides.

Owono was walking off the field after being shown the red card but turned around and joined the other players rushing to check on De Miguel.

Heartbroken fans shed tears while paying tribute to de Miguel. (Andres Gutierrez/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Another player with the same last name of Owono, Michel Owono, who plays for sixth-division Spanish club Can Vidalet, denounced a wave of racist insults against him by people thinking he was the Andorra goalkeeper.

De Miguel, a Madrid native, began his senior career with Leganés B in 2015 and later played for several lower-division clubs in Spain. He joined Tenerife last year.

No local media reported that De Miguel had a pre-existing health condition. The precise medical cause of death was not immediately disclosed.

Spanish media said De Miguel is survived by his wife and their daughter.

"There are no words of comfort," the club statement read. "There is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this profound sense of sorrow. We stand with his devastated family, his loved ones, and the entire Tenerife community."

Gerard Pique (pictured), owner of FC Andorra, paid tribute to de Miguel alongside several other football icons. (Walter Cunha/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Tributes poured out for De Miguel after news of his death broke. Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo, Kylian Mbappé and Gerard Piqué, the owner of Andorra, all extended their condolences, while Real Madrid, Manchester United and Liverpool also paid tribute.

The Spanish football federation postponed all Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina matches scheduled on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. UEFA said it would observe a moment of silence at all its matches this week.

Life-threatening injuries from collisions in football are extremely rare.

Last year in Spain, a 19-year-old goalkeeper died from head injuries suffered during a collision in a fifth-division match. Colindres goalkeeper Raúl Ramírez had two cardio-respiratory arrests, one on the field and then in the ambulance while being transported to a hospital. He was declared brain dead two days later.

In 2001, Ukrainian goalkeeper Serhiy Perkhun died from head injuries sustained in a collision during a match while playing for CSKA Moscow.

Malaga goalkeeper José Antonio Gallardo died in January 1987, more than three weeks after a collision with Celta Vigo forward Baltazar in a second-division game.

AP

World.title: Djokovic breaks Paris Masters record and sets up clash with Aussie
World.content:
Novak Djokovic is looming ominously as a threat to Alex de Minaur's hopes of reaching the ATP Finals with his opening victory at the Paris Masters — but a fellow Sydneysider will be out to do 'Demon' a big favour.

Djokovic, a seven-time champion in the ATP 1000 event, had to negotiate a scare late in the second set before ousting the in-form Monegasque Valentin Vacherot 6-7 (5-7), 7-5, 6-1 in the first round on Tuesday (Wednesday AEDT).

Serving at a set down and 4-4, the 24-time grand slam champ had to save three break points to prevent Vacherot, fresh from winning the Swiss Indoors in Basle, from serving for the match at the Plenitude Arena before he rallied to grab a hard-fought win.

At 39, Djokovic set yet another record as the oldest winner in the tournament's history, and couldn't resist a little shot at those who've dared suggest he's over the hill by declaring: "For an old guy, not so bad, huh?!

"People think I am too old and slow, but somehow I find a way to win these kinds of matches that go the distance. I am still there, and I am still holding on and trying to find my best tennis when it matters."

The win strengthened his 10th position, just one behind Alex de Minaur, in the live Race to Turn standings as the pair both jostle to be among the eight qualifiers for the ATP Finals.

Should Djokovic and de Minaur meet in the third round, the loser may well see his Finals hopes end, but before then, the Australian must beat Argentine Tomas Martin Etcheverry while Djokovic will have to defeat de Minaur's Davis Cup teammate Rinky Hijikata in round two.

Hijikata is having a great week after three victories — two in qualifying and one first-round win — without dropping a set, and he could take extra confidence after Djokovic needed a medical timeout in the second set against Vacherot to have his right shoulder treated.

Djokovic will face Australia's Rinky Hijikata (pictured) next. (Getty Images: Steven Paston/PA Images)

An early off-day could spell curtains for either Djokovic or de Minaur, who began the week in eighth spot before young Spanish star Rafael Jodar edged ahead in the live standings with his first-round win.

World no.31 Etcheverry will be a potentially awkward hurdle for world No.9 de Minaur but the Australian may well have preferred to play him than old foe Andrey Rublev, who lost 6-4, 6-7 (4-7), 7-6 (7-3) to the Argentine on Tuesday.

The fight is really on now to get to Turin with Taylor Fritz, just behind Djokovic in the race, having also won on Tuesday against Frenchman Benjamin Bonzi 3-6, 6-3, 6-4.

In other first-round matches on Tuesday, French teenager Moïse Kouame, the young home sensation at the French Open earlier in the year, bowing out 6-3, 6-1 to Nuno Borges, while 2022 champion Holger Rune, on the comeback trail after his Achilles injury, lost 7-5, 6-4 to No.12 seed Tommy Paul.

Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we’ve been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye’s journey through the Everywhen. We don’t take for granted the trust placed in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans.
